Title: Four arrested for impersonating National Security, NAIMOS officers to extort miners at Nweneso No. 2
Content: Four persons have been arrested by the Ashanti National Security operatives for allegedly parading themselves as National Security and National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) officials to extort money from miners at Nweneso No.2 in the Atwima Kwanwoma District in the Ashanti Region. The suspects, who are part of an alleged eight-member syndicate, are said to have been moving around mining communities in a pickup vehicle, posing as security operatives and demanding money from miners under the pretext of carrying out official security and anti-illegal mining operations. The activities of the group, according to the Ashanti Regional National Security Coordinator, Captain (Rtd) Jabari, have allegedly been ongoing for the past three months. Speaking to the media following the arrest, on Monday, November 16, 2026,Captain (Rtd) Jabari revealed that the suspects had devised an organised operation through which they allegedly intimidated miners and extorted money from them. He explained that although the suspects dressed like National Security operatives, they did not possess any official identification cards or documents authorising them to undertake security operations. According to him, preliminary information indicates that the group comprises eight members, with four of them successfully arrested during the operation. Captain(RTD) Jabari described the syndicate as highly organised, raising concerns about the activities of individuals who impersonate state security personnel to exploit unsuspecting members of the public. The four suspects arrested have been identified as David Ablor, 51; Samuel Nyarko, 34; Prince Mangomia, 34; and Agyemang Stephen, 34. Captain (Rtd) Jabari indicated that the suspects would be conveyed to the national headquarters of NAIMOS for further interrogation and subsequent prosecution. The arrest is expected to serve as a warning to individuals and groups who allegedly exploit the identities of state security institutions to engage in criminal activities, particularly in mining communities where efforts are being intensified to tackle illegal mining. The activities of the alleged syndicate also raise concerns about the growing threat posed by impostors who take advantage of the public’s trust in security agencies to intimidate residents and extort money. Authorities are expected to intensify investigations to establish the full extent of the group’s activities, identify other members and determine whether additional individuals may have been involved in the alleged scheme. The suspects are presumed innocent until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

Title: GRA directs ports not to release right-hand steering vehicles without Ministry of Transport permit
Content: The Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) has directed all ports and stations not to process or release any right-hand steering vehicle unless the importer produces a valid permit from the Ministry of Transport. The directive is contained in a memorandum dated November 16, 2026, addressed to all ports and stations and signed by the Commissioner of the Customs Division, Aaron Kanor. It carries the reference H/PREV/1 and is titled “Directive on the processing and release of right-hand steering vehicles”. The memo says management has noticed that some right-hand steering vehicles are being presented for clearance without the requisite approval. It does not say how many vehicles are involved or where they were presented. The memo draws attention to Section 58 of the Customs Act, 2015 (Act 891). According to the memo, the section provides that a person shall not import a right-hand steering motor vehicle into the country unless approved by the Minister. It further provides that a prohibited motor vehicle shall be seized and forfeited to the State. Based on this provision, all Sector Commanders have been directed to ensure that no right-hand steering vehicle is processed or released unless the importer produces a valid permit from the Ministry of Transport authorising its importation. The memo adds that any right-hand steering vehicle presented for clearance without such a permit should be detained and dealt with in accordance with the provisions of Act 891. Sector Commanders are also to bring the directive to the attention of all officers at the frontier stations, ports, and Collections under their command, and to ensure strict compliance. The memo was copied to the Commissioner-General, all Deputy Commissioners, and all Assistant Commissioners. What it means for importers The directive places the burden on the importer. Anyone bringing in a right-hand steering vehicle must now present a Ministry of Transport permit at the point of clearance. Without it, the vehicle risks being detained and, under the law as described in the memo, seized and forfeited to the State. Importers, clearing agents, and car dealers who handle used vehicles may therefore need to confirm the steering configuration of any consignment and check its paperwork before shipment, rather than at the port. The memorandum does not give a deadline or an effective date beyond its own date. It does not explain how an importer can obtain the Ministry of Transport permit, who qualifies for one, or whether any categories of vehicle are exempt. It also does not say whether vehicles already at the ports are covered.

Title: Do not increase hall fees by more than 10% - GTEC to Public universities
Content: The Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) has directed public universities not to increase residential fees in publicly funded halls of residence by more than 10% of the amount charged in the preceding academic year. The directive, issued on November 16, 2026 and signed by the Deputy Director-General of GTEC, Professor Augustine Ocloo, follows an instruction from the Minister for Education and is aimed at protecting students from excessive accommodation charges. In a letter addressed to all Vice-Chancellors of public universities, GTEC said the 10% ceiling applies to all halls of residence constructed, maintained or funded through public resources, regardless of their management arrangements. The Commission has consequently directed universities to review their approved or proposed residential fees to ensure compliance with the prescribed limit. "Accordingly, universities are required to review their approved or proposed residential fees to ensure strict compliance with the prescribed ceiling. "Where residential fees have already been approved or announced in excess of the stipulated ten percent (10%), the affected institutions are required to revise such fees accordingly and communicate the adjustments to students and other relevant stakeholders," the letter stated. Institutions that have already approved or announced increases exceeding the 10% ceiling have been instructed to revise the fees and communicate the adjustments to students and other relevant stakeholders. GTEC stressed that no university is permitted to impose an increase beyond the stipulated threshold for any publicly funded hall of residence. It also urged university authorities to ensure transparency and fairness in determining and communicating residential fees. The Commission said it would monitor compliance with the directive and undertake the necessary measures to ensure its effective implementation.

Title: Abu Trica faces February jury trial in US fraud case with December plea deadline
Content: Frederick Kumi, the Ghanaian socialite known as Abu Trica, goes before a US jury on February 8, 2027, over an alleged US$8 million romance fraud that targeted elderly Americans. Both sides have until December 15, 2026, to tell the court whether they have reached a plea agreement. The new timetable replaces a September trial date set when he wasarraigned in July after his extradition. A final pre-trial conference is scheduled for January 13, 2027, at 11am, with the jury trial to begin at 9am on February 8. Kumi remains in US federal custody. A grand jury returneda two-count indictmentagainst him, one for conspiring to commit wire fraud and one for conspiring to launder money, with a forfeiture specification attached. He has pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he could be jailed for up to 20 years. The US Attorney's Office in northern Ohio says the group met elderly victims on dating platforms and social media and courted them with constant, intimate messages. Then came the requests for money, for urgent medical bills, travel or investments. Prosecutors countmore than 80 victims and over US$8 milliontaken between April 2023 and November 2025. Court documents state that Kumi and co-defendant Daniel Yussif acted as leaders of the group, which used AI-driven video tools and fictitious personas to deceive victims. Prosecutors link a mansion in Ghana and luxury vehicles, including a Lamborghini and a Tesla Cybertruck, to the alleged scheme. Ghanaian and US authorities arrested Kumi, who is from Swedru, on December 11, 2025. He arrived in the United States on July 9, 2026, after acontested extradition process. US prosecutors thanked Ghana's Attorney-General's Office, EOCO, the police, the Cyber Security Authority and NACOC for their help. If no deal is reached by December 15, the case moves on to the January conference and the February trial. An indictment is only an accusation, and Kumi is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Title: Agyinasare says Mahama is doing better in his second term than in his first
Content: Archbishop Charles Agyinasare saysPresident John Mahamais doing a better job now than he did in his first spell in office. "I think he's done better than the first term," the founder of Perez Chapel International told Bernard Avle on Channel One TV's The Point of View on Monday. It was the same interview in which heasked to see the National Cathedral accountsbefore churches put in any more money. Mahama wassworn in for his second termon 7 January 2025, eight years after he left office. His first term ended in January 2017. Agyinasare's first evidence was the currency, and the money the state owes. "I see the cedi has done well. I see we've been able to pay some of our bills," he said. Mahama said last week he wasconfident in the cedi's futureas the new Heritage series of notes was unveiled. Health Minister Mintah Akandoh said this month that the government hadpaid the arrears of 13,500 health workersposted without financial clearance. He also drew on a trip home from India in September. "They told me Emirates was coming to Ghana twice a day. So I came with the midnight flight, and there was a seven o'clock flight," he said. To him, the extra flight meant more people were travelling to shop. "Now, that should show you that people have started going out to buy things. That alone, for me, was an encouragement," he said. Agyinasare also welcomed the2027 Budgetthat Finance Minister CassielAto Forsonread to Parliament last Thursday. "Some of the projects we are doing, we are not borrowing money for them. That, for me, I think, is progress," he said. Others have been harder on the budget. The think tank ISODEC told the minister thatstabilisation must now make room for jobsand production. IMANI's Kofi Bentil claims Ken Ofori-Atta's first two years as Finance Minister were better than Ato Forson's. Weput the two records side by side. On galamsey, Agyinasare wantsa state of emergency in the worst-hit areas, where forests and rivers have been ruined.

Title: Fill Ghana's middle-level skills gap to drive industrial growth — Otumfuo charges Takoradi Technical University
Content: The Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, has challenged Takoradi Technical University (TTU) to lead the charge in closing Ghana's critical middle-level skills gap that continues to hinder industrial development and the growth of the creative economy. Speaking as the Grand Guest of Honour at the Open Day Celebration of the Faculty of Applied Arts and Technology (FAAT) at TTU, the Asantehene said while Ghana has a brilliant record in tertiary education, the nation can no longer ignore the deficit in technical and vocational skills. "Ghana has had a brilliant record in tertiary education, and yet no one can deny the gap in the middle-level skills so vital to economic development," Otumfuo stated. "Industries face critical shortages in the middle-level skills they need in manufacturing. Lack of similar skills continues to hinder the construction industry from achieving the quality standards commensurate with our efforts." Otumfuo warned that Ghana is missing out on global creative wealth because technical skills to harness local talent remain underdeveloped. "Worse still, the opportunities now available to tap into global wealth for our creative talents are passing us by," he said. He described TTU and its Faculty of Applied Arts and Technology as uniquely positioned to reverse the trend. "Your university has the opportunity to make a great impact upon the economy of the nation by taking up the training of the technicians who will fill the skills gap hindering our development efforts." The Asantehene, who was honoured with a Lifetime Achievement Award at the event under the theme "Celebrating Heritage, Innovation and Excellence: A Tribute to Otumfuo Osei Tutu II's Legacy", urged the university to become a bridge between tradition and innovation. "You can connect indigenous knowledge with formal education, experienced artisans with young designers, and community traditions with modern technology." Otumfuo expressed delight that the celebration brought together diverse creative disciplines — sculpture, painting, graphics and textiles — and said he was looking forward to the innovations of the students. "I am pleased that this celebration brings together sculpture, painting, graphics and textiles. We are looking forward with great anticipation to the creations of our budding painters and sculptors as well as textile designers at your exhibition and fashion show soon to follow." The Open Day, which attracted dignitaries including the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, and the President of the Western Regional House of Chiefs, Nana Kobina Nketsia V, showcased student works, innovations by deaf students in Applied Arts, and a fashion show. Otumfuo's visit marks the first time a reigning Asantehene has officially visited any tertiary institution in the Western Region, a historic moment TTU described as a symbolic deepening of national unity.

Title: NACOC says India-bound passenger swallowed 58 suspected cocaine pellets before flight
Content: TheNarcotics Control Commission (NACOC)says a 58-year-old passenger it stopped at Accra International Airport (Kotoka) had swallowed 58 pellets suspected to be cocaine before a flight to India. Officers picked him out during routine pre-screening of passengers. The Commission said the checks are part of a stepped-up drive to stop illicit drugs passing through the points where travellers enter and leave Ghana. Last week, the Commission also arrested aTema freight forwarderover the 2.6-tonne cocaine shipment seized in Spain, in a separate case. A later examination reportedly showed he had swallowed the pellets, which NACOC said looked like an attempt to hide the substance and carry it to India. Kotoka has seen similar cases before: in February, NACOC arrested amanufacturing firm's managerover an alleged attempt to smuggle cocaine through the airport. The Commission announced the arrest in a statement on its official Facebook page on Monday, with photographs of the pellets. The statement did not give the man's name, the airline or the weight of the pellets, nor when the arrest was made. NACOC said it would keep tightening surveillance and enforcement at the country's entry and exit points so that traffickers cannot use Ghana as a transit hub. The Commission's director-general said earlier this month that NACOC will go after drug traffickers"wherever they are". NACOC cautioned prospective drug traffickers that "attempts to evade law enforcement through the concealment or ingestion of narcotic substances will be detected", as it works with national and international partners to dismantle trafficking networks.

Title: The United Nations: Choosing a successor for António Guterres
Content: The United Nations is preparing to select its tenth Secretary-General, succeeding incumbent António Guterres, whose term ends on December 31, 2026. The new Secretary-General is set to assume office on January 1, 2027, for a five-year term. Under Article 97 of the UN Charter, the Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council, which plays a pivotal role in the process. A candidate must secure at least nine votes out of 15, without a veto from any of the five permanent members: the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom. Preparations to select Guterres' successor come at a time when the United Nations faces a complex array of challenges. Protracted wars, polarisation among major powers, declining confidence in the effectiveness of international institutions and mounting humanitarian demands have all placed the office of Secretary-General under a formidable test. No woman has ever held the position of UN Secretary-General, amid growing calls for that to change. The election of a woman would embody the United Nations' founding principles of fairness and equality in rights and opportunities. Against this backdrop, Emirati diplomat Lana Zaki Nusseibeh emerges as a prominent candidate, bringing an extensive diplomatic record spanning more than a decade (2013–2024), which has given her an in-depth understanding of the intricacies of multilateral diplomacy and the workings of the international organisation. Drawing on her extensive experience within the corridors of the United Nations, Nusseibeh brings a forward-looking vision for leading the organisation over the next five years and rebuilding confidence at a time when the world continues to suffer the devastating consequences of wars and conflicts. *Lana Nusseibeh's Vision for the United Nations* Nusseibeh has previously outlined her vision for leading the United Nations, emphasising that she would act early, before disputes escalate into wars. Acknowledging the pressures facing the organisation, she has affirmed her belief in its mission and said she would work with partners to rebuild trust and reinvigorate the organisation through philanthropy and a recognition of the value and dignity of every human being. She has also pledged to defend human rights rigorously and without double standards, warning that every promise the organisation fails to fulfil will carry a heavy price: "We will pay for it with the most precious thing we have." Preventive diplomacy stands at the forefront of Nusseibeh's priorities. Her approach centres on early intervention to contain disagreements before they escalate into conflicts, while working to build practical understandings even in circumstances where comprehensive political settlements remain elusive. Her vision also encompasses reforming the performance of UN institutions, reducing duplication across their work, improving spending efficiency and strengthening accountability, alongside a focus on technology, artificial intelligence, youth employment and sustainable development. She has also advanced the concept of "First Agreements", which involves beginning with achievable, implementable steps, such as securing humanitarian corridors, exchanging prisoners and reaching localised ceasefires, before building on these measures to achieve broader and more sustainable agreements. Young people occupy a central place in Nusseibeh's vision for advancing international cooperation through the United Nations. She emphasises the need to place them directly "in decision-making positions", rather than confining them to marginal roles, and underscores the importance of equipping young people with the tools of the future and access to technology. She also seeks to develop the concept of partnerships with the private sector and financing mechanisms, moving beyond decades of traditional reliance on direct official government assistance and conventional donations as the primary sources of project funding. Nusseibeh's vision calls for adopting blended finance models in partnership with the private sector and philanthropic institutions, correcting the mispricing of risk to lower the cost of capital in fragile environments, and measuring success through "capital mobilised and jobs delivered". As part of her forward-looking vision, Nusseibeh also considers the rigorous application of Article 100 of the UN Charter essential to ensuring an unwavering commitment to acting exclusively in the interests of the United Nations. As a practical and immediate measure to safeguard neutrality, she has pledged to take formal leave from her position as Minister of State at the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation. She further stresses that human rights are universal values embodying equality, and that the credibility of the United Nations is entirely dependent on consistency and uniformity in their application, without double standards. This comes at a time when the UN's traditional approach to human rights issues faces accusations of double standards and selective treatment, alongside significant funding gaps between the mandates assigned to the human rights pillar and the actual budgets allocated to it. *An Impressive Career* Born in Abu Dhabi in 1978, Lana Nusseibeh has served as an adviser to the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the Gulf Research Center. She was the UAE's Permanent Representative to the United Nations from 2013 until April 2024. She presided over Security Council sessions during the UAE's two presidencies of the Council, during its elected membership in 2022 and 2023. Throughout her tenure, she demonstrated extensive experience in managing files relating to peace and security, humanitarian affairs, sustainable development, security risks associated with climate change, women's affairs and reform of the multilateral system. She led efforts to secure the adoption of resolutions that the UAE helped draft, including Resolution 2686, which, for the first time, recognised that hate speech, racism, gender discrimination and disinformation contribute to the outbreak, escalation and recurrence of conflicts. In 2017, Nusseibeh served as President of the Executive Board of UN Women and later as Vice-President of the 72nd session of the UN General Assembly. She also co-chaired the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform. In 2010 and 2011, she served as the UAE's Joint Special Envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan, and as Deputy UAE Sherpa to the G20 Summit during France's presidency of the group in 2011. The significance of Lana Nusseibeh's candidacy lies in the fact that work within the United Nations is not driven by speeches alone. It depends to a considerable extent on understanding procedures, managing negotiations, building alliances and recognising the distinction between publicly declared positions and what can ultimately be translated into workable agreements. Her candidacy also reinforces the UAE's standing as an active player in international diplomacy, capable of putting forward figures with the experience required to manage complex issues and engage with a wide range of global powers. By Eric Mawuena Egbeta, Ghanaian Journalist

Title: Korle Bu replaces a teenager's heart valve through her thigh in Ghana first
Content: Doctors at Korle Bu have replaced a damaged heart valve in a 14-year-old girl by threading a new one through a blood vessel in her thigh, without opening her chest. Korle Bu's National Cardiothoracic Centre (NCTC)announced the operation on Monday, calling it a first for Ghana. The procedure took about an hour. Korle Bu says checks afterwards showed she was recovering well, with the new valve "functioning excellently". She has been told to take a week's rest and to stay away from heavy lifting while the wound in her leg heals. It was done during this year's partnership visit, when about 30 doctors, nurses, physician assistants and intensive care staff join the NCTC forcomplex heart operations on children. The technique is called Transcatheter Pulmonary Valve Replacement. The girl had been diagnosed with severe pulmonary valve regurgitation, and doctors implanted a device called the Harmony Valve, which is designed for patients with enlarged pulmonary arteries. Doctors passed the valve through a blood vessel in her thigh and steered it up to the heart, where it now does the work of the damaged one. Because the chest is never opened, the technique is gentler than conventional open-heart surgery and may shorten recovery. The operation was a joint effort between the NCTC and two German partners, Kinderherzen International and the Gerald Asamoah Foundation. The visiting team also carried out open-heart surgery and catheter procedures on children born with heart disease. The German team's lead, Dr Katja Pauli, said heart conditions need to be caught early and treated promptly. Isolated pulmonary valve insufficiency can occur even when there is no other heart disease, she said, so proper assessment and regular check-ups matter. Dr Pauli added that some heart conditions can be detected during pregnancy, making early screening and prompt medical attention important for better treatment outcomes. The NCTC's director, Dr Kow Entsua-Mensah, called it a significant milestone in the centre's drive to bring advanced heart care closer to home. Ghana, he said, is now among the countries that can carry out the procedure. He said the Harmony Valve is an advance in transcatheter valve technology that is gaining acceptance around the world. Working with the partners has also let babies and children have catheter procedures and surgery in the centre'snew catheterisation laboratory, which replaced its older facility. More procedures are planned, including closing a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), an abnormal link between two large blood vessels near the heart, and an atrial septal defect (ASD), a hole between the heart's two upper chambers. Parents of children treated during the visit thanked the Ghanaian and German teams. They said getting such specialised care free of charge, made possible by the NCTC, the visiting team and theGhana Medical Trust Fund, had brought them hope and relief. Korle Bu says the procedure shows the NCTC can now take on complex heart work at home, so fewer patients should need to travel abroad for specialised care.

Title: Agyinasare wants a state of emergency where galamsey has ruined forests and rivers
Content: Archbishop Charles Agyinasare wants emergency rule in the parts of Ghana wheregalamseyhas done the worst damage, though not across the whole country. The founder of Perez Chapel International made the call in the same interview in which heasked to see the National Cathedral accounts. "There has to be a state of emergency in some places," he told Bernard Avle on Channel One TV's The Point of View on Monday. His call came two days after theCatholic Bishops' Conference demanded the samefor galamsey hotspots. In a communiqué from their plenary at Jamasi, in the Ashanti Region, on Saturday, the bishops said the crackdown so far had not broughtillegal miningunder control. President Mahama has said he willdeclare one only if the National Security Council advises it. Climate Frontier Advocacymade the same targeted appeal to himin December 2025. Agyinasare drew the line between the country as a whole and its worst-hit forests and rivers. "I also think that for some areas, there should not be a general state of emergency, but for some areas where the forest is desecrated and where the rivers are bad, there should be some form of state of emergency, because some areas are getting worse gradually," he said. He said the government should be specific about where it acts and why. "The government needs to be decisive in some of those places and say that in this particular area, because of what has happened to this forest and because of what has happened to this river, we declare a state of emergency," he said. Lands Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah has warned that"no tourist travels to see a poisoned river". The EPA has told people in mining areas thatboiling river water poisoned by galamseykills germs but leaves the mercury in. Agyinasare said he had been to mining sites in and around Dunkwa, in the Central Region. "From the pictures I have seen and the videos I have seen, some places are being reclaimed. But I think more needs to be done," he said. Enforcement is still dangerous. TwoNAIMOSofficers wereshot when an armed mob attacked an anti-galamsey teamat Manso Keniago last Wednesday. In the same interview, Agyinasare saidMahama has done better in his second termthan in his first.

Title: CIB Ghana and GhISP strengthen SME financing capacity among financial institutions in Kumasi and surrounding areas
Content: Efforts to strengthen access to appropriate financing for businesses across Ghana received further support as the Ghana Investment Support Programme (GhISP) and Chartered Institute of Bankers, Ghana (CIB Ghana) extended their financial institutions capacity-building initiative to Kumasi. The two-day workshop, held on 5th and 6th November 2026 at the Public Service Workers Union, Conference Centre, TUC , provided a platform for financial sector professionals to examine practical approaches for improving SME lending while strengthening financial inclusion and sustainability. The workshop brought together professionals from banks, financial NGOs and community banks serving SMEs across Ghana’s regional economies. Participants shared perspectives on the financing needs and challenges of businesses operating in different markets and explored practical approaches for expanding access to appropriate financing for SMEs. According to British International Investment (BII) Country Director, Kwabena Asante-Poku, the workshop also highlights GhISP’s efforts to step up its support to Ghana’s financial institutions through the organisation’s technical assistance offering. “GhISP has already demonstrated its ability to strengthen SME investment readiness through company-level technical assistance. Now, we are taking lessons from this work, combined with insights from BII’s technical assistance partnerships with financial institutions in the region and our wider ecosystem work, and applying this to tailoring support to Ghanaian financial institutions. Our partnership with CIB to deliver these workshops mark the beginning of an exciting chapter.” In a message conveyed on his behalf, the Chief Executive Officer of Chartered Institute of Bankers, Ghana, Robert Dzato, FCIB, underscored the importance of strengthening the capacity of financial institutions to respond effectively to the financing needs of SMEs. The message highlighted CIB Ghana's commitment to equipping banking professionals with practical skills in credit assessment, inclusive lending and sustainable finance, while emphasising the importance of translating knowledge gained from the workshop into improved lending practices that support SME growth across Ghana. Participants in the Kumasi workshop examined how financial institutions can better understand the realities of SMEs operating within different markets and design financing solutions that respond to their business models, cash-flow patterns and growth potential.Particular attention was given to strengthening credit assessment practices, cash-flow-based lending, climate-responsive financing and gender-smart approaches to SME finance. Participants also considered how inclusive financial products can help viable but underserved enterprises gain improved access to formal financing. The workshop facilitators emphasised the importance of moving beyond conventional collateral-based lending towards a more comprehensive assessment of SME business performance and repayment capacity. Discussions highlighted how a better understanding of cash-flow patterns, business models and sector-specific risks can enable financial institutions to make more informed lending decisions while expanding access to financing for viable SMEs. The practical nature of the workshop was reflected in participants’ discussions on how the lessons could be applied within their respective institutions. Reflecting on the insights gained, one participant remarked, “The sessions have challenged us to look beyond collateral and pay closer attention to the cash flows and business realities of SMEs. This is particularly relevant to the customers we serve in our communities.” Echoing this perspective, another participant highlighted the importance of developing financing solutions that respond to the diverse needs of businesses, noting that “One important takeaway is that financial inclusion requires more than making credit available. We must also understand the different needs of businesses and develop financing solutions that support their long-term growth.” The workshop created an opportunity for participating institutions to share practical experiences from their respective markets and discuss common challenges affecting SME financing. This peer-learning approach is an important component of the initiative, which seeks to facilitate learning among banks and community banks while strengthening engagement between financial institutions and SMEs. Participants were further encouraged to develop institutional action points that could be implemented after the workshop, ensuring that the programme translates into changes in lending practices rather than ending with classroom learning.The Kumasi workshop marked the second of the two national ecosystem engagements being implemented under the GhISP–CIB Ghana partnership and reinforced the partners' commitment to building a financial ecosystem capable of supporting SMEs through inclusive, gender-responsive and climate-conscious financing solutions.

Title: Ghana's exports to China hit $290 million in June under zero-tariff policy
Content: Ghana's exports toChinareached US$290 million in June 2026 under Beijing's zero-tariff policy for African goods, Chinese Ambassador to Ghana Cong Song has announced. He gave the figure on Friday at a forum in Accra on the zero-tariff policy, held alongside a reception for Ghanaians who studied on Chinese commerce ministry scholarships. Their alumni body, MOSAAG, organised it. Finance Minister Ato Forson has called for a shift towardvalue-added trade and local manufacturing with China. June shipments were up 166 per cent on May and 6.1 per cent on June 2025, Cong said. They made up 27 per cent of everything China bought from Ghana in the first half of the year. Bilateral trade hit a record US$14.12 billion in 2025, with Ghana's exports to China at US$2.67 billion, up 33.9 per cent year on year. Since 1 May 2026, China has given duty-free, zero-tariff treatment to goods from the 53 African countries it has diplomatic relations with, Ghana among them. Eligible products include cocoa, cashew, shea butter, textiles and handicrafts. Some Ghanaian cocoa products previously faced tariffs of eight to 22 per cent. He told the forum the policy is "offered unilaterally, with no requirement for African countries to open their markets reciprocally", places "no ceiling on the volume of African exports to China" and "comes with no political strings attached". "For African countries, this means the door of opportunity to China's mega-market of 1.4 billion people is wide open," he said. At a separate zero-tariff forum in Accra in October, theChinese Embassy in Ghanasaid, Cong urged participants to make full use of the policy and turn it into real gains. Ghana has also urged action on theChina-Africa Green Pledges. In a speech read on his behalf, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said the government seeks partnerships that build local production facilities, domestic supply chains and decent, sustainable jobs. "The real measure of a successful partnership is not simply how much we trade but how sustainable the trading arrangements are," he said. MOSAAG president Leonard Edem Cosmos said the removal of duties is "only the first step". Exporters still have to meet "sanitary and phytosanitary standards, packaging regulations, rules of origin, logistics, and Chinese buyer expectations", which he said is "where real trade happens". Cong also pointed to cooperation across themining value chain, from geological exploration to local processing, value addition and skills development, and urged Chinese businesses in Ghana to comply with local laws.

Title: Boankra terminal 85% complete in the 2027 Budget, but 2026 Budget said feasibility had started
Content: Ghana's 2027 Budget says the Boankra Integrated Logistics Terminal is 85 per cent complete, a year after the 2026 Budget said feasibility work had only started on the project. Prof Isaac Boadi raised the mismatch in a TV interview on Monday, November 16, days after the2027 Budget Statementput the project at that figure. He is a professor at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA). "But then when we have a project, the Boankra Integrated Logistics Terminal, repeated in 2025, was stated in the budget as 85% complete," he said. "Then in 2026, they tell us in that budget, feasibility work has started. Then in 2027, they state in the same document, still 85% complete." He accepted that some projects genuinely run across several budget cycles, because budgets plan over the short, medium and long term. His concern is the same figure coming back two years apart, with no account of what changed. The Budget, presented by Finance Minister Ato Forson on Thursday, November 12, states at paragraph 1341: "Mr. Speaker, the Boankra Integrated Logistics Terminal (BILT) is 85 percent complete." It describes the facility as a strategic inland logistics hub for shippers in the middle and northern belts and for transit cargo to Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. Nothing in the paragraph says what the 85 per cent covers or when it was measured. The 2026 Budget, presented in November 2025, took a different starting point. Its paragraph 543 reads: "Feasibility work has started on the Boankra Inland Port, with full construction expected in 2026 to ease congestion and support northern trade corridors." Neither statement reconciles the two positions, and neither says what became of the feasibility work or the full construction promised for 2026. Aneconomist has criticised the government for defaulting on promises made in that Budget. The agency overseeing the project gave a lower figure six weeks before the Budget was read. After the Ashanti Regional Security Council toured the site on 30 September, theGhana Shippers' Authoritysaid in a 2 October release that "Phase One of the project is currently estimated to be 65 per cent complete." Its chief executive, Prof Ransford Gyampo, told the visitors that funding constraints and the wider economy, not technical problems, had set the pace. The release said a roadmap to finish Phase One would go to the Finance Ministry for approval, with full government funding now preferred to a public-private partnership. Public figures for the project have moved all year. In February, the Transport Minister put it at50.54 per cent complete. The 2027 Budget does not say whether its 85 per cent refers to Phase One or to the whole terminal.

Title: Ghana is now Africa's eighth-largest economy, Mahama tells investors
Content: President John Dramani Mahamahas told investors that Ghana is now Africa's eighth-largest economy and the second biggest in West Africa. "In 2025, Ghana's Gross Domestic Product reached approximately $114 billion, positioning the country as the 8th largest economy in Africa and the 2nd largest in West Africa," he said as he opened the Ghana Investment Summit in Accra on Monday. The same summit heardDangote Group set out plans for sugar and cocoa factories in Ghana. TheIMFexpects the economy to reach about US$128.64 billion by the end of 2026, Mahama said, which would keep Ghana in both places. Growth came in at 6 per cent last year and is forecast at 5.7 per cent for 2026. "This figure would have been much higher if the bombs had not started flying in Iran," he said. Inflationhas dropped from 23.5 per cent in January 2025 to 5.5 per cent last month, he said, in line withOctober's official inflation reading. Gross reserves were US$12.05 billion in September, enough for 4.5 months of imports. A US$8.86 billion trade surplus over the first eight months of the year helped build them. The government ran a primary surplus worth 1.6 per cent of GDP, better than its fiscal target, he said. Public debt, he said, was broadly stable at 45 per cent of GDP in July. Former Finance Minister Dr Mohammed Amin Adam disputes that debt figure, putting debt at 47.5 per cent of GDP by October. Mahama said a badly handled debt restructuring could have dragged Ghana into a second catastrophic default. Fiscal discipline had kept the country on track with its obligations, he said, and the aim now is an investment-grade rating by 2030. The cedi gained 40.7 per cent against the dollar in 2025, he said, and was about 7 per cent stronger in September 2026 than a year earlier. Business confidence was at 107.8 and consumer confidence at 111.9 in August. The composite index of economic activity was up 14.9 per cent on a year earlier in July. S&P Global has kept Ghana at B-/B with a stable outlook, he said. Fitch now rates Ghana B, up from B-, with a positive outlook. Moody's has upgraded its long-term issuer ratings and moved the outlook to stable. One private forecaster is less upbeat on prices:Fitch Solutions sees inflation back above 10 per centin the second half of 2027. Ghana hosts the AfCFTA secretariat, he told investors, which opens a market of roughly 1.4 billion people whose economies together produce about US$3.4 trillion. Exporters also get duty-free, quota-free entry to the UK and the EU under interim trade deals, he said, along with preferential tariffs in China and access to the US under AGOA. Three decades of constitutional democracy, peaceful handovers and the rule of law give investors predictability, he said. He said the recovery had to show up in people's daily lives, such as a farmer being able to sell more of a harvest to a processor close by.

Title: 2027 Budget: Beyond the promises, what did government leave out?
Content: A US$20.49 billion asset recovery exercise, a US$235 million international arbitration award, a central bank with negative equity exceeding GH¢96 billion and several unresolved public infrastructure commitments. These are among the issues that received little or no specific attention in Ghana’s 2027 Budget Statement. On Thursday, November 12, Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson presented the 2027 Budget to Parliament under the theme The New Economy, New Ghana, Jobs and Prosperity. At the heart of the budget is an ambitious US$10 billion economic transformation programme spanning agriculture, energy, industrialisation and employment. The proposals are ambitious, but beyond the new commitments lies another important conversation: the status of existing obligations, unresolved financial liabilities and promises made in previous years. An examination of the 316-page budget statement by By the Numbers identified ten issues of significant national interest that either received no specific mention or lacked critical details necessary for measuring progress. The billions Ghana hopes to recover Perhaps one of the most striking omissions is Operation Recover All Loot (ORAL), an initiative that featured prominently in President John Dramani Mahama’s campaign ahead of the 2024 general elections. Established as part of the government's broader anti-corruption agenda, the committee was tasked with gathering information on suspected corruption and the misappropriation of public assets. On February 10, 2025, the committee presented its findings to President Mahama, identifying 36 financial cases with an estimated value of US$20.49 billion. The President subsequently referred the report to the Attorney-General for investigation. The figure was substantial, particularly for a country emerging from a sovereign debt crisis. For perspective, the estimated value of the cases was nearly seven times the size of Ghana’s US$3 billion IMF Extended Credit Facility programme. However, almost two years into the government's tenure, the 2027 Budget provides no consolidated update on how much has been recovered specifically through ORAL, how many cases have progressed to prosecution, or what financial recovery targets have been set for the coming year. It is important to distinguish between the estimated value of cases under investigation and money that can actually be recovered. Not every allegation will result in a successful prosecution or financial recovery. Nevertheless, publishing measurable outcomes would provide an important basis for evaluating the effectiveness of the initiative. The unresolved financial burden of the Bank of Ghana Another significant omission concerns the financial position of the Bank of Ghana. The central bank’s financial difficulties became particularly pronounced following Ghana's domestic debt restructuring exercise. In 2022, the Bank recorded a loss of GH¢60.8 billion, of which GH¢53.1 billion was attributed to the government's domestic debt restructuring. By the end of 2025, its negative equity had increased considerably. This represents a deterioration of approximately 57% within one year. Unlike commercial banks, central banks can continue operating with negative equity. However, prolonged financial weakness can create challenges for monetary policy, institutional independence and financial credibility. In its 2026 Article IV consultation, the IMF identified the need for a credible recapitalisation plan, with full recapitalisation expected by the end of 2032. Despite this, the 2027 Budget does not outline a specific government funding commitment towards the recapitalisation exercise. The fundamental question is not simply whether the central bank will be recapitalised, but how the government intends to finance it and what implications this could have for future budgets. The National Cathedral and the cost of an unfinished project The National Cathedral remains one of Ghana’s most controversial public infrastructure projects. In July 2025, the government disclosed that beyond the previously reported US$58 million in payments and commitments, an additional US$39 million was reportedly outstanding to the contractor. This brought the reported combined financial exposure to approximately US$97 million, although the entire amount should not be interpreted as money already spent. Following an audit by Deloitte and Touche, President Mahama directed the dissolution of the Cathedral's Board of Trustees and the closure of its Secretariat. However, dissolving the institutions responsible for managing the project does not automatically extinguish its contractual obligations. The 2027 Budget offers no project-specific update on the outstanding liabilities, the future of the infrastructure, or the potential recovery of public funds. For taxpayers, the question is whether the financial cost of the Cathedral has ended or whether further obligations will eventually find their way into the national expenditure framework. A US$235 million water project liability The financial implications of the Teshie desalination plant present another concern. The facility, originally established to improve water supply to communities in eastern Accra, became the subject of an international arbitration dispute following the termination of its water purchase agreement. In September 2026, an International Chamber of Commerce tribunal awarded approximately US$235 million to Befesa Desalination Developments Ghana Limited and Standard Bank of South Africa. Government subsequently announced that it was negotiating to acquire the facility at a lower cost, potentially avoiding payment of the full arbitration award. However, two months after the announcement, the 2027 Budget provides no specific update on the proposed acquisition, settlement arrangements or financing requirements. The concern is not only about the financial liability but also the country's ability to provide reliable water supply to affected communities. Whether government eventually pays the arbitration award or negotiates an alternative settlement, the transaction could have implications for public finances. The SML contracts and the question of recovery The controversial contracts involving Strategic Mobilisation Ghana Limited (SML) generated considerable public debate over procurement practices, revenue assurance and value for money. According to the Office of the Special Prosecutor, SML had received approximately GH¢1.44 billion in payments by December 2024. Following investigations and an external audit, government terminated the contracts. Criminal allegations arising from the investigations remain matters for judicial determination. The termination of a controversial contract, however, represents only one aspect of accountability. There are equally important questions regarding the recovery of public funds, outstanding contractual obligations and the financial savings arising from the termination. The 2027 Budget provides no specific breakdown of these issues. Judgment debts: A financial risk without a consolidated figure Unlike some of the other issues, judgment debts are explicitly acknowledged in the budget. Government reveals that more than 80% of the value of substantial judgment claims is denominated in foreign currencies, exposing the country to additional exchange-rate risks. The budget also discloses that a court order prevented government from accessing its Contingency Fund to respond to flooding in June 2026. Government intends to amend the State Proceedings Act to address challenges associated with the enforcement of judgments against public institutions. What remains unclear, however, is the consolidated value of the outstanding judgment claims. If government cannot quantify its overall exposure, how can citizens properly assess the associated fiscal risk? There is also a distinction between pending legal claims, final judgments and amounts approved for settlement. Each category carries different financial risks and must be accounted for separately. The Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921), and its accompanying regulations recognise the importance of identifying and quantifying fiscal risks, including contingent liabilities. GH¢1 billion for national service, but no new allowance rate For thousands of young graduates, the silence surrounding national service allowances is particularly significant. Government has allocated GH¢1 billion for the payment of national service allowances in 2027. However, the budget does not specify whether the monthly allowance, currently approximately GH¢715, will be increased. In July 2026, the National Service Authority disclosed that it was pursuing an increase to at least GH¢1,200. This would represent an adjustment of approximately 68%. Using GH¢715 as the monthly benchmark, the GH¢1 billion allocation could theoretically support approximately 116,550 personnel for twelve months. At the proposed GH¢1,200 monthly rate, the same allocation could support only about 69,444 personnel for the same period. These are illustrative calculations, assuming the entire allocation is used exclusively for twelve monthly allowance payments. Without information on the number of beneficiaries or the approved monthly rate, it is difficult to determine whether the allocation is adequate or whether personnel should expect an increase. Agenda 111: Another year, another completion target The healthcare sector presents a similar accountability challenge. Agenda 111 was introduced under the previous administration to expand healthcare infrastructure across the country, particularly in districts without hospitals. In March 2022, then-President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo indicated that all 111 hospitals would be commissioned before the end of his tenure in January 2025. That target was not achieved. The 2026 Budget subsequently targeted the completion of ten of the stalled hospital projects. Now, the 2027 Budget allocates GH¢1 billion towards the completion of 35 district hospitals under the initiative. While this represents a more ambitious target, the budget does not identify the specific 35 facilities, their individual completion rates or the outstanding cost of each project. Distributing the allocation equally would amount to an average of approximately GH¢28.6 million per hospital, although actual completion costs will differ depending on the stage of construction. Beyond the announcement, communities deserve to know whether their hospitals are among those scheduled for completion. More importantly, completing a hospital building is not the same as making it operational. Equipment, staffing, utilities and recurrent expenditure must also be considered. An economic transformation agenda without an annual jobs target Job creation is central to the government's new economic transformation programme. The 2027 Budget acknowledges that Ghana recorded an unemployment rate of approximately 12.8% in 2025 and targets a reduction to below 8% by 2030. This would require a reduction of more than 4.8 percentage points. However, despite several programme-specific employment projections, the budget does not provide a consolidated nationwide job creation target for 2027. This matters because economic growth does not automatically translate into employment. An economy driven largely by capital-intensive sectors such as mining and oil production can record impressive growth figures without generating enough jobs to absorb its expanding labour force. Government must therefore establish measurable annual employment targets against which the success of its economic transformation programme can be assessed. Fighting galamsey: Beyond arrests and seizures The government's fight against illegal mining is another area where the distinction between activities and outcomes becomes critical. Between January and August 2026, the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat reported: For 2027, government has allocated GH¢200 million to NAIMOS and GH¢400 million towards land reclamation. However, the budget does not provide corresponding figures on prosecutions, convictions or the final legal status of the 349 individuals arrested. Neither do the arrest figures alone establish the extent to which illegal mining has declined or degraded water bodies have recovered. Arrests are a measure of enforcement activity. Convictions, sustained reductions in illegal mining and improvements in environmental conditions are measures of effectiveness. A comprehensive assessment must account for both. Beyond the promises: The real test of accountability The omissions identified in the 2027 Budget do not necessarily mean government has abandoned these issues. Some may be addressed through separate ministerial budgets, ongoing investigations or subsequent policy decisions. Nevertheless, the national budget remains one of the most important instruments through which government communicates its priorities, financial obligations and performance to citizens. Its credibility must therefore be measured not only by the size of new allocations and the ambition of new promises, but also by how transparently it accounts for previous commitments. Announcements create expectations. Clear figures establish benchmarks. Measurable targets allow citizens to track progress. And without these, promises become increasingly difficult to evaluate. Ultimately, the purpose of a national budget is not merely to announce what government intends to do. It is also to account for what government has done, what remains outstanding and how public resources have been managed. That is the foundation of accountability.

Title: Price of LPG projected to increase by 21.10%
Content: The second pricing window of November for petroleum products has brought mixed adjustments to petroleum prices, with petrol and diesel expected to decline while Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) is projected to increase by 21.10 per cent. These changes have drawn varied reactions from consumers, as some weigh their options amid the latest price projections. For some households, Liquified Petroleum Gas is becoming an increasingly expensive necessity. While some say they will continue buying according to what they can afford, others fear that further increases could force them to consider other alternatives. "Yes, the price has been increased. I used to buy it at 120, now it's 130. We will manage. We are praying that things will go well, so that there will be a reduction," one explained. For Margaret, a food vendor, if the price escalates beyond her ability, she will add it to her cost. "I sell jollof and chicken. I sell from 25 cedis with salad. But if it continues like that, then I may have to increase to maybe 30, 35 going. I will still use the gas because I see the charcoal to be much more expensive." The Chamber of Petroleum Consumers projects LPG will sell at GH¢23.17 per kilogram, compared with the previous indicative price of about GH¢19.14. The latest development follows several upward adjustments in LPG prices since October. The Chief Executive Officer of the Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies (COMAC), Riverson Oppong, explained the reason behind the adjustment in an interview with 3 News. "What is happening is that petrol and diesel are both going down. Diesel has gone down by 5% and petrol by 16%. Ideally, on the global market, LPG also went down by 6%. That should have been reflected here. But currently, the industry applies a tendering process for LPG in the country. So that means that until the product that is in the market is finished, we don't price LPG." He suggests that the government take a second look at the methodology that is used today for importing LPG, although the price of LPG may see a reduction in the coming weeks. "Achieving a 75% DMO is ideal for any developing market. Today, Atuabo produces LPG, TOR, Sentuo and other refineries. And if they are going to use the international benchmark prices, then their LPG price should go down. So, the question you're going to ask yourself is, even if they come, what is the pricing method for LPG that you're going to adapt to? Are you going to adapt to the bidding rounds or actual price or the average price that we apply to the diesel and petrol?" Meanwhile, the National Petroleum Authority says the government is also considering developments in the petroleum market, with the Finance Minister agreeing to suspend the GH¢1 Energy Sector Shortfall and Debt Repayment Levy on diesel for November. "We are trying to ramp up domestic production and what we are bringing. And one of the things that has been greatly affected is the LPG prices. We will keep monitoring and, as and when we do, we'll update the public about this development. But we are confident that with the stability that we are seeing, things will improve in the coming months." For households already adjusting their spending to meet the rising cost of cooking gas, the concern is how much further prices could climb and whether alternatives will become necessary. For now, consumers are left to navigate another round of price adjustments.

Title: GhanaPay offers zero-charge transfers and bank loans based on your wallet history
Content: Users of GhanaPay can send money and pay everyday bills without transaction fees while building a digital record to qualify for bank loans, theGhana Association of Bankssays. Speaking at a GhanaPay Awareness Campaign media engagement in Accra on Friday, November 13, association chief executive John Awuah said the bank-backed wallet is meant to cut transaction costs and bring unbanked customers into formal banking. "Whatever you do on GhanaPay is free of charge. So you can make whatever transfers on GhanaPay to pay for data, water, school fees, to pay for your transport; it is all free," Awuah said. The banking industry created the service together with GhIPSS, theGhana Interbank Payment and Settlement Systems. Universal banks offer it, as do rural and community banks as well as savings and loans companies, all ranked among Ghana'sapproved electronic money issuers and payment service providers. Anyone with a mobile phone can open a wallet without holding a traditional bank account. Customers on MTN, Telecel and other networks can register with their existing numbers by dialling `*707#` or using the GhanaPay Customer app. During registration, a user selects a participating bank to host the wallet and validates the account at a branch with a Ghana Card. The platform also supports savings pots and digital susu contributions. Beyond transfers, Awuah said banks will use a customer's transaction history on the wallet to assess creditworthiness for direct loans, addressing complaints over collateral even asaverage bank lending rates eased to 15.9 per cent in August. "Instead of asking you for collateral, we'll just use your digital footprint, and you'll be able to have direct access to funding from the banks at a lower interest rate," he said. Awuah did not announce a start date or specific interest rates for the digital-footprint loans, which offer a regulated alternative tounlicensed loan apps flagged by the Bank of Ghana.

Title: Ghana re-elected to ITU Council with 121 votes in Doha
Content: Ghana has been re-elected to the Council of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), securing 121 of 173 valid votes in Region D at the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference 2026 (PP-26) in Doha, Qatar. The result renews Ghana's seat on the Council of the United Nations specialised agency for digital technologies and telecommunications, and extends the country's long record of engagement in the Union's governance. The victory follows an appeal by the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, to ITU member states to back Ghana's candidature. Speaking at a Ghanaian luncheon on the sidelines of the conference, he noted that Ghana has served on the Council without interruption for 24 years, since 2002. He pointed to Ghana's active participation in all three ITU sectors, its contributions to regulatory and institutional reforms, its cybersecurity initiatives, and its efforts to advance inclusive connectivity and digital development. The re-election gives Ghana the opportunity to continue contributing to the ITU's strategic direction, policy development, and decisions shaping the global telecommunications and digital ecosystem. It also underscores Ghana's commitment to ensuring that African perspectives and priorities remain part of global conversations on connectivity, emerging technologies, and telecommunications development. Ghana says it looks forward to working with member states to build a more inclusive, secure, and connected digital future.

Title: Femi Adebayo explains why he left law for acting: “It was paying more”
Content: Nigerian actor and filmmaker Femi Adebayo has revealed that acting offered him both better pay and greater personal fulfilment than the legal profession, prompting him to abandon law just two years after qualifying as a lawyer. Adebayo, who was called to the Nigerian Bar in 2003, said he spent about two years practising litigation before leaving the profession in 2005 to concentrate on acting and film production. Speaking in an interview on a podcast published in November 2026, the actor explained that performing had started as a childhood interest inspired by his father, veteran Nollywood actor Adebayo Salami, popularly known as Oga Bello. “It was actually hobby turned profession for me,” Adebayo said, explaining that he eventually discovered he felt happier acting than practising the profession he had studied. He added that the financial rewards of entertainment also influenced his decision to change careers. “I realised that it was paying more and I felt more passionate about it. I feel happy when I do that more than the law that I went to school to study,” he said. A difficult choice between two careers Adebayo’s decision carried particular significance because law had been an important ambition within his family. According to the actor, his father had wanted to study law himself but could not pursue the dream because of financial limitations. When Adebayo expressed an interest in the profession, his father was pleased that his son could achieve what he had been unable to do. However, the younger Adebayo’s growing commitment to acting eventually placed him at a crossroads. After appearing in court and handling legal cases, he decided to leave the profession in 2005, despite having spent years studying to become a lawyer. He described his departure as a difficult moment for his father, who was pleased to see him follow the family’s acting tradition but also had to accept that his son was giving up the legal career he had hoped to see him pursue. Adebayo said his father eventually came to appreciate the decision. From lawyer to established filmmaker Since leaving legal practice, Adebayo has built a career as an actor, producer, and filmmaker within Nigeria’s film industry, popularly known as Nollywood. He is known for projects includingKing of Thieves (Agesinkole)andJagun Jagun, productions that have strengthened his profile beyond acting and established him as a filmmaker in his own right. His career also reflects the influence of growing up around the film industry. His father, Oga Bello, is a veteran of Yoruba-language cinema, and Adebayo has previously acknowledged the role his family played in his introduction to acting. Nevertheless, his recent comments suggest that family influence was only part of the story. The decision to make entertainment his full-time profession came after he experienced both careers and concluded that acting offered him greater satisfaction. Choosing passion over a conventional career Adebayo’s experience highlights the difficult decisions people can face when the profession they studied does not align with the work they ultimately find rewarding. His story is not simply about abandoning a qualification. He completed his legal training, qualified to practise, and gained experience before deciding that another career better suited his interests and ambitions. For Adebayo, the choice eventually led to a life in filmmaking, where he has continued to act in and produce projects for audiences in Nigeria and beyond. More than two decades after leaving legal practice, his explanation offers a glimpse into the thinking behind that decision: a career is not always determined by the degree a person earns, but by where their abilities, passion, and opportunities meet. For Adebayo, that place was not the courtroom but the film set.

Title: Grammy Awards 2027: Beyoncé makes history with 100th nomination
Content: American singer Beyoncé achieved the milestone on Monday, 16 November, after receiving a nomination for Best R&B Solo Performance for her song “MORNING DEW (DONK)” ahead of the 69th Grammy Awards, according to the Recording Academy. The nomination brings Beyoncé’s career total to 100, while she remains the most-awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins. The latest recognition adds another chapter to a career that has taken her from girl-group success to international stardom as a solo performer. From Destiny’s Child to a solo career Born Beyoncé Giselle Knowles on 4 September 1981 in Houston, Texas, Beyoncé first rose to prominence as a member of Destiny’s Child. The group became one of the most successful girl groups of its era, gaining international attention with songs including “Bills, Bills, Bills” and “Say My Name”. She began her solo career in 2003 with the release ofDangerously in Love. The album topped the US Billboard 200 chart and produced hit singles including “Crazy in Love” and “Baby Boy”. At the 2004 Grammy Awards, Beyoncé won five awards as a solo artist, including Best Contemporary R&B Album forDangerously in Love. Those victories established her as a major solo force beyond her success with Destiny’s Child. Her Grammy recognition has continued through successive albums and performances, with nominations spanning R&B, pop, rap, country, dance, and other musical categories. A record built across musical genres Beyoncé’s Grammy history reflects her willingness to explore different sounds rather than remaining within a single musical style. Her 2016 albumLemonadecombined elements of R&B, rock, country, and hip-hop while exploring themes of identity, relationships, pain, and resilience. The project earned several nominations at the 2017 Grammy Awards and became one of the most discussed releases of her career. In 2022, she releasedRenaissance, a dance-focused album influenced by house and disco music. The project won Best Dance/Electronic Music Album at the 2023 ceremony, while the song “Break My Soul” won Best Dance/Electronic Recording. Her move into country music brought another major achievement. In 2024, Beyoncé releasedCowboy Carter, an album that drew on country, blues, folk, and other American musical traditions. At the 2025 Grammy Awards,Cowboy Carterwon Album of the Year and Best Country Album. The Album of the Year victory was her first in the category after multiple nominations over the years. The album’s success added to her Grammy record and demonstrated the range of musical styles she has explored throughout her career. What the 100th nomination means Beyoncé’s latest nomination is for “MORNING DEW (DONK)” in the Best R&B Solo Performance category. The category recognises excellence in contemporary R&B performances by individual artists. Her record of 100 nominations includes recognition across her solo career and her group or collaborative projects. It therefore reflects not only her work as a lead performer but also her contributions to recordings created with other musicians. The Grammy Awards are decided by voting members of the Recording Academy, which represents professionals working across the music industry, including performers, songwriters, producers, composers, and engineers. Beyoncé’s 35 wins make her the most-awarded artist in the awards’ history, while the latest nomination extends her lead in the nominations record. Beyoncé’s 100th nomination is a historic achievement, regardless of the outcome of the ceremony. From her early success with Destiny’s Child to her solo career and experiments across musical genres, she has built a body of work that continues to attract recognition from the recording industry. The ceremony will offer another opportunity to add to a record that has taken more than two decades to build.

Title: Ghana's King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni land 2027 Grammy nomination as Raye leads with 11
Content: King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni have carried Ghana onto the 2027 Grammy nominations list, with No Tradition, No Africa up for Best African Music Performance as British singer Raye leads the field on 11. The Recording Academy announced the nominees for the 69th Grammy Awards on Monday, November 16, in afull list of 100 categories published on grammy.com. No Tradition, No Africa is credited to King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni. Dawuni spoke to 3Xtra's Behind the Hustle in September aboutthe sacrifices behind his Grammy nominations. King Ayisoba, whotold 3News last yearhe hoped to be considered for a diplomatic passport, now has a Grammy nomination to his name. Raye, born Rachel Keen, leads the field with 11 nominations.Her mum and uncle were both raised in Ghana, and she grew up in south London. Ghana has a third name on the list. Producer GuiltyBeatz shares the Best R&B Song nomination with Tems for What You Need, afterrecounting how he came to work with Beyoncé. The five Best African Music Performance nominees are Gratitude by ASAKE; Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?) by Angélique Kidjo and Ayra Starr; No Tradition, No Africa by King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni; Big Daddy by Tems; and Jogodo by Wizkid and ASAKE. Africans appear elsewhere too. Davido's Oriadé, Kidjo's HOPE!!, Ayra Starr's Starrgirl and Tems's Love Is A Kingdom are up for Best Global Music Album against Anitta's EQUILIBRIVM. In Best Global Music Performance, Kidjo joins Pharrell Williams and Quavo on Bando [Orchestral]. Burna Boy pairs with Shakira on Dai Dai, almost seven years after Kidjodedicated her 2020 Grammy win to him. Tems adds a Best R&B Solo Performance nomination for What You Need. Album of the year: Phoebe Bridgers' Lost Weekend, Olivia Dean's The Art of Loving, Ella Langley's Dandelion and Bruno Mars' The Romantic. Also up for album of the year are Raye's THIS MUSIC MAY CONTAIN HOPE, Olivia Rodrigo's you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love, ROSALÍA's LUX (Complete Works) and Taylor Swift's The Life of a Showgirl. Record of the year: Man I Need (Olivia Dean), Choosin' Texas (Ella Langley), I Just Might (Bruno Mars), WHERE IS MY HUSBAND! (Raye), the cure (Olivia Rodrigo), Berghain (ROSALÍA with Björk and Yves Tumor), The Fate of Ophelia (Taylor Swift) and Dracula (Tame Impala with JENNIE). Song of the year: Berghain, Choosin' Texas, the cure, hate that i made you love me (Ariana Grande), I Knew It, I Knew You (from Toy Story 5) (Taylor Swift), Man I Need (Olivia Dean), Risk it All (Bruno Mars) and WHERE IS MY HUSBAND! (Raye). Best new artist lines up Angine de Poitrine, Geese, Ella Langley, Slayyyter, Sienna Spiro, Don Toliver, Remi Wolf and The Womack Sisters. The producer of the year, non-classical, nominees are Tony Berg, Dernst "D'Mile" Emile II, Noah Goldstein, Miranda Lambert and Mike Sabath. For songwriter of the year, non-classical, they are Amy Allen, Edgar Barrera, Raye, Joybeth Taylor and Theron Thomas. Raye's 11 include record, song and album of the year, her first nods in those categories, plus songwriter of the year, a run of pop slots and a music video nod for Click Clack Symphony with Hans Zimmer. Her total equals the 11 Beyoncé earned at the 2025 Grammys, still the most for any woman in one year. Beyoncé herself reaches 100 career nominations with Morning Dew (Donk), up for best R&B solo performance. ROSALÍA follows on nine, every one of them in a category she has never been nominated in before. First-time nominee Ella Langley has seven, as do Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Rodrigo and Miranda Lambert. Olivia Dean, Leon Thomas III and Bruno Mars have six. Five new categories debut this year: Best Asian Pop Music Performance, Best R&B Collaboration or Duo/Group Performance, Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, Best Traditional Folk Album and Best Latin Song. The69th Grammy Awardswill be presented on Sunday, February 7, 2027, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, live across ABC, Disney+ and Hulu at 4pm PT/7pm ET, the show's first time back on ABC since 1972. The Premiere Ceremony, where most categories are handed out, streams exclusively on Disney+ for the first time from the Peacock Theater, starting at 11:30am PT/2:30pm ET. Final-round voting, which decides the winners, runs from December 10, 2026 to January 7, 2027, covering recordings released between August 31, 2025 and August 28, 2026.

Title: Raye, whose mother was raised in Ghana, leads 2027 Grammy nominations with 11
Content: British singer Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11, including album, record and song of the year. TheRecording Academy announced the nominations on Monday, with Raye ahead of Rosalía on nine. That matches Beyoncé's 11 at the 2025 Grammys, the most any woman has earned in one year, the Academy says. Raye, born Rachel Keen, has Ghanaian roots on her mother's side. On theBroken Record podcast, she said her mum and her uncle were both raised in Ghana. Her mum moved to the UK at about 22 or 23, and her uncle moved to America. That uncle bought her first laptop, a MacBook, for her 13th birthday. She said the demos she made on it sparked her passion for production. Ghana's King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni are also nominated,for best African music performance with No Tradition, No Africa. Her single WHERE IS MY HUSBAND! is up for best pop solo performance, record of the year and song of the year. The Academy credits the song to songwriters Rachel Keen and Mike Sabath. Her album THIS MUSIC MAY CONTAIN HOPE has two nods: best pop vocal album, and album of the year.Her Academy artist page lists all 11 nominations, taking her career tally to 15. Click Clack Symphony, her collaboration with Hans Zimmer, is nominated for best pop duo/group performance, best music video and best arrangement, instruments and vocals. Life Boat is up for best dance pop recording. I Hate The Way I Look Today is nominated for best traditional pop vocal performance, one of five categories new this year. She is also nominated for songwriter of the year, non-classical. A 2017 profiledescribed a Croydon childhood in south London, with an English dad, a Ghanaian-Swiss mum and a Ghanaian grandmother. That profile said her early music leaned on Afrobeats rhythms, an echo of the Ghanaian records her grandmother played at home. She left Polydor after creative differences and went independent with Human Re Sources, which put out her debut album, My 21st Century Blues, in 2023. Escapism, from that album, gave her a first UK number one. At the 2024 Brit Awards she took home six, more than any artist had won in one night. She was also the first woman named songwriter of the year at the Brits. Her new album, THIS MUSIC MAY CONTAIN HOPE, topped the UK albums chart in April. The Academy's records show four earlier Grammy nominations: best new artist, songwriter of the year and best engineered album in 2025, and best music film in 2026. She has never won a competitive Grammy. She has received the Academy's noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award. Raye watched the announcement with her mum, while her sister Amma stood nearby, and posted the video soon after. "What is happening? What is happening? 11 Grammy nominations, including Album of the Year," she wrote. As she wiped away tears, her mum told her to "let it out". Winners will be decided by final-round voting from 10 December to 7 January. They will be announced on Sunday, 7 February 2027 at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, live on ABC, Disney+ and Hulu.

Title: Kumawood actress Maame Serwaa joins law firm Kissiedu@Law
Content: Kissiedu@Law has welcomedKumawoodactress Maame Serwaa, naming her Clara Amoateng Benson. The firmwrote on Instagram on 16 November 2026: "Welcome to the Kissiedu@Law family, Clara Amoateng Benson!" "We are happy to have you with us." It added: "Welcome aboard, Clara!" The post is shared with her verified account,@officialmaameserwaa, whose display name is CLARA A BENSON. 3News has reported her as Clara Benson, popularly known as Maame Serwaa. The welcome names the firm and greets her. It does not give her a job title. The firm's site uses the title "Strategic Legal Counsel".
