On her own accountshe wrote that, after four years, she had completed "a Bachelor's Degree at Knutford University". That is her spelling. The post is tagged at Knutsford University College. Knutsford Universityspells the name with an s. It describes itself as a private university in East Legon, accredited by theGhanaTertiary Education Commission. She did not name a degree subject.3News publishedher March 2025 Onua FM interview, in which she spoke about life after school. She said: "When I completed school, I met with my management and told them I want to start my own production and also audition for young talents." She called the degree a testament to "the power of determination, faith, and the unwavering support of my loved ones", and she looked ahead to "new beginnings, greater heights".

Title: Sarkodie's fashion venture shows why artistes need strong teams – Nana Yaw Wiredu
Content: Media entrepreneur Nana Yaw Wiredu saysSarkodie's attempt to build afashionbusiness shows why Ghanaian artistes need strong teams behind their brands. Wiredu, founder of Oneplay Africa, made the case on Woezor TV's Breakfast Café, hosted by Evergreen Asantewaa, in a discussion titled "Famous Is Not a Brand: Turning Popularity into Lasting Value". "We've seen Sarkodie try to do a fashion brand. It didn't work." "We've seen Sarkodie try to do a water brand, HOLIC H2O. It didn't work." "Not because he can't do it, because when you venture into such spaces for so long, what happens is that the music becomes a challenge. Now you have to find a way of balancing going to the studio, and running the business," he said. The label, Sark Collection, was launched in April 2013 with designer Yas, selling men's shirts, jeans, sneakers, caps and belts from a shop in Dzorwulu, Accra. By July 2016 it had gone quiet, andSarkodiesaid at the time that it was beingrebranded and restructuredbecause fans struggled to get the products. "We were just based in the shop," he said then. He had also announced a HOLIC H2O bottled-water line in January 2013. "A proper system, a structure behind an artist is what makes the artist. It's not the artist," Wiredu said. His argument is that a capable team should run bookings, production and sales while the artiste concentrates on the music, so that a venture does not live or die with the celebrity. That message echoes what the fashion industry itself has been told: a public relations expert recently called for stronger business structures across Ghana's fashion industry, and the country istargeting global fashion markets with a US$1 billion textile investment. For young creatives, the lesson in Wiredu's telling is to build the system first. Sarkodie's own playbook has since leaned on structure: hisRapperholic concertdrew a massive crowd in Kumasi in October, and he has urged investors to back the creative economy.

Title: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond in Amazon MGM's next 007 film
Content: Amazon MGM Studios has named Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, with Denis Villeneuve directing the studio's first 007 film. The studioannounced the casting on Monday, ending years of speculation over who would succeed Daniel Craig. Villeneuve will direct from a script by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce the film, with Tanya Lapointe as executive producer, the announcement says. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said. He added that he was "deeply grateful" to the creative team for their belief in him. "There can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond," Villeneuve said. In his view, Pattinson "has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new". Pascal and Heyman said the legacy of the character "is in great hands with Robert Pattinson", calling him "the perfect Bond for our times". Pattinson, 40, becomes the seventh actor to play Bond on the big screen, after Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig. Craig's five-film run began with Casino Royale in 2006 and closed withNo Time to Die in 2021. The announcement gives no title or release date for the new film. It will be the first Bond film made under Amazon, which bought MGM in 2022. Amazon took creative control in March 2025 through a joint venture with long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Pattinson broke through in the Twilight films and later led 2022's The Batman. He is currently filming its sequel, The Batman Part II, for Matt Reeves, and will appear in Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three. His other credits include Tenet, The Lighthouse and Good Time.

Title: Eddie Eckstein, the South African singer and actor, has died at 86
Content: South African entertainer Eddie Eckstein has died at 86, his family has told SABC News. SABC Newsreported on Sunday, 15 November 2026, that the family had confirmed his death. They said he died the night before at 86, surrounded by his loved ones. Singing, acting and cabaret made him famous. Eldest son John confirmed the family's loss as friends and former colleagues sent tributes. The family said: "our beloved husband, father and Papu passed away peacefully, surrounded by his family at nine minutes past six last night." They said they were humbled by the outpouring of love. "Ever since we were children, we realised that we shared dad with the whole of South Africa," the statement said. It was signed "The diminished Eckstein clan." A later SABC reportsaid he died on Saturday night. It described him as a singer, musician, actor and cabaret performer, surrounded by family and friends. Mel Miller, a friend and colleague, told SABC: "I knew Eddie for fifty years as a friend and a colleague, and I will really, really miss him." He remembered "his wonderful smile and his positive outlook." He called Eckstein "a wonderful, wonderful comedian" and "a great, great man", and offered his "sincerest condolences to Marie and her family." SABC Newssaid popular SABC shows he appeared in included Biltong & Potroast. Neither the family nor SABC gave a cause of death. The Department of Sport, Arts and Culturesaid Eckstein died in Johannesburg on 14 November 2026 at the age of 86. Its statement called the death a significant loss forSouth Africa's entertainment industry.

Title: US visa restrictions force African contestants out of Miss Universe 2026
Content: The dream of competing for the Miss Universe crown has been disrupted for some African beauty queens, with US visa restrictions forcing two contestants to withdraw from the 2026 competition in Puerto Rico and leaving two others uncertain about their participation. The affected contestants include Zambia’s Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka and the Republic of Congo’s Georgina Kambongo, who have both been unable to secure the necessary travel approval. Zimbabwe’s representative, Roseanna Hall, is also facing difficulties obtaining a visa despite months of preparation for the competition. Hall expressed her frustration over the situation. “We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved,” she said. She added that she was supposed to have travelled to Puerto Rico but had been unable to do so because of the restrictions. South Sudan’s representative, Adut Deng, is also facing uncertainty over her participation, with organisers still working to secure the necessary travel documents and approvals. The challenges are linked to US travel restrictions introduced under Presidential Proclamation 10998, which affects nationals of several countries, including Zambia, Zimbabwe, the Republic of Congo, and South Sudan. The situation has raised concerns about African representation at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, particularly as contestants from other parts of the world prepare for the competition. The grand finale is scheduled for 24 November at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The visa difficulties have cast a shadow over this year’s pageant, raising questions about equal access to international competitions and the challenges African contestants face in representing their countries on the global stage.

Title: Why Ghana must mandate mixed-gender presidential tickets
Content: Over time, I have come to believe that one of the most compelling democratic reforms our nation can pursue is the mandatory adoption of mixed-gender presidential tickets. If we genuinely celebrate women's participation in public life and champion gender inclusion, then our political system must make it possible and ordinary for women to occupy the highest offices of the state. A country's commitment to gender equality should not be judged only by the number of women in public office. It should also be measured by whether women have a fair and realistic path to the highest leadership positions. When those opportunities are limited, inclusion becomes more symbolic than real. This is why I believe women in top leadership positions represent more than inclusion for its own sake. Their presence shows that democracy and equal opportunity are working in practice. Women should not have to struggle for recognition at the highest levels of governance; their place in a nation's presidential leadership should be seen as normal, expected, and essential to public life. To the best of current knowledge, no country requires its President and Vice President to be of opposite sexes. This gives Ghana a rare opportunity to lead the world by mandating mixed-gender presidential tickets and setting a new standard for inclusive leadership. Some may see this proposal as unconventional. I see it as a necessary step forward. If we are serious about tackling gender imbalance and expanding opportunities for women, then we must be willing to adopt bold reforms that turn inclusion from rhetoric into reality. Ghana Must Lead the Way with Mandatory Gender-Balanced Presidential Tickets Such a reform would strengthen Ghana's commitment to gender equality and make inclusive leadership a defining feature of our democracy. Rather than treating inclusion as an aspiration, we should embed it in the very structure of the Presidency. If we are serious about balanced representation, then we must be intentional about ensuring that both women and men have a place at the highest level of national leadership. As a media practitioner, I have witnessed women make exceptional contributions to Ghana's development across politics, business, education, healthcare and community leadership. Their achievements prove that leadership is defined not by gender, but by competence, vision, and dedication. A gender-balanced presidency would therefore be more than a symbolic gesture; it would be a deliberate recognition of the value that both women and men bring to national governance. Ghana speaks often about gender balance and equal opportunity. Yet I believe the political class must do more than champion the rhetoric. It must give practical expression to the cause by adopting reforms that place gender inclusion at the centre of political leadership. While current efforts to empower women are commendable, they can be elevated further through bold measures that inspire future generations and advance the broader goal of empowering the girl child. At the very least, a legal requirement for mixed-gender presidential tickets would transform the Presidency into both a driver and a symbol of gender inclusion. It would create a powerful incentive for political parties to nurture diverse leadership and help accelerate progress toward national gender representation goals. The 2024 elections marked a historic milestone with the election of H.E. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang as Ghana's first female Vice President. Rather than allowing that achievement to stand alone, we should build upon it and deepen the gains it represents. From my observation and research, her election has inspired many women and girls to see themselves as capable of reaching the highest levels of leadership. It stands as powerful evidence of what becomes possible when barriers to women's political participation are removed. Indeed, 2024 was a defining year in Ghana's journey toward greater gender inclusion. That same year also saw the passage of the Affirmative Action (Gender Equity) Act, 2024 (Act 1121), reinforcing our national commitment to equal opportunity and representation. These achievements should not mark the end of the conversation; they should serve as the foundation for even more ambitious reforms that preserve and strengthen the progress made for future generations. The passage of the Affirmative Action Act was rightly celebrated. Yet I believe Ghana can take an even bolder step by mandating gender-balanced presidential tickets. Such a reform would not only advance gender equity at home but also position Ghana as a global leader in inclusive governance. Indeed, the First Schedule of the Affirmative Action (Gender Equity) Act, 2024 sets progressive targets for female representation across public and private decision-making institutions. Building on that framework by requiring gender-balanced presidential tickets would be a logical and transformative next step in Ghana's pursuit of genuine equality. The Affirmative Action (Gender Equity) Act, 2024 sets ambitious targets: 30 percent female representation by 2026, 35 percent by 2028 and gender parity by 2034. These are commendable goals, but they raise a fundamental question: why not start at the very top, the Presidency? If we truly seek to institutionalise gender equality, then the highest office of the land should lead the way. Leadership sets the tone for society. A constitutional requirement for mixed-gender presidential tickets would move Ghana beyond targets and declarations to decisive action. By requiring every presidential ticket to comprise both a man and a woman, Ghana would transform the presidency into a symbol and instrument of inclusion. The highest office should reflect the partnership between women and men that drives national development. Whether male-female or female-male, every presidential ticket should embody equality, representation, and national unity. What I Found About Africa Africa has repeatedly shown that women can lead at the highest level. From Ellen Johnson Sirleaf in Liberia to Samia Suluhu Hassan in Tanzania, Joyce Banda in Malawi, Sahle-Work Zewde in Ethiopia and Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah in Namibia, women have demonstrated leadership, competence and resilience at the summit of political power. Yet female leadership at the highest level remains the exception rather than the norm. Ghana has an opportunity not simply to celebrate these breakthroughs, but to build on them by institutionalising gender-balanced presidential tickets. Such a reform would position the country as a continental leader in inclusive governance and transform gender equality from aspiration into constitutional practice. As Ghana approaches its 70th anniversary of independence, this milestone should represent renewal, reform and progress. The next chapter of our democratic journey should begin with a bold commitment to gender-balanced leadership. It must start here. It must end the era of the all-male presidential ticket. By Kwame Anum, Media Practitioner & Student of International Affairs and Diplomacy

Title: 2027 Budget diagnosis is right, but the cure is incomplete
Content: "These boom-and-bust cycles must cease" On the evening of Thursday, November 12, 2026, the Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, when presenting the 2027 budget told Parliament that Ghana's boom-and-bust cycles must cease. Few Ghanaians would disagree. Too many times we have lived through hope followed by hardship, a stable cedi followed by sharp depreciation, and a recovery followed by another crisis. I have read the full 2027 Budget Statement, and I want to answer one question. Does the Minister appreciate why the boom-and-bust cycles happen, and does his New Economy programme remove the cause? My answer is that the Minister has made the right diagnosis but prescribed an incomplete cure. The budget sees two causes clearly. It misses a third, and the third is the one that will bring the next bust. What the budget gets right The budget statement is more candid about the causes of our instability than most budgets before it. It says the cedi came under pressure "when prices dropped or fiscal discipline weakened" (para. 161). It concedes that "temporary booms had financed permanent commitments" (para. 168), and it blames reckless spending, weak revenue and expensive debt for the crisis of 2022. Most important, the budget statement admits that past governments repaired the public finances "but did not use the recovery to alter the structure of the economy," and so "the cycle began again" (paras. 186–187). It even pledges that fiscal discipline "will apply throughout the election cycle" (para. 239). So the Government does understand two causes: our dependence on raw commodity exports, and fiscal indiscipline. I accept both. My quarrel is with what is missing. The machine that is not in the plan Read the eight pillars of the New Economy and one thing stands out. The only imports the budget counts as a drain on the cedi are things we consume: rice, sugar, poultry, fish, vegetables and medicines. It says the food import bill "weakens the cedi" (para. 260). It promises that when Ghana grows and processes more, "the cedi will face less pressure" (para. 336). It demands that every cedi of fiscal space answer the question: "what imports will it replace?" (para. 191). The budget never asks that question of the factories themselves. Throughout the statement, machines are things to buy and finance: Cocoa grinding mills, gold refineries, alumina plants, rice mills, garment lines and pharmaceutical plants are all capital goods. Ghana makes almost none of them, and few of their spare parts. Every one will be imported and paid for in dollars, and every one will be kept running with imported spares, also paid for in dollars. The budget's own figures show where the capacity to make machines stands in the Government's order of priorities. New Economy programme, 2027 outlay (para. 249) Procurement of agricultural machinery (para. 1543) Completion of the Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre (para. 1582) GRATIS Foundation, whole year, no capital expenditure (Appendix 4A) The Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre is the one line in this budget about making machines rather than buying them. The Centre dates from my time as Minister for Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation, and six years after I left office it is still waiting to be completed. In 2027 it receives about 0.17 percent of the New Economy outlay, and one-sixteenth of what we will spend on imported farm machinery in the same year. GRATIS, built to carry engineering capability into the regions, receives less than half of one percent of the machinery budget. Nothing in the New Economy programme is set aside for machine tools, foundries, spare parts or engineering manufacturing. How the next bust will come Suppose the New Economy succeeds exactly as planned. By 2030 Ghana processes all its cocoa, refines all its gold, processes all its manganese and bauxite and mills its own rice. Food imports fall, export earnings per tonne rise, and the cedi strengthens. But each of those plants was built with imported equipment, and each needs a steady flow of imported spares, replacement parts and, in time, replacement machines. When a mill breaks down, it cannot wait for the cedi to recover. It must buy the part at whatever the exchange rate happens to be. This demand for foreign exchange is stubborn, and it grows with every factory we open. The budget itself names commodity price volatility as the first of its five principal risks (para. 1025). When commodity prices next fall, export earnings will drop, but the bill for machines and spares will not. The cedi will come under pressure again, and the cycle will begin again, at a higher level of output but under the same ceiling. That is the trap of an economy that assembles but does not make. Value addition on imported capital goods moves the bottleneck; it does not remove it. There is a fiscal test as well. The programme is financed partly by lowering the primary surplus target by one percentage point of GDP (para. 247), beginning in the year before an election. The Government will answer that a surplus of at least 0.5 percent of GDP remains (para. 221), and that is a fair answer. But the pledge of discipline "throughout the election cycle" will be tested in 2028, and Ghanaians have heard such pledges before. What a complete cure would require The modern world economy is knowledge-based and driven by science and technology. Societies that produce, adapt and commercialise knowledge have achieved sustained growth and rising living standards. Raising money to pay foreign contractors to build infrastructure, good as the projects may be, cannot by itself lead to sustained economic development. Ghana has to develop the capacity to build the machines its industries run on. The cure is not to abandon value addition. It is to add the pillar the plan lacks: the capacity to make the machines. The question every factory must answer The Minister asked every cedi of fiscal space to say which imports it will replace. I ask the same question of every factory the New Economy will build. Until Ghana can make at least some of the machines that make its goods, our booms will be paid for in dollars we will not have when the bust comes. The diagnosis in this budget is right. The cure is not yet complete. © 2026 Prof. Kwabena Frimpong-Boateng. Title: Tertiary Education can be made free in Ghana, think about it
Content: Whenever the conversation around making public university education completely free comes up in Ghana, the immediate pushback from policymakers and economists is predictable: Where will the money come from? This question is genuine, but the idea that tertiary education can be made free is not a fantasy or utopian. Follow me. With tight fiscal space, competing infrastructure demands, and ongoing debt service obligations, universal free tertiary education is often dismissed as a populist fantasy. Yet, when you place Ghana's actual higher education costs side by side with the money the country loses every single year to corruption and public-sector financial irregularities, the math tells a completely different story. Ghana does not lack the money to educate its youth through university. It simply loses it before it reaches the lecture hall. The Bottleneck at the University Gates Since its rollout in 2017, Ghana's Free Senior High School policy has dramatically expanded secondary access. According to updated government figures reconciled by Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu and former Minister Dr Yaw Osei Adutwum, between 3.5 million and 3.9 million students have benefited from the programme. However, opening the secondary floodgates has created a sharp financial bottleneck at the tertiary level. While over 512,000 students are currently enrolled across Ghana's 26 public universities and specialised degree-awarding institutions, rising facility user fees continue to lock out thousands of qualified applicants. Monitoring data from Africa Education Watch (Eduwatch) shows fresh tertiary admissions dipped to roughly 160,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, down from 195,000 the year before, largely due to financial constraints. What Free Public University Would Actually Cost The government has already laid the groundwork through the No-Fees-Stress policy, which absorbs academic user fees for all first-year tertiary students. Using the state's own spending data gives us a clear blueprint of what full coverage across all four undergraduate years would cost: Academic Fees Only (GH¢1.57 Billion – GH¢1.62 Billion): In the 2025/2026 academic year, the government spent GH¢489.46 million to cover academic fees for 159,750 first-year students, representing an average subsidy of roughly GH¢3,064 per student. In the 2027 Budget presented to Parliament on November 12, 2026, Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson allocated GH¢537 million to continue funding fresh entrants. Scaling that per-student average across the entire public tertiary population of over 512,000 students puts the total annual academic fee bill at roughly GH¢1.6 billion. Full-Cost Coverage (GH¢3.5 Billion – GH¢4.5 Billion): If the state went a step further towards subsidising campus accommodation and converting student maintenance loans (currently GH¢2,250 to GH¢4,500 under the Students Loan Trust Fund) into outright grants, then the annual bill would rise to between GH¢3.5 billion and GH¢4.5 billion, roughly matching the annual cost of Free SHS. According to disclosures by Deputy Education Minister Dr Clement Abas Apaak and the Ministry of Finance, GH¢4.2 billion is allocated through the Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund) to fund the combined Free SHS and Free TVET programmes. To put GH¢1.6 billion into context, the Ministry of Education's total allocation in the 2027 Budget stands at GH¢48 billion. Eliminating academic fees for every public university student in Ghana would require roughly tripling the current first-year tertiary fee budget, which is a modest shift in national expenditure. The Elephant in the Room: US$3 Billion Lost Every Year Now, compare that GH¢1.6 billion price tag to what Ghana loses annually to corruption. State oversight bodies and anti-corruption institutions, including the Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ), the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE), and the Ghana Anti-Corruption Coalition (GACC), consistently estimate that Ghana loses approximately US$3 billion every year to corruption, procurement inflation, tax evasion, and systemic financial leakages. That annual loss is roughly double the country's yearly foreign direct investment inflows. Even if we set aside broad economic estimates and look strictly at documented public records, the numbers remain staggering: Auditor-General Reports: In the 2025 audit reports reviewed by Parliament's Public Accounts Committee in October 2026, Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs) alone recorded GH¢5.2 billion in financial irregularities, largely driven by tax infractions. Across the wider public sector, including state-owned enterprises and statutory boards, tracked irregularities have exceeded GH¢20 billion in recent audit cycles. Direct Household Bribery: Joint survey data from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) reveals that ordinary citizens pay roughly GH¢5 billion every year in direct cash bribes to public officials, costing the average household GH¢1,440 annually in indirect corruption burdens. Doing the Simple Math At prevailing exchange rates, US$3 billion translates to tens of billions of Ghana cedis vanishing every twelve months. The GH¢1.6 billion needed to eliminate academic user fees across every public university in Ghana represents less than 5% of what the country loses to corruption in a single year. Even the most ambitious version of free tertiary education, covering tuition, facility fees, hostels, and living stipends for over half a million students, could be funded multiple times over simply by plugging a fraction of the leakages flagged every year by the Auditor-General. A Question of Political Will, Not Resources Every academic year, brilliant young Ghanaians defer their admissions, drop out mid-degree, or take on heavy debt because their families cannot raise a few thousand cedis for facility user fees. Meanwhile, billions of cedis disappear through inflated contracts, uncollected taxes, and administrative infractions with little consequence. Making public university education free in Ghana is not an unrealistic dream. The resources are already here, generated by Ghanaian taxpayers every year. The only real question is whether the nation has the political will to stop leaking its future and start funding it instead. By Ishmael Oduro-Acheampong

Title: Ghana’s 2027 Budget and the BRICS Question: A strategy without a policy is only a wish
Content: By evening, Accra had slowed down for the news. Taxis parked with engines running. Market women packed unsold tomatoes and kept one ear on the radio. Students crowded around phones. Workers stood in chop bars and watched Parliament on television. Nobody was waiting for poetry. People were waiting for proof. Would this budget change how Ghana earns a living, or only change the language again? That question carries extra weight now. Cabinet has approved Ghana’s application to join BRICS as a Partner Country. Let us be precise. That decision is a strategy. A strategy is a choice about where to go and how to win. Policy is what makes that choice real: the rules, the money, the institutions, the targets, and the consequences for failure. Every serious strategy must come with policy. Without policy, strategy is only a press statement. Without policy, BRICS is only a headline. The 2027 budget must therefore be read as a test. Does it turn the BRICS strategy into policy, or leave it floating above the budget? What Are We Really Selling? Every country sells a value proposition. It answers three questions: Who is the buyer? What problem do we solve for them? Why choose us instead of someone else? For decades, Ghana’s answer was weak: “We have gold, cocoa, and oil. Come and take them.” That is not a value proposition. That is an invitation to extract. The 2027 budget tries to rewrite it: “We process what we grow. We refine what we dig. We make medicines, garments, and food. We offer a stable, democratic, English-speaking gateway to West Africa, with products that meet international standards. ” That is stronger. It promises reliability, not just resources. Finished goods, not just raw materials. A partner, not a quarry. But a value proposition is only true if the product works. BRICS buyers will not buy Ghanaian chocolate because it is Ghanaian. They will buy it because it tastes good, arrives on time, and costs less than the alternative. Marketing can open the door. Quality, price, and delivery must keep it open. A value proposition without policy is advertising. Policy forces factories to meet standards, forces procurement to buy local, and forces government to pay on time. Finance has a theory for this: structural transformation. A poor economy moves labor and capital from low-productivity work, mainly raw extraction and subsistence farming to higher-productivity work, mainly manufacturing, processing, and services. When that shift happens, incomes rise, tax revenue widens, the currency strengthens, and debt becomes easier to carry. When it does not, a country stays exposed to commodity prices, exchange-rate shocks, and endless borrowing. Ghana has lived the second story. Gold, cocoa, and later oil dominated exports, while extractive industries drove growth without creating enough jobs. That is the classic resource trap: rich ground, thin factories. The 2027 budget tries to reverse it. Under the New Economy program, government will invest US$10 billion between 2027 and 2030. In 2027 alone, the investment is 1.5 percent of GDP, equivalent to GH¢30 billion. The pillars are production, not consumption: commercial agriculture, energy, critical minerals, tourism, textiles, pharmaceuticals, and technology. The logic is simple. Every tonne processed at home increases retained value, export earnings, skilled employment, and tax base. Every tonne exported raw does the opposite. It ships jobs abroad and imports poverty back. But allocation is not achievement. A budget line is not a factory. Strategy needs a policy chain: money released, project appraised, procurement transparent, factory operational, product certified, buyer secured. Break one link, and the strategy fails. The Receipts: Four Signs This Budget Is Dressing For BRICS The word BRICS does not appear in the budget speech. That must be stated plainly. There is no BRICS project, no BRICS loan, and no BRICS timeline. What exists is more important: policies that look like preparation for a different economy. 1.     From raw exports to finished goods. The budget states: “Ghana will process at least 50 per cent of its cocoa locally by 2028 and 100 per cent by 2030, completing the transition towards a ban on raw cocoa exports.” On gold: “At least 70 per cent of artisanal and small-scale gold will be refined locally by December 2027,” rising to 100 percent by December 2028. Manganese and bauxite follow the same road: 50 percent processed locally by end 2028, 100 percent by end 2030, with raw exports prohibited. 2.     Public money creating a local market. The budget amends procurement law so public funds spent on rice and staples in schools, hospitals, and public institutions buy only food grown in Ghana. It states: “If you spend their money to put rice on the table, that rice must come from their farms.” On medicines, public money must buy Ghanaian-produced medicines wherever they exist in sufficient quantity and meet quality standards. Ghana imports 70 to 75 percent of its medicine needs, costing about US$500 million a year. The budget commits US$1 billion to pharmaceutical hubs. This is how India and Ethiopia built local industries: give local producers a reliable buyer, demand quality, and let scale follow. 3.     Less dependence on external debt. The budget reports provisional public debt of GH¢759.3 billion at end-October 2026, with 56.4 percent domestic and 43.6 percent external. It states: “Our strategy is to reduce our external debt exposure, so that movements in the exchange rate do less damage to our total debt.” In 2027, a Loans Bill will align borrowing with development priorities and debt sustainability. A Natural Resource Revenue Management Act will bring oil, gold, lithium, bauxite, and all extractive revenues under one accountable framework. A country that wants a seat at a new table cannot arrive with old borrowing habits. 4.     Diplomacy as economic work. The budget allocates GH¢1.9 billion to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs “to enhance Ghana’s foreign policy and strengthen our standing in Africa and on the world stage.” No BRICS breakdown is given. That omission is a weakness. But it shows government understands that transformation needs diplomatic work, not only domestic spending. Together, these policies do not prove BRICS membership. They prove readiness. They say Ghana wants to trade, not beg. To process, not merely extract. To borrow with discipline, not desperation. BRICS Will Not Write the Cheque Honesty is part of maturity. BRICS will not automatically bring loans. Membership will not guarantee a seat at the New Development Bank. It will not erase obligations to the IMF, World Bank, European Union, and United States. It will not fix procurement fraud, weak factories, or poor roads. What BRICS can offer is access, bargaining power, new buyers, new investors, and a chance to trade on fairer terms. Access, however, is not achievement. India used access to build capacity. Brazil used access to build supply chains. China used access to build factories. Ghana will be judged the same way. Three questions remain. How will the US$10 billion be funded without returning to reckless debt? What will each cedi produce in tonnes processed, factories running, export orders signed, and jobs paying real wages? Who will hold the money accountable when projects fail? Strategy announces direction. Policy answers: who does what, by when, with what money, and what happens if it does not happen? Dr. Ebenezer Arthur Duncan- The writer is a Senior Lecturer at University of Professional Studies, Marketing Department

Title: Is Ghana's 2027 Budget delivering a compelling value proposition to its citizens?
Content: A National Budget is more than a ledger. It is the biggest marketing vehicle a government produces every year. A promise of what you are going to do with taxpayers’ money, a price of how you intend to spend it and a prospectus of how it is going to make citizens better off. As one would expect a Ghanaian to reply over the weekend when asked how the budget went, he would probably say 389.2 billion Ghana Cedis were spent and $10 billion of a New Economy promised. No new taxes. As marketing is understood, a product is judged by its packaging. So three harder questions must be asked of the national budget. What is being promised to the Ghanaian citizen? What does the Ghanaian have to give up to realize the budget promises? Will the promises made be kept? Dr Cassiel Ato Forson launched a brand on 12 November. The budget of the Minister of Finance for 2027 is to be marketed under the banner of The New Economy, New Ghana, Jobs and Prosperity – seventies independence symbolism and all to get stability back into the political consciousness of Ghanaians and create confidence again. Eight pillars of a four-year program to be financed with US$10 billion of which US$3 billion will go to commercial agriculture, US$2.2 billion to energy, US$1.5 billion to critical minerals, GH¢30 billion or 1.5% of GDP in 2027 to tourism and creative arts, textiles and garments, pharmaceuticals and biomanufacturing and last of all GH¢300m or about US$300m to technology. Credit where credit is due, the brand architecture to the above budget theme is perhaps the most coherent the administration has offered to date. Dr. Ato Forson outlined how all the 8 programs would form part of one big production system — “finance reaching the farmer, the farm feeding the factory, the factory running on affordable power and the mineral gaining value before it is exported”. However, all these programs form part of the main brand called National Brand — and that is what needs to be marketed and developed — not these sub-brands. And, over 2 years or so, we have been marketed to by the 24-Hour Economy brand, the Big Push brand (GH¢29.8bn in 2027), the Agenda 111 brand and now the New Economy brand. Each of these brands had great promise but were not delivered on in time to earn the trust of Ghanaians to be upgraded to be part of the National Brand — which is what they promise. Their experience of each of these brands would have given them the impression that each of these brands needed to be “rescued” and so, accordingly, a huge discount would be applied to the promise of the New Economy brand. What are we buying with our patience now to get some dividend later? For GH¢389.2 billion, interest would cost about GH¢61 billion, compensation GH¢92.6 billion and legacy arrears of GH¢13.9 billion. In the end, half of the budgeted amount would be spent to settle previous debts and pay interest on previous loans before we can begin to train a single rice farmer. While it is true that for the first time in our history, capital expenditure (GH¢100.4 billion) would even exceed both the wage bill (GH¢87.4 billion) and interest (GH¢75.3 billion) of Government, a promise of no increase in taxes for now is not value addition. A promise of no increase in taxes for now is even a reduction in the cost of being a citizen. But reducing the cost of being a citizen is not value addition. That the government is holding taxes constant and thus lowering the cost of citizenship in terms of the taxes a Ghanaian has to pay is a price cut on an unchanged product. It may win the temporary goodwill of citizens, but the promise of such services has to be fulfilled in order to create loyalty with citizens rather than mere goodwill that would fade as quickly as it was won should the expected goods and services not reach citizens in due course. While the budget identifies particular customer groups such as rice farmers who would be supported in new hubs in the Western and Northern regions of Ghana, poultry producers who would be supported with some GH¢245m, cocoa processors who would have 100% local processing of their products by 2030, small-scale gold miners whose raw exports would cease by end of December 2028, garment firms and pharmaceutical manufacturers who would replace part of the US$500m of annual imports of medicines into Ghana, it does not outline what specific service would be delivered to each of these customer groups. In particular, in the face of very high interest rates of around 16% averaging across banks, the major binding constraint for all these producers would be credit at single digit interest rates and the single instrument of credit guarantee mentioned in the document is not enough. Demandside de-risking is where the budget does well. Public funds to buy Ghanaian rice, school uniforms, hospital textiles & medicines where quality permits. Import licenses for commercial rice to be tied to local purchases & for imports to cease by 2030. This is the reverse of building dark factories & then hoping for customers to materialize. Government is acting as anchor customer for its own producers & thus this is textbook marketing for a new brand entering a competitive market of cheaper imports. Also note that these are all falsifiable commitments & thus verifiable. Bans are a form of push marketing and have the potential to create problems such as shortages, smuggling and even a price hike for consumers. As investors review potential destinations to deploy processing capital to, they will consider a ban as part of the country’s risk profile. As such, Ghana needs to create a differentiator and that differentiator needs to be rooted in reliability. Evidence of a commitment to help production increase needs to be provided. While Commercial Agriculture is promised US$3 billion, the allocation to the Ministry of Food and Agriculture for 2027 is only GH¢2.9 billion. Even so, the pillar is to run for four years mostly with private capital while public money is to be used to purchase machinery, seeds, silos and for irrigation for farmers. Importantly, the full list of projects, the amount of private capital that will be mobilised per cedi of public funds to be expended and total jobs to be created are all not specified in the budget. This is a prospectus that omits the use of proceeds and expected return. Indeed, it is even more egregious that the $10 billion is to be financed by lowering the primary surplus target by a percentage point of GDP of the amount of fiscal space that has been created and not found. This is defensible enough as economics but terrible as marketing to not have mentioned this in the document. Of course, there are many weaknesses in service delivery which need to be addressed. As the budget attempts to unlock credit to agriculture by enabling individual rice farmers to establish their own rice schemes and be supported in new hubs in Western and Northern Ghana for example, it is also important to recognize that the state owes an amount greater than GH¢4.3 billion to independent power producers. In addition, there is an outstanding GH¢13 billion for energy-related fails. If government cannot pay suppliers on time, it ruins its brand at the various points of contact with citizens and businesses alike. This is so even as Minister Forson attempts to create a buzz around an early redemption of GH¢29 billion in restructured bonds with the catchy brand line: “Your cash is ready. Come for your money!” What to measure? Not the (promised) outputs for 4 years but the (lived) outcomes after 12 months. The cost per job created. The market share of public contracts awarded to Ghanaian companies. The amount of private capital (mobilized per cedi of) public investment. The percentage of cocoa, gold, manganese, bauxite etc. that is processed and added value created in Ghana. The food-basket price to be compared to the newly introduced minimum wage of GH¢25.04 per day. A quarterly citizen experience survey with specific service standards and corresponding service delivery timeframes and a way to log and solve complaints. Even with all these events and strategies that the budget presents, it will still amount to nothing more than a heap of promises, a heap of unsatisfactory promises, if there is no delivery framework to realize these promises and an evaluation framework to hold the minister accountable for the promises made and not kept. So a last-mile delivery framework is critical. So I will pose one question to the administration to monitor in 2027. Ghana is not suffering from lack of communication of its budget but a last-mile problem. If a budget is a promise what is the receipt that one holds? And what is the refund policy if the goods promised never reach? Which one figure (and NOT a slogan) will Government hold itself accountable with by end of December 2027? By Winston Asiedu Inkumsah (PhD) Marketing Scholar and Public Policy Commentator

Title: Ghana’s Cocoa Industry: Transforming the 2027 Budget’s vision into sustainable growth and prosperity
Content: For decades, cocoa has been central to Ghana’s economic development, supporting livelihoods, generating foreign exchange, and establishing our reputation in international markets. Yet one question remains: How much of the wealth generated from our cocoa stays in Ghana? The 2027 Budget Statement, presented by Finance Minister DrCassiel Ato Forson, offers a bold, visionary, and ambitious direction for addressing this question. The government’s commitment to process at least 50 percent of Ghana’s cocoa locally by 2028 and 100 percent by 2030 marks a shift from predominantly exporting raw cocoa beans to adding more value domestically. This ambition is significant, and achieving it requires more than processing facilities. It demands reliable infrastructure, competitive financing, consistent cocoa supply, strong international markets, and effective coordination across the entire value chain. For Ghana, the objective is to earn more value from every tonne produced, demonstrating the finance minister's visionary leadership. At Cocoa Marketing Company (CMC), we recognize that Ghana’s longstanding reputation for premium-quality cocoa and dependable international trade relationships remain among our greatest strengths. As the country pursues greater value addition, we remain committed to protecting these relationships, honoring contractual commitments, and ensuring Ghanaian cocoa products stay competitive globally. Our ongoing 24-Hour Operations initiative, anchored on Offload 24, Load 24 and Export 24, reflects the importance we place on operational efficiency, reliable logistics and timely delivery. These capabilities will become even more critical as Ghana expands its participation in the global cocoa value chain. Equally important is the cocoa farmer. This forward-looking transformation will ultimately improve livelihoods, strengthen the sustainability of cocoa production and create opportunities for communities whose labor sustains the industry. The Budget’s emphasis on affordable financing and industrial development also creates opportunities for Ghanaian entrepreneurs to venture into cocoa processing, chocolate manufacturing and other cocoa-derived products. As it should, this policy ambition will be matched by disciplined implementation, sustained investment, and a clear understanding of international market dynamics. The 2027 Budget sets out a direction for Ghana’s cocoa industry. The Government has demonstrated its commitment to translating that vision into lasting economic value, in collaboration with industry institutions, private investors, farmers, and international trading partners. As Managing Director of CMC, I believe Ghana has an opportunity to strengthen its position in global cocoa trade while retaining a greater share of the value generated by its most celebrated agricultural commodity. Our success must ultimately be measured not only by how much cocoa we produce or process, but by how much prosperity we create from it. That is the defining ambition for the next chapter of Ghana’s cocoa industry.

Title: Child Abuse: Why silence does not mean consent
Content: A child’s inability to speak about abuse should never be interpreted as consent or proof that everything is well, as fear, shame, intimidation, and threats can stop children from disclosing what they have experienced. Children who experience abuse may struggle to find the words to explain what has happened to them, which makes it important for parents, guardians, teachers, and other caregivers to recognise signs of distress and create safe environments where children feel comfortable speaking up. Silence does not necessarily mean a child has nothing to say. In some cases, it may reflect fear of being blamed, punished, or disbelieved, particularly when the person responsible for the abuse is someone the child knows or trusts. Listening without judgement When a child gathers the courage to disclose an uncomfortable or troubling experience, how adults respond can influence whether the child feels safe enough to share more. Parents and caregivers are encouraged to listen patiently, remain calm, and take what the child says seriously rather than reacting with anger, disbelief, or blame. Children should be reassured that they are not responsible for the abuse and that speaking about their experiences is the right thing to do. Avoiding questions that suggest blame, or pressuring a child to provide every detail, can also help prevent further emotional distress. Creating a safe environment for children Protecting children requires more than responding when abuse is reported. It also involves creating environments where children feel respected, protected, and confident enough to express their concerns. Parents, teachers, and caregivers have an important responsibility to pay attention to changes in children’s behaviour, emotional wellbeing, and interactions with others. Where abuse is suspected or disclosed, appropriate child protection professionals and authorities should be contacted to ensure the child’s safety and access to necessary support. Adults should also avoid promising to keep abuse secret, as protecting a child may require sharing the information with people who can help. Taking children’s voices seriously Child protection begins with recognising that every child deserves to be heard, believed, and protected. A child’s silence should never be used to dismiss their experiences, while their willingness to speak should be met with compassion rather than judgement. Ultimately, preventing and responding to child abuse requires collective responsibility from families, schools, communities, and child protection institutions. Listening to children, taking their concerns seriously, and acting when something is wrong are essential steps towards ensuring that every child grows up in a safe environment free from abuse and intimidation.

Title: Assessing 'Atonomics'- Spend only what you have, finish what you start, bring down the cost of credit
Content: It is not every day that a Finance Minister stands before a university audience and asks to be checked. Yet that was the most striking line of Dr Cassiel Ato Forson's pre-budget engagement at KNUST on Monday, November 9, 2026. "Test the assumptions behind the policies we will be announcing," he told staff and students, "and show us where correction is needed." The Minister deserves credit, first, for showing up. He told the audience he had returned to KNUST "with responsibility," and he stayed to answer five rounds of questions from staff and students. Our students heard the country's chief fiscal officer explain his choices in person, and many put their own questions to him directly. Pre-budget engagements like this should become the norm. Three days before he presents the 2027 Budget on 12 November, the Minister laid out what some have begun to call "Atonomics": spend only what you have, finish what you start, bring down the cost of credit, buy Ghanaian, and write the rules into law. As an economist at his alma mater, I want to take him at his word. The Minister's diagnosis is hard to dispute. Ghana's boom-and-bust cycles have been driven largely by fiscal indiscipline, and his call for discipline to become "a culture of our entire nation" is the right one. Rules that depend on one minister's temperament do not survive elections. His case on credit is equally strong. When he took office in January 2025, the 91-day Treasury bill paid about 29% and businesses borrowed at 35–36%. He reports the bill rate is now about 4.5%, with some firms borrowing at 9–12%. He was candid that government itself crowded out private borrowers: bank credit to the private sector was only about 11% of GDP, against 25–26% in Côte d'Ivoire. His goal of lifting it above 20% is the right target. And his insistence on phasing is overdue. Starting 111 hospitals when the money could finish 10 is how Ghana fills its landscape with abandoned projects. Spreading the US$10 billion New Economy programme over four years, about US$2.5 billion a year, is sensible macroeconomics, not timidity. Where the numbers need testing The Minister invited scrutiny, so here are three places where his own 2027 Fiscal Strategy Document tells a more complicated story. First, the debt path after 2028. The Minister spoke of reducing debt by 0.5% of GDP a year. The FSD projects debt falling to about 42% of GDP in 2028 and then rising back to about 44.8% by 2034, just under the 45% legal ceiling. The New Economy uses up most of the headroom. A shock to growth, the cedi or interest rates would push Ghana to the line. Second, crowding out has not gone away. The FSD plans no Eurobonds and negative net foreign financing, so government will still borrow around 5% of GDP a year at home, mostly from banks. That sits uneasily with the goal of doubling private credit. Third, buy-Ghanaian has costs. Requiring Free SHS feeding to use local rice, and tying rice import permits to local purchases as Nigeria once did, will help farmers. But it may raise food prices, encourage smuggling, and test Ghana's commitments under the African Continental Free Trade Area. The Minister did not say how he will square these. What the room told him The most valuable evidence on Monday came not from the podium but from the floor. A young graduate who answered the call to farm described registering his two-hectare farm and being asked for an upfront tax of GH¢5,000. That bill has since more than doubled to GH¢12,000. When his plantain reached the market, he was offered GH¢20 a bunch. A colleague who works with market women explained why: market queens control access and set prices, leaving farmers little bargaining power. A lecturer asked how his students could get an affordable loan of GH¢50,000 to GH¢150,000 for a truck to aggregate maize. A student asked what institution will give young people a real voice in economic policy, not just a place in government programmes. These are not complaints about the vision. They are the points where the vision meets the market. The New Economy will succeed or fail at the farm gate, the tax office and the loan desk, not in the Budget Statement. What to watch on Thursday The Minister promised policies on agriculture, textiles, local procurement, AI and affordable credit. Citizens should judge the Budget against five simple tests: 1. Does the primary surplus target of 0.5% of GDP hold, on a commitment basis? 2. Are the New Economy's projects named, costed and phased, starting with about GH¢30 billion in 2027? 3. Do new taxes and levies fall on loopholes rather than on the young people starting businesses? 4. Is there a concrete plan for farm-gate prices: storage, aggregation and fair access to markets? 5. Will jobs be measured by independent labour surveys, not by enrolments in government schemes? The Minister closed by telling students they are "the very reason" for this effort. KNUST, and every university in Ghana, should now do what he asked: measure the results honestly, publish what we find, and hold the policy, not the personality, to account. Prof. Eric F. Oteng-Abayie is an economist in the Department of Economics, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kumasi. The views expressed are his own.

Title: More cocaine busts linked to Ghana: better policing or leakier ports?
Content: When Spain announced on Wednesday that two containers of coconuts loaded at Tema in August had been carrying2,600kg of cocaine, the news landed in a country that has grown used to seeing its name in drug stories. Amsterdam, Antwerp, Dunkirk, Beirut and now Valencia: the list of places wherecocainefrom Ghana has turned up keeps growing. Each new case restarts the same argument at home. One side reads the busts as progress. Under the previous administration, it says, checks were weak and theNarcotics Control Commission (NACOC)was kept at arm's length, so we rarely heard of seizures; now that NACOC has been empowered, the cases are finally coming to light. The other side reads them as a warning. We are hearing about more drugs, it says, because more drugs are getting through, and our ports and airports have become easier to slip past. Both positions are argued with confidence, and both can be tested. Every seizure leaves a trail: a date, a place, a quantity and an agency that made the find. Lined up together, those trails say a good deal about which side is closer to the truth. The idea that the earlier years were silent does not survive a look at the archive. In September 2020, officers intercepted152kg of cocaine mixed into sugar from Brazilat Tema. In 2021, Britain's National Crime Agency broke up a ring moving cocaine from Accra through Heathrow, while NACOC arrested connected suspects at home; four Ghanaians were later jailed in Britain for more than 28 years between them. In 2024, a courier who boarded at Kotoka was caught in Brussels with 8.5kg, and NACOC and the British agency stopped two Britons at Kotoka with 166.88kg before they could fly to Gatwick. Even in 2017, reports thatcocaine worth US$30 million had disappeared at Tema, whichCustoms denied, kept the subject in the headlines. What those years lacked was scale. From public reports, we counted 13 Ghana-linked drug seizures between 2017 and 2024, and none of the cocaine finds among them went above 200kg. For 2025 and 2026, the count already stands at 24, and the quantities have changed beyond recognition. Look at where the bigger hauls turned up. Dutch customs found about 4.5 tonnes in timber from Ghana at Amsterdam in June 2025. Belgian officers found 2,829kg in cassava flour from Tema that November andanother 1,158kga month later, and Australian officers later found320kg of methamphetaminein coconut charcoal shipped from Tema. This year, French customs tookabout 3.9 tonnesout of a container of plastic waste from Ghana at Dunkirk in September, and in October a courier who had flown out of Kotoka was stopped atBeirut airport with 46.7kg. Then came Valencia, whereSpain's Tax Agency saysits officers flagged the Tema containers as high-risk on arrival, found false bottoms in the coconut crates and followed the cargo to a warehouse in Almería before arresting two men. Add those up and roughly 15 tonnes of drugs passed through Ghanaian exit points in less than two years before foreign officers caught them. The largest consignments stopped in Ghana on the way out were small by comparison:89.74kg in 73 slabs at the Swissport cargo terminalin April 2025, and 866 parcels hidden in gari sacks at Tema in August 2026. None of the foreign agencies involved has publicly credited a Ghanaian tip-off for any of those finds. A seizure in Valencia tells us how carefully Spain checks what arrives. It tells us very little about how carefully Ghana checks what leaves. The ports explain a good part of the pattern. The paperless reform of July 2018 cut the number of agencies carrying out joint inspections from 16 to three, with NACOC to join only "based on intelligence". A month earlier, the Ghana Shippers' Authority had told a stakeholders' meeting at Tema that the single scanner at the export terminal had been taken away. NACOC stayed outside routine container checks until President Mahamarestored it to the joint inspection regimeon 17 September this year. That gap opened under the previous government and ran on for 20 months into this one. The Dunkirk case shows how an exit can fail even when the equipment works. According to the charge sheet, scan images of thefour containerswere assessed as "abnormal" on 12 August, and the containers still left Tema a week later. Four customs officers of the Ghana Revenue Authority are among those charged. They are presumed innocent until the court decides, but if the prosecution's account holds, the scanner did its job and the people around it did not. The trade itself has also changed. The UN drugs office put global cocaine manufacture at a record3,708 tonnes in 2023, the same year seizures in the European Union reached a record419 tonnes. As Brazil began screening export cargo at Santos and Europe's big ports tightened their checks, traffickers went looking for routes that drew less attention. ASeptember 2025 studyby the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime warned that scanning at West African ports was "limited by resources" and "focused on imports", so that "increases in containerized exports could pass unnoticed". By January this year,Belgian customs figureshad placed Ghana among the top five countries shipping the cocaine seized at Antwerp, the first time it had appeared there. None of this makes the old silence innocent. The Africa Organised Crime Index, published by ENACT and the Global Initiative in November 2025, has scored Ghana's cocaine market at 6.5 out of 10 in every edition since 2021, andits Ghana profilegoes further. As cocaine seizures and media coverage declined, it records, law enforcement officials and civil society stakeholders suggested that "political protection being given to illicit markets, particularly the cocaine trade, by sections of the government is the main reason for a drop in visible trafficking". The same profile says reporting on cocaine had become more limited, "reportedly because of threats made to journalists". The Index does not name the officials it has in mind or say which years it means, and its claim rests on what its sources told it. Still, it lends weight to one half of the better-enforcement argument: fewer busts in the past did not mean less trafficking. It does nothing for the other half, because whatever kept the trade quiet then, the tonnes being seized now are still being found in Europe. There is real work to acknowledge. NACOC's arrestsrose from 73 in 2024 to 217 in 2025. In March 2025, the National Intelligence Bureau seized about 3.3 tonnes of cocaine hidden under sand in a tipper truck at Pedu Junction in Cape Coast, a consignment laterburned at Bundase, though that haul was coming into the country rather than leaving it. Couriers have been stopped at Kotoka, and suspects have been arrested at home after the Dunkirk and Beirut seizures. But arrests are not convictions, and no conviction rate for drug cases is published. That is why neither side can yet prove its case: the figures that would settle it are not public. The most recent official cocaine seizure figures we could find stop at 2022, at 158.91kg in 2020, 32.50kg in 2021 and 117.01kg in 2022. The roadmap President Mahama ordered from his inter-agency task force in September was due around 1 October and is still unpublished, despite the opposition'sseven-day ultimatum, and so is the revenue authority's preliminary report to the President. If the government wants credit for better enforcement, it should publish both, along with seizure figures for 2023 to 2026, the number of export containers scanned at Tema and Takoradi each year, the outcome of drug prosecutions, and the share of hauls caught before they leave the country. Prof H. Kwasi Prempeh of the Ghana Centre for Democratic Developmenthas urged the Presidentto hold every appointee responsible for port security to account. Names matter, and so do numbers. The day more cocaine is caught at Tema than in Valencia is the day the better-enforcement argument wins.

Title: H.E. Dr. Christian Rogg writes: Facing our past and shaping our future together
Content: Britain and Ghana cannot change the past, but we can face it honestly, listen carefully and strengthen a modern partnership founded on dignity and mutual respect. A few weeks ago, I sat in Ghana’s National Theatre and watched "The Darkest Chapter", a moving play by Latif Abubakar. It traces a path from the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade through decolonisation and independence to modern Ghana. One line has stayed with me: “before diplomacy, before policy, before resolutions, there were human beings”. That is where any conversation about the slave trade must begin. With the millions of people torn from their homes, families and communities. With those whose labour and suffering enriched others. And with the descendants and societies that continue to live with that history today. The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation. People were denied their humanity, separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. The UK Prime Minister has expressed his “sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people” and recognised the way this history “still shapes our world today.” Ghana has helped ensure that the world does not look away. Its leadership in shining a spotlight on the slave trade has brought renewed attention to questions that are difficult, deeply felt and important. Ghana’s perspectives have helped shape the wider Commonwealth conversation. At the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) last week, Commonwealth leaders agreed that the time had come for a meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation to forge a common future based on equity. They welcomed the UK Government’s agreement to engage in a structured, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties, addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms. The Prime MinisterThe Rt Hon Andy Burnham MPalso met with President Mahama during CHOGM to set out these plans and welcomed the President’s support. This is an important step, and the United Kingdom enters the dialogue seriously and respectfully. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of the process, and the Prime Minister has said that he is open to them. A dialogue of this importance must allow those most affected to help shape it. Its outcome should not be predetermined, but neither should the depth or difficulty of the conversation be underestimated. The first responsibility is to listen. One of the privileges of serving as British High Commissioner is gaining a view of the many layers of the UK’s and Ghana’s shared history. At the British Museum this summer, I saw how one object, the Asante Ewer, can tell a story spanning medieval England, trans-Saharan trade, Asante ceremonial life and the violence and pillage of the Anglo-Asante wars. Such objects do not offer simple stories. They ask us to confront complexity and understand what they mean to different communities. Other moments remind us how relationships can change. Last year at the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park, I stood with the Duke of Edinburgh before the image of Queen Elizabeth II dancing with President Kwame Nkrumah in Accra in 1961. Ghana had won its independence only four years earlier and was inspiring movements across Africa. That photograph captured our countries’ relationship being reshaped at a decisive moment. Today, the United Kingdom and Ghana meet as sovereign partners. Our relationship is rooted not only in history, but in people, education, culture, business, security and a shared interest in prosperity. That modern partnership gives us a strong foundation for difficult conversations. We should be confident enough to discuss both progress and pain, allow space for honest disagreement, and recognise that listening is part of an equal partnership. As Ghana approaches its 70th anniversary of independence, there will be many opportunities to reflect on the journey from colonial rule to the Black Star of Africa, and on Ghana’s continuing influence in the world. The United Kingdom should take part in those conversations with humility, openness and respect. We gather to remember. We also need to listen. The dialogue agreed at CHOGM will not be simple, and there will be strongly held views. But our bilateral relationship is mature enough to face difficult history honestly, to hear each other with respect and to work together towards a common future based on dignity and equity. H.E. Christian Rogg is the British High Commissioner to Ghana.

Title: Turning high cocoa prices into lasting national prosperity is an economic strategy
Content: When the world price of cocoa surges, the assumption is that producing countries must be celebrating. If the world is paying more for a commodity, surely the countries that grow it are earning more. It is an understandable assumption. It is also an incomplete one. In Ghana, the cocoa industry links farmers to purchasing institutions, international buyers, processors, financiers and shippers. For such a country, the path from a high market price to real economic prosperity is far from straightforward. The critical question is not what cocoa fetches on international exchanges. It is how much of that value is realised, retained, distributed and converted into lasting economic opportunity. That question deserves more attention after the extraordinary volatility of recent years. A high market price is not the same as higher national income International cocoa prices respond to a web of influences: supply expectations, weather, production estimates, inventories, processing demand and financial-market activity. When supply falls short of demand, prices rise; when production recovers or demand weakens, they retreat. These adjustments can come faster than producers, exporters and policymakers can absorb. The International Cocoa Organization's (ICCO) August 2026 statistical bulletin illustrates the shift. For the 2024/25 cocoa year, it estimates world production at about 4.733 million tonnes and grindings at 4.649 million tonnes, leaving a global surplus of 37,000 tonnes once weight losses are accounted for. The market can swing between scarcity and improving supply, and commercial decisions must be taken knowing that today's expectations may differ sharply from tomorrow's outcomes. Rising benchmark prices, moreover, do not necessarily translate into equivalent gains in export revenue. A producing country may already have sold part of its expected crop forward. Output may fall short of expectations, cutting export volumes while financing and operating costs remain high. The exchange price is therefore not the average price realised on physical export contracts, and a higher price does not automatically raise the income of individual farmers.contracts. Nor does a higher price automatically guarantee a corresponding improvement in the income of individual farmers. The outcome depends on the whole commercial chain that carries cocoa from farm to international customer. The overlooked relationship between prices and production Consider a hypothetical cocoa-producing economy that exports 800,000 tonnes at an average realised price of US$3,000 per tonne. Its gross export sales come to US$2.4 billion. In a second season, the average realised price rises to US$4,000 per tonne, but exports fall to 500,000 tonnes. Despite the much higher price, gross export sales drop to US$2 billion. These are illustrative figures, not Ghanaian production or export statistics; the point lies in the relationship they show. Higher prices cannot indefinitely compensate for shrinking productive capacity. This matters most in agriculture, where crop disease, ageing farms, weather shocks and productivity constraints can cut the volume available to sell. A boom can lift the value of each available tonne while also signalling deeper supply problems. For Ghana and other producers, the priority must therefore go beyond favourable prices to sustained investment in productivity, resilient farms, reliable purchasing arrangements and dependable export supply. A country that grows less cocoa at a higher price may look more prosperous in the headlines without strengthening the foundations of its cocoa economy. Why forward sales should not be judged by hindsight Forward selling is often read as giving up the chance to benefit from later price rises. That reading misses its main commercial purpose: managing uncertainty. In international commodity markets, buyers and sellers commonly contract before delivery. Such commitments give greater predictability for sales planning, financing and operational coordination. When prices later rise, an earlier contract can look less attractive than the new spot price. When prices fall, the same contract protects against the downturn. A forward-selling decision should be judged against the information available when it was made, the risks it was meant to manage and the commercial obligations it supported. It would be neither economically sound nor institutionally responsible to judge every earlier sale against the highest price subsequently recorded. This does not place forward sales beyond scrutiny. Their timing, governance and risk-management frameworks deserve rigorous assessment. But that assessment must rest on commercial principles, not hindsight. Who captures the benefit of a cocoa boom? There is a broader question of who captures the value. The global cocoa economy is not a single transaction between a farmer and a chocolate consumer. It spans cultivation, aggregation, quality assurance, trading, processing, manufacturing, branding, distribution and retailing. Each stage carries costs, investment needs and risks, and each offers a chance to create and capture value. A rise in the bean price affects them differently. Farmers benefit where higher producer prices are effectively transmitted. Exporters may see better revenue opportunities, though their contractual commitments and financing structures matter. Processors and manufacturers face higher input costs that they cannot always pass on at once. Consumers may eventually meet higher retail prices, thinner promotions or reformulated products. It is misleading to assume that everyone in the chain gains equally from a rising cocoa price. The larger development question is whether producing economies have the commercial and industrial capabilities to take part in a wider range of value-creating activities. A temporary price advantage should not be mistaken for a lasting gain in economic bargaining power. From price opportunity to lasting prosperity For Ghana, the policy implications are substantial. First, productivity must stay at the centre of cocoa-sector development. Better yields, disease management and production efficiency matter whatever happens to international prices. Second, producer remuneration should be assessed by the combined effect of prices, yields, production costs and payment reliability. A high nominal price is welcome, but a farmer's welfare depends on the conditions under which that income is earned. Third, cocoa-marketing institutions must protect their commercial credibility through disciplined contracting, reliable supply coordination and effective risk management. Fourth, the industry needs transparent, reliable market information. Better data improves public understanding and supports sounder commercial and policy decisions. Finally, favourable market conditions should be used to invest in the capabilities that keep the sector strong when prices turn. These principles reach well beyond cocoa. From coffee and cotton to copper and petroleum, resource-producing countries periodically find that high international prices raise hopes of national prosperity. History shows that commodity wealth is volatile, and that genuine transformation requires lasting institutional and productive capacity. The real test for a commodity exporter is not whether it benefits from a rally, but whether it emerges from one with more resilient producers, stronger commercial institutions, better infrastructure and greater economic opportunity. A rising cocoa price is a market event. Turning that price into lasting national prosperity is an economic strategy. That is the distinction Ghana and other cocoa-producing economies must continue to make.

Title: CAF Awards: Kim Lars Björkegren nominated for Women’s Coach of the Year
Content: Black Queenshead coach Kim Lars Björkegren has been shortlisted for the 2026 CAF Women’s Coach of the Year award. The Swedish coach is among 10 nominees announced by the Confederation of African Football on Tuesday, with his recognition coming from his work with Ghana’s senior women’s national team. Björkegren guided the Black Queens to the knockout stage of the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco, where Ghana’s campaign ended in the quarter-finals following a 2-1 defeat to Malawi. The nomination also comes after a period in which Björkegren has taken on an additional role with the Black Stars, leading Ghana on an interim basis for the November 2027 AFCON qualifying double-header against Somalia. He completed that assignment with two wins, as Ghana beat Somalia 2-0 in the first leg before securing a 1-0 victory in the return fixture to collect all six points. However, it is his work with the Black Queens that has earned him the CAF Women’s Coach of the Year nomination. Björkegren is competing against Algeria’s Farid Benstiti, Cabo Verde’s Silveria Nédio, Cameroon’s Valentine Nguele, Malawi’s Lovemore Fazili, Hicham Drissi and Jorge Vilda of Morocco, Nigeria’s Akeem Busari, South Africa’s Desiree Ellis and Tanzania’s Bakari Nyundo Shime. The nomination gives Ghana representation in another major individual category at this year’s CAF Awards, with the Black Queens, Portia Boakye and Cynthia Konlan also nominated in the women’s categories. The 2026 CAF Awards will be held at the National Theatre in Lagos, Nigeria, on December 2.

Title: Black Challenge face USA in Amputee World Cup round of 16 on Wednesday
Content: Ghana'sBlack Challengeface the United States on Wednesday for a quarter-final place at the Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico, afterthrashing Iraq 6-0to reach the knockout stage. The last-16 tie kicks off at 5pm Mexican time, 11pm in Ghana, at the Santa Lucía 2 field in San Juan de los Lagos, according to thetournament schedule. Ghana are one of 24 teams at thetournament, which began on November 13 and runs until Sunday, November 22. The group stage featured 36 matches in six groups of four, with Ghana drawn alongside Angola, Colombia and Iraq in Group D. Monday's 6-0 win over Iraq was Ghana's first victory of the tournament. The Black Challenge needed it, having lost 2-0 to Angola in their opener and held 1-1 byColombiaon Sunday, with a positive result in the final group game required to keep the knockout hopes alive. Hamza Mohammed and Yussif Yahaya scored twice each against Iraq, with Mohammed Mubarik andRichard Ekwamadding the other goals. Thetwo-time African championsfinished second in Group D behind group winners Angola, who beat Colombia 2-0 in the other final fixture. The United States won their other two group matches, against Uzbekistan and Uruguay, to finish runners-up in Group E behind Morocco.
