The Governor noted that the committee would use the meeting to take stock of macroeconomic developments throughout 2026 and assess the effectiveness of measures implemented by the central bank. He said the MPC would also determine whether further adjustments to its policy instruments are necessary to preserve the gains made in restoring price stability. The 133rd MPC meeting is the Bank's final monetary policy meeting for 2026, with its outcome expected to provide direction on monetary policy heading into 2027.

Title: Fuel prices fall as Star Oil cuts petrol to GH¢14.97, diesel to GH¢17.95
Content: Fuel prices have begun to fall at the pumps, with Star Oil reducing petrol to GH¢14.97 per litre and diesel to GH¢17.95 per litre from Monday, November 16, 2026. The reductions coincide with the start of the latest two-week petroleum pricing window, following industry projections of lower pump prices. Checks by JoyBusiness on Monday morning showed that Star Oil had cut petrol from GH¢15.55 to GH¢14.97 per litre, a reduction of 58 pesewas. Diesel fell from GH¢18.37 to GH¢17.95 per litre, representing a cut of 42 pesewas. Other Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) told JoyBusiness they also intended to adjust their prices. However, they did not disclose the size of the expected reductions. Uncertainty remained over whether some companies would reduce prices immediately or maintain their existing rates. Several had already cut prices multiple times ahead of the November 16 pricing window. The Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies attributes the reductions to lower international prices of refined petroleum products, the cedi’s recent appreciation and government support to cushion diesel prices. The chamber had projected a petrol price reduction of more than 8% and a diesel cut of just over 4% per litre for the new window. Actual adjustments will vary among OMCs, as reflected in the prices announced so far.

Title: Energy and Works Ministries to anchor building, power and energy expo on December 1
Content: The Ministries of Energy and Works and Housing and Synergice Events will, from December 1, 2026, bring together players in the building, power, and energy industries at the largest expo and exhibition fair in West Africa. The event is also being supported by key stakeholder associations in the country such as the Ghana Electrical Contractors Association, Association of Building & Civil Engineering Contractors, Ghana Electrical Dealers Associations, Ghana Union of Traders Association, the Energy Chamber of Ghana, Ghana Chamber of Construction Industries, and other stakeholders including international partners like CCI France Ghana and KOTRA. Building construction with power and energy is one of the most significant sectors supporting the growth and sustainability of the Ghanaian economy, infrastructure, and industries and contributing significantly towards the income of the country, including energy exports. The event is expected to bring together 100+ exhibitors from China, Ghana, Nigeria, South Korea, India, Portugal, Spain, France UAE, and Qatar. Over 4,000 businesses and professionals from Ghana, Nigeria and West Africa are also expected to take part. The exhibition will cover sectors including electrical, power energy, solar, battery, transmissions, wires, cables, construction equipment, building materials and chemicals, ceramic tiles and sanitary ware, granite stone and flooring, plumbing, hospitality among other. According to the organisers, the event gives the opportunity to meet and engage in business-to-business discussions and explore business partnerships with manufacturers, exporters, suppliers, distributors, importers, wholesalers, contractors, retailers and consultants. It is expected to address the growing building and construction requirements, along with the power and energy supply demand and issues in the country, so that the sector can be built and developed in the country. This aligns with the vision of the Government of Ghana to have a strong industrial support infrastructure for export and job creation. Ghanaian and West African companies will have the opportunity to connect, collaborate and create distribution arrangements, joint ventures, and investments.

Title: African oil producers urged to balance local content with investment
Content: African oil-producing countries have been urged to strengthen local content development by creating a sustainable pipeline of upstream investments and projects, while maintaining an enabling business environment that attracts international investors. The call was made at just ended Local Content Conference and Exhibition (LCCE), where industry stakeholders stressed that building a resilient, competitive and sustainable oil and gas sector requires more than policies promoting indigenous participation. It also demands continuous exploration, new project development and strategic partnerships capable of generating lasting opportunities for local businesses. Contributing to a panel discussion on enhancing local content for sustainable growth, Deputy Managing Director of Eni Ghana, Mr Baluri Kassim Bukari, said Ghana’s experience demonstrated that local content development was intrinsically linked to the level of activity and investment within the upstream sector. He cited Ghana’s Offshore Cape Three Points (OCTP) project, operated by Eni Ghana, which currently supplies more than 70 per cent of the country's domestic gas for power generation, as an example of how upstream investments could generate significant opportunities for indigenous businesses. Mr Bukari recalled that during the project's development phase, several international companies entered Ghana, established joint ventures with local partners and secured contracts under the country's local content framework. He disclosed that Eni Ghana awarded more than US$4 billion in contracts to local companies, including indigenous businesses and joint ventures, generating employment and stimulating economic activity. He noted that Takoradi experienced a significant increase in commercial activity during the development phase, with hotels and other businesses benefiting from the presence of companies and workers engaged in the project. However, economic activity slowed following the completion of the development phase, leaving many local businesses with fewer opportunities. According to him, this experience highlights a fundamental requirement for successful local content development: a sustained pipeline of upstream investments and projects. “You can't have local content without content,” he said, urging Ghana to accelerate the award of petroleum blocks, encourage exploration and facilitate the development of new projects. Mr Bukari cautioned against a situation where indigenous companies obtain regulatory permits, establish offices and employ workers but struggle to secure contracts because of insufficient industry activity. He stressed the need for Ghana to move beyond memoranda of understanding (MOUs) towards concrete agreements backed by firm investment commitments and Final Investment Decisions (FIDs). On the capacity of indigenous companies, he observed that opportunities existed across the entire oil and gas value chain, although certain specialised activities required advanced technologies and technical competencies that were not yet fully developed locally. He therefore called for deliberate investment in technical training, health and safety, operational standards and other specialised skills to strengthen the capacity of Ghanaian companies to compete for more complex industry assignments. In highlighting local business participation, Mr Bukari emphasized the broader economic contribution of OCTP, particularly the supply of gas to the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) for domestic thermal power generation. He noted that the gas continued to support electricity supply to households, schools, churches, commercial establishments and industries. Deputy Chief Executive for Finance, Commercial and Administration of GNPC, Mr Hamis Yussif, said Ghana’s local content strategy had been shaped by the need to attract international partners while progressively developing indigenous capabilities. He explained that following the discovery of oil, GNPC's accelerated growth strategy identified local content development as one of its key priorities. He said Ghana’s ambition should extend beyond local employment and procurement to building indigenous companies capable of owning assets, developing technical expertise and competing in international markets. Achieving this, he noted, would require sustained investment and a consistent pipeline of opportunities to enable local businesses to maintain, strengthen and expand their capabilities. Mr Yussif cautioned, however, against viewing local content and foreign investment as competing objectives, stressing that without projects and investments from international oil companies, opportunities for indigenous businesses to participate in the industry would remain limited. Sharing Nigeria’s experience, Eng. Bashir Ahmed, a representative of the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), underscored the importance of adapting local content policies to changing industry conditions. He explained that Nigeria's local content framework became more structured following the establishment of the NCDMB in 2010, after earlier policies failed to achieve the desired results. Nigeria initially pursued an aggressive local content strategy, which contributed to the development of domestic fabrication, engineering and manufacturing capabilities. Eng. Ahmed cited the integration of topside modules in Nigeria around 2013 as a significant milestone, alongside the growth of local manufacturers providing goods and services to the oil and gas industry. However, he noted that the subsequent slowdown in major deepwater projects exposed the challenges of building local capacity without corresponding industry activity. Although Nigerian companies had invested in fabrication facilities and engineering capabilities, the absence of new investment decisions by international oil companies limited the availability of projects and commercial opportunities for local businesses. He said Nigeria subsequently reviewed its approach through executive orders, regulatory adjustments and tax incentives introduced around 2022 and 2023, with the aim of making its local content framework more supportive of investment while sustaining the country's indigenous participation objectives. Representing Angola, Ms Maura Nunes of the National Agency for Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG) said the country's local content policy was anchored on the principle of “For Angolans, by Angolans, with Angolans.” She explained that a presidential decree introduced in 2020 established two principal objectives: increasing the participation of Angolan companies in the oil and gas industry and developing the skills and capabilities of the country's human resources. The panel discussion was moderated by the Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Upstream Chamber, Mr David Ampofo.

Title: COP31: Two-thirds of Africa’s US$2.2bn clean cooking pledges yet to be delivered
Content: Two years after leaders pledged US$2.2 billion to expand clean cooking in Africa, only about US$740 million has been paid out, leaving roughly two-thirds of the money, about US$1.46 billion, still to be delivered. The figures were presented at a Leaders’ Roundtable on Clean Cooking in Africa at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on 12 November. The meeting was co-hosted by the COP31 Presidency of Türkiye, the United Republic of Tanzania, the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the Clean Cooking Alliance. The pledges were made at the first Summit on Clean Cooking in Africa, held in Paris in 2024 and co-chaired by Tanzania’s President Samia Suluhu Hassan. The IEA has been tracking the commitments since, and its Executive Director, Fatih Birol, told the roundtable that about a third of the money had been disbursed (about 34 cents of every dollar pledged). “Where did this money go? It went to 28 African countries supporting concrete projects,” Birol said. President Samia said she was “encouraged that our collective efforts are beginning to deliver tangible results.” According to her, “by July 2026 approximately US dollar 740 million of the commitment made in Paris has been deployed across 22 African countries.” She said a further US$900 million in commitments had been mobilised since the Paris summit, bringing the total to about US$3.1 billion. “Our success must be measured not only by the resources mobilized but also by the number of families gaining access to affordable, reliable and sustainable clean cooking solutions,” she told the leaders. Nearly one billion Africans (about six in every ten people on the continent) still lack access to clean cooking, contributing to about 850,000 premature deaths every year (more than 2,300 a day), President Samia said. To Birol, it is “one of the greatest injustices in this world.” Traditional cooking, he said, generates 1.2 gigatonnes of greenhouse gases a year. “If you want to know what is 1.2 gigaton, it is equal to the emissions from international aviation and shipping put together.” “Why I say it’s a big injustice … because it is easily solve problem if we have the finance for that,” he added. Kenya’s special envoy, Ambassador Ali Mohamed, who spoke on behalf of President William Ruto, said Africa’s clean cooking challenge “requires at least $2 billion every year.” “Our success of course will be measured not just by commitment. It will be measured by the financing that is deployed,” he said. The President of the OPEC Fund for International Development, Abdulhamid Alkhalifa, cited a different figure: “The IEA estimates that Africa needs $4 billion a year for clean cooking issue.” That amount, he said, is “less than … what the world invest in energy in a single day.” “Let us make the smoke-filled kitchen a chapter of Africa’s past, not future,” he urged. For Norway’s special envoy, Hans Olav Ibrekk, the message was clear: “Clean cooking is climate action. We need to move from commitments to implementation at scale.” Lesotho’s Deputy Prime Minister, Justice Nthomeng Majara, warned that “isolated projects and pilot interventions will not be sufficient to achieve universal access.” “Uganda recognizes that access to clean cooking is not merely an energy issue,” said Uganda President Yoweri Museveni’s representative. She said the country’s strategy targets universal access to clean cooking “by 2040 with an intermediate target of 50% access by 2030,” and that President Museveni has issued Executive Order No. 3 banning charcoal. The next test comes at the second Summit on Clean Cooking in Africa, to be held in Nairobi, Kenya, on 27–28 January 2027, which Birol will co-chair with President Ruto. “We are going to fix this problem and solve this biggest injustice of the humanity,” Birol told the meeting.

Title: Ghana High Commission UK, Okyeman Amanonehene deepen diaspora development partnership
Content: The Ghana High Commission in London and the Okyeman Amanonehene, Otuapem Oduduobiribi Benkyi, have agreed to strengthen collaboration to channel diaspora skills, expertise and capital into Ghana’s national development agenda. The agreement is aimed at ensuring that Ghanaians in the diaspora are meaningfully involved in national development, beyond their traditional role of providing financial support through remittances. The Okyeman Amanonehene, who is also the Honorary Consul of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg to Ghana and Secretary of the Honorary Consular Corps of Ghana (HCCGH), said the diaspora possessed significant professional expertise and resources that could be harnessed to support the country's development priorities. Speaking at a meeting at the Ghana High Commission in London on Thursday, he said the initiative would create opportunities for diaspora members to contribute more actively to Ghana's development. Ghana's High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Her Excellency Mrs Sabah Zita Benson, welcomed the proposed collaboration, describing the Amanonehene as a partner and stakeholder in advancing the Mission's development priorities. She said the High Commission's existing programmes focused on women's empowerment, youth development, health and environmental sustainability, areas in which closer engagement with diaspora organisations could deliver meaningful results. Mrs Benson emphasised the importance of creating employment opportunities for young people to address broader social challenges, while ensuring that women were fully included in development initiatives. She also expressed the Mission's readiness to work with the various cultural groups and communities already engaged in activities connected to Ghana. Mobilising diaspora investment Discussions also focused on trade and investment, particularly the need to direct a greater proportion of diaspora financial resources towards productive ventures. The Okyeman Amanonehene cited diaspora remittances of US$7.5 billion in 2025, arguing that more of these inflows could be channelled into investments capable of generating economic activity and supporting national development. Among the projects discussed were the Accra Marine Drive development and larger land-based cultural and investment initiatives requiring additional capital to advance. The High Commissioner underscored the connection between culture, business and development, indicating that the Mission was prepared to facilitate partnerships and support collaborative initiatives built around events. Both parties agreed to institutionalise their engagement through regular meetings, potentially on a quarterly basis, while working towards developing the initiative into an annual event that would demonstrate tangible progress and measurable outcomes. The meeting ended with a commitment from both sides to sustain the partnership, maintain regular communication and provide updates on progress towards the agreed objectives.

Title: AETC, Ministry of Youth Development sign MoU to strengthen strategic collaboration, advance youth innovation and entrepreneurship
Content: As part of its commitment to advancing youth empowerment, entrepreneurship and sustainable development across Africa, the leadership of the Africa Energy Technology Centre (AETC) has paid a courtesy visit to the Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment to strengthen institutional collaboration and explore strategic opportunities to support Ghana’s national youth development agenda. The engagement reaffirmed AETC’s commitment to working alongside government and key stakeholders to equip young people with the skills, opportunities and support systems required to become drivers of Africa’s energy transition and economic transformation. The delegation was received by the George Opare Addo, Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment, who welcomed AETC’s vision and acknowledged the important role that indigenous Pan-African institutions can play in supporting Ghana’s development priorities. The meeting provided an opportunity for AETC to share the Centre’s strategic initiatives while exploring areas of collaboration that align with the Ministry’s vision of empowering young people through innovation, entrepreneurship, leadership development and sustainable job creation. Speaking during the engagement, Founder & President of the Africa Energy Technology Centre, Emelia Akumah, reaffirmed AETC’s commitment to serving as a leading Pan-African platform that convenes governments, policymakers, industry leaders, development partners, academia, investors and innovators to promote dialogue, strengthen partnerships and develop practical solutions that advance Africa’s energy and technology sectors. She emphasised that empowering young people must remain central to Africa’s long-term development strategy, particularly as the continent seeks to accelerate industrialisation, innovation and inclusive economic growth. Ms. Akumah also highlighted the vision of the Youth Energy Entrepreneurship & Incubation Programme (YEEIP), one of AETC’s flagship initiatives designed to nurture the next generation of African entrepreneurs, innovators and business leaders. She explained that the programme seeks to provide young people with technical capacity building, entrepreneurship training, mentorship, business incubation and strategic industry partnerships that will enable them to develop innovative solutions while creating sustainable employment opportunities within the energy and technology sectors. She further noted that the programme closely aligns with the Ministry’s mandate to empower young people through innovation, entrepreneurship and leadership development. Building on this, Ms. Akumah introduced the Africa Building on this, Ms. Akumah introduced the Africa Energy Youth Forum (AEYF), an initiative of the YEEIP that gives young people a voice of their own in the energy, oil and gas and technology sectors. She explained that the Forum provides a dedicated platform for young professionals, students, entrepreneurs and innovators to engage directly with policymakers, industry leaders and investors, to share their perspectives on the issues shaping these sectors, and to contribute ideas and solutions for Africa’s energy future. Through the AEYF, AETC seeks to ensure that young Africans are not only beneficiaries of the continent’s energy transition, but active participants in shaping the policies, investments and innovations that will define it. The Minister commended AETC for its strategic vision and expressed appreciation for the Centre’s growing contribution towards youth development and innovation. He underscored the importance of creating sustainable pathways that enable young Ghanaians to develop practical skills, build successful enterprises and actively contribute to the country’s socio-economic development. He further encouraged stronger collaboration between government and indigenous institutions whose programmes complement national development priorities and create meaningful opportunities for young people. A key outcome of the engagement was the mutual commitment to commence the development of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment and the Africa Energy Technology Centre. The proposed framework is expected to establish a long-term strategic partnership that will provide a structured platform for implementing practical, measurable and sustainable interventions aimed at advancing youth empowerment across Ghana. Discussions explored several priority areas of collaboration, including the implementation of the Youth Energy Entrepreneurship & Incubation Programme (YEEIP), youth engagement and joint policy dialogue through the Africa Energy Youth Forum (AEYF) to strengthen youth participation within Ghana’s energy, oil and gas and technology sectors, entrepreneurship and leadership development programmes, resource mobilisation and strategic partnership development, collaborative needs assessments to inform programme implementation, and the establishment of a Joint Technical Working Group to develop an implementation roadmap and facilitate effective coordination between the Ministry and AETC. Both parties reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining close engagement as technical teams work towards formalising the proposed partnership framework. The envisioned collaboration reflects a shared commitment to developing innovative, youth-centred programmes that create sustainable livelihoods, strengthen entrepreneurship ecosystems and position young people as active contributors to Ghana’s economic transformation. The meeting concluded with a shared commitment to strengthening collaboration between the Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment and the Africa Energy Technology Centre, paving the way for a long-term strategic partnership that will expand opportunities for Ghana’s youth while advancing innovation, entrepreneurship, leadership development and sustainable national development.

Title: Government to invest US$1bn in textile and garment industry – Ato Forson
Content: Government will invest US$1 billion to transform Ghana's textile and garment industry into a competitive manufacturing hub, capable of supplying global fashion markets. Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson said the investment is aimed at expanding local production, increasing exports and creating employment opportunities under the government's 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme. Presenting the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, he said the initiative will focus on modernising existing textile mills, expanding garment factories and establishing dedicated industrial enclaves for textile and garment production. The enclaves will be equipped with essential infrastructure, including reliable electricity, industrial water, laboratories, warehouses, treatment facilities and factory buildings to help manufacturers reduce production costs and handle large orders. Government will also support local fashion designers, tailors and dressmakers with modern equipment, technical assistance and commercial partnerships to enable them to access regional and international markets. Dr Forson said the investment will help build a competitive local industry capable of producing fabrics, garments and Ghanaian fashion brands for global markets. “Our ambition is to put Made-in-Ghana fashion into wardrobes around the world and put dependable incomes into Ghanaian homes,” he told Parliament. The government plans to begin developing industrial enclave infrastructure and modernising priority facilities in 2027, with new and upgraded production lines expected to become operational in 2028. By 2030, the target is to establish a textile and garment industry operating at commercial scale and supplying wider international markets.

Title: Ghana Police intercepts GH₵20m worth of fake GTP fabric
Content: The Special Operations Team of the Inspector General of Police has intercepted counterfeit wax prints from Nigeria with imitated designs of Tex Styles Ghana Limited, producers of GTP fabrics. This follows a tip off received by the special team. The product, mainly wax prints from Nigeria was smuggled into the country without paying the required taxes to the state. The exercise forms part of an anti-counterfeit campaign by Ghanaian textile manufacturers and the Ghana Police. Speaking to journalists, Environmental Sustainability Manager at Tex Styles Ghana, Schandorf Nii Obodai, disclosed that the ceased textiles are worth about GH₵ 20 million. “When you check all the materials here including the ones in the truck load, it’s about GH₵ 20 million worth of cloth which is just going to enter the local market but for the vigilance of the team”, he said. He stated that the activities of smugglers affect the nation and tax collection and also adversely impact the operations of legal companies operating in the country. “This (smuggled goods) can be in the market for about two months even after the festive season and you can imagine the amount of taxes the state may be losing just because of these smuggled items and we as a company will be struggling to sell or produce more for the local market”. Outlining the negative impact on business operations, Mr. Obodai said the increase in smuggling of fake wax prints is the reason for the collapse of many local textile companies in Ghana. “The impact of this is deeper than you can imagine because it affects production which turns to have an impact on job for our citizens in Ghana” he said. He advised the general public to note that GTP does not operate other factories in in Africa, hence any GTP fabrics produced on the continent apart from Ghana are fake and illegal. “Often traders are being bait with the myth that this is printed by GTP in Nigeria or Côte d'Ivoire. I want to put it on record today, that GTP doesn’t have any factory in Nigeria or elsewhere in Africa producing GTP or Vlisco cloths. GTP cloths are only produced in Ghana but they copy our designs and the stamps to reproduce the imitation products”, he warned. The Intelligence Unit of the Ghana Police has taken over the investigation to apprehend all perpetrators.

Title: Obuasi Trade Show 2026 to bring businesses together for four-day exhibition in December
Content: The 2026 Obuasi Trade Show is scheduled to take place from December 21 to 24 at the Obuasi Black Park, bringing together businesses, entrepreneurs, manufacturers and traders from across the Ashanti Region. The four-day exhibition is expected to provide a platform for businesses to showcase their products and services, connect with potential partners and investors, and explore opportunities to access new markets. The initiative is being spearheaded by the Obuasi Trade Show Consortium, with AngloGold Ashanti Obuasi Mine as headline sponsor. It forms part of the Mine’s 10-year Socio-Economic Development Plan (SEDP 2022–2031), which seeks to promote local entrepreneurship, expand opportunities for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) and support efforts to diversify Obuasi’s economy beyond mining. Speaking at the official media launch on November 10 at Tutuka in Obuasi, the Mine’s Director of Sustainability Management, Edmund Oduro Agyei, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to initiatives that create sustainable economic opportunities in its host communities. He said the trade show aligns with the objectives of the development plan, particularly its focus on strengthening local businesses, promoting entrepreneurship and building a resilient local economy. Mr Oduro Agyei encouraged businesses to use the exhibition to showcase their products, establish commercial connections and explore markets beyond their immediate communities. Board Chairman of the Obuasi Trade Show Consortium, Aboagye Ohene Adu, said the organisers intended to develop the event into a major regional commercial exhibition, attracting businesses from across the Ashanti Region and beyond. He said the platform would help connect entrepreneurs, investors, businesses and consumers while strengthening Obuasi’s position as a destination for commerce and investment. The Ashanti Regional Director of the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Mrs Diana, also commended the initiative, saying it could support entrepreneurship, local industrialisation and regional economic development. She urged business owners to participate in the exhibition to promote their products, access new markets and build networks that could support business growth. This year’s edition is expected to feature businesses from across the Ashanti Region, with exhibitors showcasing a range of products and services. In addition to the exhibition stands, visitors can expect networking opportunities, cultural displays and entertainment. The initiative is supported by the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, the Obuasi Municipal Assembly, the Obuasi East Municipal Assembly and the Ghana Enterprises Agency. Organisers are encouraging businesses, entrepreneurs, traders and members of the public to attend the exhibition from December 21 to 24. Through its support for the trade show, AngloGold Ashanti says it is advancing its commitment to sustainable livelihoods, local enterprise development and inclusive economic growth as part of its broader socio-economic development programme in Obuasi.

Title: Eni Ghana pledges more opportunities for local firms in upstream sector
Content: The Managing Director of Eni Ghana, Mr Federico Ricco, has reaffirmed the company’s commitment to strengthening local content development and expanding opportunities for local businesses in the country’s upstream petroleum industry. Speaking at the 2026 Local Content Conference and Exhibition in Takoradi, Mr Ricco said Eni’s experience with the Offshore Cape Three Points (OCTP) project demonstrated the value of combining international investment with a strong commitment to developing local capabilities. The conference was held on the theme:“Enriching Local Content for Sustainable Growth: Building a Resilient Upstream Sector through Reforms and Partnerships to Spur Competitiveness and Investment.” Since the start-up of the Sankofa field, he said, Eni and its partners had made significant investments not only in infrastructure and production facilities but also in people, skills development, technology transfer and the strengthening of the local supply chain. He revealed that approximately 90 per cent of the company’s workforce were Ghanaians, while a substantial proportion of its operational activities were carried out by local companies. He attributed these achievements to years of investment, collaboration and a shared commitment involving Eni, the government, the industry regulator, the Petroleum Commission, its partners and businesses that had grown alongside its operations. Mr Ricco emphasised that local content was not merely a regulatory requirement but an integral part of how Eni operated, developed its projects and created lasting value in the countries where it operated. He noted that the progress made so far had transformed investments into opportunities, opportunities into capabilities, and capabilities into lasting value for the industry in the country. The achievements, he said, represented the beginning of a more ambitious journey, with the next priority being to expand the role of Ghanaian companies in the development and execution of major upstream projects. He said local companies that had progressively developed the capacity to support and manage complex operational activities must now be given opportunities to participate in increasingly complex engineering, construction and project execution activities. He also identified opportunities for Ghanaian businesses to expand beyond the domestic market and position themselves as regional service providers. With significant upstream investments expected across West Africa in the coming years, he said Ghanaian companies could support projects across the wider West African energy industry, strengthening their capabilities and competitiveness. Mr Ricco stressed that realising these opportunities would require collective efforts to unlock the next wave of upstream investments in the country. New investments and attraction He acknowledged the continued efforts of the government, the sector ministry and the Petroleum Commission to strengthen the competitiveness of Ghana’s upstream sector and attract new investments. The Managing Director also expressed appreciation for ongoing industry engagement and initiatives aimed at creating a more attractive and predictable investment environment. He said these efforts should translate into concrete agreements and new projects reaching Final Investment Decision (FID), opening a new chapter of growth and opportunities for local businesses. Mr Ricco further indicated that additional resources had already been identified through Eni’s exploration activities, making their development and eventual production a shared priority with the government and partners. He said continued exploration of new blocks would be necessary to identify the resources required to power the country for decades, while maintaining a steady pipeline of new development projects. He added that this was essential in an industry characterised by long investment cycles. Mr Ricco observed that Ghanaian companies had invested significantly in people, equipment and technical capabilities to support petroleum operations. A steady flow of new projects, he said, would give them the confidence and opportunities to sustain these investments, retain skilled professionals and undertake increasingly complex activities. Eni Ghana reiterated its commitment to working closely with the government, the Petroleum Commission, its partners and the local business community to translate these opportunities into tangible outcomes for the country’s economy and local industry.

Title: Ghana’s lithium future: Will local communities get a fair share?
Content: Ghana's ambition to become a lithium producer is entering a new phase as Chinese mining giant Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt moves closer to gaining control of Atlantic Lithium, the company behind the country's first proposed commercial lithium mine. The development is raising questions about what the country and communities hosting the mine stand to gain, particularly as concerns over compensation and environmental responsibility emerge from the company's operations elsewhere. The questions come after a subsidiary of Huayou was ordered by authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to pay US$6 million in compensation to three communities affected by an industrial wastewater spill. Congo Dongfang International Mining, a Huayou subsidiary, was ordered to pay US$2 million each to Kasapa, Kamatete and Kamisepe following a November 2025 incident at its Lubumbashi operation. The company's operations were subsequently suspended, but Congo's Mines Ministry insists that the suspension does not remove its obligation to compensate affected residents. Reuters reported on November 6 that the compensation payments had been delayed, with the company citing financial difficulties. Although the incident happened in Congo and does not establish that similar problems will occur in Ghana, it highlights the importance of enforcing environmental and compensation obligations as Huayou expands its mining interests. The Ewoyaa Lithium Project in the Central Region is expected to become Ghana's first commercial lithium mine. The government granted a 15-year mining lease to Barari DV Ghana Limited, a subsidiary of Atlantic Lithium, in October 2023. However, the agreement faced delays in Parliament amid disagreements over the financial terms, particularly the royalty Ghana would receive. After further consultations and revisions, Parliament finally ratified the lease on March 19, 2026. The revised agreement introduced a sliding-scale royalty system, allowing Ghana to receive higher royalties when international lithium prices rise. Under the arrangement, royalties range from 5% to 12%, depending on the price of lithium concentrate. The ratification removed a major obstacle to the project, but commercial production is not automatic. Financing, development work and outstanding community-related matters remain important to its progress. Huayou's interest in the project has developed through two separate transactions. In May 2026, the Chinese company proposed a US$210 million takeover of Atlantic Lithium. Separately, it completed an agreement in October to acquire Elevra Lithium's interests in Atlantic Lithium's Ghana portfolio. The completed transaction gives Huayou an initial 22.5% interest, with the opportunity to increase this to 50% by providing additional development funding. Atlantic Lithium remains the project's operator under the existing arrangement. But, the proposed takeover of Atlantic Lithium would give Huayou control of the company itself. In an announcement dated November 5, Atlantic Lithium disclosed that the Supreme Court of Western Australia had approved a meeting for shareholders to consider the proposed takeover. The meeting is scheduled for December 14, 2026, at 7:00 a.m. Ghana time. Atlantic Lithium's board has unanimously recommended that shareholders vote in favour of the transaction, provided there is no better offer and an independent expert continues to consider the deal to be in shareholders' best interests. The takeover is not yet complete. It still requires shareholder approval and the fulfilment of other conditions, including relevant regulatory approvals. But what does this mean for Ghana? Huayou's entry could provide the financial resources and technical experience needed to advance the Ewoyaa project. But the bigger question is whether Ghana and its communities will receive lasting benefits from the investment. For residents around Ewoyaa, one immediate concern is compensation for land, farms and other properties affected by the project. Delayed payments could leave some residents facing financial difficulties, particularly where access to their farms and other properties has been restricted. The experience in Congo also brings attention to the importance of ensuring that mining companies meet their obligations to communities, even when their operations face financial or operational difficulties. Ghana must therefore ensure that compensation arrangements are clear and enforceable, and that environmental protections are not compromised in the pursuit of investment. Beyond compensation, the country must also consider how much value it can retain from lithium production. That means looking beyond royalties and taxes to local jobs, opportunities for Ghanaian businesses, skills development and the possibility of processing more of the mineral locally.

Title: Partnerships key to unlocking Ghana’s mineral wealth – MIIF CEO
Content: The Chief Executive Officer of the Minerals Income Investment Fund (MIIF), Justina Nelson, has stated that deeper partnerships with international investors are key to unlocking Ghana’s mineral potential and driving greater value addition in the mining sector. According to her, Ghana’s mineral wealth offered significant opportunities for investors, particularly in bauxite, iron ore, manganese and graphite, as the country seeks to move beyond the export of raw minerals towards value addition and industrial production. Speaking on the sidelines of the 2026 China (Guangxi)–ASEAN Mining Cooperation Conference in China on Friday, November 6, Mrs. Nelson presented Ghana’s mineral resource potential and outlined investment opportunities for companies seeking to establish partnerships in the country. The conference on the theme: “Empowering China-ASEAN Mining Cooperation, Innovation and Development” brought together government officials, mining industry leaders, investors and other stakeholders across the world to explore investment opportunities, forge strategic partnerships and promote cooperation across the mining value chain. Ghana has an estimated 920 million tonnes of bauxite resources, while iron ore deposits at Sheini Hills are estimated at more than 1.7 billion tonnes. The country also has about 5.2 million tonnes of manganese resources, alongside opportunities for graphite exploration and further development within the Cape Coast lithium belt. Mrs Nelson outlined several areas for potential investment, including new and existing mining projects, joint ventures between foreign mining companies and Ghanaian contract miners, as well as the local manufacture of mining consumables.She further identified opportunities in alumina refining, smelting technology, iron and steel production, and the manufacture of battery-grade manganese, all of which could support the development of Ghana’s domestic mineral processing industry.A key area she highlighted was the development of an integrated iron and steel industry. According to her, domestic mine-to-steel production could potentially replace about US$528 million in annual iron and steel imports, based on 2023 figures.Mrs Nelson’s engagement at the conference forms part of MIIF’s broader efforts to promote Ghana as an investment destination and position its mineral resources as a catalyst for industrialisation, job creation and sustainable economic growth. The Deputy Minister of Lands and Natural Resources, Alhaji Yusif Sulemana, said Ghana’s laws and policies were open to investment, adding that the government was committed to creating favourable conditions for international businesses. He said the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources and relevant government agencies remained ready to support investors and facilitate partnerships that would contribute to the development of the mining industry. Therefore, he encouraged Chinese companies to explore opportunities in Ghana's mining, mineral processing and related industries, emphasising the importance of long-term partnerships that would benefit both countries.

Title: Rethinking the Ghanaian compound house: Co-living as part of the housing solution
Content: When we discuss Ghana’s housing challenges, the conversation often turns to acquiring more land, building new estates, and finding the money to finance construction. These are important. But I believe another question deserves attention: What can we do with the buildings we have already started? There are unfinished properties that could potentially provide accommodation if they were completed and put to productive use. At the same time, there are people who need somewhere decent to live but cannot afford an entire house or a self-contained apartment. Could co-living help bring these two needs together? I believe it is worth exploring—not as a complete answer to Ghana’s housing crisis, but as a practical alternative that could provide accommodation, create investment opportunities, and unlock some of the capital tied up in unfinished buildings. A familiar Ghanaian foundation The term “co-living” may sound new to some readers. The underlying arrangement, however, has a familiar Ghanaian foundation.Consider the compound house. Different households occupy their own rooms while sharing a courtyard and, depending on the property, kitchens, bathrooms, and other facilities. People maintain their individual lives within a shared residential setting. Co-living can build on that familiarity. Residents could have private, lockable bedrooms, with shared kitchens, sitting areas, laundry facilities, and other amenities. Some properties might offer private bathrooms; others could provide adequately maintained shared facilities. Another way to understand the idea is through shared student accommodation in Ghana’s colleges and universities. Depending on the hall or hostel, students may share bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchens, or common areas. They have individual responsibilities while observing rules that allow people to live together.[5] Co-living for working adults could apply a similar principle, with greater emphasis on private bedrooms and the needs of people at different stages of life. A young graduate leaving university may no longer want to share a bedroom but may be comfortable sharing a kitchen or sitting area if the arrangement is affordable, secure, and properly managed. The comparison helps explain the concept; it does not mean every college hostel has the same facilities or that an adult co-living home should operate exactly like a student residence. The aim should be to adapt shared living to the needs and expectations of today’s residents. Privacy, sanitation, security, maintenance, and clear household rules must be part of the design from the beginning. We should also recognise that people have different preferences. Some will always want a self-contained home. Others may welcome a well-managed room if it offers an affordable and convenient place to live. The opportunity in unfinished buildings Ghana Statistical Service’s final 2021 census report found that approximately 15 percent of residential structures had some form of roofing but were not fully completed. In Greater Accra, the proportion was 17.6 percent.[1] These are 2021 figures, rather than a current inventory of available properties. They also do not tell us that every unfinished building is vacant, structurally sound, or suitable for conversion. Nevertheless, they give substance to the question: Could we bring some of this existing investment into productive use? An investor might identify a suitable unfinished building near employment, a university, a hospital, or a reliable transport route. After verifying ownership and assessing its condition, the investor could examine whether completing it as shared accommodation makes commercial sense. Land, foundations, walls, and roofing may already represent substantial investment. Where those elements are sound and the price is reasonable, completing an existing structure could offer an advantage over starting again. That advantage must be established through proper inspection and costing. The objective should be to create decent places to live. Simply dividing a building into as many rooms as possible would miss the point. What Airbnb can teach us Airbnb offers a useful comparison. The platform came from outside Ghana, but it has found a place in the country’s accommodation market. In November 2024, the Ghana Tourism Authority reported a significant rise in listings on platforms such as Airbnb and introduced a registration regime for short-term rentals.[2] Its growth suggests that an accommodation model can gain acceptance when owners and users see value in it.That does not mean co-living will automatically follow the same path. Airbnb largely serves a short-stay market, while the opportunity considered here is accommodation for people who need a place to live for longer periods. Still, if we have been willing to adopt a platform developed elsewhere, we should be willing to examine a professionally managed housing model with roots in a familiar Ghanaian arrangement. The lesson is to study what people need and adapt the model accordingly. The PadSplit example in the United States There is also a practical example in the United States: PadSplit, a platform where housing providers list rooms in shared homes and people looking for accommodation can search for and book available rooms. PadSplit describes its model as providing private, furnished bedrooms, shared facilities such as kitchens, and either shared or private bathrooms, depending on the listing. Its advertised weekly payments include utilities and internet.[4] This illustrates how shared housing can be supported by an organised platform that helps people find accommodation and understand what is included in the price. For Ghana, the opportunity would be to explore an approach suited to local incomes, payment patterns, housing rules, and expectations. A locally appropriate platform could advertise available rooms, show facilities and charges clearly, and help connect residents with responsible property operators. The buildings and management would still have to deliver what the listings promise.PadSplit offers an example to study. I am not suggesting that the company currently operates in Ghana, or that its payment arrangements should simply be copied here. Why serious investors should pay attentionAs a real estate investor and educator, I look at both the housing need and the economics. A property must serve its residents, and it must generate enough income to maintain itself and justify the capital committed. Co-living could appeal to investors because several individually affordable room rents may together produce more income than letting the entire property to one household. One vacant room would also leave income from the others, although several rooms could become vacant at the same time. Shared facilities may allow more efficient use of suitable floor space. Completing an unfinished property could also turn an asset producing no income into one generating rental receipts. But gross rent is only the beginning. More residents can mean more maintenance, greater utility consumption, more frequent tenant changes, and more management work. Improved cash flow and return on investment are possibilities to evaluate after these costs, rather than benefits to assume. Serious investors should compare what residents can actually pay with the full cost of completing and operating the property. A housing shortage does not guarantee demand for every room at every price. Partnerships could unlock stalled projects An outright sale is not the only route. An owner with a suitable unfinished property could partner with an investor who provides completion funds. A capable operator could manage the accommodation. The parties would agree on the property’s value, the capital required, responsibilities, income distributions, and how the arrangement ends. Such a partnership could allow an owner to put an unfinished asset to work while giving an investor access to a project without purchasing the property outright. However, the owner’s contribution still has value. The agreement must account for it, alongside the completion investment. Ownership, control, capital recovery, and exit rights need to be clear before work begins. Affordability must be meaningful The potential residents could include young workers, students, national service personnel, and people relocating for employment.For them, affordability involves the total cost of living: rent, utilities, transport, and the money required before moving in. A reasonably priced room far from work may become expensive once commuting is included. Good co-living should give residents clarity about what they are paying for, access to adequate facilities, and a reasonable balance between privacy and shared life. Existing residents also matter. Ghana Statistical Service reported that 79,721 urban households were already living in uncompleted buildings in 2021.[3] Improving such properties should take their circumstances into account. A conversion involving occupied accommodation cannot simply be counted as entirely new housing supply. Start with disciplined pilots I would encourage interested owners and investors to begin with a carefully selected pilot property.Verify ownership. Obtain a structural assessment and a reliable completion budget. Confirm the required permissions with the relevant assembly. Design sufficient bathrooms, cooking areas, ventilation, and safe access. Establish clear tenancy agreements and appoint someone accountable for management. Then measure the results: occupancy, collections, operating expenses, maintenance, resident satisfaction, and net cash flow.That evidence would tell us far more than an attractive brochure. Ghana will continue to need new homes and broader reforms in housing finance and infrastructure. Alongside those efforts, we should examine how to complete and use suitable existing buildings more effectively. The compound-house tradition gives us a familiar starting point. Shared student accommodation provides another useful comparison. The growth of Airbnb shows a willingness to adapt accommodation models, while PadSplit illustrates how a platform can connect people with rooms in shared homes. Co-living offers an opportunity to bring these lessons together with local experience and investment discipline. A carefully completed building can provide homes, generate income, and support the community around it. That is a possibility worth taking seriously—one property at a time. George Ansong is a real estate investor, Georgia-licensed agent, author and educator based in Atlanta. He wrote The Cash Flow Real Estate Agent: A Step-by-Step Guide to Working with Investors and teaches investment strategies, creative financing and working with investor clients. Sources[1] Ghana Statistical Service, 2021 Population and Housing Census, General Report Volume 3N: Structures.https://census2021.statsghana.gov.gh/subreport.php?Volume-3N-Structures=&readreport=NTgwNjExMjQ4LjI4Mw%3D%3D[2] Ghana Tourism Authority, “GTA Finalises Engagements with Airbnb to Regularise Operations,” 21 November 2024.https://visitghana.com/press-release-gta-finalises-engagements-with-airbnb-to-regularise-operations/[3] Ghana Statistical Service, release on urban housing, water and sanitation conditions, 5 October 2023.https://census2021.statsghana.gov.gh/presspage.php?1-4-million-households-in-urban-areas-were-without-water-on-their-premises=&readmorenews=MTg0NzM5OTQyNi4zNTU%3D[4] PadSplit, “What is PadSplit?” and room listings.https://www.padsplit.com/what-is-padsplithttps://www.padsplit.com/rooms-for-rent[5] Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Housing and Accommodation.https://www.knust.edu.gh/index.php/students/housing1

Title: GHIB partners with property specialists to connect African clients with London residential developments
Content: Ghana International Bank plc (GHIB) has announced a collaboration with Daniel Ford International and the Berkeley Group to provide African clients with information on selected residential developments in London, alongside access to the bank’s UK banking services. The initiative was unveiled at an event in Accra, targeting high-net-worth individuals, entrepreneurs, business owners and senior executives across the continent who have international banking needs. Through the collaboration, prospective property buyers can access information on selected residential developments within the Berkeley Group’s portfolio, with property advisory services provided by Daniel Ford International. GHIB said its role would be limited to providing banking services to eligible customers and would not extend to recommending, advising on, arranging or endorsing any particular property purchase. The initiative comes as Africa’s affluent population continues to attract attention from international financial institutions and property businesses. The Africa Wealth Report 2026, published by New World Wealth, estimates that the continent has just over 127,000 US-dollar millionaires, defined in the report as individuals with at least US$1 million in liquid wealth. Nigeria accounts for an estimated 8,100 millionaires, while Ghana has approximately 2,600, according to the report. GHIB says the collaboration forms part of its efforts to expand its personal banking services to affluent customers across its African markets, particularly those seeking UK-based banking solutions. Established in London in 1959, GHIB has operated for more than six decades, supporting trade, investment and corporate banking relationships between Africa and international markets. The bank is now seeking to broaden its personal banking proposition through services for affluent African clients with cross-border financial requirements. Commenting on the collaboration, GHIB Chief Banking Officer, Ophelia Attobrah, said the initiative responds to the growing international banking needs of African professionals and business leaders. “At GHIB, we understand that many successful African professionals, entrepreneurs and business leaders increasingly have international banking needs, including when considering residential property ownership in the United Kingdom. Our proposition is designed to provide banking services that can support customers with their UK banking requirements, should the customer elect to pursue them,” she said. She said the bank’s Premier and Classic Accounts were UK-based services intended to help customers manage their international banking requirements, including those that may arise in connection with property acquisitions. “Our role is limited to providing appropriate banking services to eligible customers. Decisions concerning whether to acquire property, and which property to acquire, remain entirely with the customer,” she added. Mrs Attobrah said although the initiative was launched in Ghana, it was intended to serve existing and prospective customers across the bank’s African footprint. “This proposition is open to both existing and prospective GHIB customers in all the African markets we serve. We see significant opportunity to support affluent clients across West Africa and beyond as their international banking needs evolve, helping them manage cross-border financial requirements while maintaining strong connections to the continent,” she said. GHIB said access to its accounts would remain subject to its eligibility requirements, onboarding procedures, customer due diligence and applicable terms and conditions. The bank also clarified that it does not provide property, investment, mortgage, tax or legal advice through the collaboration. Customers interested in any of the developments are expected to make their own assessments and seek independent professional advice where necessary.

Title: Ghanaian rice quality has improved significantly – CSIR-CRI Chief Director
Content: The Chief Research Scientist and Director at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research–Crops Research Institute (CSIR-CRI), Professor Maxwell Darko Asante, says the quality of locally produced rice has improved significantly, dismissing concerns that poor processing is responsible for its low patronage. He said Ghana's rice industry has moved beyond the days when locally produced rice was commonly associated with stones and other impurities due to inadequate processing. According to him, improvements in the country's rice production and processing systems have addressed some of the quality challenges that previously affected consumer confidence in local varieties. "People talk about quality, but it is not true, we have gone past the quality issues long ago. Well, I should admit that a few times farmers don't treat the paddy well, and it doesn't mill well, but we have gone past the stage where there were stones in it," he said. Prof. Asante said this onJoy FM's Super Morning Show, challenging the perception that Ghanaian rice is not selling because farmers and processors fail to sort their paddy or maintain acceptable quality standards properly. He then attributed the low patronage of Ghanaian rice to the cheap importation of foreign rice, "the challenge we are facing is cheap import." He maintained that the country's locally produced rice is now of good quality and should be able to compete with imported varieties on the market. His comments come amid concerns about the growing dominance of imported rice and the difficulties local farmers face in selling their produce. Prof. Asante has previously warned that the situation is discouraging farmers from continuing rice cultivation, with some reportedly abandoning the activity after struggling to sell their harvests. He believes the challenges confronting local rice production require greater attention to market access and support for farmers to ensure that improvements in the quality of Ghanaian rice translate into increased patronage.

Title: Don Little accuses female police officer of verbal abuse during encounter in Kumasi
Content: Ghanaian actor Don Little has expressed anger and disappointment towards an unnamed female officer of the Ghana Police Service following an alleged unpleasant encounter with a female police officer at Kumasi Breman. In a viral video shared on X on November 17, 2026, the actor recounted how the officer allegedly stopped his vehicle and verbally assaulted him during a confrontation. According to Don Little, the incident began when he failed to notice a torchlight the officer had flashed towards him. He claimed that the officer became upset and started hitting his vehicle, prompting him to question her conduct. Narrating his experience, the actor criticised the behaviour of some police officers, insisting that those entrusted with maintaining law and order should treat members of the public with respect. Don Little further alleged that the confrontation escalated when the female officer made a derogatory remark about his height, reportedly comparing it to the size of her clitoris. Some people are mean o eiii. how can you look at Don Little and tell him your clit is longer than him? 🤦‍♂so mean. Kafra Don. https://t.co/kdoHd80tHY He disclosed that the comment deeply offended him, describing the officer's alleged behaviour as unacceptable and disrespectful. The actor also issued a strong warning to the Ghana Police Service, cautioning that he would not tolerate a similar incident in the future. He threatened to take drastic action should another officer mistreat him without justification. In his remarks, Don Little questioned the professionalism of the officer involved and called attention to what he considers inappropriate conduct by some members of the police service. The allegations have drawn attention to the importance of professionalism, respectful communication and accountability in interactions between police officers and civilians.

Title: Otumfuo pushes for creative industry investment to boost Ghana’s economy
Content: The Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II has called for increased investment in Ghana’s creative industry, stressing its potential to generate employment, create wealth and drive economic growth. He believes the country can unlock greater economic benefits from its arts, fashion and cultural sectors through improved technical training, stronger local production and adequate investment in creative enterprises. The Asantehene made the call at the Faculty of Applied Arts and Technology (FAAT) Week celebration at Takoradi Technical University (TTU), where he challenged the institution to develop the skills and expertise needed to transform Ghana’s creative industry. Highlighting the economic potential of the fashion sector, Otumfuo disclosed that the industry was estimated to contribute about GH¢2 billion to the national economy, with considerable room for growth if given the necessary support. Despite the increasing international recognition of Ghanaian designers and artists, locally manufactured fashion products remain underrepresented in shops and markets, with imported goods continuing to dominate. “What you cannot find in the shops, though, are Made-in-Ghana labels and sadly, even on the domestic market, our shops are dominated by foreign products, save for the growing indigenous sector,” he observed. The situation, he said, reflected Ghana’s inability to translate the international recognition of its creative talents into meaningful commercial opportunities for locally manufactured products. Artists, designers and students were consequently encouraged to prioritise quality, embrace innovation and meet international standards while preserving the country's cultural identity through their work. Otumfuo also identified the shortage of middle-level technical skills as a major obstacle to industrial development and the expansion of the creative sector. He tasked Takoradi Technical University with bridging this gap by connecting indigenous knowledge with formal education, experienced artisans with emerging designers, and traditional craftsmanship with modern technology. “Your university stands at the critical point in the value chain where heritage and culture meet economic value,” he said. Ghana’s rich traditions in weaving, pottery, metalworking, woodcarving, architecture and visual communication, he stressed, provide a strong foundation for developing a globally competitive creative industry. Integrating these traditional skills with contemporary design and production techniques would help local artisans and designers develop products capable of competing in international markets. As part of the celebration, the Asantehene cut the sod for the proposed Otumfuo Osei Tutu II Art Museum at Takoradi Technical University. The facility is expected to promote artistic expression, preserve Ghana’s cultural heritage and provide a platform for advancing the country's creative arts industry. The celebration, held under the theme, “Celebrating Heritage, Innovation, and Excellence: A Tribute to Otumfuo Osei Tutu II’s Legacy,” featured cultural performances, an exhibition of artistic creations and a fashion show showcasing designs by students of the Faculty of Applied Arts and Technology. The Asantehene praised the university for making arts and cultural heritage integral to its academic programmes, urging it to strengthen its role in developing the skilled artists and designers needed to drive Ghana’s creative industry and economic growth.

Title: KGL Group’s Alex Apau Dadey wins top honour at Ghana CEO Vision and Awards
Content: Alex Apau Dadey, Executive Chairman and Group Chief Executive Officer of KGL Group, has been named CEO of CEOs at the fifth Ghana CEO Vision and Awards, where 39 corporate leaders were recognised for their contributions to business development and leadership. The ultimate award was presented at a ceremony in Accra held under the theme, “Reimagining Ghana’s Future: CEOs at the Heart of the Reset Agenda.” The event also featured calls for business leaders to translate Ghana’s improving economic conditions into increased investment, industrial growth and job creation. Delivering a speech on behalf of the Chief of Staff, Dr Julius Debrah, Presidential Advisor on National Resilience and Emergency Preparedness, Ernest Brogya Gyemfi, urged the private sector to take an active role in the country’s economic reset agenda through investments in production, industrialisation, tourism and the creative economy. Dr Debrah said improvements in inflation, foreign exchange conditions and investor confidence had created an enabling environment for businesses to expand. He, however, stressed that economic stabilisation must translate into lasting prosperity through increased production, innovation, exports, value addition and employment. “Macroeconomic stability alone cannot guarantee national prosperity. While stabilisation provides the foundation, transformation builds the nation,” he said. Touching on the Government’s upcoming 2027 Budget, Dr Debrah said it would outline a new economic blueprint anchored on the commitment: “Ghana producing, Ghanaians working, prosperity growing.” He said the proposed framework would shift the economy away from excessive dependence on borrowing for consumption towards strategic investments in production, productivity and enterprise development. At the centre of the agenda is a proposed US$10 billion, five-year domestic investment framework intended to attract and mobilise private capital into strategic sectors. Half of the proposed investment is expected to go into commercial agriculture, irrigation infrastructure, agro-processing and agribusiness value chains. Dr Debrah said the initiative was expected to strengthen food security, reduce dependence on food imports, expand manufacturing and create jobs for young people. He urged business leaders to move from business preservation to expansion and from local ambition to continental competitiveness, arguing that government alone could not deliver the country's economic transformation. “Policy can establish the framework. Public investment can provide infrastructure. But it is the private sector that drives sustainable economic growth,” he said. He also called for greater investment in local processing and manufacturing, particularly in agribusiness, pharmaceuticals, textiles and critical minerals. Ghana’s deposits of lithium, manganese, bauxite and gold, he said, presented opportunities for investment in processing, refining and manufacturing rather than continued reliance on raw material exports. He further encouraged businesses to adopt digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital payments and data analytics, while strengthening corporate governance, risk management and environmental sustainability. Minister of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts Abla Dzifa Gomashie called on corporate Ghana to increase investment in tourism, culture and the creative arts, describing the sectors as important sources of employment, foreign exchange and economic growth. She said Ghana’s heritage, festivals, music, film, fashion, gastronomy, hospitality and creative talent represented economic assets that could strengthen the country's international profile. Madam Gomashie urged business leaders to go beyond hiring creative professionals to perform at corporate events and support businesses and institutions operating within the creative economy. “I know that when CEOs organise events, there is always room for performances. But right after the performances, the CEOs forget us. I accepted to come this evening just so I can remind you that we are here for you. Please, do for us too,” she said. She added that investment in the sector could also benefit financial institutions, as creative professionals and entrepreneurs would channel their earnings into the banking system. “When the creative makes money, they bring it to your banks. Remember that when you are thinking about the development of your institutions,” she said. Founder and Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana CEO Vision and Awards, Latif Abubakar, said Ghana’s economic transformation drive must move beyond discussions in boardrooms to practical implementation. He said the private sector had a critical role in attracting investment, creating jobs and stimulating innovation, adding that national development required the collective efforts of government, businesses and other stakeholders. Mr Abubakar said the reset agenda required bold ideas, responsible leadership and strategic partnerships, urging business leaders to help turn the country's challenges into opportunities. Beyond Mr Dadey’s recognition as CEO of CEOs, Mukesh V. Thakwani, Founder and Group Chairman of B5 Plus Group, was named CEO of the Decade, while Dr Maxwell Ampong, Chief Executive Officer of Maxwell Investments Group, received the Promising CEO of the Year award. Dr (Mrs) Maame Yaa Afriye, Chief Executive Officer of St. John’s Hospital and Fertility Centre, was named Female CEO of the Year. Ing. Patricia Obo-Nai, Chief Executive Officer of Telecel Ghana, received the Woman of Excellence award. Ivan Oppong, Chief Executive Officer of Palm Island, received the Discovery of the Year award. Dr Nick Danso Adjei, Chief Executive Officer of Ghana Link Network Services Limited, was named Entrepreneur of the Year, while Dr Daniel McKorley, Founder and Group Chairman of McDan Group, received the Entrepreneur of the Decade award. Eunice Asemnor, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Nehemiah Energy, was named Promising Entrepreneur of the Year. Dr Ishmael Evans Yamson, Board Chairman of MTN Ghana, received the Board Chair of the Year award. Chief Dr Doli-Wura Zakaria of National Investment Bank (NIB) PLC was recognised for Transformational Leadership, while Albert Kwabena Dwumfour, President of the Ghana Journalists Association, received the Outstanding Leadership award.

Title: Tourism Authority shuts down over 20 hotels, restaurants in Ashanti Region over licensing violations
Content: The Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) has shut down more than 20 hotels and restaurants operating within the Kumasi and Konongo enclaves in the Ashanti Region for operating without valid licences. The affected establishments, comprising both locally and foreign-owned businesses, were found to be operating without obtaining or renewing their operating licences from the Authority. Ashanti Regional Director of the Ghana Tourism Authority, Frederick Rudolf-Adjei, explained that prior to the shutdown, he had personally visited some of the affected establishments and urged their management to visit the Authority's office to initiate the licensing process, but they failed to comply. “I personally visited some of these facilities and asked them to come to our office to begin the licensing process to enable them to operate legally. However, they failed to heed the warning, compelling us to shut them down. They can only resume operations after acquiring the required licences,” he said. The Authority has commenced a 21-day enforcement exercise to clamp down on hospitality facilities operating without the requisite permits. About 13 facilities were shut down in Kumasi, while more than eight others were closed in Konongo as part of the exercise. Mr Adjei warned that all facilities served with closure notices were prohibited from operating until they regularised their licensing status. He cautioned that operators who defy the directive and continue to operate risk apprehension. The Regional Director further urged all businesses within the tourism and hospitality industry to obtain the necessary licences to avoid being shut down during the ongoing enforcement exercise. He also disclosed that the operation had uncovered some establishments that had previously obtained licences but failed to renew them, describing such businesses as being in violation of the Authority's regulations.
