Title: Obasanjo, Kufuor and Mahama join UK delegation to mobilise investment for Africa’s infrastructure1 hour
Content: Africa’s quest to close its estimated US$170 billion annual infrastructure financing gap will take centre stage in Accra as Powered by Africa (PBA) 2026 convenes approximately 100 influential political leaders, investors, business executives and infrastructure pioneers from 17–21 November 2026. The gathering seeks to address one of the continent’s most pressing development challenges by connecting investment capital, political influence and global expertise with opportunities across Africa. Beyond convening political and business leaders, Powered by Africa is positioning itself as an international platform for turning Africa's economic potential into tangible development outcomes. Headquartered in the United Kingdom and Accra, the initiative seeks to mobilise institutional investment, diaspora wealth and international partnerships while strengthening African ownership of the industries and infrastructure that will shape the continent's future. A high-level UK delegation will lead Powered by Africa 2026, comprising Helen Grant OBE MP, Chair of Powered by Africa; Baroness Patricia Scotland KC; and Abena Oppong-Asare MP. They will be joined by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, Patron of Powered by Africa; former Ghanaian President John Agyekum Kufuor; and President John Dramani Mahama. President Obasanjo is expected to officially open the initiative at the AfCFTA Secretariat on 18 November 2026, while Presidents Mahama and Kufuor are expected to address the Infrastructure and Investment Conference on 19 November 2026. Addressing the need for stronger collaboration to unlock Africa’s infrastructure potential, Samuel Kasumu, Founder, Convenor and Campaign Director of Powered by Africa, highlighted the importance of aligning political commitment, global partnerships and local enterprise. "Africa's future cannot be built in isolation, and neither can its infrastructure ambitions be realised through capital alone. We need political leadership, international partnerships and African enterprise working together towards a common purpose. "Powered by Africa is about bringing those forces into the same room and turning shared ambition into investments that change lives and economies," he stated. The flagship Infrastructure and Investment Conference on 19 November 2026 will provide a platform to discuss mobilising capital and accelerating development across critical sectors, including energy, transport, real estate, digital infrastructure, and industrialisation. The discussions will explore how international investors, development finance institutions, African businesses and the diaspora can work together to unlock opportunities, strengthen indigenous enterprise and address the continent's infrastructure financing challenges. A defining feature of the gathering will be the unveiling of the Powered by Africa 100: The Most Influential Africans in Infrastructure, a continental recognition initiative celebrating 100 individuals whose investments, innovations and leadership are shaping Africa's infrastructure and industrial development. Representing more than 20 African countries, the featured leaders include Ghanaian industrialists and business figures Ibrahim Mahama, Daniel McKorley (McDan), Solomon Asamoah, Moses Kwesi Baiden Jr. and Emelia Akumah, alongside other influential figures driving progress across the continent. On the significance of the Power List, Kasumu said the individuals being recognised represent the kind of African leadership and enterprise needed to shape the continent's economic future and contribute to global development. "The next chapter of the global economy must be one in which Africans are not simply consumers of infrastructure and industries built elsewhere, but owners, financiers, innovators and builders. The people featured on the Powered by Africa 100 are demonstrating that this is possible. "Their contributions are not only transforming communities and economies across Africa; they are helping to shape industries, create solutions and influence the wider world. We want their work recognised, their influence amplified and their achievements connected to even greater opportunities," he added. The five-day gathering will culminate in a prestigious black-tie gala on 20th November 2026, coinciding with the United Nations' Africa Industrialisation Day. The gala will formally unveil the Powered by Africa 100 and celebrate the individuals advancing infrastructure investment and industrial transformation across the continent. "With approximately 250 participants expected across the programme, Powered by Africa aims to establish a lasting platform for collaboration, investment and partnerships that move Africa closer to becoming a greater beneficiary of its own wealth and economic potential.

Title: When budgets are used for propaganda and not planning – The Interesting case of Democratic Ghana1 hour
Content: In the simplest terms,a budget is a financial plan for a set period (like a month or year) that tracks expected income versus expenses, helping individuals, businesses, or governments manage money, set priorities, and achieve financial goals by ensuring spending aligns with resources, preventing debt, and allocating funds for savings or specific purposes. It acts as a roadmap for your money, showing where it comes from (income) and where it goes (expenses).This is an Investopedia definition, but it will suffice for the purposes of this citizen discourse For the life of any business or government that runs well, budgets are tools used for planning. They give the business an opportunity to conceive ideas and devise strategies based on a certain future prediction or expectation. If today Ghana sets for itself a vision for 2050, it envisages what it wants to see of Ghana by that time. Such a vision may have qualitative and quantitative expectations. For instance, the vision could have a dream to halve illiteracy by 50%, eradicate poverty by that time or achieve 100% electricity access to every Ghanaian. Permit my use of these elementary examples so you can follow me on this journey. That vision will then be broken down into yearly deliverables, with the expectation that as the yearly allocations of the plans are executed, they will all together count towards a certain cumulative result by the end of the program. The yearly portion of the overall strategy is then broken into monetary units so it can be easily measured. The 1992 Constitution(Article 179 )  gave us a lot of prescriptions that require Parliament to ensure that we have a national budget and that planning is ingrained into our national life. Section 21 of the Public Financial Management Act ( PFM ) is one such Act, and there are many other pieces of legislation that exist primarily to enforce this planning into our lives. Like the many other laws on statute books, our politicians have found ways to implement it their way. The PFM requires the Minister of Finance to lay a budget before Parliament in November so that the House can review and approve it before the start of the fiscal year in January. The format for the budget is set by the Act, and the Minister is required to present, among other things, the Annual Report on the Petroleum Funds, in accordance with Section 48 of the Petroleum Revenue Management Act, 2011 (Act 815), as amended; and the Annual Report on the Collection and Utilisation of the African Union Import Levy, in line with Section 7 of the African Union Import Levy Act, 2017 (Act 952 etc. The entire budget is sometimes a whole volume and, together with its appendices, can be a time-consuming script to read. It may be technical and requires time and some basic financial literacy to appreciate the hidden weaknesses, political promises and the aspirations of the government under whose authority the budget is presented. Interestingly enough, the budgets have not identified their connection to the “National Plan”, which I believe the NDPC has done. I know for a fact that the government that left power in 2024 did not give that much credence to the NDPC’s plan because the plan had been made by a government that came before it. That is one beautiful mess of our democracy. The two main parties, the NDC and NPP, cannot even agree on what the common good for Ghana is. Let me not digress. In modern times, you see a lot of social media leaflets and snippets of the budget that are purposely reproduced by the “party communication people” for “citizens” and are shared on many social media platforms. These usually show revenue expected, expenses planned and then most importantly, “infrastructure projects”, which are usually the catchy areas that most people look at. Sometimes you see very nice artist impressions of the planned projects. If there is a planned tax bill in the offing, these messages will also have some background vibes to convince people to support the move – C, D and E- levy, etc.) It is interesting to note that most of the projects (Infrastructure and programs) that appear in our budgets never get executed and nothing is said about them when the budget comes for review. So, I would expect that when the 2017 Midyear budget promised a railway Line from Accra to Paga, and it did not happen, the Minister would ordinarily explain to Parliament in November 2017, when the 2018 Budget was being laid, why the Rail project did not happen, whether it was a case of revenue that was not met or something else. Typically, the current budget should seek to give some background as to why targets in the previous ones were missed, and that should inform the outlook for the current one. In our case, however, it appears that ministers and their sponsoring government can put in all manner of projects in a budget and read it in Parliament, knowing fully well that the projects won’t be done and they know for sure Parliament would not do anything about it.But for fear of being summoned before Parliament, I dare say that the Parliamentary Oversight on the Budget is very weak and requires some improvement. The ICAG and relevant bodies must take interest and ensure the budget becomes an active, real document and not just a piece of paper meant to mark an event and then we go back to sleep. If you almost concluded on the 2017 Mid-Year Budget alone, just go back to last year’s 2025 Mid-Year Budget (Paragraph 211, Page 32) and see the numerous projects that were outlined. They never saw the light of day, and nothing was said about them in the 2026 budget presented in November of last year. I am not here to condemn Ato or his predecessors because these examples abound in all the budget documents from 2016, when I started following this discourse with passion, but I do believe the structure and format of our budgets as presented to Parliament serve more of a cosmetic, mischievous, propaganda purpose than one meant to guide planning and to give some form of accountability to citizens, whose representatives sadly approve the budget all the time.I take a look at the  2025 Mid-Year Budget Statement, the 2026 Budget Statement and the most recently read budget for 2027-2030 statement and will identify a few themes, projects that get lost from the successive budget. In some instances, the macro targets even get misreported.  In the 2025 Budget, for instance, the government sets out to launch the “Nkoko nkitinkiti” project and a budget of close to GHS 400 million is voted for the program. It is only fair that the 2026 budget reports on the program and its results, lessons learnt and any modifications for the coming year. If it is being withdrawn, those who approve the expenditure must know. It is also a fair expectation to see progress made on the BIG Push Infrastructure program and the projects that were being funded under that budget head. How many of those roads are at what stage of completion, and how much more money will the people’s representatives be required to approve to complete the projects? If these do not appear in the subsequent budgets, what message is being sent to the people who approved the budget? These are but a few areas I have selected for the purposes of this article to highlight the silent disconnect in our planning documents These are a few observations that run through the three budget statements used, but the trend has been consistent in previous budget statements, subsequent mid-year reviews and the budgets for the ensuing years. There are themes that disappear, deadlines that shift and numbers that sometimes do not reconcile Other observations worth noting These observations do not make the budgets unfit for use, nor do they condemn their appropriateness or sufficiency in terms of meeting the statutory requirements. Consistency is required to measure progress, and so a good budget reporting practice would require us to identify themes and programs against which targets are set, measured and reported. In our case, we have a lot of inconsistencies, and it makes tracking our progress very difficult. This is a call for some reform at the budget preparation and reporting level to rid it of too much “political “ loose talk and propaganda and make them useful planning documents. Yaw Owusu-Brefo is a member of the ICAG and a resident in East Legon Hills. (0208216936)

Title: Open Letter To the Government: Who’s protecting young Ghanaians travelling to Russia? Are they safe?
Content: Dear President John Dramani Mahama and Honourable Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister for Foreign Affairs, I write as a concerned Ghanaian journalist, increasingly worried about reports of young Ghanaians being lured into the Russia-Ukraine war, with some losing their lives, others ending up as prisoners of war and several more remaining missing. My concern is not about Ghana's diplomatic relations with Russia or an attempt to discourage legitimate educational and employment opportunities abroad, in general. It is about the responsibility of government to protect Ghanaian citizens, particularly young people who may be vulnerable to deception and exploitation. My question is simple but urgent: What specific safety and security alerts are being given to young Ghanaians travelling to Russia, particularly students and beneficiaries of scholarship programmes, to ensure they do not become victims of recruitment networks allegedly luring foreigners into the war? This question has become even more pertinent following the disturbing revelations about Ghanaians who have died or gone missing in the conflict and the recent departure of scholarship beneficiaries to Russia. The frightening numbers we cannot ignore This is no longer speculation. Ghana's own Foreign Affairs Minister, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has repeatedly confirmed the scale of the problem following engagements with Ukrainian authorities. In February 2026, following his visit to Ukraine, the Minister disclosed that at least 55 Ghanaians had been killed while fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war,with two others being held as prisoners of war. He also revealed that approximately 272 Ghanaians had been lured into the conflict since 2022 through transnational recruitment networks. Across Africa, an estimated 1,780 people from 36 countries were believed to have been recruited to fight for Russia. Some of the affected Ghanaians were reportedly attracted by opportunities advertised as civilian employment, including construction, hospitality, logistics and security jobs, only to find themselves involved in the war. The situation became even more troubling in August 2026 when Mr Ablakwa disclosed that the number of Ghanaians killed had risen to 62, with another 15 missing. Read Also:62 Ghanaians killed, 15 missing in Russia-Ukraine war – Ablakwa Speaking during his visit to Russia, the Minister reiterated Ghana's concerns and efforts to engage Russian authorities to address the situation. His position was particularly emphatic: "This is not our war, and it should not be claiming Ghanaian lives." These are not merely statistics. They represent families whose sons, brothers, husbands and relatives may never return home. They represent young people who may have travelled in search of better economic opportunities but ended up fighting in a war in which Ghana has no stake. The government must therefore move beyond expressing concern and prioritise preventive measures. John Dumelo's scholarship initiative: An opportunity, but are the necessary precautions being taken? My immediate concern was heightened by the recent announcement by the Member of Parliament for Ayawaso West Wuogon and Deputy Minister for Food and Agriculture, John Dumelo, that the first batch of beneficiaries under his scholarship initiative had departed Ghana for Russia to pursue further studies. The initiative is expected to support more than 40 students by the end of 2027. The effort could be viewed as commendable. At a time when many Ghanaian families struggle to finance tertiary education, providing young people with opportunities to study abroad deserves recognition. However, while I welcomed the announcement, I could not help but ask some uncomfortable questions. What happens when these young people arrive in Russia? Who takes responsibility for their safety beyond providing scholarships and admission arrangements? Have they received adequate security orientation about the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and reports of foreign nationals being lured into the Russian military? Have they been warned about individuals or organisations that may approach them with attractive financial offers, employment opportunities or promises of a better life in exchange for signing military contracts? Do they know that some Ghanaians reportedly travelled to Russia for civilian employment but eventually ended up on the battlefield? Have their sponsors established reliable channels through which their welfare can be monitored throughout their stay? And have their parents and guardians been informed about the potential risks and provided with emergency contacts should anything go wrong? I raise these questions without suggesting that Mr Dumelo's scholarship initiative is connected in any way to the reported recruitment activities. There is no basis for such an allegation. My concern is that a good educational opportunity can become a vulnerable entry point for exploitation if beneficiaries are not adequately prepared and protected. The fact that these young people are travelling primarily to study does not automatically make them immune to approaches by individuals seeking to exploit their financial circumstances, ambitions or unfamiliarity with the country. I would therefore expect that every Ghanaian public official, institution or individual facilitating educational opportunities in Russia works closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ghana's diplomatic mission to ensure that beneficiaries receive proper security briefings before departure. The question is whether we are doing enough to ensure they return safely after completing their studies. Ghana-Russia labour recruitment agreement: Are adequate safeguards in place? My concerns are further heightened by another development reported by Citi Newsroom on October 29, 2026. According to the report, Ghana signed an agreement with Russia to facilitate the recruitment of Ghanaian workers for industrial and manufacturing jobs. The agreement was signed by Labour Minister Emmanuel Agyekum and the director of Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, an industrial hub comprising 48 companies with a reported requirement for more than 75,000 workers. Alabuga is a name known to many.Stories have been published about young women being tricked into going to Alabuga to work in drone factories used by Russia to attack Ukraine. Under the arrangement, Ghana's Labour Ministry is expected to coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation to safeguard the interests of Ghanaian workers. While creating legitimate employment opportunities for young Ghanaians is commendable, the timing of this agreement raises important questions that the government must address. Considering the disturbing reports of Ghanaians being lured to Russia with promises of lucrative civilian employment before allegedly ending up on the battlefield, what additional safeguards have been incorporated into this agreement to prevent a recurrence? What specific companies will employ the Ghanaian workers, what jobs will they perform, and who will independently verify their employment contracts and working conditions? Will the government ensure that every prospective worker understands the nature of the job, the terms of engagement, their rights and the procedures for leaving employment should the circumstances differ from what was promised? More importantly, what guarantees exist that these workers will not be approached, pressured or deceived into signing military contracts after arriving in Russia? The Labour Minister's assurance that the Ministry will verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation is important. But given what Ghana has already experienced, I believe the government must go further by establishing independent monitoring, accessible complaint mechanisms and clear protections against any attempt to recruit these workers into military service. We cannot be facilitating the movement of Ghanaian workers to Russia through official government arrangements without first demonstrating that we have put adequate safeguards in place to protect them. The opportunity to work abroad should never become a pathway to a foreign battlefield. Ukraine's warning should not be taken lightly Ghana has received warnings from Ukrainian authorities about the dangers facing its citizens in Russia. During his February 2026 visit to Kyiv, Mr Ablakwa held discussions with his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, who raised concerns about the recruitment of African nationals into the Russian military. The Ukrainian Foreign Minister warned that Africans, including Ghanaians, were being drawn into the conflict through deceptive recruitment arrangements. More recently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, identified Ghana among 47 countries whose citizens, he said, were being used in Russia's war against Ukraine. Read Also:‘Do not let Russia pay for its madness with lives of your people’ – Zelensky to Ghana, 46 other countries He urged the affected countries to protect their nationals and prevent them from ending up on the battlefield, highlighting the use of deception and other tactics to recruit foreign nationals. Ghana was specifically mentioned. What more warning does our government need to appreciate the urgency of this situation? Is Ghana doing enough to alert prospective travellers? The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously issued travel advisories cautioning Ghanaians against travelling to conflict areas and warning them about middlemen and agents who promise employment and other opportunities in countries experiencing armed conflict. But the circumstances have since become even more alarming. We now have official figures indicating that dozens of Ghanaians have died, others are missing, and some have been captured as prisoners of war. The question is whether the Ministry has moved beyond general travel advisories to a targeted and sustained public education campaign addressing the dangers facing Ghanaians travelling to Russia. How many prospective students are aware of the reported recruitment tactics? How many scholarship beneficiaries have been reached? How many travel agencies, universities and educational facilitators have been engaged? And how many parents and guardians have been sensitised? It is not enough for the Ministry to issue statements on its website or social media platforms and assume that everyone who needs the information has received it. A warning is only useful when it reaches the people it is intended to protect. It is also important to acknowledge that Russia has rejected allegations of deliberately recruiting African nationals unlawfully into its military. Russian Ambassador to Ghana, Andrei Ordash, has maintained that foreign nationals can voluntarily enlist through contractual arrangements under Russian law. However, the concern is not simply that a Ghanaian may voluntarily choose to join a foreign military. It is that people travelling in search of legitimate civilian employment or educational opportunities could allegedly be deceived, coerced or manipulated into participating in a war. Ghana cannot leave the protection of its citizens entirely to assurances from foreign governments. Putin's assurance: Is that enough? At the recent Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, President John Dramani Mahama raised Ghana's concerns about recruiting its citizens into the Russia-Ukraine war during bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to the Ghanaian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, President Putin gave an assurance that Ghanaians would no longer be permitted to participate in the war. The commitment, as communicated by the Ghanaian government, is expected to address both irregular recruitment arrangements and voluntary enlistment. The development is welcome, and President Mahama deserves commendation for raising an issue that has caused so much pain to Ghanaian families. However, is President Putin's assurance sufficient reason for Ghana to relax its vigilance and allow its citizens, particularly young people, to continue travelling to Russia without comprehensive security education and precautionary measures? A diplomatic assurance, however significant, must be followed by practical measures, monitoring and accountability. The government must also ensure that recruitment networks allegedly operating to lure unsuspecting Africans are identified and dismantled. What happens to the 15 Ghanaians reported missing? What about those already in captivity or serving in the Russian military? How will Ghana verify that the commitment announced after the summit is being implemented? What I expect the government to do Mr President and Honourable Minister, I believe the time has come for Ghana to introduce a more deliberate security education programme for all Ghanaians travelling to Russia. Specifically, I would respectfully suggest the following: These measures are not intended to discourage legitimate educational or economic relations with Russia. They are intended to ensure that such relations do not expose Ghanaian citizens to preventable dangers. Our young people deserve opportunities, but above all, they deserve protection Ghana has every right to pursue diplomatic, economic and educational partnerships with Russia. There is nothing inherently wrong with Ghanaian students travelling there to acquire knowledge, build careers and contribute to national development. But we must not let the excitement around international opportunities overshadow the realities confronting some of our citizens. When 62 Ghanaians have reportedly died, and 15 others are missing in a foreign war, we cannot afford to treat the matter as an ordinary diplomatic disagreement. When the Ukrainian President has specifically mentioned Ghana among countries whose citizens are allegedly being lured into the conflict, our response must go beyond statements of concern. And when our own Foreign Affairs Minister acknowledges that criminal networks are exploiting young Ghanaians through deceptive employment arrangements, the government must ensure that prospective travellers understand those dangers before leaving the country. I am particularly worried that, in our enthusiasm to promote international educational opportunities, we may be overlooking the need to educate young people about the security implications of travelling to a country involved in an active war. A scholarship should be an opportunity to acquire an education, not an avenue through which a young person becomes vulnerable to exploitation. A job offer should provide an opportunity to earn a living, not become a deceptive pathway to the battlefield. Mr President and Honourable Minister, Ghanaians should not have to choose between pursuing opportunities abroad and remaining safe. The government must find a way to guarantee both. My question, therefore, remains: Following the deaths, disappearances and imprisonment of several Ghanaians in the Russia-Ukraine war, what specific safety and security alerts are being given to young Ghanaians travelling to Russia today, and what concrete measures are in place to ensure they are not lured into this war? President Putin may have given his assurance, but can Ghana afford to simply look on and watch its young people travel to Russia without first ensuring that they understand the risks and know how to protect themselves? I believe the answer should be an emphatic no. We have already lost too many lives. We should not wait for another Ghanaian family to receive devastating news before taking preventive action. The government's responsibility is not only to negotiate the safe return of citizens who have fallen victim to dangerous circumstances. It is also to prevent more citizens from becoming victims in the first place. Our young people deserve opportunities. But above all, they deserve to live long enough to benefit from them. Yours in the interest of Ghana and the protection of its citizens,

Title: Religion must not become a pawn in geopolitical power plays
Content: Religion has always played an important role in Ghanaian society. Churches have contributed to education, healthcare, community development and the moral upbringing of generations. They have supported vulnerable people and helped strengthen communities. Ghana's tradition of religious freedom and peaceful coexistence is an important national asset that must be protected. However, protecting religious freedom also means paying attention to how religious institutions operate, particularly when foreign organisations seek to expand their influence. One development deserving attention is the growing presence of the Russian Orthodox Church in Africa and its emerging links with religious and educational institutions in Ghana. This is not an argument against Christianity, foreign churches or anyone's right to worship. It is a recognition that religion, like other influential institutions, can sometimes become a channel for advancing political and geopolitical interests. Why the Russian Orthodox Church deserves attention In December 2021, the Russian Orthodox Church established its Patriarchal Exarchate of Africa, following a disagreement with the Orthodox Church of Alexandria over the recognition of the independent Orthodox Church of Ukraine. The move brought 102 clergy from eight African countries under Moscow's authority, according to Interfax'sreporton the establishment. Ghana was included among the countries placed under the Exarchate's declared pastoral responsibility. The Church has alsoreportedsending African students to Moscow for theological education. In December 2023, for example,nine students from four African countriesarrived at the Moscow Theological Academy. International religious partnerships are not unusual. Churches have long worked across borders to exchange knowledge, train clergy and support missionary activities. Such relationships can be beneficial when based on genuine faith, mutual respect and transparency. However, the circumstances surrounding the Russian Orthodox Church's expansion deserve closer attention. Its establishment of separate church structures across Africa has raised questions about church authority, jurisdiction and the wider implications of its activities. There is also the historically close relationship between the Moscow Patriarchate and the Russian government. A 2022 academicstudypublished in the journal “Religions” examined how the Russian Church and government have worked together to promote shared social and political interests internationally. Similarly, Georgetown University'sBerkley Centrehas examined the Church's role in Russia's international soft-power strategy. These studies do not establish that every Russian Orthodox activity is politically motivated. However, they demonstrate why the relationship between religious institutions and state interests deserves attention. When religion becomes a tool of influence Concerns about the political use of religious institutions are not merely theoretical. In September 2025,Reuterspublished an investigation into allegations that Russia used Moscow-linked Orthodox Church networks in Moldova to influence political opinion ahead of parliamentary elections. The investigation reported alleged payments to some clergy and coordinated messaging against European integration. Church officials denied political motives, describing the activities differently. Although this involved Moldova and does not establish similar activities in Ghana or elsewhere in Africa, it illustrates how religious networks can potentially become channels for political influence. These concerns provide reason for Ghanaian religious leaders and citizens to approach foreign religious engagements with informed caution.My particular concern is the potential impact on young Christians. For many young people, the Church is more than a place of worship. It provides spiritual guidance, education, mentorship and a sense of belonging. This gives religious institutions considerable influence over how the next generation understands society and the wider world. Young Christians receiving theological training through foreign institutions should understand who runs these organisations, where their funding comes from and what values they promote. Religious education must strengthen faith, encourage independent thinking and develop responsible Christian leaders. Young people should never unknowingly become instruments in political or ideological projects disguised as religious opportunities. Transparency and accountability are essential The answer to these concerns is not fear, hostility or discrimination. It is transparency and accountability. Whenever foreign religious organisations seek to establish churches, recruit students, train clergy or partner with local institutions, there should be clarity about their leadership, funding, affiliations and objectives. Local churches and theological institutions must carefully examine potential international partners and ensure that agreements protect their independence. The spiritual needs of Ghanaian congregations must remain the priority, not the interests of external organisations or their political partners. Government, civil society, academia and the media also have a role in promoting informed public discussion and ensuring that all religious organisations operate within Ghana's laws. Such scrutiny must be fair and consistent. It should not target particular nationalities or denominations. Every religious organisation, local or foreign, must respect the same standards of accountability and Ghana's sovereignty. Religious freedom must come with responsibility Ultimately, the question is not whether foreign churches should be welcomed in Ghana. They should be free to contribute to our religious and social development, provided they respect our laws, institutions and independence. The real question is whether we are sufficiently informed and prepared to ensure that their presence serves genuine spiritual and social purposes. Religious freedom does not mean religious institutions should operate without accountability. Equally, asking questions about their activities is not religious intolerance. Ghana must protect the independence of its religious institutions and preserve the trust communities place in them. Our churches must remain places of faith, service, fellowship and hope, not channels for advancing the geopolitical interests of foreign powers. Our faith must not become a weapon in someone else's power struggle. The Church must never become a pawn in geopolitical power plays. President, Anglican Young People's Association (AYPA), St. Peter Anglican Church, Nungua, Accra Diocese

Title: A heritage special
Content: On the day the government’s 24-hour economy began losing its hours to a “New Economy”, the Bank of Ghana unveiled new money to celebrate our heritage. The finance minister was changing the name of the future while the governor was changing the faces of the past. A full day’s work, even if we can no longer account for all 24 hours. In Ghana, when a public decision makes no sense, ask who stands to profit. It is not to suggest wrongdoing. It is simply a useful point at which to request the invoice. What particular anniversary required this celebration? What made it a priority now? The Bank cited security and durability. Fair enough. But why did the Big Six group portrait have to go? Were the gentlemen helping counterfeiters? Our history is certainly larger than six men. Many others deserve recognition. But a country should be able to enlarge its memory without first conducting an eviction. The President’s own memory also deserves preservation. In opposition, Mr Mahama condemned the introduction of GH¢100 and GH¢200 notes. Why introduce higher denominations when Ghana was heading towards a cashless economy? Now he has unveiled redesigned versions of those same notes. Of course, introducing denominations and redesigning them are different exercises, but his enthusiasm deserves an explanation. Apparently, the road to a cashless economy passes through a printing press, provided one is travelling in a presidential convoy. Then came the history lesson. The Bank said the woman on the GH¢50 note is Theodosia Okoh. Her nephew disputed the likeness. The Bank explains that photographs were combined and her familiar head-tie replaced with a hairstyle, producing a resemblance to her sister. I call this national gaslighting: the portrait needs correcting, but the public is being asked to adjust its eyesight. Eii!!! We invited Theodosia Okoh onto our currency, sent her to the makeup salon, and are now asking the family to identify who came out. The woman who gave us our unmistakable flag has been honoured with a face that requires a press release. Then there is the Zimbabwean model whose image appears in the market scene on the GH¢1 note. She visited Makola once and ended up on our currency. Generations of Ghanaian market women must wonder why nobody mentioned this opportunity. The Big Six have lost their group portrait, while a visitor has secured a place in our national imagery. Our heritage is evidently more accessible to tourists than we realised. One hopes the Tourism Authority is taking notes: “Visit Ghana. You may leave as legal tender.” Presiding over this exercise is a Governor whose criminal charges were withdrawn by the Attorney-General. That is not to suggest wrongdoing. It certainly does not relieve him of the duty to account. The questions about this exercise cannot also be withdrawn by a nolle prosequi. How much did it cost? Who received the contracts? Who researched the images? Who approved the designs? When did the work begin, and what explains the timetable? Surely the portraits could have been checked with a little more diligence before they were presented to us. It is generally cheaper to correct a photograph before printing money around it. But perhaps this is the heritage we are celebrating: launch first, answer questions later, and issue a press release when somebody notices the mistakes. We have certainly preserved that tradition. A comedy of errors indeed! But before we applaud, let us see the bill.

Title: The future of banking in Ghana: Why execution matters in the digital age
Content: Banking in Ghana is changing as more customers use digital channels to make payments, transfer funds, manage accounts and conduct business. Electronic payments, real-time services, and interoperable platforms now play a greater role in everyday economic activity, increasing demand for high-quality, reliable, and secure financial services. According to the Bank of Ghana’s2025 Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report, emerging technologies, changing customer behaviour, and collaboration across the financial sector have supported more efficient, secure, and accessible payment channels. The Bank’sFinTech Sector Report for the First Quarter of 2025also recorded increases in mobile money transaction values and volumes compared with the corresponding period in 2024. Digital banking can reduce barriers created by distance and extend services to more individuals and businesses. Its value, however, depends on how effectively financial institutions turn technology into secure, reliable, and accessible customer experiences. A new platform achieves little if customers cannot complete a transaction, obtain help when something goes wrong or trust that their money and information are secure. Digital Banking at the Centre of Customer Experience Customers increasingly expect to transfer funds, make payments and manage their accounts without visiting a branch. Businesses expect services that help them operate efficiently, monitor cash flow and make decisions using current information. When these services are difficult to use, the consequences can extend beyond inconvenience. A delayed transaction can affect a household obligation, supplier payment or business opportunity. Customers judge a digital service primarily by whether it works when they need it. Branches and human interaction still have an important role. Some customers need help with complex decisions, disputed transactions, or services that cannot be completed effectively through digital channels. A strong service model should make routine banking easy digitally while keeping employees accessible when customers need explanation or support. The experience should remain coherent whether a customer uses a mobile device, contacts a service centre or visits a branch. Technology Does Not Guarantee Better Banking A successful digital programme converts investment into better customer and business outcomes. Execution begins with identifying a specific customer problem. Before introducing a service or feature, an institution must establish who needs it, what difficulty it addresses and what outcome will show that it is working. Consider the full customer journey. A digital onboarding process may look successful based on how many customers start it. A better assessment considers completion rates, time to completion, where customers abandon it, and whether help is available. Performance after launch matters equally. Transaction success rates, service availability, complaint volumes, resolution times and sustained customer use provide a clearer view of whether a service creates value. An ambitious digital strategy will still disappoint customers if services are unreliable, difficult to navigate or poorly supported. Effective execution also depends on alignment across the organisation. Technology teams may build a platform, but operations, risk, compliance, customer service, product teams and frontline employees all shape the experience. Manage digital transformation as a business priority, with clear ownership and measurable outcomes. Moving an inefficient process to a digital channel won't fix its underlying weaknesses. Inclusion Requires More Than Digital Access Ghana’s expanding digital-finance system can extend services to people and businesses with limited access to traditional banking infrastructure, reducing the time, distance and cost involved. Digital access does not amount to full financial inclusion. A customer may have access to a payment channel without suitable savings, credit, insurance or investment services. Others may remain excluded because of connectivity costs, limited digital or financial literacy, documentation requirements, unreliable infrastructure or concerns about fraud. Assess inclusion by the value customers obtain. They need to understand a service, afford it, use it safely, and get help when needed. Registrations or downloads give an incomplete picture without evidence of sustained use and customer outcomes. Digital services must also account for differences in language, literacy, ability, and familiarity with technology. Data, Artificial Intelligence and the Next Phase of Banking Artificial intelligence and data analysis may help institutions provide more relevant information, identify unusual transactions and support faster credit assessments. Their value will depend on the quality of the data and the controls governing its use. An automated decision may be flawed if its reasoning cannot be explained or its outcome unfairly disadvantages customers. Personalisation may also become intrusive when customers do not understand how their information is used. Institutions will need clear standards for privacy, consent, fairness and human oversight. Accountability must remain with the institution, even when technology informs or automates a decision. Embedded finance is also likely to grow, with commercial platforms offering payment and credit services. This may improve access, but it can also make financial commitments less visible to customers. Clear disclosure and appropriate consumer protection will remain necessary as financial services become more closely integrated into everyday transactions. Trust Will Determine Sustainable Adoption The Bank of Ghana’sNational Payment Systems Strategy 2025–2029identifies interoperability, centralised fraud monitoring, stronger information sharing and enhanced security controls among the country’s payment-system priorities. Customers must believe that their money is safe, their information is protected, and their financial institution will respond effectively when something goes wrong. Financial institutions must strengthen fraud detection, cybersecurity, system resilience and incident-response capabilities as risks change. Customers also need practical information to recognise suspicious requests, protect their credentials and use authorised channels. Education cannot replace effective institutional controls or shift primary security responsibility to customers. Reliability also affects trust. Customers are more likely to continue using digital services when transactions are completed consistently, information is accurate, and failures are resolved promptly. An institution’s response to a failed transaction or suspected fraud can influence confidence as much as the original service. Ghana does not lack digital ambition. The harder task is turning that ambition into services customers can use reliably, understand clearly, and trust with their money. Execution quality will determine whether digital banking merely adds more channels or builds a financial system that works better for the people and businesses it is meant to serve. Francis Amoako, Head of Strategy and Execution, Absa Bank Ghana LTD

Title: Rashid Seidu writes: Madina at the crossroads – Why Siidi must go unopposed
Content: Madina is tired of waiting. Tired of promises that fade after the votes are counted, and of roads, jobs and hope that never arrive. Now, as 2028 draws near, the constituency has one question to answer: who will finally deliver? I have spent time listening to the people. I have sat with elders, youth, traders, students and party faithful across Madina. Whatever the neighbourhood, the answer is the same: *Siidi Abubakar Musah. According to the significant number of people I have engaged so far, they are all calling for him. They describe him as a good man with a good heart, whose hand has touched many lives, both nationally and here at home in Madina. Then they add the part that stops you: he did all of it quietly, in secret, without a camera, a banner or a request for applause. In politics, that is rare. Most people announce their generosity. Siidi simply gets on with it. A man who is already built? Too many seekers of office arrive with a personal project: a house to build, a fortune to secure, a name to polish. By the time they remember the people, the energy is spent. Siidi comes the other way round. He does not need Madina to build him. He is already built, and what he has left to give, he wants to give to Madina. A door that never closes? Ask the young people of this constituency what Siidi has meant to them. Many will tell you of education he supported, businesses he helped start and government jobs he helped them reach. For the people of Madina he has become the lender of last resort. When a family has nowhere left to turn, they turn to him. When he cannot solve a problem immediately, he does not shrug and send them away. He makes the call, pulls every string and knocks on every door until a way opens. That comes from character, and no campaign stage can fake it. A record the youth wing still feels? As National Youth Organizer, Siidi turned the party’s youth wing into a place young people were proud to belong to. He raised literacy among them, and he opened pathways for many young members into the security services. His impact left a mark that keeps the youth wing attractive today. A man who could energize the youth of a whole nation can surely awaken the youth of Madina. Why must Siidi Abubakar Musah be made to run unopposed? A bruising contest would leave wounds that take years to heal, and the NDC family in Madina needs healing more than it needs another fight. Siidi is the one figure who can gather the elders, the women, the youth and the grassroots under one tent. Heading into 2028, he is the candidate best placed to bring in the votes, and a resounding win in Madina will echo across the nation. Dear Discerning stakeholdersTo the elders, executives and opinion leaders of Madina, this moment will not wait for us. Protect it. Rally behind Siidi, let consensus carry him, and let us offer the constituency the leadership it has long deserved. Madina is at the crossroads. The people have already spoken, and all that remains is for the party to listen.Siidi for Madina MP. Madina for the NDC. Together, we rise!Author: Rashid SeiduResident of Madina, Madina-Washington SDA and Former Madina West UBH Communications Officer

Title: Ghana can grow the rice it eats
Content: I have worked as a rice breeder in Ghana for two decades. In that time, people in Ghana and abroad have often asked me the same question. “If you and your colleagues have released so many good rice varieties and developed technologies to help farmers grow them, why is Ghana still importing rice?” Research can give farmers better varieties and ways to grow them. For that work to make a difference across Ghana, the private sector must invest and the government must put the right policies in place. Even the best variety will make little difference if farmers cannot get seed and fertiliser on time, have no means to expand production or cannot find buyers for the rice they harvest. That is why I welcome the rice measures in the 2027 Budget. The government plans to use public procurement to create a market for Ghana-grown rice, link import licences to verified local purchases and end commercial rice imports by 2030. I believe Ghana can grow the rice it eats. The first thing I would do is buy the rice our farmers have already grown.[1] Rice farmers have taken a hard hit over the past two years. In November 2026, farmers at Asutsuare reported that they still had unsold rice and that some stocks had spoiled. The Peasant Farmers Association of Ghana has reported similar difficulties across major rice-producing regions. Put yourself in the position of a farmer who has paid for seed, fertiliser, labour and harvesting and still has rice sitting in storage. What would persuade you to invest in another crop?[2, 3] The government should release funds now to buy Ghana-grown rice at farm gates, in warehouses and at mills. Where farmers have paddy, the government can work with millers to buy and process it. Milled rice that meets the required standards can go to schools, hospitals, prisons and other public institutions. Prompt payment will help farmers settle their debts, buy inputs and prepare for the next season. While the government buys the rice already in stock, public institutions should estimate what they will need for the next season. The government can then contract farmer groups, millers and rice businesses to supply agreed volumes. Before planting, farmers need to know how much to grow, what price they will receive, what grade they must meet and where to deliver. The requirement to buy Ghana-grown rice should apply when institutions buy through caterers and other contractors as well. The government should set aside the money when it awards the contracts and pay suppliers as soon as their deliveries are accepted. In the same Budget, the Finance Minister announced thatGH¢29 billionwas available for an early redemption offer on Domestic Debt Exchange Programme bonds due in February 2027. The Budget also made specific allocations for road works and maintenance. I would apply the same discipline to rice procurement. Farmers who wait months to be paid can miss the next planting season, even with a contract in hand.[1, 4] A funded purchase contract gives farmers a reason to plant, millers a reason to invest and lenders a basis for financing the next crop. The Minister for Food and Agriculture, Eric Opoku, put Ghana’s annual demand at about1.71 million tonnes of milled rice. He reported that Ghana produced about960,000 tonnesin 2025, or roughly56%of what the country consumes. That leaves a gap of about750,000 tonnesof milled rice.[5, 6] To work out what we need to grow, start with the rice people eat and work back to what farmers harvest. Some paddy is retained for seed, some is lost after harvest, and milling removes the husk and bran. Using the Feed Ghana Programme’s planning assumptions of 65% milling recovery, 13% post-harvest losses and 2.3% retained for seed, Ghana would need to harvest about3.11 million tonnes of paddyto meet the reported demand. Better drying, storage and milling would yield more saleable rice from every tonne harvested.[7] For the land and seed estimates, I use the Ministry of Food and Agriculture’s (MoFA) provisional 2024 baseline of434,266 hectaresunder rice and1.13 million tonnes of paddy. That works out to2.6 tonnes per hectare.[7] At Dawhenya, some of the lead farmers we work with have harvested8 metric tonnes of paddy per hectare, even in seed production fields, where we normally expect lower yields. That shows what our varieties can deliver under good management. National averages reflect growing conditions across all rice farms. In 2023/24, the US Department of Agriculture reported average paddy yields of 7.14 tonnes per hectare in China, 6.12 in Vietnam, 4.32 in India and 2.85 in Thailand.[13]Given the scale of production Ghana needs and the range of conditions farmers will face, I would plan on a national average of4.5 to 5.0 tonnes of paddy per hectare. Land and seed requirements for 1.71 million tonnes of milled rice a year Illustrative estimates using MoFA’s provisional 2024 baseline and Feed Ghana’s paddy-to-milled-rice assumptions. Seed estimates assume 80 kg of certified seed per hectare across the full area.[7, 8] At the provisional 2024 yield of 2.6 tonnes per hectare, Ghana would need to harvest nearly1.2 million hectares a year. At a national average of 4.5 to 5.0 tonnes per hectare, the same demand could be met with about621,000 to 690,000 hectares harvested annually, or roughly 1.53 to 1.71 million acres. That is about half a million fewer hectares than at the 2024 yield. Tanzania shows what bringing more land into production can achieve. In 2023/24, Tanzania’s Ministry of Agriculture reported that harvested rice area rose by 22.4% and the average paddy yield increased from about 3.0 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare. The ministry put rice self-sufficiency at 112% that season. Ghana can expand cultivation on suitable land while raising yields on existing rice farms.[14] The 2027 Budget proposes putting100,000 additional hectaresinto production through rice development hubs, with yields of5 to 6 tonnes per hectarein the hubs. We also need investment in farms outside the hubs. Where irrigation allows two crops a year, the same hectare can contribute two harvests. Both crops need seed, water and a buyer. At a national yield of 4.5 to 5.0 tonnes per hectare, every additional 100,000 tonnes of milled-rice demand would require roughly36,000 to 40,000 more hectares harvested annually. The 2030 plan should be based on what Ghanaians are expected to consume by then.[1, 7] Where will the seed come from? Sowing the full area with certified seed at80 kilograms per hectare, the lower end of MoFA’s recommended rate for broadcasting, would require about49,700 to 55,200 tonnes a year. The final requirement will depend on the area planted, the share sown with certified seed and the mix of broadcasting, drilling and transplanting.[8] Producing certified seed at that scale starts several seasons earlier with breeder and foundation seed. MoFA has set targets for all three classes. The government should use the production plan to determine how much seed of each variety is needed, where and by when. Research institutions need funding in time to produce breeder seed and support foundation seed multiplication. Seed companies with a record of producing quality seed should receive contracts early enough to multiply the seed and allow for inspection and certification.[7] Fertiliser must reach farmers when the crop needs it. Irrigation schemes must provide reliable water by planting time. Farmers need access to extension advice throughout the season, and drying, storage and milling facilities must be ready when the extra paddy comes off the field. Rice farmers also need affordable machinery for land preparation, planting and harvesting. The 2027 Budget allocatesGH¢800 millionto procure machinery for Phase 2 of the government’sFarmer Service Centres. Farmers should be able to book tractors, seed drills and combine harvesters through the centres at published rates. Timely access matters because a farmer who has seed and fertiliser ready can still miss the planting window if the tractor arrives late.[1] We have seen what importers’ distribution networks can do for Ghana-grown rice. During the 2019–2020 push for local rice, Olam brought Ghana-grown jasmine rice to market under the Mama Gold brand, and Wilmar launched local rice under its Fortune and Viking brands. The new policy gives importers a reason to build on that experience.[9, 10, 11] Before issuing an import licence, the government should ask the importer to show where the Ghana-grown rice was produced, how much was bought, where it was delivered and who was paid. Each lot should count only once. If the importer buys paddy, a published conversion rate can establish its milled-rice equivalent. The government can then reduce quotas in step with verified supplies of Ghana-grown rice reaching consumers. The government must also curb rice smuggling. As the General Agricultural Workers’ Union has warned, traders who evade duties and taxes can sell imported rice more cheaply, undercutting Ghanaian producers and importers who pay what they owe. The National Rice Policy calls for stronger customs valuation, border surveillance and enforcement. Customs should increase surveillance at unapproved crossings and check that import permits and duty payments match shipment records.[11, 15] At CSIR and in Ghanaian universities, we have developed improved aromatic rice varieties, most of them jasmine-type. At Dawhenya, we asked farmers and millers to assess improved varieties in the field and after milling. Farmers singled out CRI-Agyapa for its aroma, early maturity and milling performance. The 2027 Budget records that MoFA secured300 tonnes of Agyapa seedthrough KOPIA for subsidised distribution. That is one example of how Ghana’s partnership with the Republic of Korea has helped get varieties developed here into farmers’ fields.[1, 12, 17] When we release a variety, farmers also need to know when and how to plant it and how to manage water, fertiliser, weeds, pests and diseases under local conditions. The work continues after harvest. We need practical ways to thresh on time, dry paddy safely and store and mill it without avoidable losses or damage to grain quality. Researchers should test these practices with farmers and millers and work with extension officers to put the findings into use.[8] Producing rice in Ghana is expensive, and research can help bring costs down. We should test planting methods that save seed or labour, ways to get more from fertiliser and irrigation, and harvesting and milling practices that deliver more saleable rice from the same crop. I would measure the cost per tonne of paddy in farmers’ fields and the cost per tonne of saleable rice at the mill.[11] As rice production expands, we must keep monitoring diseases. When farmers grow a popular variety over large areas, changes in pathogen populations can erode its resistance. Changes in rainfall and temperature can also affect where a variety performs well. Breeding and testing climate-smart varieties under Ghanaian conditions must be part of the production plan. Over the past decade, our rice research and development at CSIR–CRI has relied mainly on funding from international partners. The most consistent support has come from theRural Development Administration (RDA) of the Republic of Korea, which has helped us develop improved varieties and get quality seed to farmers. We value that partnership. Ghana’s government should commit more of its own resources to rice research through predictable, multi-year funding. It takes several seasons to develop and test a variety. By the time farmers need one better suited to their conditions, we should have tested it and be ready to advise farmers on growing it and millers on preserving its quality.[16, 17, 18] When properly dried, stored and milled, Ghana-grown jasmine-type rice matches imported jasmine rice in aroma, taste and grain quality. Most people who have tasted good-quality Ghana-grown rice prefer it to imported rice. Our task now is to make rice of that quality consistently available at a price Ghanaians can afford. By Prof. Maxwell Darko Asante Prof. Maxwell Darko Asante is Director of CSIR–Crops Research Institute, Chief Research Scientist in Rice Breeding, and an AfricaRice Council of Ministers laureate for excellence in rice research and development. 1.Ministry of Finance. 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy, paragraphs 273–287, 1190, 1543 and 1550–1551. 2.3News.
