Title: Ghana’s GH¢28.8 Billion Bond Buyback: A step towards restoring financial confidence
Content: Government’s planned buyback of GH¢28.8 billion in domestic bonds is an important development in Ghana’s continuing effort to restore confidence in its public finances. Although the figures may appear technical, the underlying issue is quite simple. Government is preparing to settle a substantial debt obligation before it becomes due in February 2027. It is a move that deserves attention, not merely because of the amount involved, but because of what it says about the management of public money. To understand the significance of this decision, it is necessary to understand what a government bond is. A bond is essentially a loan. Government borrows money from investors, including banks, pension funds and individuals, with a promise to repay the amount at an agreed date. In return, investors receive interest for allowing Government to use their money. This is a normal feature of modern economies. Governments borrow to finance development, support public services and meet other national obligations. The difficulty arises when borrowing becomes expensive, repayment obligations accumulate and the country struggles to meet its commitments. That was the position Ghana found itself in towards the end of 2022. The Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP) was introduced as part of efforts to address the country’s debt crisis. Government asked holders of certain domestic bonds to exchange their existing investments for new securities with different repayment periods and lower interest rates. In practical terms, investors agreed to receive their money over a longer period and under revised financial conditions. The exercise helped Government reduce immediate pressure on its finances. However, it also placed considerable responsibility on Government to honour the new repayment arrangements. The bonds did not disappear. Their repayment dates simply changed. Some of those obligations are now approaching maturity. Government is therefore preparing to buy back approximately GH¢28.8 billion in DDEP bonds originally scheduled to mature in February 2027. The proposed transaction is intended to settle the bonds ahead of their original repayment date. It is part of a broader debt management exercise designed to address upcoming obligations in an orderly manner. The important question is where the money will come from. During the presentation of the 2027 Budget, Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson announced that Government had accumulated approximately GH¢29 billion in the Cedi Sinking Fund as of November 11, 2026. A sinking fund is simply money set aside over time to meet a future financial obligation. The idea is familiar to most households. Rather than waiting until a major bill arrives, one puts money aside in advance. When the payment date comes, the resources are already available. Governments can apply the same principle to public debt. The Finance Minister also indicated that the February 2027 obligations comprised approximately GH¢29 billion in principal and GH¢11.1 billion in interest. Together, these amount to GH¢40.1 billion. It is important to understand the distinction. The principal is the original amount borrowed, while interest is the additional cost Government pays for using investors’ money. The proposed GH¢28.8 billion buyback concerns the bonds targeted under the current transaction, while the GH¢40.1 billion represents the wider principal and interest obligation associated with the February maturity. For ordinary Ghanaians, these figures may seem distant from everyday concerns. They are not. Government’s ability to manage its debts affects the wider economy. When public debt becomes difficult to service, the consequences can extend to interest rates, business financing, public investment and the cost of living. It can also reduce the resources available for essential services such as education, healthcare and infrastructure. There is also an important institutional dimension. Banks, pension funds and insurance companies hold government securities as part of their investments. When Government fails to meet its obligations, the effects can extend beyond the immediate bondholders. Financial institutions may face pressure, and the savings and investments of ordinary citizens can be affected. This is why the proposed buyback matters. It offers Government an opportunity to demonstrate that debt restructuring must be followed by responsible repayment. The DDEP was an exercise in managing a financial crisis. The next stage must be about rebuilding confidence in the institutions and financial arrangements that support the economy. However, we should not mistake an early repayment exercise for the complete resolution of Ghana’s debt challenges. Buying back one set of bonds does not mean that the country’s entire debt burden has been settled. Government has already indicated that approximately GH¢58 billion in DDEP bonds will mature in 2027, with a further GH¢53 billion expected in 2028. The challenge, therefore, extends beyond February 2027. Ghana must develop a consistent approach to managing these obligations without returning to the conditions that made the debt exchange necessary in the first place. This requires discipline in public expenditure, stronger domestic revenue mobilisation and greater care in the way Government contracts new loans. It also requires a clearer relationship between public borrowing and productive economic activity. Borrowing should support investments capable of improving national productivity, expanding employment and strengthening the country’s capacity to generate revenue. There is little value in repeatedly borrowing to meet expenditure without building the economic capacity to repay those loans. A sustainable economy must be able to finance its ambitions while meeting its obligations. The Government’s proposed bond buyback is therefore a welcome opportunity to demonstrate financial responsibility. Its ultimate value, however, will depend on the consistency with which the Government manages the wider debt portfolio and protects the public purse. For investors, the most important assurance is that agreements will be respected. For businesses, it is that economic stability will be sustained. For ordinary citizens, it is that the management of public finances will eventually translate into better opportunities, more reliable public services and a stronger economy. Ghana has already paid a considerable price for the mistakes of its recent debt crisis. The lesson should not be forgotten. Financial confidence is not restored by announcements alone, but by the steady fulfilment of obligations and the responsible management of national resources. The proposed GH¢28.8 billion buyback is a step in that direction. The greater task is to ensure that Ghana never again has to ask its citizens and investors to bear the cost of an avoidable debt crisis. A country’s creditworthiness is ultimately built on the confidence that it will honour its word. The writer is V. L. K. Djokoto, Director, Institute of Presidential Research.

Title: Stones cannot replace trees and landscape plants: Is Accra’s beautification turning our capital into a concrete jungle?
Content: Accra's Disappearing Green Heritage Something disturbing is happening to Accra's urban landscape. Along some of the capital's major roads, established flowering shrubs, ornamental plants and mature trees are being removed and replaced with decorative stones, plastic ground coverings and other hard-landscaping materials. At first glance, these arrangements may appear beautiful. The white and brown stones, carefully arranged into attractive patterns, create an impression of modernity. But beneath this temporary aesthetic appeal lies a serious environmental concern:Are we beautifying Accra or gradually transforming our capital into a concrete jungle? Government has invested substantial resources in improving major road corridors, including the stretch from the National Theatre towards the Pantang Hospital Intersection. These investments are commendable. However, beautification should not come at the expense of environmental sustainability. As a landscape management practitioner, I find it troubling that established vegetation, which has survived years of exposure to vehicle emissions, dust and harsh climatic conditions, are being removed in favour of predominantly decorative materials.Since when did the destruction of healthy vegetation become a measure of urban development? The Destruction of Established Road-Median Vegetation The stretch from the 37 Military Hospital through the Jubilee House vicinity towards the Ako Adjei Interchange is one area which has suffered such destruction. For years, beautiful pink-flowering oleanders adorned sections of this corridor, softening the harsh appearance of the road infrastructure. Today, sections of these established plantings have been removed and replaced with decorative stones. Similar changes are occurring around the Association International School, Airport Police Station, Airport traffic intersection and adjoining road medians. In some locations, the existing vegetation and topsoil have been removed, plastic coverings laid and decorative stones arranged into ornamental patterns. Within the Airport enclave, this approach has already become noticeable. Elsewhere, mature trees have reportedly been felled, while established trees at Togo Roundabout have undergone severe pruning. The concern is not opposition to landscape improvement, but rather, it is the unnecessary replacement of functional green infrastructure with materials whose long-term environmental benefits remain questionable. Ironically, many road medians and public spaces across Accra remain bare and neglected. Why not invest in landscaping those areas instead of destroying already established landscapes?Development should improve our environment, not erase its living assets. Landscaping is more than Aesthetics Urban landscaping is not merely about planting flowers to beautify roads. It is an essential component of environmental management, climate adaptation and public health. Trees and shrubs contribute to the interception of airborne particulate matter, while certain plant species can absorb some gaseous pollutants. Vegetation also moderates local temperatures through shading and evapotranspiration, supports biodiversity, improves visual amenity and contributes to psychological well-being. In heavily trafficked environments, appropriate vegetation can form part of a broader strategy for managing dust and air pollution, although it cannot eliminate vehicle emissions. This is why professional landscape management requires careful plant selection based on environmental conditions, pollution tolerance, safety, soil characteristics and maintenance requirements. The oleander (Nerium oleander), for example, is recognized for its tolerance of heat, drought and challenging urban conditions. Its attractive flowers and hardy nature have made it useful in selected roadside landscapes. Why remove plants that have adapted successfully to these difficult conditions without first demonstrating that the alternatives offer greater benefits?A landscape should not be judged merely by how beautiful it looks today, but by how effectively it serves the environment over time. Decorative stones cannot perform the functions of living plants Decorative stones have legitimate uses in landscape design. However, they should complement vegetation rather than indiscriminately replace it. The growing practice of covering road medians with plastic sheets and decorative stones raises important questions about soil health, water infiltration, surface temperatures and long-term maintenance. Unlike living vegetation, stones do not provide evapotranspirative cooling, biological pollutant uptake or biodiversity habitat. Furthermore, Accra's dusty environment and heavy vehicular emissions may gradually discolour these decorative materials. The attractive white stones seen today may become stained with soot and dirt, requiring regular cleaning or replacement. What will these installations look like in five years? What will it cost to maintain them? If the objective is to avoid maintaining living vegetation, we may eventually discover that the supposedly cheaper alternative is more expensive.The solution to inadequate landscape maintenance is not to eliminate vegetation. It is to provide proper maintenance and professional management. Accra is getting hotter: Why remove the vegetation? Accra is already experiencing the environmental pressures associated with rapid urbanization, expanding infrastructure and increasing areas of exposed hard surfaces. Vegetation helps moderate urban temperatures by providing shade and supporting evapotranspiration. Its removal can contribute to hotter surface conditions, depending on the characteristics of the replacement materials and surrounding environment. Anyone travelling through the Airport area or other heavily developed sections of Accra during the afternoon can appreciate the discomfort associated with intense sunshine, traffic congestion and exposed road surfaces. Imagine removing substantial areas of vegetation from such environments and replacing them with predominantly mineral surfaces. What environmental purpose does this serve? Cities worldwide are increasingly exploring nature-based solutions to reduce urban heat and improve climate resilience. Accra should be expanding its green infrastructure rather than unnecessarily diminishing it. The situation is particularly worrying because urban heat affects everyone, especially pedestrians, roadside traders, transport operators and people who spend long hours outdoors.We cannot continually complain about rising temperatures while removing vegetation that contributes to making our city more comfortable. Air pollution and the importance of roadside vegetation Air pollution remains a major environmental and public health concern in Accra. Vehicle emissions, road dust, construction activities and other urban sources contribute to atmospheric pollution, including fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide. Prolonged exposure to elevated concentrations of these pollutants can have serious implications for respiratory and cardiovascular health. Appropriately selected roadside vegetation can intercept some airborne particles and contribute to environmental quality. The removal of established vegetation from heavily trafficked corridors should therefore be approached cautiously and supported by technical assessments. It is especially worrying when mature shade trees and landscape plants are removed from busy city centers, where pedestrians, traders and commuters already experience significant environmental pressures. A mature tree or landscaping represents decades of growth and ecological development. Its environmental contributions cannot be immediately replaced by planting a seedling. Where trees interfere with utilities or infrastructure, professional arborists should assess alternatives such as selective pruning, appropriate root management or design modifications before removal is considered. The contradiction of Ghana's greening agenda Ghana has promoted national tree-planting and environmental restoration initiatives, including Green Ghana and Trees for Life. These initiatives are commendable, but their objectives must be reflected in how we manage existing vegetation. What is the justification for investing resources in planting new trees while established trees and shrubs are being removed from public spaces without clearly demonstrated necessity? Why celebrate the number of seedlings planted while paying insufficient attention to the mature trees we lose? Protecting existing vegetation should be as important as planting new trees and shrubs. The contradiction becomes even more striking when we consider countries in the Middle East, where cities invest in urban greenery despite severe water scarcity. Ghana, with its tropical climate and seasonal rainfall, has significant opportunities to develop environmentally functional landscapes using appropriately selected plants. Yet we appear increasingly attracted to stone-dominated landscaping styles.Why should a country capable of supporting rich vegetation voluntarily replace living landscapes with predominantly artificial surfaces? Where are our environmental institutions? These developments raise important questions about institutional responsibility and professional oversight. Where are the Environmental Protection Agency, Department of Parks and Gardens, Metropolitan and Municipal Assemblies, and the relevant road authorities when established urban vegetation is being removed? Are qualified horticulturists, landscape architects, arborists and environmental scientists consulted before these decisions are taken? What technical assessments justify the removal of these healthy plants? Who approves these projects, and who evaluates their long-term environmental consequences? The Ghana Institute of Horticulturists and other relevant professional bodies should have opportunities to contribute their expertise to public landscape development. The Environmental Protection Agency, Parks and Gardens, road authorities and local assemblies should strengthen collaboration to ensure that landscaping interventions comply with sound environmental management principles. These questions are not intended to assign blame without evidence. They are a call for transparency, professional accountability and better coordination.Public landscaping should be guided by science and professional competence, not simply by the preferences of those financing or implementing projects. The way forward: Protecting Accra's green infrastructure Accra urgently needs a coordinated approach to sustainable urban landscaping. Conclusion: Leave our vegetation alone I wish to make a passionate appeal to those responsible for the planning, financing and execution of public landscaping projects in Accra. We appreciate efforts to beautify our capital. We welcome modern infrastructure and attractive public spaces, but please,do not destroy established vegetation in the name of beautification.These plants have served us quietly for years. They have endured intense sunshine, dust, vehicle emissions and the pressures of urban development. They have contributed colour, greenery and environmental value to our city. They cannot speak for themselves. We must speak for them. The ordinary Ghanaian spending hours in traffic deserves a pleasant environment. The roadside trader deserves relief from excessive heat. The pedestrian deserves shade. Our children deserve to inherit a city where trees and flowering plants remain part of everyday life. Let us remember that a flowering shrub is more than a decorative object, a mature tree is more than an obstacle to construction, and a green road median is more than a strip separating traffic. They are components of the living infrastructure upon which the health and environmental quality of our cities depend. Accra can be modern, beautiful and environmentally sustainable at the same time. These objectives are not mutually exclusive. Let us beautify Accra, but let us not destroy its green heritage in the process. Because stones cannot replace trees, concrete cannot replace living ecosystems, and artificial beauty cannot compensate for the unnecessary destruction of nature. When the last flowering shrub has been uprooted, the last mature tree has been felled and our once-green road medians have been covered with stones, will we still proudly call Accra a beautiful city? Or will we finally realize that, in our attempt to beautify the capital, we have gradually turned it into a concrete jungle? Philip Quaye, FGhIH; MGhISEPFellow, Ghana Institute of Horticulturists (GhIH)Former Vice-President and Former Honorary Secretary, GhIH philip18q@yahoo.com; 0506712973

Title: The Inconvenient Truth: We applaud Africa at the summit, then frown at it on the supermarket shelf
Content: Made in Africa, Produced in Ghana. Made in Africa, Produced in South Africa. Made in Africa, Produced in Nigeria. One continental identity, many national centres of excellence. Until we learn to honour where a product is made without letting national pride erase where it belongs, our dream of an industrialised, integrated Africa will remain hostage to the very divisions we claim to have outgrown. By Ing. Prof. Douglas Boateng, Chartered Director UK | Chartered Engineer UK | Fellow, Institute of Directors UK | Fellow, Ghana Institution of Engineering | Governance, Industrialisation and Supply Chain Strategist | Founder, Boardroom Governance Summit | Founder and Scriber, NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) The Product That Needed A Diplomatic Passport Imagine a Ghanaian entrepreneur who manufactures an excellent product that meets international standards, is competitively priced and could succeed anywhere on the continent. She sets off to win buyers in Lagos, Johannesburg and Nairobi, expecting questions about quality, price and delivery. Instead, she is too often asked why anyone should buy something made in Ghana when they ought to be supporting their own industries, while imported goods from far beyond Africa glide past her into the same shops on long established distribution networks. Perhaps African products should travel with diplomatic passports. A Ghanaian biscuit entering Nigeria could carry a certificate confirming that its crunchiness poses no threat to Nigerian industrial ambition, and a South African appliance bound for Kenya could come with a solemn undertaking not to wound national pride. It would be hilarious if the economic consequences were not so serious. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom):When neighbours treat one another's products as foreign threats, the continent becomes a marketplace for everybody except itself. The Border We Carry In Our Heads This is not an argument against national identity, domestic manufacturing or healthy competition. Every African country should build its productive capabilities and pursue excellence with pride. The trouble begins when national pride, instead of fuelling continental prosperity, quietly blocks it. We celebrate unity at conferences and sign integration treaties with ceremonial pens, yet the moment an African product crosses an African border, our enthusiasm can develop an acute case of identity anxiety. The inconvenient truth is that the most stubborn borders in Africa are not drawn on maps; they are drawn in minds. Fifteen Per Cent And A Mirror The numbers tell the story with uncomfortable clarity. Recent reporting on Afreximbank data suggests that trade among African countries accounted for only about fifteen per cent of the continent's roughly US$1.47 trillion in total trade in 2025, compared with about sixty per cent within Asia and close to seventy per cent within Europe. Comparisons demand care, since structures and measurement differ, but the message is unmistakable. A continent of more than a billion consumers is still selling mostly to strangers and buying mostly from them, while its own neighbours remain, commercially speaking, distant relatives we greet warmly at funerals but rarely visit. A Label That Could Change A Mindset Consider a simple proposition: Made in Africa, Produced in Ghana; Made in Africa, Produced in Kenya; Made in Africa, Produced in Morocco. Such a label honours two truths at once, recognising the country where the work was done while placing the product within a wider African industrial family. One identity does not erase the other; each strengthens the other. Made in USA carries the products of fifty states with competing interests, and Made in China covers provinces that compete fiercely for investment. Africa, of course, comprises fifty four sovereign nations, and no national model can simply be transplanted. But the branding lesson travels well: a shared identity can amplify recognition without diminishing local pride, just as South Africa's own Proudly South African campaign has shown how a credible mark can nudge consumer loyalty. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom):A product can proudly carry the name of its birthplace without being denied the larger name of its family. Fifty Four Bakeries And One Nervous Banker Industrial ambition without coordination is an expensive hobby. When one country wants a complete automotive industry, another an entirely independent pharmaceutical sector and a third every component of renewable energy equipment, the result is duplication at uneconomic scale. Picture fifty four households in one compound, each insisting on its own industrial bakery, flour mill, transport fleet and packaging plant. The households grow very proud, their bankers grow very nervous, and the village eventually discovers that cooperation would have produced more bread at far lower cost. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom):National pride becomes economically expensive when every country insists on duplicating what its neighbour could produce more competitively. From Bean To Bar, Or From Bean To Boat? Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire together grow the bulk of the world's cocoa, yet much of the value in processing, branding and retail is captured elsewhere, so that the beans leave by boat and too often return as a premium bar at an airport duty free counter. Their joint cocoa initiative deserves credit. Now imagine two rival chocolate brands, one labelled Made in Africa, Produced in Ghana and the other Made in Africa, Produced in Côte d'Ivoire, competing ferociously on taste and price while jointly building global recognition for African chocolate. Ghana would remain Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire would remain Côte d'Ivoire, and Africa would at last own a share of the shelf rather than merely the farm. The same logic applies to vehicles assembled in South Africa or Morocco with components from qualified suppliers across the continent, and to batteries built on copper and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom):Owning the mineral beneath the soil is not the same as owning the industry built above it. Lessons From Those Who Learned To Share The Shop Europe and Southeast Asia have shown what scale can achieve. The European Commission estimates that the single market has raised EU GDP by three to four per cent and created 3.6 million jobs since 1993, while trade among ASEAN members accounted for about 21.5 per cent of that bloc's total trade in 2023, much of it in components that cross several borders before becoming finished goods. Neither region abolished competition; both simply stopped letting it close the shop. The Customer Is Also A Citizen Governments cannot do this alone, because consumers vote every day with their wallets. Many Africans understandably associate certain imported brands with reliability or prestige, sometimes rightly and sometimes because of decades of advertising. A Made in Africa identity must therefore never become a patriotic excuse for mediocrity. Medicines must be safe, vehicles must meet technical standards, food must satisfy hygiene requirements and digital services must work when the customer needs them. At the same time, consumers should give competitive products from neighbouring countries a fair hearing rather than assuming that anything African must be second best. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom):Patriotism may persuade a customer to buy once, but only quality, value and reliability will persuade her to return. A Practical Plan, Not Another Communiqué Good intentions need machinery. In the first year, the African Union and the AfCFTA Secretariat in Accra, working with regional economic communities, the African Organisation for Standardisation and industry associations, should establish a voluntary Made in Africa certification mark governed by an independent body with private sector representation. Eligibility should be anchored in the AfCFTA rules of origin, with clear minimum thresholds for African value addition, so that no imported product becomes African simply because a distributor changed its packaging. Every certified product should carry a digital code that allows buyers, customs officers and consumers to verify its origin and certification instantly, and misuse should attract published penalties and withdrawal of the mark. Within three years, the mark should be piloted in a handful of sectors where Africa already has credible capacity, such as processed cocoa, pharmaceuticals, automotive components, textiles and agro processing, using the AfCFTA Guided Trade Initiative as the launch pad. Mutual recognition of standards and conformity assessments among participating countries would ensure that a product tested in one market need not be retested in the next. Afreximbank and national development banks could offer preferential trade finance to certified exporters, while the Pan African Payment and Settlement System allows them to trade in local currencies without first converting into dollars. Governments could introduce modest, transparent preference margins for certified African suppliers in public procurement, consistent with trade obligations and value for money, and retailers encouraged to give African products visible shelf space. Each year, an independent scorecard should report the number of certified products, cross border sales, rejected applications and enforcement actions, so that success is measured in containers shipped rather than speeches delivered. Underpinning all of this must be a more inclusive mindset. Small and medium enterprises, women traders who dominate many cross border markets, young innovators and the diaspora must be able to access the mark affordably rather than watching it become a privilege of large corporations, and governments must learn to celebrate a neighbour's industrial success as an African success. The Question The Unborn Child Will Ask One day an African child not yet born may ask why, knowing that Africa needed larger markets and stronger industries, we allowed African products to become foreign the moment they crossed an African border. Shall we reply that Ghanaian products were too Ghanaian for Nigeria, that Nigerian goods were too Nigerian for South Africa, or that we preferred fifty four separate ambitions to one shared industrial identity? History may listen politely, but the child will inherit the consequences. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom):A nation does not become less proud when its neighbour succeeds; a continent becomes stronger when their achievements reinforce one another. Ghana must remain proudly Ghanaian, Nigeria proudly Nigerian, South Africa proudly South African, and every nation should celebrate its own centres of excellence. But the inconvenient truth is that we cannot build a continental market while treating a neighbour's industrial success as a threat to national prestige. We must compete on quality, cooperate on capability and celebrate African production wherever it occurs. The Africa we desire is in our own hands, provided those hands stop pulling our industries apart and start building an identity capable of competing with the world. Ing. Professor Douglas K. Boateng is a strategist in governance, industrialisation and supply chains, and serves as a professional chairperson, an international Chartered Director (UK) and a Chartered Engineer (UK). A Pan-Africanist and social entrepreneur at heart, he has spent his career working across public institutions, corporate boards and industrial policy, in Africa and beyond, guided by the conviction that strong institutions are built one honest decision at a time. His contributions to industry and academia have earned him more than six lifetime achievement awards. He is the founder of NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom), a collection of daily aphorisms he has written and shared since late 2019, distilling decades of experience advising governments, boards, and enterprises on governance, accountability, and institutional resilience into words meant to challenge and endure. He convenes the Boardroom Governance Summit, Africa’s largest boardroom-focused summit, and writes a widely read weekly op-ed series titled “Inconvenient Truth” and “What Is Wrong With Us”, featured on some of the region’s leading digital media platforms. Professor Boateng can be reached via LinkedIn or atinfo@panavest.com. © 2026 Ing. Prof. Douglas Boateng. All rights reserved.

Title: Daily Insight for CEOs: The CEO’s role in strengthening corporate governance
Content: By Ernest De-Graft Egyir Strong corporate governance is essential to building a credible, accountable and sustainable organization. It provides the structures, policies and processes through which an organization is directed, controlled and held accountable. The CEO plays a central role in making governance effective. This requires maintaining a constructive relationship with the board, providing accurate and timely information, respecting the distinction between board oversight and executive management, and ensuring that decisions are made in the best interests of the organisation. Good governance should not exist only in policy documents. It must be reflected in daily leadership conduct, decision-making, financial management, risk oversight and stakeholder relationships. A CEO who takes governance seriously strengthens institutional credibility and protects the long-term interests of the organization. CEO Leadership Actions. ✅ Review the effectiveness of the organization’s governance framework and identify areas requiring improvement. ✅ Ensure that board members receive relevant information ahead of meetings to support informed discussions and decisions. ✅ Hold the executive team accountable for compliance with governance policies, internal controls and delegated authorities. Strong governance protects the organization from avoidable failures, improves the quality of leadership decisions and strengthens confidence among shareholders, employees, regulators and other stakeholders. It also ensures that the organization is built around sound institutions rather than depending solely on the personality or influence of individual leaders. Ernest De-Graft Egyir, CEO advisor, Thought Leader and Founding CEO of Chief Executives Network Ghana, convenes the Ghana CEO Summit and served on Ghana’s Economic Dialogue Planning Committee.

Title: New Cedi notes: What does Ghana stand to gain?
Content: Beyond a new appearance, will Ghana’s redesigned currency deliver meaningful value to the economy and the people who use it? On December 1, 2026, Ghanaians will begin using a new series of cedi banknotes, unveiled on November 12, by President John Dramani Mahama. The redesigned banknotes are known as the Ghana Cedi Heritage Series. According to the Bank of Ghana (BoG), the redesign is intended to strengthen currency security, improve convenience and ensure the banknotes withstand the demands of frequent circulation. But beyond the new appearance and official explanations, a bigger question remains: Does Ghana really need new cedi notes, and what difference will they make to ordinary Ghanaians? The Heritage In Our Money Each denomination carries a distinct national theme, represented by the personality featured on its front. The GH¢1 note celebrates commerce through market trader Agnes Oforiwa Tagoe-Quarcoopome; the GH¢2 represents religious freedom through Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery; and the GH¢5 highlights education through renowned educationist Dr J.E.K. Aggrey. The GH¢10 represents justice and equality, featuring female pioneering judge Justice Annie Jiagge, while the GH¢20 celebrates arts and entertainment through composer Dr Ephraim Amu. The GH¢50 highlights nationalism through Theodosia Salome Okoh, designer of Ghana’s national flag. The GH¢100 represents peace, featuring former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, the first African to hold the position, while the GH¢200 celebrates sovereignty through Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah. Regina Akie Mensah, a young Ghanaian says, “it's beautiful, because it has brought back memories, we wont forget those people again. When I first saw the new faces I asked who are these people. But now we will learn about them and wont ask those questions again”. New Notes, Same Economic Realities A redesigned banknote does not mean a stronger currency. While the new series promises improvements in durability, security and convenience, it does not automatically improve the purchasing power of the cedi. For Osman Abdul Latif Cheboo, President and Founder of the Youth Parliament Ghana, the redesign can be a positive development, provided it serves a clear national purpose. He, however, cautions against allowing the exercise to become an unnecessary financial burden. “Redesigning banknotes should not simply be about changing their appearance. We must also consider the economic implications and ensure that the exercise does not impose unnecessary costs on the country. Every decision must be guided by value for money and the national interest”, he said. The Cost Of A New Look Redesigning a national currency involves more than producing new banknotes. It comes with expenses associated with design, printing, distribution, public education and the gradual withdrawal of older notes. The BoG argues that improved durability will help the new notes last longer, potentially reducing the frequency and cost of replacing damaged currency, but at what cost of production? In 2007, the BoG publicly reported an expenditure of approximately GH¢89 million for the redenomination exercise, while the introduction of the GH¢100 and GH¢200 notes in 2019 was reported to have cost US$8.97 million to print. How much will this heritage series amount to, when the BoG announces the audits in 2027? Beyond The Design: Are The New Security Features Enough? Counterfeiting is a persistent concern for currencies globally, making security one of the most important considerations in any banknote redesign. The Bank of Ghana says the Heritage Series incorporates enhanced security features intended to make counterfeiting more difficult and help the public identify genuine notes. However, introducing improved security measures is only part of the solution, people will still counterfeit, making public awareness important. Cheboo believes the introduction of the new notes should also create an opportunity to improve financial education among young people. “I also see this as an opportunity for financial education. The Bank of Ghana and relevant institutions should engage young people, especially students in secondary schools and universities, to educate them about the new currency, its security features and the reasons behind the redesign.” The central bank’s planned public education campaign will therefore be important in helping citizens familiarise themselves with the new features. Ultimately, the effectiveness of the redesign will depend not only on the security measures incorporated into the notes but also on how well they protect the currency in everyday circulation. Will Everyone Be Able To Use The New Notes? Accessibility is another important consideration in currency design, particularly for persons with visual impairments. Identifying different denominations can be challenging for people with limited or no sight. Tactile markings, distinguishable note sizes, high-contrast colours and assistive technology are among the measures that can make banknotes more accessible. The Bank of Ghana has introduced the Cedi App to help the public understand the security features of the new notes, with particular attention to assisting visually impaired users, but the physical notes should be easily identifiable as well. A national currency should be designed with the needs of all its users in mind, including those who cannot rely on sight to identify denominations. As the new notes prepare to enter circulation, one question deserves to remain at the centre of the conversation: Beyond giving the cedi a new face, will this exercise make a meaningful difference to Ghana and its people?

Title: The New Cedi at the Altar: Beyond the portrait, beneath the gift
Content: Money occupies an important place in human society. From the bustling markets of Makola to the smallest village shops across Ghana, money facilitates the exchange of goods and services, supports livelihoods and drives economic activities. It enables individuals to meet their daily needs, businesses to operate and governments to undertake development projects. Beyond its economic functions, however, money also carries historical, cultural and national significance. The personalities, landmarks and symbols displayed on currency notes often communicate the values, achievements and aspirations of the societies that issue them. In this sense, currency represents not only purchasing power but also a nation’s identity, heritage and collective memory. In Ghana, the evolution of currency reflects the country’s economic transformation and historical development. From traditional systems of exchange involving cowrie shells and gold dust to the introduction of the cedi and subsequent monetary reforms, Ghana’s currency has undergone several changes. These developments have largely been influenced by economic needs, technological advancements and the desire to preserve national identity. The Bank of Ghana’s introduction of the Ghana Cedi Heritage Series on November 12, 2026, represents another significant development in this journey. The redesigned banknotes incorporate enhanced security features while celebrating distinguished personalities, national landmarks and Ghanaian cultural symbols (Bank of Ghana, 2026; Ghana News Agency, 2026). One particularly interesting feature of the Heritage Series is the appearance of Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery, a distinguished Ghanaian Catholic religious leader, on the new GH¢2 note. The reverse of the note features the historic Larabanga Mosque, reflecting Ghana’s religious diversity and tradition of peaceful coexistence (Incoom, 2026). Although the inclusion of these religious symbols is intended to recognise national heritage, it has also generated interesting conversations about the relationship between money, religion and Christian giving. Following the unveiling of the new currency, I received a humorous message from a friend suggesting that the GH¢2 note had effectively become the appropriate denomination for church offerings because it bears the portrait of a Christian religious leader. Initially, I regarded the message as an ordinary joke. Upon further reflection, however, I realised that it raised a more important question about how Christians understand the spiritual significance of money and the biblical principles governing offerings. The issue is not whether Christians may give GH¢2 during worship, since there is nothing inherently wrong with giving that amount. Rather, the concern is whether the appearance of a religious leader on a currency note should influence, determine or restrict the amount a Christian chooses to offer to God. Does religious imagery confer special spiritual significance on a particular denomination? Can a national decision to honour a religious personality be interpreted as an instruction concerning Christian giving? More importantly, what does the Bible teach about the motives, attitudes and circumstances that should guide believers when they give? These questions deserve careful consideration because confusing the symbolic meaning of currency with the spiritual meaning of offerings may lead to a misunderstanding of Christian stewardship. The central argument of this article is that although the new GH¢2 note appropriately honours Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery and celebrates Ghana’s religious heritage, its religious imagery does not make it spiritually superior to other denominations or establish it as the prescribed currency for church offerings. Biblical giving is determined not by the portrait or denomination of a banknote but by the giver’s willingness, gratitude, financial circumstances, generosity and sincerity before God. To develop this argument, the discussion examines the evolution of Ghana’s currency, the significance of the Heritage Series, the symbolism of the GH¢2 note and Cardinal Dery’s contributions to national development. It then considers relevant biblical teachings on giving and their implications for Christian stewardship. 2. BEYOND THE CEDI: NATIONAL HERITAGE, RELIGIOUS SYMBOLISM AND BIBLICAL GIVING 2.1 From Cowries to Cedis: Understanding Ghana’s Currency Journey The history of money in Ghana provides an important starting point for understanding the significance of the Heritage Series. Long before the introduction of modern currency, people living in present-day Ghana engaged in trade through barter. Under this arrangement, goods and services were exchanged directly for other goods and services. A farmer could exchange yams for fish, while a trader could exchange salt for cloth or other necessities. Although barter facilitated economic interaction, it presented practical difficulties because each trading partner needed to possess something the other wanted. This limitation encouraged the gradual adoption of commodities that could serve as generally accepted mediums of exchange. Over time, items such as cowrie shells and gold dust became important in commercial transactions. The wordcediitself originates from the Akan wordsedie, meaning cowrie shell, reflecting the historical importance of cowries in Ghana’s trading activities (Bank of Ghana, n.d.). As economic activities expanded and monetary institutions developed, modern banknotes and coins gradually replaced traditional mediums of exchange. On 19 July 1965, Ghana introduced the cedi to replace the Ghanaian pound. Subsequent reforms included the introduction of the new cedi on February 17, 1967. Another major development occurred on July 1, 2007, when Ghana redenominated its currency by converting 10,000 old cedis into one Ghana cedi (Bank of Ghana, 2007, n.d.). These changes illustrate that currency is not a permanent or unchanging institution. Its design, denomination and physical appearance may be altered to respond to economic conditions and national priorities. However, such alterations do not automatically change the spiritual or moral meaning of the money people possess. While the state may use money to commemorate historical figures, the presence of those figures does not confer religious authority on the currency itself. 2.2 Why Nations Introduce New Currency Notes The printing and issuance of currency are among the major responsibilities of central banks. In Ghana, the Bank of Ghana manages the issuance and circulation of the national currency. Currency notes perform several economic functions, including facilitating transactions, serving as a medium of exchange, providing a common measure of value and enabling people to hold purchasing power. Nevertheless, physical banknotes deteriorate through regular handling and circulation. They may become worn, torn, dirty or damaged. Moreover, advances in printing and reproduction technologies create opportunities for currency counterfeiting. Central banks therefore periodically introduce redesigned or upgraded banknotes to improve their security, durability and ease of identification. Currency redesigns may also provide opportunities to celebrate historical achievements, recognise distinguished personalities and promote national identity. The Ghana Cedi Heritage Series reflects these considerations. According to the Bank of Ghana (2026), the redesigned notes incorporate improved security features, greater durability and distinctive designs that celebrate Ghanaian history and culture. Their introduction therefore serves both practical monetary purposes and broader national commemorative objectives. It is important, however, to distinguish currency redesign from currency appreciation. Introducing a new banknote does not, by itself, increase the purchasing power of money. The strength of a currency depends on broader economic conditions, including inflation, productivity, public confidence and effective monetary and fiscal management. Similarly, incorporating the portrait of a religious leader into a banknote does not transform its economic value into spiritual value. The state determines the denomination and legal status of currency, but Christian teachings provide a different basis for understanding the spiritual significance of offerings. 2.3 The Ghana Cedi Heritage Series: Celebrating National Identity On November 12, 2026, President John Dramani Mahama officially launched the Ghana Cedi Heritage Series at the Bank of Ghana’s headquarters in Accra. The redesigned banknotes are scheduled to enter general circulation on December 1, 2026, alongside the existing notes, which remain legal tender (Ghana News Agency, 2026). The Heritage Series comprises eight denominations, each featuring a distinguished Ghanaian personality, an important national landmark and an Adinkra symbol. Together, these elements celebrate Ghana’s historical development, cultural identity and contributions to national and international progress (Incoom, 2026). The GH¢1 note features Agnes Oforiwa Tagoe-Quarcoopome, a pioneering Ghanaian market woman and entrepreneur. Its reverse depicts market women engaged in trading activities, recognising commerce, entrepreneurship and the contributions of women to national development. The GH¢2 note honours Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery, a distinguished Catholic religious leader, while the historic Larabanga Mosque appears on its reverse, communicating the values of religious freedom, tolerance and peaceful coexistence. The GH¢5 note features Dr James Emman Kwegyir Aggrey, an influential educationist associated with the establishment of Achimota School, which appears on the reverse. This denomination emphasises the importance of education in national development. The GH¢10 note celebrates Justice Annie Jiagge, a pioneering female judge and advocate for human rights. The Supreme Court of Ghana appears on its reverse, symbolising justice, equality and the rule of law. The GH¢20 note honours Dr Ephraim Amu, whose contributions to music enriched Ghana’s cultural heritage, while the National Theatre on the reverse celebrates the arts and their contribution to national identity. The GH¢50 note recognises Theodosia Salome Okoh, the designer of Ghana’s national flag, with Jubilee House appearing on the reverse to symbolise national independence, patriotism and sovereignty. The GH¢100 note celebrates Kofi Annan, the former Secretary-General of the United Nations. The reverse features the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre, reflecting Ghana’s contributions to international peace and diplomacy. Finally, the GH¢200 note features Dr Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first President, with the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park on the reverse. It commemorates Ghana’s independence, sovereignty and struggle for self-determination. These personalities represent different dimensions of Ghana’s national experience, including commerce, religion, education, justice, culture, nationalism, peace and sovereignty. Their appearance on the banknotes allows Ghanaians to encounter important aspects of the country’s history through everyday economic transactions. The Heritage Series therefore communicates more than monetary value; it reminds present and future generations of individuals whose contributions helped shape the nation. Nevertheless, the significance of these portraits must be understood within their intended national context. Just as the appearance of a judge on the GH¢10 note does not make that denomination the official currency for paying legal fees, the presence of a cardinal on the GH¢2 note does not make it the prescribed denomination for church offerings. 2.4 The GH¢2 Note and the Offertory: A Message That Got Me Thinking Following the unveiling of the Heritage Series, a friend forwarded a message to me that read: ‘They’ve certified the new GHC 2 note for offertory with a Reverend Minister on the currency note. Now diɛɛ GHC 2 nkoaaa I go give as offering in church.’ In other words, because the new GH¢2 note bears the portrait of a Christian religious leader, my friend had concluded, perhaps humorously, that GH¢2 had become the appropriate amount for church offerings. I smiled when I read the message. However, as I reflected on it, I realised that beneath the humour was an important issue deserving Christian consideration. Has the Bank of Ghana designated the GH¢2 note for church offerings? Does the presence of a religious leader’s portrait make the note spiritually superior to other denominations? Should Christians now restrict their offerings to GH¢2 because of the personality displayed on it? Certainly not. The Bank of Ghana issues currency to serve the economic needs of the country. Its responsibility is not to prescribe how much Christians should give during worship. The decision to feature a religious personality on a banknote is an act of national recognition, not a theological declaration concerning offerings. The humour in my friend’s message becomes even more interesting when we examine the two sides of the GH¢2 note. While the portrait of Cardinal Dery appears on the front, the Larabanga Mosque appears on the reverse. If the cardinal’s portrait means that the note has been designated for Christian offerings, what would the presence of the mosque imply? The question exposes the weakness of interpreting the denomination through the religious identity of the person appearing on it. The two images are not competing religious instructions. Rather, they communicate a shared national commitment to religious freedom and peaceful coexistence. The issue therefore requires a clear distinction between recognising a religious leader’s contribution to national development and understanding the spiritual principles that guide Christian giving. 2.5 Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery: A Life Worth Celebrating Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery was born on May 10, 1918, in Zemuopare, in present-day Ghana. He was ordained a Catholic priest on February 11, 1951, and subsequently became the first Bishop of Wa and the first Archbishop of Tamale. On March 24, 2006, Pope Benedict XVI elevated him to the rank of cardinal (Holy See Press Office, n.d.). Throughout his ministry, Cardinal Dery demonstrated a strong commitment to Christian leadership, education, community development and human dignity. He contributed to the establishment of numerous educational institutions, including schools and a minor seminary. He also promoted the inclusion of appropriate Ghanaian cultural expressions in Christian worship, helping to make Christian religious practice more meaningful within local cultural contexts. His influence extended beyond his responsibilities as a church leader. Through educational development, pastoral service and engagement with communities, he contributed to social progress, particularly in northern Ghana. Cardinal Dery died on March 6, 2008, leaving a legacy of faith, service, educational advancement and religious leadership (Holy See Press Office, n.d.). His inclusion in the Heritage Series is therefore a fitting recognition of his contribution to Ghanaian society. Equally important is the decision to pair his portrait with the Larabanga Mosque, one of Ghana’s historically significant Islamic religious landmarks. This combination communicates an important national message: people of different religious traditions can contribute to the development of the same country while maintaining mutual respect. The GH¢2 note consequently represents more than the celebration of a Catholic cardinal. It recognises religious diversity as an important part of Ghana’s national heritage. However, honouring Cardinal Dery does not mean that his portrait determines the value of Christian offerings. He could equally have been honoured by a different denomination without changing the biblical principles of giving. We must therefore distinguish between a banknote that honours a servant of God and an offering that honours God Himself. The former represents national recognition of human achievement and service, while the latter concerns the believer’s relationship with God, expressed through worship, gratitude, obedience and generosity. 2.6 Beyond the Portrait: What Does the Bible Teach About Giving? Having considered the historical and national significance of the GH¢2 note, the more important question concerns the biblical understanding of offerings. Christian giving extends beyond the denomination of a currency note. It is an expression of worship, gratitude, generosity, obedience and trust in God. Although money is the physical substance often presented during offerings, the spiritual significance of giving cannot be determined exclusively by its monetary amount. Several biblical teachings help explain this distinction and provide guidance on how Christians should understand their responsibility to give. 2.6.1 God Loves a Cheerful Giver In the second book of Corinthians, the apostle Paul teaches that believers should give according to what they have decided in their hearts, rather than reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7). This passage highlights the importance of willingness and sincerity in Christian giving. An offering should not be motivated by pressure, embarrassment, competition or the desire to satisfy other people’s expectations. The same principle applies to the new GH¢2 note. A Christian who willingly gives GH¢2 according to their financial circumstances may be expressing genuine worship. Likewise, another Christian who gives GH¢20, GH¢50, GH¢100 or more with a sincere and cheerful heart may also be acting in accordance with biblical teaching. The issue is not which banknote carries a religious personality. Rather, it is whether the giver’s decision reflects genuine willingness and devotion to God. Christians should therefore avoid interpreting the presence of Cardinal Dery’s portrait as a reason to limit their giving to a particular denomination. The appropriate question is not, ‘Which note has a religious leader printed on it?’ but ‘What can I willingly and responsibly give in gratitude to God?’ This understanding encourages believers to make thoughtful decisions about their offerings instead of relying on the symbolic appearance of currency. 2.6.2 Giving Should Reflect Gratitude to God The psalmist raises a profound question about what one can offer to the Lord in response to His goodness. ‘What shall I return to the Lord for all his goodness to me?’ (Psa. 116:12). This passage presents giving as an expression of gratitude rather than a mere financial obligation. Christians recognise many blessings that cannot be adequately measured in monetary terms. These include life, health, strength, family, protection, opportunities, peace and the hope of salvation through Jesus Christ. Offerings provide one means through which believers express appreciation for God’s goodness. From this perspective, adopting GH¢2 as a permanent ceiling for one’s offerings solely because the note bears a religious leader’s portrait would misunderstand the purpose of giving. However, gratitude should not be confused with financial wealth. Someone with limited resources may express deep appreciation through a small offering, while another person with greater financial capacity may choose to give substantially more. The biblical emphasis remains on sincere gratitude rather than the outward appearance of the gift. An offering therefore becomes meaningful when it expresses genuine appreciation for God’s goodness and is given in accordance with the believer’s circumstances and convictions. 2.6.3 God Looks Beyond the Amount to the Heart of the Giver One of the clearest biblical illustrations of giving is found in parallel accounts in two of the Synoptic Gospels (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4). Jesus observed wealthy individuals contributing money to the temple treasury. He also noticed a poor widow who gave two small coins. Although her contribution was financially insignificant compared with those of the wealthy, Jesus drew attention to her extraordinary sacrifice. The widow’s offering was remarkable not because of the denomination of the coins but because of the circumstances under which she gave. This account challenges the assumption that the spiritual significance of an offering can be assessed simply by examining its monetary value. A GH¢2 offering from someone who genuinely cannot afford more should never be despised because it may represent considerable sacrifice and sincere devotion. On the other hand, a GH¢2 offering does not automatically become spiritually sufficient because the note carries Cardinal Dery’s portrait. The widow’s example teaches that Christian giving must be understood in relation to the giver’s resources, sacrifice and commitment. At the same time, the account should not be used to pressure financially vulnerable believers into giving beyond their capacity. Jesus’ recognition of the widow’s sacrifice does not justify exploiting those who are already experiencing hardship. The lesson is that the spiritual significance of giving cannot be read from the denomination of a banknote. 2.6.4 Giving Should Be Proportionate to One’s Resources In his first letter to the church in Corinth, the apostle Paul encourages believers to set aside money in proportion to their income: ‘On the first day of every week, each of you should put aside and store up in keeping with how he has prospered, so that when I come no collections will need to be made’ (1 Cor. 16:2). Similarly, in his second letter to the same church, the apostle Paul emphasises that the acceptability of a gift depends on the giver’s willingness and available resources rather than what the individual does not possess: ‘For if the willingness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have’ (2 Cor. 8:12). These passages establish an important principle of Christian stewardship: giving should reflect the resources available to the individual. Christians do not possess identical financial capacities. A student dependent on limited financial support, a parent struggling to provide for a family and a successful businessperson may not be in positions to give the same amount. What represents considerable sacrifice for one person may be relatively insignificant to another. For this reason, the Bible does not establish a uniform currency denomination that every Christian must present during worship. The principle is faithfulness in stewardship, not sameness of amount. Consequently, Christians should neither use the GH¢2 note as an automatic justification for reducing their offerings nor feel compelled to give beyond their reasonable means to impress others. Giving should be intentional, thoughtful and consistent with one’s financial circumstances and sincere conviction. This approach recognises that responsible stewardship involves generosity as well as the wise management of resources entrusted to the believer. 2.6.5 Giving Is an Expression of Worship, Love and Service King Solomon, in the book of Proverbs, encourages believers to honour God with their wealth: ‘Honour the LORD with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops’ (Prov. 3:9). Similarly, the author of Hebrews reminds Christians that giving extends beyond financial offerings to include acts of kindness, generosity and practical support for others: ‘And do not forget to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased’ (Heb. 13:16). These passages demonstrate that Christian giving is not merely a financial transaction performed during a church service. It is closely connected to worship, generosity and practical expressions of love. Offerings contribute to the activities and mission of the church. They may support religious programmes, pastoral work, evangelism, community development and assistance to people experiencing hardship. The purpose of giving therefore extends beyond placing money in an offering basket. A Christian who understands this responsibility will recognise that the value of an offering is connected to the purpose, willingness and commitment behind it. The portrait of a priest, pastor, cardinal or other religious personality on a banknote cannot replace these considerations. Furthermore, genuine Christian generosity should extend beyond church offerings to include caring for vulnerable people, assisting those in need and demonstrating compassion through practical actions. A generous Christian life cannot be reduced to the denomination placed in an offering basket on Sunday, because worship and love must also be expressed through everyday relationships and acts of service. 2.6.6 Giving Should Not Be Motivated by Public Recognition In the Gospel according to Matthew, the first book of the New Testament, Jesus warns believers against performing charitable acts merely to attract public attention or receive praise from others. He cautions: ‘Be careful not to practice your righteousness in front of others to be seen by them. If you do, you will have no reward from your Father in heaven’ (Matt. 6:1). He further teaches: ‘But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you’ (Matt. 6:3–4). These teachings highlight the danger of allowing social recognition to influence religious behaviour. In some situations, believers may feel pressured to give large amounts because they want others to regard them as generous. Others may give simply to conform to prevailing expectations within their congregations. Both situations raise important questions about motive. Are we giving to honour God or to attract attention? Are we giving out of gratitude and love, or merely to satisfy social expectations? Are we being faithful stewards, or are we allowing convenience and outward appearances to determine our decisions? These questions cannot be answered by examining the portrait or denomination of a currency note. They require sincere personal reflection about the intentions behind one’s actions. The biblical teaching is therefore clear: the spiritual meaning of giving lies beyond the external appearance of the money presented. Christians are encouraged to demonstrate generosity without making public recognition the basis of their giving, recognising that sincere worship is not dependent on the approval or admiration of others. 2.7 The GH¢2 Note Is Not the Problem; Our Understanding of Giving Is The preceding discussion demonstrates that there is nothing inherently wrong with putting a GH¢2 note into the offering basket. Once the new Heritage Series enters circulation, the GH¢2 note can be used for church offerings like any other legal currency denomination. Its use for religious giving is neither inappropriate nor spiritually inferior. The difficulty arises when Christians interpret the portrait of Cardinal Dery as a divine instruction, an official religious endorsement or a justification for restricting their offerings to GH¢2. Such an interpretation confuses two different matters. First, the Bank of Ghana’s decision to feature Cardinal Dery is an act of national recognition, celebrating his contribution to religious leadership, education and Ghanaian society. Second, Christian giving is governed by biblical principles that emphasise willingness, gratitude, generosity, proportionality, sincerity and responsible stewardship. These two matters should not be treated as interchangeable. If a Christian has only GH¢2 to give, that amount may be offered with joy and sincerity. Similarly, if another believer has the financial capacity and genuine willingness to give more, there is no biblical reason to restrict that person’s offering to GH¢2 simply because the denomination carries a religious leader’s portrait. The presence of Cardinal Dery on the note neither increases nor diminishes the spiritual value of the gift. For individual Christians, the new GH¢2 note provides an opportunity to reflect on the relationship between money, faith and responsible giving. Rather than allowing religious imagery to determine their offerings, believers should examine their motives, appreciate their circumstances and make thoughtful decisions grounded in biblical teaching. For church leaders, the discussion reinforces the importance of teaching balanced principles of Christian stewardship. Congregations should be encouraged to give willingly and responsibly without being subjected to unnecessary pressure, public embarrassment or unrealistic financial expectations. For Ghanaian society more broadly, the Heritage Series reminds us that national symbols can communicate important historical and cultural messages without necessarily carrying religious instructions. The appearance of Cardinal Dery and the Larabanga Mosque on the same note demonstrates that Ghana can honour its religious heritage while recognising the different traditions that contribute to national life. The GH¢2 note should therefore be appreciated for the values it represents rather than assigned a spiritual purpose that was never intended. In all, the central issue is not the amount printed on the note but the meaning attached to the act of giving. The introduction of the Ghana Cedi Heritage Series represents an important development in Ghana’s monetary history. Beyond improvements in security, durability and design, the new banknotes celebrate distinguished personalities, important national landmarks and the country’s cultural heritage. They remind Ghanaians that currency can serve not only as a medium of exchange but also as an expression of national identity and collective memory. Within this broader context, the recognition of Cardinal Peter Porekuu Dery on the GH¢2 note is particularly meaningful. His contributions to religious leadership, education, community development and the promotion of human dignity deserve national appreciation. The inclusion of the historic Larabanga Mosque on the reverse further reinforces Ghana’s commitment to religious freedom, mutual respect and peaceful coexistence. However, the recognition of a religious leader on a banknote should not be confused with the biblical meaning of giving. As the discussion has established, the Bank of Ghana’s decision to feature Cardinal Dery does not make GH¢2 the prescribed denomination for church offerings or confer special spiritual value on that note. The biblical passages examined consistently emphasise that Christian giving should be cheerful, voluntary, sincere, proportionate to one’s resources and motivated by gratitude and love. The accounts of the poor widow, Paul’s teachings on generosity and Jesus’ warnings against seeking public recognition demonstrate that the spiritual significance of giving cannot be determined solely by monetary value or outward appearance. These teachings have practical implications for Christians. A GH¢2 offering made sincerely by someone with limited resources should never be regarded as insignificant. Equally, the presence of a religious personality on the note should not become an excuse for limiting generosity when a believer is willing and reasonably able to give more. Christian stewardship requires thoughtful decisions that recognise both God’s goodness and the giver’s financial circumstances. The broader lesson is that national recognition and religious devotion, although both worthy of respect, serve different purposes. Ghana may honour its distinguished religious leaders through currency designs, monuments and other national symbols. Christians, however, must continue to understand their offerings through the teachings of Scripture rather than the images appearing on money. We should therefore celebrate our national heroes without misinterpreting the purpose of their recognition. We should appreciate the cultural and religious symbolism of our currency without allowing that symbolism to replace biblical principles. And to my dear friend who has already resolved that the new GH¢2 note will henceforth be the only denomination for church offerings, as well as others who share this sentiment, I offer this gentle reminder: The Bank of Ghana may determine whose portrait appears on the cedi, but it does not determine what you should give to God. The image on the note may remind us of a faithful servant, but our giving should reflect our own faithfulness to the Lord. After all, the value of an offering before God is not determined by the face printed on the currency, but by the heart from which the gift proceeds. May our offerings always reflect grateful hearts, willing spirits and genuine love for God. Bank of Ghana.
