Title: Ghana’s 2027 Budget: Investing in Ghana’s energy future
Content: The intersection of energy reliability and industrial capacity remains the most critical determinant of economic growth in developing economies. Historically, Ghana's energy system has expanded, yet it has been burdened by high tariffs, distribution losses, weak revenue collections, and accumulated obligations to Independent Power Producers (IPPs). In 2025, the annual energy sector shortfall reached approximately US$1.4 billion, with arrears to IPPs and fuel suppliers standing at US$1.7 billion. Ghana's 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy appears to introduce a paradigm shift. The budget outlines a decisive move toward energy sovereignty, anchoring national industrialisation on state-owned, affordable, and reliable power generation. This article details the specific energy infrastructure projects, funding allocations, and policy frameworks embedded in the 2027 budget. Key Energy Initiatives (Pillar Three: US$2 Billion Energy Infrastructure) Pillar Three of the New Economy, New Ghana framework in the 2027 budget is dedicated to overhauling the national energy architecture. The government has allocated US$2 billion to this pillar, aiming to end dependence on costly emergency power by 2030 and reduce generation costs from 16 US cents per kilowatt-hour (kWh) to 8 US cents/kWh or less. State-Owned Thermal and Renewable Power Generation To secure baseload and peak power demands, the government is investing heavily in state-owned generation assets:• 1,450 MW Thermal Power Plant: Construction will commence in December 2026 at Kafodzidzi Abrobeano in the Central Region. The plant will be fully state-funded and owned. The first 600 MW will be operational by December 2028, and the remaining 850 MW by December 2030. It will utilise approximately 150 million standard cubic feet of additional gas per day from the Sankofa and Jubilee fields.• 600 MW Solar Power Plant & Battery Storage: A fully state-owned 600 MW solar facility will be constructed, supported by a massive 2,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery storage. This storage capacity is designed to shift daytime solar generation into peak evening periods, ensuring grid stability. Grid Modernisation and Distribution Reforms Recognising that generation capacity must be matched by efficient transmission and distribution, the budget outlines strict policy sequencing.• Transmission Modernisation: US$500 million is allocated from 2027 to 2030 to modernise the transmission system. GRIDCo will utilise these funds to strengthen the north-south network, connect new generation to demand centres, and provide dedicated connections to strategic industrial enclaves. • Distribution Efficiency: To combat distribution losses, the government will deploy 2 million prepaid meters. Furthermore, a performance-based private-sector participation model in electricity distribution will be fully implemented by the end of 2027, protecting strategic public assets while leveraging private-sector expertise.Nuclear Energy Readiness ProgrammeThe 2027 budget officially initiates Ghana's transition to nuclear baseload power, treating the future plant as a strategic national asset rather than an IPP.• Funding & Timeline: US$200 million is dedicated to a 24-month nuclear-readiness programme running from January 2027 to December 2028.• By December 2028, the goal is to complete site studies, technology selection, environmental assessments, financing, and licensing preparations, culminating in the signing of the EPC (Engineering, Procurement, Construction) and financing contract.• The programme includes the training of over 2,000 scientists to build local expertise, ensuring technology transfer and domestic capability.Synergy with Industrialisation (Pillar Four: US$1.5 Billion Critical Minerals)Energy capacity is economic capacity. The energy infrastructure developed under Pillar Three is explicitly designed to power Pillar Four: a US$1.5 Billion investment in Critical Minerals Value Addition.The budget proposes creating a 24-hour critical-minerals processing enclave in the Western Region, powered directly by the new energy backbone. Key policy targets include:• Refining at least 70% of artisanal and small-scale (ASM) gold locally by December 2027, and 100% by December 2028 (prohibiting raw ASM gold exports).• Processing 50% of manganese and bauxite locally by 2028, and 100% by 2030.• Constructing a new railway line from Takoradi to Nyinahin (starting 2027) to transport minerals to the processing enclave. Funding Allocation and Financial Breakdown The following table and chart detail the specific financial commitments outlined in the 2027 Budget Statement regarding energy and related industrial infrastructure. The 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy represents a definitive pivot towards energy sovereignty for Ghana. By allocating US$2 billion to energy infrastructure and US$1.5 billion to mineral value addition, the government aims to eliminate the US$1.4 billion annual fiscal drain caused by energy sector shortfalls. Through strategic investments in state-owned generation, grid modernisation, and nuclear readiness, Ghana is laying the foundational infrastructure required to transition from an exporter of raw materials to a hub of green industrialisation and value-added manufacturing.

Title: Ghana needs a kenkey index!
Content: I have a suggestion for how we should measure economic progress in Ghana. Perhaps we should stop getting too excited about GDP growth and start paying more attention to how much kenkey the average Ghanaian can afford! For many decades, Ghana's progress as a nation has been measured using various economic indicators: GDP growth, inflation, interest rates, foreign direct investment, exchange rates and so on. These are important, but I sometimes wonder whether we have become too obsessed with measuring the economy rather than measuring how people are actually living. Take GDP, for example. GDP largely measures the monetary value of goods and services produced in an economy. But does everything that contributes to human wellbeing have a monetary value? Imagine two people. One buys vegetables from a supermarket. The other grows the same vegetables in a community garden. The supermarket purchase contributes to GDP. The vegetables harvested from the community garden generally do not. Yet, both people have food. The second person may actually be better off financially, nutritionally and socially. I have made a longer post on this specific issue in the past here:https://www.facebook.com/share/19xfDXVC5f/ Similarly, a mother who stays home to care for her children contributes enormously to society, but much of that work is invisible in GDP calculations. A country can therefore record impressive economic growth while its citizens struggle to afford food, rent, transportation and electricity. So, what exactly are we celebrating when GDP grows but people's purchasing power declines? This brings me to my proposal. Introducing the Ghana kenkey index! I propose that Ghana establishes a national Kenkey Index (KI) to measure the purchasing power of ordinary Ghanaians. The methodology is quite simple. 1. Identify 10 popular kenkey joints in each of Ghana's 16 regions. That's 160 joints nationwide. 2. Every month, survey these sellers to establish the price and actual weight of their kenkey. 3. Compare the price and weight against Ghana's daily national minimum wage. 4. Calculate how many kilograms of kenkey a minimum-wage earner can afford with one day's earnings. 5. Publish the results monthly, including regional comparisons. The news headlines following a budget presentation could be any of the following: * Ghana's GDP grows by 5%, but kenkey purchasing power declines by 20%. * Workers in Central Region can afford twice as much kenkey as workers in Greater Accra. * The average minimum-wage earner can now afford only 1.2 kg of kenkey per working day, down from 2 kg last year. These would be headlines and economic indicators that ordinary Ghanaians can relate to! Of course, the index will have limitations. Not everyone eats kenkey. Kenkey prices and portion sizes differ across regions. Weight doesn't necessarily tell us about nutritional quality. And the minimum wage does not represent everyone's income, particularly in Ghana's large informal sector. I acknowledge all these limitations. The Kenkey Index is not intended to replace GDP, inflation or other conventional economic indicators. It is intended to challenge the idea that economic growth automatically translates into improved living standards. Because, frankly, I am becoming less interested in how many billions of cedis are being generated in the economy and more interested in how much of that economic prosperity finds its way into the pockets and kitchens of ordinary Ghanaians. We need to measure development in ways that reflect people's lived experiences. If GDP is growing but the average Ghanaian can afford less kenkey, can we honestly say that life is getting better? Perhaps the time has come to move beyond GDP. Perhaps we need a Kenkey Index! By: Dr. Fred Otu-Larbi, Head of Strategic Research of the Economic Fighters League

Title: Deceptive marketing in the digital era
Content: A single Instagram post can fill a vendor’s DMs with hundreds of orders. A good photo, low prices, or a word from a popular influencer can close a sale within minutes. Some businesses use that reach to mislead. They edit product photos until the item looks better than it is. They exaggerate what a product can do. Some pay for fake reviews or cut prices that never existed. The sales come fast, and so does the damage to customer trust, which is hard to win back once it is gone. When the product does not match the post Deceptive marketing is any false, misleading, or incomplete information a business uses to get someone to buy. Most online shoppers in Ghana have a story like this. The dress arrives in thinner fabric and a different shade. A shop advertises “50% off” on a price it raised the week before. An influencer raves about a cream without mentioning the brand paid her. A service quotes one figure and adds fees at checkout. So much buying happens through social media pages, online shops and WhatsApp. Customers usually pay before they see the item, and they have only the seller’s word to go on. That makes honesty the seller’s responsibility. How deception hurts businesses Some owners argue that with so much competition, they have to push hard to survive. Here is what misleading customers does to a business. A customer who feels cheated seldom orders again. She tells her sister, her colleagues, and her church WhatsApp group too. Complaints travel fast online. One angry post can reach thousands of potential buyers, and a complaint that goes viral can undo years of goodwill within hours. Losing customers is expensive. Each one who leaves has to be replaced with fresh advertising, so the business pays again and again to attract buyers who never stick around. The law matters here too. Ghana’s Consumer Protection Bill is still being debated, yet current laws and regulators already deal with advertising, trade practices, and consumer rights. A business that ignores them is taking a real risk. Good marketing gets someone to buy and then gives them a reason to buy again. Photos, product descriptions, prices and promotions should show customers exactly what they will get. Any claim about quality or results should be something you can back up. Customers should know the full cost before they pay, including delivery, extra fees, and any subscription terms. Nobody forgets a surprise charge at the end. Reviews should come from real buyers. Ask for honest feedback, reply to complaints with courtesy, and sort out the problem. Customers notice when a business owns its mistakes. Paid endorsements need a clear label. If you pay an influencer to promote your product, the post should say so, because followers have a right to know. Clicks and first-time sales only show the start. Repeat orders, retention, satisfaction, referrals and complaints tell you whether customers are coming back or drifting away. Social media lets a small business reach more buyers than any shopfront could. Trust takes more than reach. An ad might get someone to place a first order. What arrives in the package decides whether they place a second. When the product falls short of the post, customers stop believing your ads, and the loss runs well past that single order. Misleading customers puts profits and reputation on the line, and over time it can sink the business. Count the customers who come back because you delivered what you advertised. That number tells you whether your marketing works. Keep your word with every order, and you build a business people return to. Dr. Genevieve Sedalo, Department of Marketing, University of Professional Studies. gdsedalo@gmail.com

Title: Every family should have a Family Pharmacist: The future of personalised pharmaceutical care in Ghana
Content: Healthcare is changing rapidly, and Ghana must keep exploring innovative approaches to improve its population's health and well-being. One such approach is to introduce and promote Family Pharmacist services, so every family can access a designated pharmacist who understands their pharmaceutical and medication-related needs. I strongly advocate that every family in Ghana should have the opportunity to engage a Family Pharmacist who can provide continuous pharmaceutical care, medication counselling, health education, preventive health advice, and support for the safe and effective use of medicines. Pharmacists are among society's most accessible healthcare professionals. However, the pharmacist's role extends far beyond dispensing medicines. Modern pharmacy practice has evolved into a highly specialised clinical profession, with pharmacists contributing to patient care across a wide range of therapeutic and public health areas. Today, pharmacists have advanced expertise in oncology and chemotherapy, neuropharmacy, clinical pharmacy, infectious diseases, critical care, cardiology, paediatrics, geriatrics, psychiatry, public health, pharmacogenomics, antimicrobial stewardship, nuclear pharmacy, and several other specialised areas. These specialist pharmacists possess advanced knowledge and clinical skills that enable them to contribute meaningfully to the care of patients with complex diseases and medication needs. They work as part of multidisciplinary healthcare teams alongside physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals. Ghana should therefore consider a more structured model of pharmaceutical care in which the Family Pharmacist serves as a trusted pharmaceutical healthcare partner for the family, while patients with complex conditions can be referred to the appropriate specialist pharmacist. The Family Pharmacist could provide services including medication reviews, medication reconciliation, identification of potential drug interactions, support for medication adherence, counselling on the appropriate use of medicines, guidance on over-the-counter medications, health education, and advice on disease prevention. The Family Pharmacist could also maintain an appropriate medication record for family members and, where necessary, collaborate with doctors, nurses, hospitals, and specialist pharmacists to ensure continuity of care. For patients with complex medical conditions, the Family Pharmacist could help facilitate access to specialised pharmaceutical care. For example, a patient undergoing cancer treatment may need an Oncology Pharmacist with specialised knowledge of chemotherapy and supportive cancer care. A patient with complex neurological conditions may benefit from a Neuropharmacist, while patients with serious infections may need pharmacists specialising in infectious diseases and antimicrobial stewardship. This creates a continuum of pharmaceutical care: Family Pharmacist → Specialist Pharmacist → Multidisciplinary Specialist Care The Family Pharmacist would not replace the physician, nurse, or other healthcare professionals. Instead, the Family Pharmacist would become an important member of the family's healthcare team, working collaboratively with other professionals to ensure patients receive appropriate pharmaceutical care at the right time. Families could voluntarily engage Family Pharmacists and pay professional fees or subscriptions for agreed services, depending on their healthcare needs and the scope of care provided. This approach could create a sustainable model of personalised pharmaceutical care while recognising pharmacists' professional value and clinical expertise. Such a model could contribute to addressing major health challenges, including medication errors, adverse drug reactions, drug interactions, polypharmacy, inappropriate self-medication, poor adherence to treatment, irrational use of antibiotics, and medication-related hospital admissions. It could also strengthen preventive healthcare by giving families regular access to a healthcare professional who can identify potential medication-related problems early and provide evidence-based advice before such problems become more serious. As a public health professional and specialist public health pharmacist, I believe Ghana must begin to think beyond the traditional boundaries of healthcare delivery. We must build a preventive, patient-centred, multidisciplinary, accessible, and increasingly personalised healthcare system. The Family Pharmacist concept offers an opportunity to bring pharmaceutical care closer to the family and ensure people have a trusted professional to guide them in the safe, effective use of medicines throughout their lives. Every family should have access to a trusted Family Pharmacist. Every patient with a complex condition should have access to the appropriate specialist pharmacist. Every pharmacist should be empowered to practice at the highest level of their training, competence, and specialisation. Ghana's healthcare system must evolve towards a model in which the right patient receives the right care from the right healthcare professional at the right time. The future of healthcare is not simply about treating illness after it occurs. It is about prevention, early intervention, personalised care, medication safety, rational use of medicines, and multidisciplinary collaboration. I therefore call for a national conversation among the Ministry of Health, Ghana Health Service, Pharmacy Council, Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana, health insurers, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and the public on developing a sustainable framework for Family Pharmacist services in Ghana. Let us recognise the pharmacist not merely as the professional who dispenses medicines, but as a highly trained healthcare professional and an essential partner in disease prevention, medication safety, health promotion, and the management of complex health conditions. Let us make the Family Pharmacist an essential partner in family healthcare and harness the full potential of specialist pharmacists to build a healthier Ghana. Dr Sheikh Ibrahim Ibn Saana, FGCPharm, MPH

Title: Kester Osei Mensah writes: Mfantsipim has shown us what school pride, unity and collective love can achieve
Content: I have watched with admiration the excitement and razzmatazz surrounding Mfantsipim’s 150th anniversary. From the build-up to the actual celebrations, the energy, togetherness and love for the school have been beautiful to behold. And it hasn’t been Mfantsipim alone. This past weekend, we have also witnessed other schools, including St. Monica’s Senior High School, Accra Senior High School, Archbishop Porter Girls’ Secondary School and Armed Forces Senior High Technical School, celebrate their homecomings with pride, excitement and a wonderful sense of belonging. It has been beautiful to see old students reconnect, relive cherished memories and celebrate the institutions that helped shape them. But it got me thinking: What would it take for us to celebrate our own schools with that same passion and enthusiasm? Every school has a story, and every old student is part of that story. The friendships, experiences, lessons and memories we gathered along the way helped shape who we are today. Life may have taken us in different directions, but our connection to those institutions remains. Perhaps it’s time we did more than reminisce about the good old days. Let’s reconnect, show up, support our schools, mentor the younger generation and contribute in whatever way we can. To all alumni, regardless of the school you attended, let Mfantsipim and the other schools celebrating this weekend inspire you. The school made you who you are today. Now, do your part to make the school better than you met it! And to my dear Ghanacoll family, this is a special appeal. Osagyefo’s own school, Ghana National College, is already 78 years old! In just two years, we celebrate our 80th anniversary. That’s a milestone worth preparing for, and we have every reason to build the same excitement, unity and collective pride around our beloved school. Our history is even intertwined with Mfantsipim, St. Augustine’s and Adisadel, as some of our pioneering students came from these institutions following the establishment of Ghana National College by Osagyefo Dr. Kwame Nkrumah. Fellow Ghanacoll alumni, it’s time to step up! Wherever you are, whatever you do and whichever year you left school, Ghanacoll is still part of your story. Whether you are an established professional, entrepreneur, public servant or still finding your feet, you have something to offer. Let’s not leave the responsibility of building our school to a handful of committed old students. Let’s all take ownership. Join the alumni initiatives, attend reunions, support school projects, mentor students, open doors for one another and contribute your time, ideas, networks and resources. Don’t just wear the school badge or celebrate your year group. Be present. Be involved. Be counted! And let’s not wait until the 80th anniversary is upon us before we start showing up. The excitement, the planning and the commitment must begin now. Let’s make our 80th a celebration that reflects not just how old our school is, but how much its people care. The school made us. Now it’s our turn to make the school great!

Title: The stench of cocaine and Ghana’s new cedi – Occasional Kwatriot Kwesi Yankah writes
Content: On my global rounds last year, I was shocked to see at airport shops perfume names that shook me to the core: a perfume called ‘Cocaine,’ then another designer perfume. ‘Opium.’ But the killer of them all was ‘Sinners Perfume,’ apparently the fastest ticket to Hell. Surprisingly, the accompanying aromas were smooth, except that no Daddy in his right senses would want ‘Cocaine Perfume’ even mistakenly seized by Customs officials. Those were on sale for $175 to $200, and attracted a small queue of young men. The trip to the cocaine world is not as long as you thought. Who knows if we have a cocaine heritage on our hands in Ghana, in search of heritage items on a new currency. Our beloved country has now launched new currency bank notes, called the ‘heritage series’: a label we are scratching our heads to understand. Are the current cedi notes that weak and fragile, their batteries about to die? Or does the Bank of Ghana seek an excuse to print new money and fill the till to rescue 2028? ‘There is no money in the system,’ market women complain of low sales; so ‘let’s simply print more money and give it an elegant pseudonym, Heritage? Were the signs not clear? Did you notice the speed, the rush, the sense of urgency, and eventually the anti-climax: a comedy of errors on our sovereign cedi. National mourning, indeed, tears for a sinking Ghana. For once, the entire public is part of this debate on our national heritage; and we are together debating wrong faces matched to human names on new currency notes; and we lament essentials missing in the national heritage. Indeed, faces on our new cedi notes have sparked so much debate that we forget the likelihood that Artificial Intelligence may have fooled us all. Let Ghana wait until rumours spread that the man we see as Kofi Annan on the new 100 cedi note is really not Kofi Annan but our friend Kevin Taylor; and that the lady displayed as Justice Annie Jiagge on the new 10 cedi note is ‘before God and man,’ probably Akosua Jollof? Simply imagine the stampede online. It is now unclear whether the Bank of Ghana will swallow its pride and go back to school for remedial education: honouring the name Theodocia Okoh with the true Face of Theodocia Okoh, the true designer of the national flag. Letitia Obeng, the mistaken identity, was well known to us fellows of the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences. She was an award-winning scientist who, in 2006, succeeded Nana Dr S.K.B. Asante as the first female President of the Academy. ‘Auntie Leti’ must be stirring in her grave over her mixed identity with Theodosia. Then comes, of late, a damning verdict on the picture representation of Cardinal Peter Dery on the two cedi note. Says a worried Ghanaian: “It is simply disheartening and baffling that a national tribute meant to honour an iconic figure of our faith, the late Cardinal Peter Dery of blessed memory, could be marred by such a glaring oversight.” Then was this blatant omission of five of the Big Six on the heritage bank notes, leaving a lone Kwame Nkrumah. Remember the Big Six statue in Accra was demolished in 2024 by an anonymous Ghanaian at dawn, who had enough time to videotape the entire event in full view of cheering spectators. It was during the Nana Addo era. No arrests were made by the police, who were three hundred meters away. When the Mahama party won power in late 2024, the Big Six roundabout was redesigned, with the Big Six statue conspicuously deleted. The Big Six, with Nkrumah, Danquah, Edward Akufo Addo, Obetsebi Lamptey, Ako Adjei, and William Ofori Atta, is apparently no longer a heritage priority? But wait till power changes hands in 2028; Ghana’s toy play may bounce back. And what do we do with this bizarre incident? 2021 one Esther Bosha a Zimbabwean national and crew member of Emirate Air, visits Ghana as tourist, poses for a picture among market women in Accra; then says a word or two in praise of Ghana. A kind-hearted Bank of Ghana adds her picture among traders, as qualified to stick on Ghana’s one cedi banknote. Esther Bosha as Ghana’s heritage icon? Zimbabwe currently chuckles hearing this. I myself visited Zimbabwe in 2006 and felt at home seeing Mugabe’s Zanu-PF headquarters in Harare, hoisting the Red Cockerel flag of Kwame Nkrumah’s CPP. I warmly applauded, but did that qualify me to appear on the Zimbabwean currency? Where is our state protocol? Our parliament? Ghana, when did we drop the baton and lose the plot? And how did we sink this low? Our state emblems now run the ship of state aground, and all is quiet? Akom ko, the elders say. ‘The pristine dance of the high priest is no more, leaving the field for those that merely twirl around in raffia skirts… Ghana is no longer the state we knew: now plunged into a crisis of identity, prewired with a badge of dishonour. We miserably flopped at the soccer World Cup, but beat our chest with pride, excelling in a global cocaine league. Daily news breaks of Drugs shipped through our ports, sometimes officially escorted. Our port officials see no cocaine, speak no cocaine, smell no cocaine and do no cocaine. But kids do cocaine at home and school. The scandal breaks only after the horse has left the stable…When cocaine arrests are made, no names and no faces. Indeed, a silent cocaine prosecution in a nation that is not angry enough to crack the whip. Yes, we have a heritage to protect, and display on bank notes, but it is Negative Heritage. A sordid heritage of moving sewage that was once called rivers; a heritage of toxic streams, poisoned crops, dangerous turbidity. No river has been spared, including the great Volta River, and with it the diverse fish species it hosts. The school kids are busy too, learning the sport of poisoning; they have abandoned school and now mine in poisonous waters. After all this, we finally set our sights on the sea, to seal the shipment of floating sewage. But we shouldn’t omit paedophilia from the emerging heritage. Our moral compass is gone; elders and security now look on while school kids are defiled. Is anybody home, Ghana? A new cedi note has been launched in the filth of a negative heritage. That is the legacy we leave for future generations: the stench of cocaine across the landscape, in schools, a nation high on drugs, and a polluted banknote that says it all: A rotten heritage can only be returned to the Sender. How much has Ghana lost in all this? There is something they call Financial loss to the state. Hello Attorney General! Next Post: Yours truly as a Drug Suspect at Heathrow. kyankah@ashesi.edu.gh

Title: The right diagnosis, an incomplete cure – Frimpong Boateng writes on 2027 budget
Content: "These boom-and-bust cycles must cease" On the evening of Thursday, November 12, 2026, the Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, when presenting the 2027 budget, told Parliament that Ghana's boom-and-bust cycles must cease. Few Ghanaians would disagree. Too many times we have lived through hope followed by hardship, a stable cedi followed by sharp depreciation, and a recovery followed by another crisis. I have read the full 2027 Budget Statement, and I want to answer one question. Does the Minister appreciate why the boom-and-bust cycles happen, and does his New Economy programme remove the cause? My answer is that the Minister has made the right diagnosis but prescribed an incomplete cure. The budget sees two causes clearly. It misses a third, and the third is the one that will bring the next bust. What the budget gets right The budget statement is more candid about the causes of our instability than most budgets before it. It says the cedi came under pressure "when prices dropped or fiscal discipline weakened" (para. 161). It concedes that "temporary booms had financed permanent commitments" (para. 168), and it blames reckless spending, weak revenue and expensive debt for the crisis of 2022. Most importantly, the budget statement admits that past governments repaired the public finances "but did not use the recovery to alter the structure of the economy," and so "the cycle began again" (paras. 186–187). It even pledges that fiscal discipline "will apply throughout the election cycle" (para. 239). So the Government does understand two causes: our dependence on raw commodity exports, and fiscal indiscipline. I accept both. My quarrel is with what is missing. The machine that is not in the plan Read the eight pillars of the New Economy and one thing stands out. The only imports the budget counts as a drain on the cedi are things we consume: rice, sugar, poultry, fish, vegetables and medicines. It says the food import bill "weakens the cedi" (para. 260). It promises that when Ghana grows and processes more, "the cedi will face less pressure" (para. 336). It demands that every cedi of fiscal space answer the question: "what imports will it replace?" (para. 191). The budget never asks that question of the factories themselves. Throughout the statement, machines are things to buy and finance: the "manufacturer investing in new machinery" is offered equipment leasing (paras. 228, 231);the rice hubs receive tax incentives for "irrigation, mechanisation, silos, modern mills" (para. 276);GH¢800 million is allocated "to procure agricultural machinery" (para. 1543);the review of Chapter 98 of the Customs Tariff concerns duty concessions on imported "machinery and other inputs" (para. 860);the textiles pillar promises jobs for machine operators, not machine makers (para. 448);for the nuclear plant, "international partners will only provide technology, finance, engineering and specialist services" (para. 380).Cocoa grinding mills, gold refineries, alumina plants, rice mills, garment lines and pharmaceutical plants are all capital goods. Ghana makes almost none of them, and few of their spare parts. Every one will be imported and paid for in dollars, and every one will be kept running with imported spares, also paid for in dollars. The budget's own figures show where the capacity to make machines stands in the Government's order of priorities. New Economy programme, 2027 outlay (para. 249) Procurement of agricultural machinery (para. 1543) Completion of the Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre (para. 1582) GRATIS Foundation, whole year, no capital expenditure (Appendix 4A) The Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre is the one line in this budget about making machines rather than buying them. The Centre dates from my time as Minister for Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation, and six years after I left office, it is still waiting to be completed. In 2027 it receives about 0.17 per cent of the New Economy outlay, and one-sixteenth of what we will spend on imported farm machinery in the same year. GRATIS, built to carry engineering capability into the regions, receives less than half of one per cent of the machinery budget. Nothing in the New Economy programme is set aside for machine tools, foundries, spare parts or engineering manufacturing. How the next bust will come Suppose the New Economy succeeds exactly as planned. By 2030 Ghana processes all its cocoa, refines all its gold, processes all its manganese and bauxite and mills its own rice. Food imports fall, export earnings per tonne rise, and the cedi strengthens. But each of those plants was built with imported equipment, and each needs a steady flow of imported spares, replacement parts and, in time, replacement machines. When a mill breaks down, it cannot wait for the cedi to recover. It must buy the part at whatever the exchange rate happens to be. This demand for foreign exchange is stubborn, and it grows with every factory we open. The budget itself names commodity price volatility as the first of its five principal risks (para. 1025). When commodity prices next fall, export earnings will drop, but the bill for machines and spares will not. The cedi will come under pressure again, and the cycle will begin again, at a higher level of output but under the same ceiling. That is the trap of an economy that assembles but does not make. Value addition on imported capital goods moves the bottleneck; it does not remove it. There is a fiscal test as well. The programme is financed partly by lowering the primary surplus target by one percentage point of GDP (para. 247), beginning in the year before an election. The Government will answer that a surplus of at least 0.5 per cent of GDP remains (para. 221), and that is a fair answer. But the pledge of discipline "throughout the election cycle" will be tested in 2028, and Ghanaians have heard such pledges before. What a complete cure would require The modern world economy is knowledge-based and driven by science and technology. Societies that produce, adapt and commercialise knowledge have achieved sustained growth and rising living standards. Raising money to pay foreign contractors to build infrastructure, good as the projects may be, cannot by itself lead to sustained economic development. Ghana has to develop the capacity to build the machines its industries run on. The cure is not to abandon value addition. It is to add the pillar the plan lacks: the capacity to make the machines. Make capital goods a ninth pillar of the New Economy, with its own budget, targets and delivery unit, as the other eight have.Fund the Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre to operate, not merely to be completed, and link it to the processing enclaves as a supplier of spare parts. Establish the Design and Manufacturing Technology Centre called for at the conference of Ghanaian scientists and engineers that the Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation and the Ghana Institution of Engineering convened at Peduase in January 2019. The foundry can cast and machine parts; the Centre would let Ghana design the machines themselves, working with the processing enclaves on the equipment they need. Apply the budget's own local-preference principle to machines. If public money spent on rice must buy Ghana rice (para. 283), public money spent on silos, mills, dryers and processing equipment should, where quality allows, buy from Ghanaian fabricators: Suame Magazine, the regional centres of GRATIS, KNUST's Technology Consultancy Centre, and the private engineers who have already shown what they can do. Reform Chapter 98 so that duty concessions on imported machinery are matched by incentives to make the same machinery here, and are phased down as local capacity grows. Judge every New Economy project by its import content, not only by the jobs and exports it creates.The question every factory must answer The Minister asked every cedi of fiscal space to say which imports it will replace. I ask the same question of every factory the New Economy will build. Until Ghana can make at least some of the machines that make its goods, our booms will be paid for in dollars we will not have when the bust comes. The diagnosis in this budget is right. The cure is not yet complete. © 2026 Prof. Kwabena Frimpong-Boateng.

Title: To judge and to teach: 150 years of the Supreme Court and Mfantsipim
Content: In 1876, two institutions were born on the Gold Coast within three days of each other. On 31 March, the Supreme Court Ordinance created a Supreme Court for the whole colony. On 3 April, the Wesleyan High School, later Mfantsipim, opened in Cape Coast under its 18-year-old principal, the Rev. James Picot. One institution was made to judge, the other to teach. A hundred and fifty years later, Ghana’s story is hard to tell without either of them. The coincidence gained a fitting footnote this year. On the same day in September 2026, two Mfantsipim old boys, Edward Amoako Asante and Anthony Forson Jnr, were sworn in as Justices of the Supreme Court. The moment invites a bigger question: what makes an institution last? SupremeCourt History Built for more than one generationAt the School’s founding, Rev. Thomas Birch Freeman spoke of ‘the pressing necessity for higher schools,’ to train the teachers the colonial government would not. The Court began as a colonial superior court with roughly the powers of the English High Court. Today the School prepares boys for every kind of career, and the Court is the nation’s final court of appeal. The real test of an institution is whether it keeps its purpose as the world changes around it. Measured by its people In 1908, Mfantsipim’s Principal Rev W T Balmer set out to ‘raise up a generation of men… who will be brave enough to face the problems of their own continent practically and unselfishly.’ Fittingly, few people judge Mfantsipim by its buildings, but by its people, from Kofi Annan to a long line of national figures, judges among them. Sir Samuel Quashie-Idun acted as Chief Justice of the Gold Coast, became Chief Justice of Western Nigeria and was the first African President of the Court of Appeal for Eastern Africa. Edmund Bannerman became Ghana’s fourth Chief Justice in 1971, and Isaac Abban, formerly Chief Justice of Seychelles, was its ninth. Other old boys on the Supreme Court include W B Van Lare, W S Bruce-Lyle, G E K Aikins, I N K Wuaku, I K Amuah, T K Adzoe and B T Aryeetey. Four have served as Attorney-General: Aikins, E G Tanoh, Paapa Owusu-Ankomah and Joe Ghartey. The two new Justices continue that line. Justice Asante served three terms as President of the ECOWAS Court of Justice and steered it online when COVID-19 closed courtrooms. Justice Forson sat on the 1992 Consultative Assembly that drafted the present Constitution and later led the Ghana Bar Association as its President. Adapting without losing purpose Neither institution has had a smooth road. The School changed its name and endured lean years. In 1905 it merged with the school founded by John Mensah Sarbah, dropped the motto Honour et Honores for Dwen Hwɛ Kan, meaning ‘Think and Look Ahead,’ and chose black and red, for African skin and blood, as its colours. Its lowest point came perhaps in 1907, when the staff and most students left, and eight boys stayed on to teach themselves: the ‘Faithful Eight’ of school legend. In 1931, the School moved to Kwabotwe Hill, land whose history is still disputed. Independence brought fresh trouble, as successive governments removed three headmasters in a row: Rev Brandful under the CPP in 1963, J W Abruquah in the ‘Apollo 568’ dismissals of 1970, and O K Monney under the Supreme Military Council government in 1976. The Court’s experience was harsher still. The Constitutions of both 1957 and 1960 gave judges security of tenure, but that protection did not last. In 1963, a three-judge panel acquitted the accused in the Adamafio treason trial. President Nkrumah removed the presiding judge, Chief Justice Arku Korsah, and a second panel member, Van Lare (an old boy), resigned. When the third, Justice Akufo-Addo, refused to go, the Constitution was amended to let the President remove judges at will, and Nkrumah removed him too. After the 1966 coup, the military regime ‘retired’ judges, among them Bruce-Lyle (an old boy). The Court itself was abolished in 1966, restored in 1969 and abolished again in 1972, and Chief Justices were removed in 1972 and 1977, Bannerman among them. Only in 1979 was the Court fully restored; today it rests on the 1992 Constitution. Both stories show that an institution can be interrupted and still return renewed. Excellence must be earned again History guarantees nothing. Mfantsipim cannot live off its famous old boys, nor the Court off 150 years of history. Each generation must earn public trust again through independence, rigour and loyalty to the Constitution. Nor is an old boy’s appointment a win for one school over others: appointments rest on merit, and the Court belongs to all Ghanaians. A legacy is a debt to be honoured, not an inheritance to be spent. For the Supreme Court, the challenge is urgent: public trust in the judiciary is under real strain. The answer is not to chase popularity but to show, repeatedly, that decisions follow the law rather than politics, give clear reasons and arrive without needless delay. The executive and Parliament must respect the Court’s independence; lawyers, the media and civil society must examine its work fairly and fearlessly. Building a nation is a relay. Mfantsipim, especially after 1905, gave itself to the nationalist cause. The Court was largely deferential to colonial rule for 80 years, and it is still debated whether it has become the court a free nation deserves. How the two new Justices serve will be their true measure. The real achievement of 1876 is not that two institutions have survived for 150 years. It is that they still matter. The task for the next 150 years is to make sure they always will. The writers, Ace Anan Ankomah, Esq., FGA & Dr Nana Dadzie Ghansah, are from MOBA'84 [A fuller version of this article has been published in the Mfantsipim Speech Day brochure].

Title: Mfantsipim School and the founding of Ghana National College – Egbert Faibille Jnr writes
Content: On the occasion of the 150th Anniversary of Mfantsipim School, it is imperative that we share one significant impact of that School on the independence struggle of the Gold Coast. The record stands that in the wake of the Christiansborg Cross-Roads Shootings on 28th February, 1948, then Gold Coast Governor, Gerald Creasy, ordered a crackdown. That resulted in the arrests of 5 of the Big Six- J.B. Danquah, Ako Adjei, Edward Akufo-Addo, William Ofori Atta, and Emmanuel Obetsebi Lamptey in Accra on suspicion of complicity in the protest march of the ex-servicemen. They were arrested in the immediate aftermath of the disturbances and detained. The other member of the United Gold Coast Convention's (UGCC) Working Committee, Kwame Nkrumah, was initially fortunate to escape arrest because he had been requested by the others named above to rush to the UGCC's Saltpond offices to secure it and their documents. Kwame Nkrumah proceeded to Saltpond and, after carrying out the tasks assigned to him, went into hiding in Cape Coast. The Colonial Police took almost 14 days to locate Kwame Nkrumah to arrest him. Pursuant to a Removal Order under the hand of Governor Gerald Creasy dated 12th March, 1948, Kwame Nkrumah was arrested in Cape Coast on that same day. As fate would have it, Kwame Nkrumah was with his then Private Secretary, Saki Scheck, an alumnus of Mfantsipim School at the time of his arrest. With Nkrumah arrested, MOBA Saki Scheck set a scheme in operation when he chanced upon some students of Mfantsipim School in Cape Coast in the immediate aftermath and recounted to them the arrest. Saki Scheck also requested the Mfantsipim students to accompany him to Mfantsipim School to sensitise the students about the arrests of the Big Six. At Mfantsipim School, a student gathering was called for Saki Scheck, who seized the moment to ginger the students to boycott classes and to petition the Colonial government for the immediate release of the Big Six. That Petition was effectively written. From Mfantsipim, Saki Scheck moved to St. Augustine's College and Adisadel College respectively to undertake the same sensitisation campaign. FindSchools With that, boys and some teachers from the three all-boys schools in Cape Coast embarked on a strike dubbed 'political' to demand the release of the Big Six. The strike lasted from 13th March to 20th March, 1948. Mfanstipim School was thus the nerve centre of the strike action. The Colonial government acted swiftly by closing down the three schools. Further, a Conference on the Cape Coast Secondary Schools was called to investigate the strike action and make recommendations. In the end, some 150 boys were expelled for their joint roles in the strike action. Also expelled were four teachers, one of whom was Henry Werner Aryee Kofi Sackeyfio of Mfantsipim School. FindSchools On the release of the Big Six, Kwame Nkrumah seized the opportunity to found Ghana National College on 16th July, 1948 for the dismissed students. On such an occasion, and as a proud alumnus of Ghana National College, I salute Mfantsipim School for its stance in March 1948 and the outcome in July 1948 being the founding of my alma mater. Ghana National College today stands as a nationalist school and the Gold Coast's defiant response to colonialism. Mfantsipim is the oldest secondary school in Ghana, and Ghana National College is the only school that bore the name 'Ghana' almost nine years before the Gold Coast attained independence and assumed the name Ghana. FindSchools Congratulations to Mfantsipim School! The author is Egbert Faibille Jnr is former President of the Ghana National College Old Students Association.

Title: When even your Traffic Fine is a scam!
Content: Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, the government decided that Ghanaian motorists had enjoyed too much freedom on the roads. Some drove as though speed limits were recommendations from elderly relatives, deserving respectful consideration but not necessarily obedience. Others regarded traffic lights as Christmas decorations, beautiful to behold but entirely optional. The authorities therefore introduced electronic traffic enforcement, hoping cameras would accomplish what policemen, road signs and decades of public education had struggled to achieve. It was a brilliant idea. Cameras do not accept apologies, recognise party colours or appreciate the significance of a driver's uncle being a Deputy Minister. They simply record offences and leave the authorities to do the rest. Unfortunately, the Republic's fraudsters were also watching. And being patriotic citizens with an extraordinary appetite for business opportunities, they apparently decided that government should not enjoy a monopoly over the collection of money from frightened motorists. Thus was born Ghana's newest potential growth industry: Traffic Fine Entrepreneurship. For years, our enterprising fraudsters concentrated on traditional sectors of the deception economy. They promised unsuspecting citizens foreign visas, miraculous investments, parcels of gold and romantic relationships with wealthy strangers who mysteriously required financial assistance before declaring their undying love. But every industry must innovate or perish. Why promise somebody an inheritance from a dead millionaire in London when you can simply inform him that his Toyota Corolla has offended the Republic? No complicated love story. No inheritance documents. Just a threatening message, an alleged traffic offence and instructions to pay before trouble arrives. The Ghana Police Service warned motorists about fraudulent traffic penalty notices on 4 November 2026, while the Cyber Security Authority followed on 9 November with concerns about fake messages and payment websites. Evidently, some people had discovered that where government establishes a collection system, unofficial competitors may soon arrive with their own invoices. In the Republic of Uncommon Sense, even criminality believes in public-private partnership. Consider the predicament of the ordinary Ghanaian motorist. He leaves home determined to obey every traffic regulation. At the first junction, a taxi overtakes him from the wrong side. At the next, an aboboyaa carrying enough merchandise to establish a branch of Kejetia Market passes him with the confidence of a presidential convoy. Before reaching his destination, three motorcycles have demonstrated that road markings are merely artistic expressions on asphalt. Our gentleman, meanwhile, is doing 50 kilometres per hour, glancing nervously at his speedometer as though it contains the examination results of his firstborn. Then his telephone announces the arrival of a traffic penalty. He checks the message, his registration number and his memory. Was it yesterday? Last Tuesday? Perhaps the day he accelerated slightly to escape an impatient truck whose driver appeared to believe that brakes were invented for cowards. The message demands payment. But is it genuine? One friend advises him to ignore it. Another warns that failure to pay could lead to prosecution. A third suggests visiting the police station. A fourth, who considers himself an expert in digital governance because he once successfully renewed his passport online, recommends checking the official platform. By the time our motorist finishes his consultations, he has spent enough airtime to finance a small telecommunications company. And he still cannot establish whether he owes the Republic money or whether the Republic's unofficial business community is attempting to collect a private tax. Our ancestors warned that when two elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers. In modern Ghana, however, the elephants have discovered mobile money, and the grass is being asked to enter its PIN. The tragedy is that electronic traffic enforcement is not inherently a bad idea. Ghana's roads have witnessed enough recklessness to convince even the most stubborn optimist that something must change. We cannot continue treating road safety as a seasonal sermon delivered during Christmas and Easter, only to return afterwards to the national sport of overtaking death at dangerous bends. But technology without adequate public education can become an elaborate invitation to confusion. When motorists are uncertain about how official notices are delivered, where penalties should be verified and which payment channels are legitimate, fraudsters need little imagination. They merely dress deception in the respectable clothing of government authority and wait for frightened citizens to open their wallets. As the elders say, when the owner of the house fails to identify his children, the stranger may enter the compound and demand supper. Indeed, perhaps the Republic should introduce a compulsory examination for motorists: Advanced Traffic Fine Authentication. Question One: You receive a message claiming that your vehicle exceeded the speed limit. What should you do? A. Pay immediately before the police arrest your ancestors. B. Forward the message to your family WhatsApp group for collective interpretation. C. Consult your pastor to determine whether the offence is physical or spiritual. D. Verify the notice through the officially authorised channel. Naturally, the correct answer is D. Unfortunately, in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, many citizens may have exhausted A, B and C before discovering D. And therein lies the serious matter beneath the laughter. The success of electronic enforcement depends not merely on detecting wrongdoing but also on public confidence. A genuine penalty must be distinguishable from a fraudulent demand without requiring the investigative resources of EOCO, the patience of Job and the technical expertise of a cybersecurity consultant. Government must make verification simple, publicise authorised payment channels and ensure suspicious notices can be reported without unnecessary bureaucracy. Otherwise, motorists may ignore legitimate penalties because they suspect fraud, while others pay criminals because they fear prosecution. The criminal wins either way. Perhaps the greatest irony is that the Republic has invested in technology to detect motorists exceeding speed limits, only to discover that fraudsters are equally determined to overtake the enforcement system in the race for the motorist's money. And so, in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, government is pursuing speeding motorists, fraudsters are pursuing frightened motorists, and frightened motorists are pursuing somebody who can explain which pursuit is legitimate. Perhaps the next generation of traffic cameras should be programmed to detect not only speeding vehicles but also speeding fraudsters. For in a country where even a traffic fine can be counterfeit, the only thing travelling faster than the motorist is the criminal's imagination. And unlike the unfortunate driver, that imagination appears to have no speed limit.

Title: Ghana’s new export miracle: From Cocoa to Cocaine!
Content: Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, a country famous for producing cocoa, gold and excellent excuses discovered that its agricultural export industry had acquired a rather mysterious new product. The discovery was not made at the Ministry of Trade, the Ghana Export Promotion Authority or any of those important conferences where distinguished gentlemen gather to discuss value addition over bottled water and meat pies. It was made in Spain, where customs officers opened a consignment of Ghanaian coconuts and discovered that the fruits had apparently travelled with 2.6 tonnes of cocaine. For a nation that has spent decades preaching export diversification, this was an extraordinary development. Our farmers had been encouraged to add value to their produce, but nobody had explained that the value should be hidden beneath the produce in wooden crates. Somewhere along the international supply chain, certain enterprising criminals had evidently taken the government's economic transformation agenda rather too literally. The humble coconut must have been deeply embarrassed. For generations, it had served humanity faithfully, providing refreshing water, nutritious flesh and occasional employment for young men who could climb trees faster than graduates could find jobs. Now, through no fault of its own, it had become an exhibit in an international narcotics investigation. According to Spanish authorities, two containers loaded at Tema Port in August arrived in Valencia later that month. Beneath false bottoms in wooden crates containing coconuts, investigators discovered approximately 2.6 tonnes of cocaine. The consignment was subsequently tracked to Almería, where two men were arrested. The operation was publicly announced on 11 November 2026. The Spanish officers must have wondered what extraordinary agricultural technology had enabled Ghanaian coconuts to acquire such expensive foundations. A coconut ordinarily contains water, flesh and a hard shell. These particular coconuts had apparently been provided with an underground economy. And this was hardly the first time Ghanaian commodities had found themselves in such distinguished criminal company. Timber had featured in an enormous cocaine seizure in Amsterdam. Cassava flour had attracted the attention of Belgian authorities. Gari sacks had appeared in a domestic narcotics interception. Even plastic waste, which sensible nations are desperately trying to recycle, had reportedly been recruited into the international drug business. At this rate, Ghana may soon require a new department at the Export Promotion Authority: the Directorate of Unintended Value Addition. One can imagine the next international trade exhibition. Ghanaian exporters arrive proudly displaying their products. The timber merchants arrange their wood, the cassava processors exhibit their flour, and the coconut farmers carefully polish their fruits. Then a mysterious gentleman wearing dark glasses approaches the exhibition organisers and enquires whether there is sufficient space beneath the tables. Our innocent exporters may soon have to attach sworn affidavits to every shipment, declaring that their cassava is merely cassava, their coconut contains nothing more exciting than coconut water, and their timber has no ambition to become an international narcotics courier. But before we condemn our agricultural produce, let us remember that a goat does not become a thief merely because somebody hides stolen money beneath its sleeping place. The cocaine was concealed by human beings. The coconuts were innocent passengers, unfortunate enough to find themselves travelling with criminals who had mistaken agricultural exports for a branch of organised crime. The more troubling question is how such consignments enter the international shipping system in the first place. Ghana has ports, customs officers, scanners, inspection procedures, intelligence agencies and enough official acronyms to fill a small dictionary. We have institutions responsible for examining cargo, preventing smuggling and protecting the integrity of our borders. Yet the recurring discoveries raise uncomfortable questions about the effectiveness of the arrangements intended to detect illicit shipments. Modern scanning technology can examine containers without requiring an officer to unpack every coconut, count every grain of gari or interrogate every piece of timber. Unfortunately, technology is only as effective as the people and procedures surrounding it. In the investigation arising from the cocaine seizure in France, prosecutors alleged that suspicious scanning images had not been properly examined before the cargo was cleared. Customs officers were among those charged, although the allegations remain subject to judicial determination. Perhaps the Republic requires a new generation of scanners. Not merely machines capable of looking through containers, but machines capable of looking through negligence, compromised procedures and the occasional temptation to look in the opposite direction. Imagine such a device at Tema Port. A container approaches the inspection point. The machine examines its contents and announces: "The cargo contains coconuts, suspicious compartments and three explanations that do not agree with one another." The officer presses a button to silence the machine. It immediately announces: "Attempt to suppress evidence detected." Such technology would undoubtedly revolutionise port security, although its manufacturers might struggle to obtain the necessary import permits. But Ghana is not a country that sits idle when confronted with a national emergency. We have developed an impressive administrative tradition of responding to difficult problems with committees, task forces, technical teams, investigative panels and carefully worded assurances that the situation is receiving the highest attention. Following the September cocaine seizure in France, President John Dramani Mahama directed the establishment of an inter-agency task force to develop a roadmap for strengthening border security. The question now is what has happened to that roadmap. Which recommendations have been implemented? Have inspection procedures changed? Are suspicious cargoes receiving more effective scrutiny? And how will the public know whether the reforms are working? The Republic has considerable experience in preparing roadmaps. We have roadmaps for development, roadmaps for economic transformation and roadmaps for institutional reform. What occasionally defeats us is the inconvenient expectation that somebody must actually travel along the road. A roadmap that remains in a filing cabinet is merely a tourist attraction for documents. And while the security agencies investigate the cocaine, our politicians have discovered another valuable national resource: political ammunition. In Ghana, every scandal has two lives. The first concerns what actually happened. The second concerns which political party can extract the greatest advantage from the happening. The opposition has demanded accountability over the recurring seizures, including changes in security leadership. Government officials and security authorities have pointed to enforcement efforts and the wider history of the country's narcotics challenges. The spectacle is familiar enough to qualify as a national cultural festival. When a political party occupies the opposition benches, every kilogramme of intercepted cocaine becomes evidence of an alarming failure of governance. When the same party occupies the government benches, the matter suddenly acquires historical complexity, international dimensions and a pressing need for citizens to avoid premature conclusions. The cocaine itself remains politically neutral. It does not carry an NDC membership card or an NPP polling-station executive's identification. It does not attend party congresses, wear campaign T-shirts or contribute to manifesto preparation. Yet the moment it is discovered, politicians rush to claim custody of the narrative. If cocaine could speak, it might complain that it had entered the international trade system illegally but was now being used for perfectly legal political arguments. Accountability, however, should not change its meaning whenever political parties exchange seats. A proverb reminds us that the man who complains about smoke from his neighbour's kitchen should first examine the firewood burning in his own. And beyond the political exchanges lies another victim of this unfortunate national embarrassment: the honest Ghanaian exporter. Somewhere in the countryside, a coconut farmer wakes before sunrise, tends his trees, harvests his produce and struggles to find a buyer willing to pay a fair price. He knows nothing about cocaine trafficking, international criminal syndicates or concealed compartments in shipping containers. Yet every major seizure involving agricultural consignments risks casting suspicion on legitimate trade, encouraging additional scrutiny and imposing costs on innocent exporters. The coconut farmer wants his produce to reach a supermarket. The criminal wants the same coconut to reach a warehouse where nobody will ask too many questions about what lies beneath it. We must resist the temptation to conclude that every shipment intercepted abroad proves that Ghanaian security officers were compromised. International drug trafficking involves multiple countries, complex shipping arrangements and opportunities for concealment. Establishing where drugs were inserted and which safeguards failed requires evidence rather than political imagination. Nevertheless, the questions remain. Who owns these consignments? Who verifies the exporters? How are containers secured? What happens when scanners identify suspicious images? And what consequences follow when investigations establish negligence or criminal complicity? These are questions that cannot be answered by arresting the coconut. Perhaps the next time Ghana participates in an international agricultural exhibition, the organisers should provide a special pavilion where our innocent commodities can hold a press conference to defend their reputations. The cassava will insist that it has always been flour. The gari will demand an apology for the unfortunate publicity. The timber will remind journalists that it was cut down against its will. And the coconut, speaking on behalf of the entire agricultural community, will declare that it has never knowingly participated in the international narcotics trade. We have spent decades trying to convince the world that Ghanaian agricultural products deserve a place on international supermarket shelves. Now, thanks to certain criminal enterprises, some of those products are finding their way onto international police evidence tables. The coconut has committed no offence. The cassava is innocent. The gari has an impeccable character. Even the timber has refused to make a statement without its lawyer. Perhaps it is time we stopped interrogating the agricultural produce and started examining the human beings who keep giving it criminal travelling companions. For when the same farm keeps producing strange harvests, the wise farmer does not arrest the crops. He investigates who has been planting the seeds.

Title: The currency portrait blunder: heads must roll
Content: By Evans Mawunyo Tsikata The introduction of a new national currency should be a moment of pride, national reflection and celebration of Ghana's identity. It should provide an opportunity to honour distinguished Ghanaians whose contributions have helped shape our history, culture and national development. Unfortunately, what should have been a moment of national pride has been overshadowed by a deeply embarrassing controversy surrounding the alleged use of an incorrect portrait of Theodosia Okoh, the distinguished Ghanaian who designed our national flag. Let me state this without mincing words:IF IT IS ESTABLISHED THAT THE PORTRAIT USED IS INDEED NOT THAT OF THEODOSIA OKOH, THEN THE PERSON RESPONSIBLE FOR THE DESIGN, SOURCING AND VERIFICATION OF THAT IMAGE MUST BE DISMISSED. This is not a small mistake. It is not an ordinary administrative oversight. It is not something that should be swept under the carpet with an apology or an explanation about institutional procedures. We are talking about the image of a national icon being printed on the currency of an entire country. How can a project of such national significance be handled with this level of apparent disregard for basic verification? What exactly was the designer doing? What research was conducted? Who supplied the photograph? Who verified its authenticity? Who examined the final artwork before it received approval? Was there no historian, researcher, communications professional or responsible official capable of identifying such a fundamental error? Are we seriously saying that an entire chain of professionals could handle the design of Ghana's national currency without establishing whether the photographs being used actually belong to the personalities being honoured? That is simply unacceptable. If the individual entrusted with this responsibility could not undertake the most elementary task of verifying the identity of a person whose portrait was to appear on our national currency, then serious questions must be asked about their suitability for that assignment. Public responsibility is not a ceremonial title. It comes with accountability. You cannot be entrusted with an important national assignment, deliver such a fundamental failure and expect to retain your position as though nothing happened. If the portrait is confirmed to be wrong, the person responsible for the design and verification should not merely be reprimanded, transferred or asked to apologise. They should be fired.There must be consequences proportionate to the gravity of the failure. Beyond the immediate embarrassment, this incident raises a much bigger question about the standards of due diligence in our public institutions. If something as basic as verifying a historical portrait can escape scrutiny, what confidence should the public have in the quality-control processes governing other important national assignments? However, while this alleged error deserves the strongest possible scrutiny, I find the attempt by Afenyo-Markin to use it as an indictment of the government's entire economic management rather simplistic and disproportionate. A mistake in currency design and the management of the national economy are two different responsibilities. Fiscal discipline, monetary policy, inflation management, debt sustainability and the design of banknotes are not interchangeable functions. One can condemn an administrative failure without manufacturing an argument that it automatically demonstrates an inability to manage the economy. Political criticism must be intelligent, measured and supported by sound reasoning. Not every government mistake must be stretched into an argument about everything the government does. That said, the government must not use political distractions to evade responsibility. The issue deserves a proper investigation, a transparent explanation and decisive action against anyone whose negligence is established. More importantly, we must not allow this controversy to overshadow the broader significance of recognising distinguished Ghanaians beyond the familiar personalities who have traditionally dominated our national currency. The recognition of personalities such as Theodosia Okoh and Kofi Annan, alongside Kwame Nkrumah and other notable figures, provides an opportunity to appreciate the different dimensions of Ghanaian excellence and national contribution. Our national history is bigger than any political party, family, political tradition or individual historical narrative. Ghana belongs to all of us. The national currency should reflect that reality. We must move away from the unfortunate tendency to assess national recognition through the narrow lenses of political inheritance, family connections and partisan nostalgia. The worth of a Ghanaian's contribution should be measured by what that individual gave to the country, not by their political affiliation or family background. We cannot build a culture of excellence by continually making excuses for failures that should never have happened in the first place.

Title: The Right Diagnosis, an Incomplete Cure: The 2027 Budget and Ghana’s Boom-and-Bust Cycles
Content: "These boom-and-bust cycles must cease"On the evening of Thursday, November 12, 2026, the Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, when presenting the 2027 budget told Parliament that Ghana's boom-and-bust cycles must cease. Few Ghanaians would disagree. Too many times we have lived through hope followed by hardship, a stable cedi followed by sharp depreciation, and a recovery followed by another crisis. I have read the full 2027 Budget Statement, and I want to answer one question. Does the Minister appreciate why the boom-and-bust cycles happen, and does his New Economy programme remove the cause? My answer is that the Minister has made the right diagnosis but prescribed an incomplete cure. The budget sees two causes clearly. It misses a third, and the third is the one that will bring the next bust. What the budget gets right The budget statement is more candid about the causes of our instability than most budgets before it. It says the cedi came under pressure "when prices dropped or fiscal discipline weakened" (para. 161). It concedes that "temporary booms had financed permanent commitments" (para. 168), and it blames reckless spending, weak revenue and expensive debt for the crisis of 2022. Most important, the budget statement admits that past governments repaired the public finances "but did not use the recovery to alter the structure of the economy," and so "the cycle began again" (paras. 186–187). It even pledges that fiscal discipline "will apply throughout the election cycle" (para. 239). So the Government does understand two causes: our dependence on raw commodity exports, and fiscal indiscipline. I accept both. My quarrel is with what is missing. The machine that is not in the planRead the eight pillars of the New Economy and one thing stands out. The only imports the budget counts as a drain on the cedi are things we consume: rice, sugar, poultry, fish, vegetables and medicines. It says the food import bill "weakens the cedi" (para. 260). It promises that when Ghana grows and processes more, "the cedi will face less pressure" (para. 336). It demands that every cedi of fiscal space answer the question: "what imports will it replace?" (para. 191). The budget never asks that question of the factories themselves. Throughout the statement, machines are things to buy and finance: • the "manufacturer investing in new machinery" is offered equipment leasing (paras.228, 231); • the rice hubs receive tax incentives for "irrigation, mechanisation, silos, modern mills" (para. 276); • GH¢800 million is allocated "to procure agriculture machinery" (para. 1543); • the review of Chapter 98 of the Customs Tariff concerns duty concessions on imported "machinery and other inputs" (para. 860); • the textiles pillar promises jobs for machine operators, not machine makers (para. 448); • for the nuclear plant, "international partners will only provide technology, finance, engineering and specialist services" (para. 380). Cocoa grinding mills, gold refineries, alumina plants, rice mills, garment lines and pharmaceutical plants are all capital goods. Ghana makes almost none of them, and few of their spare parts. Every one will be imported and paid for in dollars, and every one will be kept running with imported spares, also paid for in dollars. The budget's own figures show where the capacity to make machines stands in the Government's order of priorities. 2027 allocation Amount New Economy programme, 2027 outlay (para. 249) GH¢30 billion Procurement of agricultural machinery (para. 1543) GH¢800 million Completion of the Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre (para. 1582) GH¢51 millionGRATIS Foundation, whole year, no capital expenditure (Appendix 4A) about GH¢3 million The Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre is the one line in this budget about making machines rather than buying them. The Centre dates from my time as Minister for Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation, and six years after I left office it is still waiting to be completed. In 2027 it receives about 0.17 percent of the New Economy outlay, and one-sixteenth of what we will spend on imported farm machinery in the same year. GRATIS, built to carry engineering capability into the regions, receives less than half of one percent of the machinery budget. Nothing in the New Economy programme is set aside for machine tools, foundries, spare parts or engineering manufacturing. How the next bust will come Suppose the New Economy succeeds exactly as planned. By 2030 Ghana processes all its cocoa, refines all its gold, processes all its manganese and bauxite and mills its own rice. Food imports fall, export earnings per tonne rise, and the cedi strengthens. But each of those plants was built with imported equipment, and each needs a steady flow of imported spares, replacement parts and, in time, replacement machines. When a mill breaks down, it cannot wait for the cedi to recover. It must buy the part at whatever the exchange rate happens to be. This demand for foreign exchange is stubborn, and it grows with every factory we open. The budget itself names commodity price volatility as the first of its five principal risks (para. 1025). When commodity prices next fall, export earnings will drop, but the bill for machines and spares will not. The cedi will come under pressure again, and the cycle will begin again, at a higher level of output but under the same ceiling. That is the trap of an economy that assembles but does not make. Value addition on imported capital goods moves the bottleneck; it does not remove it. There is a fiscal test as well. The programme is financed partly by lowering the primary surplus target by one percentage point of GDP (para. 247), beginning in the year before an election. The Government will answer that a surplus of at least 0.5 percent of GDP remains (para. 221), and that is a fair answer. But the pledge of discipline "throughout the election cycle" will be tested in 2028, and Ghanaians have heard such pledges before. What a complete cure would requireThe modern world economy is knowledge-based and driven by science and technology. Societies that produce, adapt and commercialise knowledge have achieved sustained growth and rising living standards. Raising money to pay foreign contractors to build infrastructure, good as the projects may be, cannot by itself lead to sustained economic development. Ghana has to develop the capacity to build the machines its industries run on. The cure is not to abandon value addition. It is to add the pillar the plan lacks: the capacity to make the machines. © 2026 Prof. Kwabena Frimpong-Boateng. Title: The Price and promise of a solitary monetary policy
Content: In 2025, the cedi posted its first annual gain against the US dollar in more than three decades, while the Bank of Ghana posted a combined loss of GHS 34.95 billion. Read against the Plaza and Louvre Accords, the two outcomes are not contradictory: they are the price of stabilising a currency alone. In 2025, the Bank of Ghana (BoG) accomplished something of extraordinary monetary significance. The cedi appreciated by 40.7 per cent against the US dollar, its first annual gain in more than three decades and, on IMF data, the strongest performance of any African currency. Headline inflation, which had peaked at 54.1 per cent in late 2022, fell to 5.4 per cent by year-end, and gross international reserves rose to a record US$13.83 billion. The same year produced large losses on the Bank’s balance sheet. Its audited statements, released on 30 April 2026, show a net operating loss of GHS 15.63 billion, up from GHS 9.49 billion in 2024, and a further loss of GHS 19.32 billion in other comprehensive income. The combined loss of GHS 34.95 billion pushed cumulative negative equity to about GHS 96.3 billion. Severed from their context, these figures read as catastrophe. Situated within the history of coordinated exchange-rate statecraft, they read as something else entirely: the quantified cost of macroeconomic stewardship in the absence of multilateral burden-sharing. The modern international monetary system rests on a structural paradox. Capital moves across borders in quantities that dwarf the reserves of any single monetary authority, yet central-bank mandates remain resolutely national, so that misalignments are increasingly absorbed on central-bank balance sheets. At decisive moments, the major economies answered such misalignments with coordinated intervention, whose efficacy is usually traced to the signalling channel. A unilateral stabiliser lacks that multilateral credibility by definition.
