Yet Ghana’s outcomes suggest that unilateral intervention can replicate much of what coordination achieved, provided it is sufficiently aggressive, sufficiently sustained and anchored by credible external surveillance. The price is borne in full by one institution and recorded with brutal clarity on its balance sheet. The Plaza Accord of 22 September 1985 remains the defining act of post-Bretton Woods monetary diplomacy. By the spring of that year, the dollar had appreciated by roughly 44 percent against a trade-weighted basket over five years. Its causes were well understood: American fiscal expansion, colliding with a tight Federal Reserve, had drawn in capital through real interest-rate differentials, while a widening trade deficit fed protectionist pressure in Congress. The finance ministers and central-bank governors of the G-5 (the United States, Japan, West Germany, France and the United Kingdom) responded with a communiqué of studied ambiguity but unmistakable intent. The dollar was overvalued, and they would cooperate to encourage its orderly decline through concerted intervention. Their dollar sales, about US$10 billion in the following weeks, were modest by modern standards. Their power lay in the signal. Sterilised intervention cannot durably move exchange rates through portfolio-balance effects alone; its force derives from the credible public commitment of several sovereigns, each bearing reputational and financial cost. That jointness, constitutive rather than merely logistical, is precisely what a unilateral stabiliser cannot reproduce. In the event, Plaza overachieved: by early 1987, the trade-weighted dollar had fallen by about 40 percent from its peak, and an excessively weak dollar had displaced the original problem. The Louvre Accord of February 1987 reversed the objective, seeking to halt the slide within informal reference ranges. The episode showed that defending an equilibrium is structurally different from engineering a correction. Defence requires continuous sterilisation, sustained liquidity management and interest-rate differentials wide enough to deter speculation, and each carries a direct cost to the central-bank balance sheet. The participating central banks absorbed those costs collectively. Neither communiqué said who would pay. Exchange-rate operations are quasi-fiscal in character, redistributing income and imposing costs much as explicit taxation or public expenditure would. IMF staff research notes that such losses are met from equity buffers where these suffice, or otherwise through government transfers; either way, they are fiscal costs. The G-5, with deep fiscal capacity and implicit mutual backstops, socialised those costs across their treasuries. Ghana had no equivalent mechanism. Between 2022 and 2025, the BoG performed the correction-and-defence function of the Plaza–Louvre model entirely alone. It did so under a US$3 billion IMF Extended Credit Facility, in the aftermath of the most severe domestic debt restructuring in Ghana’s post-independence history, and against a legacy of fiscal dominance and structural excess liquidity. When advanced economies tighten aggressively, capital flight and dollar strength exert depreciatory pressure on African currencies, feeding imported inflation and swelling the cost of foreign-currency debt. The cedi lacks the reserve status that the yen and the deutschmark enjoyed in the 1980s, yet the Bank of Ghana Act, 2002 (Act 612) mandates price stability and support for a stable path of the cedi. The Bank must therefore intervene alone, trading institutional equity for currency stability. The research from which this article is drawn names such an institution a solitary stabiliser, defined by three features: The Mundell–Fleming trilemma holds that no country can combine a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility and monetary independence, and Hélène Rey argues that the global financial cycle reduces it to a dilemma. Neither fully captures the BoG’s position. The Bank faced a quadrilemma, in which four objectives could not all be maintained together: Against the structural excess liquidity associated with the Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP), large policy-driven losses were not merely probable but arithmetically inevitable. Ghana was not choosing between the corners of the impossible trinity; it was attempting to occupy three adjacent policy positions at once. The losses were the clearing mechanism through which that overdetermined system resolved its contradictions, with the balance sheet as absorber of last resort. Credibility came, paradoxically, from an external constraint. The sequence of IMF programme reviews, each demanding performance on inflation, reserves and fiscal targets, formed a serial credibility mechanism that the BoG could not have generated on its own. For central banks without the geopolitical capital of G-5 membership, IMF conditionality, deployed as a substitute commitment device, is thus the closest functional equivalent of multilateral coordination. It carries sovereignty costs, but it can deliver outcomes comparable in quality, if not in mechanism, to coordinated intervention. The headline loss is not a homogeneous expression of failure. It arose from three structurally distinct mechanisms. The first and largest is the cost of open market operations (OMO),which reached GHS 16.73 billion in 2025, nearly double the GHS 8.60 billion of 2024. It is best understood as a monetary tribute: the price a post-crisis financial system, already distorted by the DDEP, exacts for withdrawing the excess liquidity that crisis-era monetary financing created. Launched in December 2022, the DDEP required domestic bondholders to swap existing securities for longer-dated, lower-yield bonds. It imposed impairments of about GHS 48 billion on the BoG’s holdings, including a 50 percent haircut on non-marketable instruments, and cut its annual interest income by about GHS 13 billion until the affected instruments mature. The restructuring also steered commercial-bank liquidity into BoG money-market instruments, which offered attractive short-term returns amid still-elevated policy rates. By 2025, the OMO book stood at about GHS 93.6 billion, at rates between 18 and 28 percent. Without sterilisation, that liquidity would have fed inflation and depreciation and unwound gains already won. The OMO bill was the price of not losing them. The second, GHS 9.05 billion in losses on gold transactions,is the most mischaracterised component. Under its domestic gold-purchase programme, run alongside the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), the Bank bought locally mined gold from artisanal and small-scale miners in cedis and converted it into reserves. The loss arises because the cedi acquisition cost, recognised at purchase, exceeds the carrying value at which the gold enters the balance sheet. It is a timing mismatch, not a destruction of value. At the end of 2025 the Bank still held about 18.6 tonnes of gold, worth roughly three times the loss attributed to the programme, having sold some 19 tonnes at a realised profit. The strategic logic reaches beyond reserve accumulation. By requiring domestic gold to be settled in cedis before export, Ghana’s gold-governance architecture routed foreign-exchange earnings through official channels, reduced illicit financial flows and gave the BoG a continuous source of dollar liquidity for intervention. The programme was instrumental in lifting gross international reserves from US$9.11 billion to US$13.83 billion. The third is an appreciation paradox,in which Ghana’s most celebrated achievement generated large losses. When a central bank holds foreign-currency reserves and its own currency appreciates, the local-currency value of those reserves falls mechanically. A US$1 billion holding is worth GHS 17 billion at 17 cedis to the dollar, but only GHS 10 billion at 10. In 2025, the cedi’s rise produced GHS 5.47 billion in revaluation losses in the operating account and GHS 19.32 billion in other comprehensive income. This is a structural feature of central-bank balance sheets in small open economies, not a policy error. The Bundesbank and the Bank of Japan experienced exactly this effect after Plaza, as their dollar sales lifted the deutschmark and the yen. The economic substance is structurally equivalent; only the distribution of the burden differs. The effect is also reversible, as Governor Johnson Pandit Asiama has noted. By May 2026, the cedi had weakened to about GHS 11.5 to the dollar from the GHS 10.4 at which the 2025 accounts were struck, the signature of a translation effect rather than a real depletion of reserves. Ghana’s experience is far from unique, and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has been emphatic that losses and negative equity do not in themselves impair a central bank’s capacity to operate. The European Central Bank (ECB) lost €7.94 billion in 2024 by paying elevated interest on banks’ reserves while earning low yields on legacy bonds, a structure that closely mirrors the BoG’s OMO costs. The ECB carries these losses forward against future profits, with no recapitalisation requirement. The Czech National Bank (CNB) is the closest precedent for Ghana’s 2025 position. Between November 2013 and April 2017, it prevented the koruna from appreciating beyond CZK 27 per euro to avert deflation, accumulating reserves on a massive scale. When the floor was removed, the koruna appreciated, the koruna value of its euro assets fell, and negative equity persisted for years without any impairment of its inflation-targeting functions. The parallel is imperfect, given the CNB’s European context, but its lesson translates: revaluation losses left by successful exchange-rate management do not compromise the institution that incurs them. Elsewhere, the Federal Reserve carries its losses as a deferred asset against future remittances to the Treasury, while HM Treasury indemnifies the Bank of England’s losses on gilt sales. The Swiss National Bank lost about CHF 132 billion in 2022, roughly a sixth of Swiss GDP, and the Reserve Bank of Australia slipped into negative equity of about A$12.4 billion. What distinguishes Ghana is not the fact of loss but its institutional context. Each of these institutions stood behind a fiscal backstop, whether a monetary union of twenty-one states, an explicit treasury indemnity or a deep-pocketed sovereign. The BoG, by contrast, has had a statutory recapitalisation framework only since December 2025, backed by a single sovereign still emerging from an IMF-supported restructuring. Until the phased recapitalisation takes effect, its losses rest almost entirely on its own balance sheet. The most frequent analytical error is to conflate accounting solvency, meaning positive equity, with policy solvency, meaning the capacity to fulfil the mandate. Central banks have historically operated successfully with negative equity, and there is no systematic relationship between a central bank’s equity and its ability to meet monetary-policy objectives. The decisive variable is fiscal backing. As Willem Buiter argues, irredeemable central-bank money is a liability in name only, so a central bank without large foreign-currency liabilities can in principle avoid insolvency by raising the present value of its seigniorage. Where that would threaten its mandates, indemnification or recapitalisation by the treasury becomes the appropriate remedy. In 2025 the BoG recorded a positive policy-solvency margin of GHS 5.5 billion: operating income of GHS 22.23 billion, from gold sales, reserve management and fees, more than covered the GHS 16.73 billion cost of sterilisation. Its negative equity traces principally to the DDEP impairment of about GHS 48 billion and to the accumulated losses of 2022–2025. The impairment was, in economic substance, a quasi-fiscal transfer from the Bank to the sovereign, which allowed the debt restructuring to proceed on terms sufficient to unlock IMF support. Ghana has taken its first steps toward formal recapitalisation: This is a material advance. Yet a statutory obligation is not yet a funded schedule, and a projected horizon is not yet a binding commitment. Hungary, whose central bank act required the state to restore any capital shortfall over five years, amended the law in 2023 to defer that obligation once large losses emerged. What Ghana needs is an explicit, transparent, fully funded and time-bound commitment calibrated to its fiscal consolidation. The OMO bill also exposes a structural problem. Most of the GHS 16.73 billion flowed to commercial banks, whose aggregate profit of about GHS 15 billion in 2025 was strikingly close to the central bank’s sterilisation cost. Banks earning risk-free returns on central-bank paper have weak incentives to build credit-assessment capacity or to lend to the firms and households of the real economy, so the instrument designed to sterilise liquidity doubles as a banking subsidy. The remedy lies beyond monetary policy: As the G-5 recognised in the 1980s, exchange-rate adjustment without structural reform cannot deliver durable rebalancing. Accounting needs reform too. Frameworks such as IFRS were designed to measure going-concern risk in profit-maximising firms, and applied raw to central banks they can create a false impression of distress. Losses from currency revaluation and urgent OMO intervention belong in a dedicated policy-stabilisation account, backstopped by long-term recapitalisation instruments. A mandate-centric reporting standard would convey the same information without inviting the category error that treats institutional sacrifice as institutional failure. Ghana is an unusually well-documented instance of a condition common across Africa’s more financially developed economies: commodity-dependent revenue, thin capital markets, persistent current-account deficits and the recurring need to navigate between IMF conditionality and domestic political pressure. The instruments of stabilisation, namely reserve accumulation, sterilised intervention and liquidity management, are precisely those that generate the largest accounting losses when a currency appreciates. African central banks that succeed may therefore look institutionally weakest on paper at the very moment of their greatest achievement. The deeper implication is normative. When the G-5 stabilised the dollar, the costs were shared; when Ghana stabilised the cedi, they were concentrated in a single institution. The asymmetry reflects not merely economic size but the absence of mechanisms through which developing-country stabilisation can attract multilateral support. The IMF’s Extended Credit Facility, essential as a commitment device, disburses liquidity; it does not absorb losses. A framework analogous in spirit, though not in form, to Plaza–Louvre coordination could rest on three elements: None of these is immediately achievable, but Ghana’s experience strengthens the intellectual case for their development. The Plaza Accord was a triumph of coordination, and the Louvre Accord demonstrated the cost that coordination must bear to defend what correction achieves. Both were possible because no single nation stood alone. The Bank of Ghana’s programme of 2022–2025 was a triumph of institutional resolve, and its balance-sheet losses demonstrate what resolve costs when it stands alone. The combined loss of GHS 34.95 billion is the quantified expression of a macroeconomic achievement obtained without multilateral subsidy. The outcomes justify the accounting cost: Africa’s best-performing currency, single-digit inflation, record reserves, policy-rate cuts of 1,400 basis points between July 2025 and March 2026, and a fall in public debt to about 45 percent of GDP. These did not emerge despite the central bank’s losses. They emerged because of the interventions that generated them. Three analytical conclusions and one normative prescription follow: The architects of the Plaza Accord understood that orderly adjustment was worth its price and that its price was worth sharing. The least the international community, and Ghana’s own policymakers and public, can do is recognise that Ghana’s adjustment was equally orderly, equally costly and equally worthy of honest institutional assessment. The writer is the author of the research paper “The Price and Promise of a Solitary Monetary Policy: Coordinated Exchange-Rate Statecraft, the Plaza–Louvre Legacy, and the Bank of Ghana’s Solitary-Stabiliser Balance-Sheet Crisis, 2022–2025” (August 2026), from which this article is drawn.

Title: Samson’s Take: Ghana’s media madness – Politicians created it
Content: Sam Nartey George says Ghana's broadcasting landscape is overcrowded, describing the proliferation of radio and television stations as pure madness. He's absolutely right about the problem. But who created this madness? Who distributed broadcasting frequencies like political souvenirs? And who frustrated attempts to bring sanity to the industry? Politicians without principles. The NDC and the NPP alike. Check the insane saturation: in 2017, this small country of ours had 471 authorised FM stations. Nigeria, big brother Nigeria, with over 170 million people at the time. Even some said it was about 200 million. Six times more than our population had fewer. They had 361. Kenya had 118. And again, big South Africa had only 59 FM stations. By 2023, Ghana had added nearly 300 more to the 471 stations. We had a staggering 747 FM authorisations. Today, according to the NCA's June 2026 figures, we have 793 authorised FM stations. Yes, only 571 are operational, though. Add 170 television authorisations, and you have almost a thousand. That's 963 radio and television stations in a small country of approximately 35 million people. Is this media pluralism or an industry drowning in political patronage, commercial desperation, and professional indiscipline? Media freedom is a constitutional treasure, but multiplying stations does not necessarily multiply quality journalism. I have personally fought this battle. I was counselled, challenging the reduction of FM transmission coverage from 100 kilometres to 45 kilometres. When Nana Akufo took over, petitions for some sanity to Minister Ursula Owusu-Ekuful and the President went unheeded. The policy created room for more frequency allocations in an already overcrowded, saturated market. The plain plan was this, very obvious. The NDC had distributed frequencies like confetti to cronies, and the NPP needed to outdo them in the race to the bottom. It is the usual senseless partisan conduct, disguised as national interest. Politicians, politically exposed persons, and their associates have acquired broadcasting frequencies frequently during their party's reign. Some obtained authorisations without the resources to operate viable stations, treating frequencies as commodities for eventual transfer. Some sold them. The public airwaves became instruments of private political advantage. You recall the crackdown under Ursula Owusu-Ekuful in 2017? 131 FM stations or authorisation holders were sanctioned. By October 2019, 57 stations had reportedly been closed down. Radio Gold and Radio XYZ became prominent casualties of the enforcement controversy. And who fiercely challenged those closures? Even the closures included the genuinely defaulting operators who needed correction and sanction. Sam Nartey George. Yes, he challenged that. Today, he is a minister threatening to shut down politically and religiously affiliated broadcasters. I welcome his recognition of the problem. But where is the consistency? What was objectionable under Ursula cannot suddenly become acceptable under Sam George, simply because political power has changed hands. Regulation must be lawful, fair, and independent of party interest. Now consider the broadcasting bill. For nearly two decades, Ghana has failed to enact comprehensive broadcasting legislation. Earlier drafts sought to prohibit political and certain religious ownership, restrict multiple frequencies, and expose beneficial owners. Those restrictions threatened powerful political and commercial interests. And that was central to the prolonged resistance and inaction. We still haven't passed it. Indeed, the 2024 draft relaxed earlier ownership prohibitions. The politicians expected to legislate against media concentration were themselves beneficiaries of the system. And now social media has multiplied the problem. That's what it has done. Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, and other platforms have opened extraordinary opportunities for free expression and citizen participation. But alongside the benefits is an epidemic of misinformation. Yes, I mean that. An epidemic of misinformation, fabricated stories, character assassination, hate speech, dangerous health claims. Some people are doing juju and multiplying money on TV. Kids have had to kill and murder their own because they were misled on these platforms. And deliberate political disinformation is going on. Reputations are destroyed for clicks. Falsehoods are monetised. Ethnic and religious tensions are inflamed. Public confidence in democratic institutions is undermined. I repeat that. Public confidence in democratic institutions is undermined. It's become very difficult to rule or to govern a small country like ours. Some political actors finance, encourage, and amplify these abuses only to complain when the same weapons are turned against them. That is political hypocrisy. Freedom of expression is not freedom from irresponsibility. Neither is it permission to endanger public health, destroy reputations, or poison democratic governance. But the solution cannot be arbitrary closures, censorship, or ministerial control of public discourse. Pass a constitutionally sound broadcasting bill. Disclose the real owners of stations. Restrict excessive ownership concentration. End speculative frequency trading. Enforce lawful conditions without political discrimination. Empower the independent National Media Commission. Stop appointing politicians to that place. Strengthen professional accountability and confront online harms through lawful proportionate measures. Sam George has correctly diagnosed a long-standing national problem. We check it now, or it will destroy this country. Now let him prove that his principles apply equally to NDC and NPP interests because the airwaves belong to Ghanaians, not politicians, party financiers, or even media moguls. Ghana needs more responsible journalism, not merely more broadcasting stations. Mr GJA President, these are really not jobs, as you complain that people's jobs are at stake. How much are they paid at these stations, these mushrooming FM stations? How much are the people paid? You see why it is so easy for them to be turned into political tools: more truth, not more noise. More public service, not political propaganda. The politicians helped create this mess. Let them now demonstrate the courage and principles to clean it up, beginning with their own interests, and that is my take.

Title: Coaching growth in Ghana: A market still in its teething Stage
Content: Profession teething in a green market with a need for major boardroom buy-in. In 2020, Zoweh Global Consult published its first survey of coaching in Ghana and six years on, our follow-up asks how far the profession has travelled. The answer is encouraging: the market is still in its teething stage, a clear message of potential and opportunity for corporate leaders and their boards. Of the 122 respondents in the latest 2026 survey, 75% say coaching in Ghana is more professional than in 2020, and 61% say it is more visible. Three in four expect demand to rise over the next five years; only one person expects it to fall. Seven in ten report a significant or moderate positive impact from coaching. That optimism extends beyond Ghana. The International Coaching Federation (ICF) counted a record 122,974 coaches worldwide in its 2025 Global Coaching Study, and found the Middle East and Africa the most optimistic region, with 71% of coaches expecting growth. Although 92.6% of respondents say the market is maturing, “the proof of the pudding is in the eating”: nearly two-thirds have more than a decade of professional experience, 17% are coaches or consultants, and 72% have been coached. These are people close to the profession. Those who have never been coached had little reason to answer a coaching survey, so their voices are largely missing. ICF’s 2026 Global Consumer Awareness Study, conducted by PwC among more than 25,000 consumers in 26 markets, offers a useful benchmark. Globally, 74% have heard of coaching, yet only 27% picked the correct definition from a list, and a third mistook it for mentoring. The lesson applies at home. In our experience, most Ghanaian managers and staff have never been coached, and many would struggle to say how coaching differs from training, advice or counselling. Even among our well-informed respondents, one in eight chose a mistaken or uncertain definition. Respondents say as much. Lack of awareness was the most-cited barrier to organisational use of coaching (37%), followed by cost and unclear benefits (20% each). Difficulty finding a qualified coach came last, named by just three people. The constraint is not a shortage of coaches. Too few decision-makers understand what coaching does and what it is worth; this is where awareness creation, visibility, coaching dialogues, and research on the impact of coaching on ROIs and return on expectation (ROEs) come in. While 91% of respondents rate coaching as valuable for leadership development, only 52% say their organisation uses it, and nearly half work in organisations that do not or are unsure. ICF sees the same pattern: interest is high, yet only 24% of consumers have ever been coached. Who opens the door matters too. Worldwide, two-thirds of coached consumers pay their own way or rely on family; fewer than three in ten have employer funding. In our sample, the workplace was the most common route in: about a third were coached through their employer, against one in eight who hired a coach privately. In Ghana, employers hold the key to wider access. For organisations, the best starting point is a leadership pilot of 10 to 20 managers with clear goals, measure progress at three and six months, and report results to the executive team. Set a minimum standard for coaches, including recognised certification, so quality is never left to chance, as 85% of our respondents and 77% of consumers worldwide rate certification as important. For coaches, the task is to speak the language of the boardroom, translating confidence, self-awareness and leadership growth into retention, team performance and decision quality, backed by evidence of impact. Respondents expect youth development coaching to grow fastest after leadership coaching, a signal worth heeding in a nation with a young workforce. A note on method: respondents opted in, largely through professional networks, so the findings describe an informed, experienced group rather than the wider workforce. Even a random sample of this size would carry a margin of error of about nine percentage points. The direction, however, is clear: demand exists, belief is growing, and professional coaches are available. What is missing is understanding in the corporate boardroom and self-sponsorship will. Ghana’s coaching market is still in its teething stage, and it is ready for more coaches and more organisations to take part. By Scofray Nana Yaw Yeboah, MCC, ACTC, MCS, FInstCM, and Afia Boatemaa Sarpong Scofray Nana Yaw Yeboah, MCC, ACTC, MCS, FInstCM, is a Transformational Executive and Team Coach and the lead consultant at Zoweh Global Consult, which conducted the survey. Ghana’s first ICF Master Certified Coach, he is also the first Ghanaian Advanced Certified Team Coach and the first Ghanaian to hold ICF’s Mentor Coach Specialisation at all three credential levels. He served as founding President of the ICF Ghana Chapter and founded Neuro-Emotional Intelligence Training (NEIT™) Afia Boatemaa Sarpong is an Author | Researcher | Faculty Intern, Ashesi University

Title: Human rights and Democratic futures: Reflections from West and Central Africa
Content: The future of human rights in Africa will not be secured by defending yesterday's institutions alone. It requires reimagining the relationship between rights, democracy, dignity, and the everyday aspirations of citizens. There is a fundamental question confronting the human rights movement in Africa today: How do we defend human rights in societies where many citizens increasingly question whether democracy, constitutionalism, and the institutions established to protect their rights are delivering meaningful improvements in their lives? This question is particularly urgent in West and Central Africa, where democratic aspirations coexist with military interventions, constitutional controversies, violent extremism, economic exclusion, and growing pressures on civic freedoms. Yet these same regions are also home to extraordinary traditions of civic resistance, community solidarity, constitutional activism, women's leadership, and youth mobilisation. The recent convening on the future of human rights in West and Central Africa provides an important opportunity to reflect on these contradictions. Beyond the immediate challenges confronting human rights defenders, it invites us to interrogate the assumptions, approaches, and institutional arrangements that have shaped human rights work over the past three decades. Our central argument is that the future of human rights and the future of democracy in Africa are inseparable. But their relationship must be understood more expansively than the defence of elections, constitutions, and formal institutions. Human rights must become meaningful in the everyday experiences of citizens, while democracy must be judged not only by how leaders acquire power but also by how power is exercised, whose interests it serves, and whether it advances human dignity. It is a warning the Nigerian political economist Claude Ake issued a generation ago: a democracy reduced to periodic elections, he argued, risks becoming the democratisation of disempowerment; a ritual of voting that leaves intact the structures that keep people poor, insecure and voiceless. It is echoed in the Indian jurist Upendra Baxi’s insistence that the legitimacy of human rights is measured not by the elegance of our norms but by their capacity to answer human suffering. The crisis is not only democratic regression. It is also a crisis of relevance. Across West and Central Africa, the democratic transitions of the 1990s generated considerable optimism. Multiparty elections returned, constitutions were rewritten, civil society expanded, and regional institutions developed increasingly ambitious frameworks for democratic governance and human rights. These were important achievements. They created opportunities for participation, strengthened normative commitments, and established institutional foundations for challenging abuses of power. Yet political liberalisation did not consistently produce economic transformation, social inclusion, or responsive governance. For many citizens, the promise of democracy has remained distant from the realities of unemployment, insecurity, inadequate public services, corruption, and unequal access to opportunities. This disconnect has profound implications for human rights. Ake saw the danger clearly. Because the colonial and post-colonial state remained the principal route to wealth and security, he observed, the struggle to control it turned politics into a form of warfare; multiplying parties without transforming that state would produce elections everywhere and popular power nowhere. The legal scholar Amy Chua sounded a complementary alarm inWorld on Fire: exporting free markets and overnight elections together into deeply unequal societies, without redistribution or social protection, can convert economic grievance into communal resentment and make democratic politics the arena in which that resentment is organised. Both warnings have aged well in West and Central Africa, where liberalisation of the ballot and of the market arrived together, and where too many citizens experienced both as systems rigged for others. When rights are presented primarily as legal guarantees, procedural protections, or international obligations, without sufficient attention to the material conditions that make their enjoyment possible, they risk appearing disconnected from the daily struggles of ordinary people. A young person who can vote but cannot find dignified employment may question the value of political participation. A woman whose constitutional equality is guaranteed but whose economic opportunities and physical safety remain constrained experiences a democracy that is incomplete. A rural community living with persistent insecurity may struggle to reconcile the language of citizenship with the absence of effective state protection. These experiences do not diminish the importance of civil and political rights. Rather, they demonstrate why such rights must be understood alongside economic, social, cultural, and collective rights. The challenge is not to replace one category of rights with another but to recover their indivisibility. Baxi’s formulation remains the sharpest test available: the foundations of human rights lie not in abstract theories of human nature but in concrete histories of human suffering. Rights that do not answer suffering will not command allegiance. When the state becomes both protector and source of insecurity The relationship between citizens and the state is undergoing significant strain. In parts of the Sahel, military authorities have justified extraordinary restrictions on political participation and civic freedoms by invoking national security and sovereignty. Elsewhere, civilian governments have faced criticism over restrictions on dissent, disputed constitutional arrangements, and the conduct of security institutions. Meanwhile, violent extremist groups, armed movements, criminal networks, and other non-state actors continue to threaten communities and undermine the protection of civilians. These developments expose a central dilemma: the state is expected to guarantee human rights, yet its institutions may themselves contribute to violations, exclusion, or insecurity. This is not an argument for weakening the state. On the contrary, effective and legitimate public institutions remain essential to the protection of rights. But state authority cannot be treated as an end in itself. Its legitimacy must rest on accountability, public trust, and the protection of the people it exists to serve. Nor should the understandable demand for security become a justification for indefinitely suspending freedoms. These dilemmas have deep historical roots. Ranajit Guha, the founding historian of Subaltern Studies, described colonial power as dominance without hegemony: rule sustained by coercion rather than consent. Too many post-colonial states inherited that grammar of rule. Where the state’s default relationship with society is domination, security easily becomes a language of repression, and citizenship remains thin in practice. Partha Chatterjee, writing in the same tradition, adds that beyond the enclaves of formal civil society, most people encounter the state not as rights-bearing citizens but as populations to be managed — negotiating survival through brokers, customary authorities and informal arrangements in what he calls political society. Human rights practice that speaks only the language of courtrooms and constitutions will struggle to reach them. Security and human rights are not competing objectives. Sustainable security depends on justice, inclusion, institutional legitimacy, and meaningful relationships between communities and public authorities. Where governments respond to insecurity primarily through coercion, without addressing the grievances that sustain conflict, they risk reproducing the conditions that undermine their own legitimacy. The future of human rights therefore requires stronger engagement with the political economy of insecurity, the governance of security institutions, and the lived experiences of communities at the margins of state protection. Human rights cannot remain the language of institutions alone One of the most consequential questions for the human rights movement concerns who defines its priorities, speaks in its name, and determines its strategies. Africa has a rich history of struggles for dignity, justice, freedom, and collective self-determination. These struggles predate contemporary international human rights institutions and cannot be reduced to frameworks imported from elsewhere. From anti-colonial movements to campaigns against military rule, from women's organising to community struggles over land and natural resources, African societies have continually articulated their own understandings of rights and justice. Yet human rights practice can become overly professionalised, urban-centred and donor-driven, with accountability flowing upwards to funders rather than outwards to communities. This is also a question of the movement’s own legitimacy and ownership. These approaches have achieved important results and remain necessary. But they are insufficient when disconnected from the communities whose rights they seek to protect. The question is not whether international human rights standards remain relevant. Their universality remains essential, particularly when governments invoke cultural relativism or sovereignty to evade accountability. Issa Shivji has been among the most unsparing critics of this drift. Human rights in Africa, he reminds us, were forged in popular struggles against slavery, colonialism and dictatorship; when the discourse is professionalised, projectised and donor-funded, it risks being converted from a weapon of the oppressed into an ideology administered over their heads; one fluent in the vocabulary of accountability yet silent about the political economy that produces violation. Shivji’s conclusion is not that rights are a foreign imposition to be discarded. It is that rights are never granted from above: they are won, defended and extended through the struggles of ordinary people, and a movement that loses contact with those struggles loses both its legitimacy and its power. Rather, the question is how universal principles can be grounded in African experiences, histories, social relationships, and aspirations without compromising their substance. This requires community-based organising, local accountability and a polycentric movement: many centres of initiative, united by shared principles rather than a single institutional voice. It also requires recognising communities as political actors and rights holders, not merely beneficiaries of programmes designed elsewhere. Gayatri Spivak’s celebrated question; can the subaltern speak poses the movement’s hardest test: whether those who claim to represent the marginalised end up effacing their voices in the very act of representation. The answer cannot be to speak on behalf of communities. It must be to build the conditions in which communities speak, organise and lead for themselves. A new generation is expanding the meaning of rights Across Africa, younger generations are increasingly challenging conventional boundaries between political rights, economic justice, and democratic participation. Their demands frequently connect accountability to employment, corruption to public services, policing to dignity, and political exclusion to broader questions of generational justice. Digital technologies have expanded opportunities for mobilisation, documentation, solidarity, and public scrutiny. They have also introduced new risks involving surveillance, disinformation, online harassment, and restrictions on digital freedoms. What is particularly significant is that many young people are not necessarily rejecting democracy. They are questioning forms of democracy that appear unable or unwilling to respond to their aspirations. This distinction matters and the response cannot simply be to persuade young Africans to appreciate existing democratic institutions. It must also involve making those institutions more responsive, inclusive, and accountable. What is emerging, in Baxi’s terms, is a shift from the politics of human rights; the management of standards by professionals and institutions  towards a politics for human rights: insurgent movements in which those who suffer become the authors of the norms meant to protect them. Guha would have recognised in these mobilisations what he called the autonomous domain of popular politics: forms of organisation, solidarity and imagination that do not wait for elite permission. The task of the established movement is not to tutor this energy but to join it, resource it and defend its space. Human rights organisations should engage younger generations not as programme participants alone but as co-creators and leaders, while confronting their own internal hierarchies and exclusions. The same principle applies to women, persons with disabilities, displaced populations, informal workers, and communities historically excluded from decision-making. A democratic future cannot be built through the continued marginalisation of those who constitute its social foundation. Reclaiming African agency without abandoning universal principles The changing international environment introduces another dimension to this debate. Geopolitical competition, shifting development priorities, declining confidence in multilateral institutions, and accusations of selective application of international norms have complicated the operating environment for human rights organisations. Criticism of double standards in the international system deserves serious engagement. The credibility of human rights principles is weakened when violations are condemned in some contexts but minimised or overlooked in others. However, the response to inconsistency cannot be the abandonment of universal standards. Shivji’s own position is instructive here. The sharpest African critic of human rights as an ideology of empire has never doubted the universality of the demand for dignity; he questions only who is entitled to define it, deploy it and speak in its name. Universality is not weakened when it is claimed from below. It is authenticated. African agency should not be confused with the unrestricted authority of governments to determine which rights their citizens may enjoy. Sovereignty belongs ultimately to people, not merely to those who exercise state power. An authentically African approach to human rights must therefore combine historical consciousness, cultural legitimacy, and regional ownership with firm commitments to accountability, equality, and freedom. Ake insisted likewise that an African democracy worthy of the name could not be an abstract template indifferent to time and place; it had to be concrete, anchored in how people actually live, labour, organise and resist. The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights provides an important foundation. Its recognition of individual rights, peoples' rights, duties, and collective wellbeing offers opportunities to reconnect human rights with questions of solidarity, development, participation, and social justice. Institutions such as the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights, ECOWAS, and relevant Central African regional mechanisms can play important roles. But their effectiveness depends not only on normative mandates. It also depends on political commitment, institutional independence, access to justice, implementation and solidarity across borders, including across linguistic divides. Regional human rights protection must become more accessible and consequential for the people it is intended to serve. From defending democracy to making democracy worth believing in For too long, democracy and human rights have sometimes been approached as separate fields of intervention. Democracy practitioners focus on elections, political participation, institutional reform, and constitutional governance. Human rights actors concentrate on freedoms, legal protections, accountability, and remedies for violations. In practice, these agendas are deeply interconnected. An election cannot be meaningfully democratic where citizens cannot freely organise, speak, associate, or challenge those in authority. Similarly, human rights protections remain vulnerable where political institutions lack accountability, checks and balances are weakened, and citizens have limited opportunities to influence public decisions. But the relationship extends beyond institutional safeguards. A democracy that protects freedom of expression while tolerating systematic economic exclusion remains incomplete. A government that promises economic development while suppressing political freedoms cannot claim to have resolved the question of human dignity. The future therefore lies in bringing together democratic governance, human rights, economic justice, and social inclusion as mutually reinforcing dimensions of public life. This means moving beyond an overwhelmingly defensive posture. Defending civic space, protecting activists, challenging unlawful detention, and resisting constitutional manipulation remain indispensable. Yet the human rights movement must also articulate a positive vision of the societies it seeks to help build. What does a rights-respecting economy look like? How should public resources be governed to advance dignity and equality? How can communities exercise meaningful influence over decisions affecting their livelihoods? What would democratic accountability mean for young people confronting unemployment, or for women whose unpaid labour sustains households and communities? These are not peripheral development questions. They are central questions about the future of rights. Ake’s answer was what he called social democracy: a democracy anchored in the material life of ordinary people, in which participation means real power over the decisions that shape livelihoods, and development is undertaken by the people and not merely for them. Chua’s analysis points to the same conclusion from another direction: a democracy that coexists with entrenched economic exclusion will eventually be consumed by the backlash it breeds. Democratic security and distributive justice stand or fall together. Reimagining the movement and its methods If the human rights movement is to remain relevant and effective, several shifts deserve consideration. First, it must reconnect rights advocacy with the lived realities of communities, recognising that dignity is experienced through both freedom and material wellbeing. It must learn to work where Chatterjee’s political society lives  in informal settlements, markets, farms, transport networks and community associations, where most people actually negotiate with power and not only in the formal civil society of registered organisations and legal claims. Second, it must build alliances across institutional boundaries, linking rights defenders with labour, women’s and youth movements, environmental advocates and community groups, while engaging non-state power, including corporations and armed actors. Third, it must invest in intergenerational leadership and the sustainability of civic movements. A movement cannot continually speak about the future while reproducing structures that limit the participation and leadership of younger generations. Fourth, it must rethink the relationship between formal institutions and informal systems of accountability. Community dialogue, mediation, customary institutions, and local solidarity networks can contribute to rights protection when they operate consistently with equality, inclusion, and fundamental freedoms. Finally, philanthropy and development partners must examine their own approaches. Short funding cycles, fragmented interventions and donor-defined indicators can undermine movement autonomy; flexible support must combine rapid protection with long-term organising. Supporting the future of human rights requires patient investment in relationships, ideas, collective agency and the movement’s capacity to learn and assess its actual effects on people’s lives. It also requires the humility to recognise that durable transformation cannot be engineered through projects alone. It requires, above all, what Baxi calls taking human suffering seriously: measuring the movement’s work not by reports produced or funds disbursed, but by the difference it makes to those who bear the weight of violation. The future is not predetermined It would be a mistake to interpret the challenges facing human rights and democracy in West and Central Africa as evidence of an inevitable democratic decline. The region's political trajectories are neither uniform nor predetermined. There are important examples of constitutional resilience, peaceful political transitions, civic mobilisation, institutional innovation, and communities organising to defend their rights. These experiences remind us that democratic progress is rarely linear. It advances through contestation, negotiation, setbacks, and renewed collective action. The task is therefore neither to romanticise the past nor to surrender to pessimism about the future. It is to learn from the limitations of previous approaches while building on the achievements that remain worth protecting. The convening on the future of human rights offers an opportunity to move this conversation beyond familiar diagnoses of shrinking civic space and democratic regression. The more consequential question is what kind of human rights movement, democratic institutions, and relationships between citizens and power will be necessary for the decades ahead. Our answer begins with a simple proposition: human rights must be reclaimed as the everyday language of dignity, justice, belonging, and collective possibility. For West and Central Africa, this means protecting fundamental freedoms while confronting economic exclusion; defending constitutionalism while demanding accountable governance; strengthening regional institutions while investing in community agency; and upholding universal principles while recognising African histories and aspirations. Baxi has described human rights as a politics of hope;  a language through which people who suffer imagine, and insist upon, a different world. That is the register in which the African human rights movement must now speak. The future of human rights will not be determined solely in courtrooms, conference halls, regional institutions, or international forums. It will also be shaped in communities confronting insecurity, among young people demanding opportunity, through women's struggles for equality, and wherever citizens insist that power must serve human dignity. The challenge before us is not simply to preserve the human rights architecture we have inherited. It is to make human rights and democracy sufficiently meaningful, inclusive, and transformative that future generations will see them not as distant promises, but as foundations of the societies they aspire to build. Guha called this the small voice of history: the persistent, often unrecorded insistence of ordinary people on their own dignity. The human rights architecture of the future will stand only if it is built around that voice; not speaking for it, not administering it, but amplifying it until power has no choice but to listen.

Title: Dead Men Can Teach: Why Ghana’s Medical Schools are running out of bodies
Content: Some months ago, a sister of one of my mentors passed away at the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra. There was no funeral because she, knowing her illness was terminal, chose to donate her body to the University of Ghana Medical School for medical research. This was my first personal encounter with such a donation. During the procedures related to the body bequest, the doctor in charge explained the challenges in securing cadavers (bodies) for medical training and mentioned that limited admissions of medical students in Ghana are partly due to this issue and not just infrastructure. This inspired me to write this article. Consider what a body represents to medical science. It is not just tissue and bone. It is a complete textbook, a laboratory that teaches and a final teacher whose lessons endure in every doctor it helps train. When a patient dies of a disease that medicine does not yet fully understand, their body holds answers. When a new medication is developed, its effects on human physiology must be studied in human bodies and not just in computer models or animal subjects. When old medicines need revision because diseases evolve or populations change, researchers must see how those medicines interact with human tissue, organs and systems. Most of the medical researchers in Ghana face this challenge. Without fresh bodies, they cannot study the effects of emerging diseases like new viral strains or resistant infections. They cannot test how new medications affect organs in real human subjects. They cannot refine surgical techniques that might save thousands of lives. Korle Bu's Medical School, like others across the country, has historically relied heavily on unclaimed bodies. Thus, those left in mortuaries with no family to claim them. But this source is no longer reliable. Mortuaries are overwhelmed, and even unclaimed bodies are often too decomposed or otherwise unsuitable for meaningful study. The hospital has had to conduct mass burials of unclaimed bodies, removing them from any possibility of contributing to medical education. The Anatomy of a Medical Student's Education Imagine the scene: one hundred first-year medical students gather around a single dissection table. They crowd, struggle for position, peer over shoulders and others. The professor points to a nerve, a vessel or a muscle, and most of these students cannot see. Then the situation means that those at the back would have to rely on textbooks and imagination. This is not an exaggeration. In Ghanaian medical schools, the student-to-cadaver ratio is a big challenge. Some institutions report having only a handful of cadavers for entire cohorts of hundreds of students. The result is that students learn anatomy through models, digital simulations and textbook diagrams, which, although very important, cannot be substituted for what is done with the cadaver. Cadaveric dissection remains the gold standard for learning human anatomy. It teaches not only structure but how bodies differ from one another. It teaches surgical technique, respect for the human body and the three-dimensional relationships that no flat image can convey. A study conducted at the University of Health and Allied Sciences (UHAS) in Ghana on 513 health science students - medicine, nursing, midwifery, pharmacy and allied health revealed that only 74.1% of these students had heard of body bequeathal, 98.3% agreed body bequeathal was important, and only 39.6% knew the requirements and processes of body bequeathal. The paper also says 214 students (41.7%) said they had no idea what was required in the process. It is obvious that there was a high awareness of the importance of body bequeathal but very low procedural knowledge, as most were unwilling to donate their body. A Culture of Funerals, A Shortage of Teachers Ghanaian culture, particularly among the Akan and many other ethnic groups, places a strong significance on funeral rites and the treatment of the dead. The body is not only a vessel that has stopped working. It is a site of ritual, a conduit for ancestral blessings and a subject of communal mourning. Funerals in Ghana are detailed, expensive and protracted affairs. Bodies are bathed, dressed, displayed and buried with ceremony. To suggest that a loved one's body be given to medical students for dissection, which means to be cut, studied, and eventually disposed of, can feel like a violation of cultural and spiritual obligations. This is not a small or dismissible concern. These are deeply held beliefs about the afterlife, about respect, about the relationship between the living and the dead. Any conversation about body donation in Ghana must begin with acknowledgement of this cultural weight and not dismissal of it. Yet there is a tension worth examining. The same culture that insists on detailed funerals also values healing, community and the preservation of life. If a body can no longer benefit the deceased, could it benefit the living? If a funeral honours a life that was lived, could a donation honour a life that could still be saved? The Law Already Allows It Ghana's Anatomy Act of 1965 (Act 280) provides a legal framework for body donation. Section 3 explicitly allows any individual to direct, either in writing or verbally before two witnesses during their final illness, that their body be used for medical education and research. Section 2 permits executors or those with lawful possession of a body to allow such use, unless the deceased expressed a contrary desire or a surviving spouse or relative objects. The law is permissive but not proactive. It does not actively encourage donation, does not create an accessible system for willing donors and does not provide the cultural and religious engagement needed to shift deeply held norms. As a result, Ghana has only two institutions with any form of body donation programme, and these receive an average of just five and two bodies per year, respectively. In a country with multiple medical schools and thousands of students, this is a drop in an empty bucket. The Way Forward: A Call for Courageous Conversation What would it take to change this? The answer must be many-sided, culturally sensitive, and sustained. First, leadership from chiefs and religious leaders is essential. As research on community responses to health crises in Ghana has shown, when traditional and religious authorities endorse changes to deeply held practices, communities are far more likely to follow. If the National House of Chiefs, the Christian Council and Islamic leadership publicly endorsed body donation as an act of service and healing, the cultural calculus would shift. Second, hospitals must create accessible and dignified donation programmes: Individuals who know they are dying, whether from terminal illness or old age, should have a clear, compassionate pathway to bequeath their bodies. The process must be respectful, transparent and honoured with acknowledgement and gratitude. Third, medical schools must invest in public education. The fact that nearly all health science students support body donation in principle but few know how to do it reveals a massive gap in information. This gap extends to the general public. Educational campaigns, testimonies from families who have donated, and visible memorials to donors can help normalise the practice. Fourth, the legal structure for body bequeathal should be strengthened. Parliament has already recognised the need for updated legislation on organ and tissue donation, noting that only 10 per cent of global transplantation needs are met and that the African region is far behind. The same legislative energy should be applied to body donation for education, with provisions for donor registries, family consent protocols and protections against commercial exploitation. Finally, we must reframe the conversation. Body donation is not abandonment of the dead. It is, in a great sense, the ultimate act of healing. A body that teaches a medical student to recognise a tumour, to perform a delicate surgery, to understand a disease does not lie idle in the ground. It works. The Teacher Who Never Speaks In medical schools around the world, cadavers are often called the "silent teachers." They do not lecture. They do not explain. They simply are. And by being, they teach what no book can. In Ghana, we have the opportunity to create a culture where donation is not taboo but honoured. Where a family's grief is joined by a community's gratitude. Where the dead continue to serve the living not through memory alone but through medicine. Korle Bu Teaching Hospital needs bodies. Ghana's medical students need bodies. The patients of tomorrow, that is, the ones who will survive because a doctor learned from someone who gave their body to science, need those bodies too. The question is whether we are brave enough to have the conversation. Whether we can hold our cultural traditions in one hand and our children's futures in the other and find a way to honour both. The dead can teach. Let them teach.

Title: Facing our past and shaping our future together
Content: Britain and Ghana cannot change the past, but we can face it honestly, listen carefully and strengthen a modern partnership founded on dignity and mutual respect. A few weeks ago, I sat in Ghana’s National Theatre and watched The Darkest Chapter, a moving play by Latif Abubakar. It traces a path from the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade through decolonisation and independence to modern Ghana. One line has stayed with me: “before diplomacy, before policy, before resolutions, there were human beings”. That is where any conversation about the slave trade must begin. With the millions of people torn from their homes, families and communities. With those whose labour and suffering enriched others. And with the descendants and societies that continue to live with that history today. The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation. People were denied their humanity, separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. The UK Prime Minister has expressed his “sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people” and recognised the way this history “still shapes our world today.” Ghana has helped ensure that the world does not look away. Its leadership in shining a spotlight on the slave trade has brought renewed attention to questions that are difficult, deeply felt and important. Ghana’s perspectives have helped shape the wider Commonwealth conversation. At the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) last week, Commonwealth leaders agreed it was time for a meaningful, truthful, and respectful conversation to forge a common future based on equity. They welcomed the UK Government’s agreement to engage in a structured, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties, addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms. The Prime Minister also met with President Mahama during CHOGM to set out these plans and welcomed the President’s support. This is an important step, and the United Kingdom enters the dialogue seriously and respectfully. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of the process, and the Prime Minister has said that he is open to them. A dialogue of this importance must allow those most affected to help shape it. Its outcome should not be predetermined, but neither should we underestimate the depth or difficulty of the conversation. The first responsibility is to listen. One privilege of serving as British High Commissioner is gaining a view of the many layers of the UK’s and Ghana’s shared history. At the British Museum this summer, I saw how one object, the Asante Ewer, can tell a story spanning medieval England, trans-Saharan trade, Asante ceremonial life and the violence and pillage of the Anglo-Asante wars. Such objects do not offer simple stories. They ask us to confront complexity and understand what they mean to different communities. Other moments remind us how relationships can change. Last year at the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park, I stood with the Duke of Edinburgh before the image of Queen Elizabeth II dancing with President Kwame Nkrumah in Accra in 1961. Ghana had won its independence only four years earlier and was inspiring movements across Africa. That photograph captured our countries’ relationship at a decisive moment as it was reshaped. Today, the United Kingdom and Ghana meet as sovereign partners. Our relationship is rooted not only in history, but in people, education, culture, business, security and a shared interest in prosperity. That modern partnership gives us a strong foundation for difficult conversations. We should be confident enough to discuss both progress and pain, allow space for honest disagreement, and recognise that listening is part of an equal partnership. As Ghana approaches its 70th anniversary of independence, there will be many opportunities to reflect on the journey from colonial rule to the Black Star of Africa, and on Ghana’s continuing influence in the world. The United Kingdom should take part in those conversations with humility, openness and respect. We gather to remember. We also need to listen. The dialogue agreed at CHOGM will not be simple, and some views will be strongly held. But our bilateral relationship is mature enough to face difficult history honestly, to hear each other with respect and to work together towards a common future based on dignity and equity. The writer,DrChristian Rogg, is the British High Commissioner to Ghana.

Title: Ghana’s cocaine seizures abroad raise questions about port security, trade integrity and national reputation
Content: Something is happening, and we cannot afford to treat it as another passing headline! According to JoyNews Research, approximately 13,876 kilogrammes of cocaine linked to Ghana have been seized abroad in five separate operations since January 2025. That is the equivalent weight of 217 bags of cocoa! Now, pause and consider the implications. How do such quantities become associated with our international trade corridors? Are our cargo inspection systems sufficiently robust? What vulnerabilities exist within our ports, shipping documentation, customs procedures and intelligence architecture? And perhaps the most troubling question: If these quantities were intercepted abroad, what does that tell us about the potential scale of trafficking that remains undetected? The figures alone cannot answer that question, but they certainly justify asking it. You see, international cocaine trafficking is not simply a narcotics problem. It is an economic governance, financial integrity and national security problem. Organised criminal networks thrive where institutional weaknesses intersect with lucrative illicit markets. The proceeds can penetrate legitimate businesses through trade-based money laundering, property acquisitions, shell companies and complex financial transactions. Over time, such illicit financial flows can distort competition, compromise regulatory institutions and weaken confidence in the financial system. Imagine the implications for Ghanaian exporters if international trading partners begin subjecting our shipments to heightened scrutiny. Longer clearance periods, increased compliance costs, disrupted supply chains and reputational damage could eventually affect businesses that have absolutely nothing to do with narcotics trafficking. Must legitimate Ghanaian enterprises pay the economic price for the activities of criminal syndicates? And this is where the responsibility of the current administration becomes particularly important. What exactly are we doing differently to strengthen our national anti-narcotics architecture? Are we sufficiently integrating customs intelligence, port surveillance, financial intelligence, beneficial ownership investigations and international law-enforcement cooperation? Are we conducting credible risk-based inspections of high-risk consignments? Are suspicious financial transactions being systematically connected to underlying trade activities? More importantly, when foreign authorities intercept Ghana-linked shipments, do our institutions pursue the entire criminal value chain, including financiers, facilitators, freight intermediaries and ultimate beneficiaries? We must also distinguish between cocaine originating in Ghana, transiting through Ghana and being concealed in shipments without the knowledge of legitimate exporters. These distinctions are essential to credible investigations and accountability. Let us not underestimate the long-term consequences. Countries do not lose their international credibility overnight. Reputational deterioration occurs gradually, particularly when repeated incidents begin to raise questions about institutional effectiveness. Ghana has spent decades positioning itself as a stable investment destination, a regional commercial gateway and a credible participant in international trade. What happens to that positioning if our export corridors become increasingly associated with narcotics trafficking? What happens to investor confidence, correspondent banking relationships, trade financing and our broader ambitions under the AfCFTA? The administration must therefore demonstrate measurable progress through coordinated investigations, stronger preventive controls, successful prosecutions where evidence warrants them and transparent institutional accountability. This is too consequential to reduce to partisan exchanges. My greatest concern is not merely the cocaine being intercepted abroad. It is what repeated Ghana-linked seizures may reveal about vulnerabilities within our economic and security systems. We cannot build a competitive export economy while leaving organised criminal networks opportunities to exploit legitimate trade infrastructure. Neither can we pursue economic transformation without protecting the institutional integrity upon which sustainable development depends. The government must act decisively, and every responsible Ghanaian must demand credible answers. Because the day Ghana becomes more internationally recognisable for cocaine trafficking than for cocoa, gold, innovation and legitimate enterprise, we will have lost something far more valuable than revenue. We will have compromised the credibility of our nation. Lecturer, University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development

Title: When the outrage dies, who remembers the victims? – The Obuasi SHTS case and our troubling habit of forgetting the people behind the headlines
Content: The speed at which victims of sexual abuse, especially children, can become less central to the public discussion of their experience once the outrage dies away is deeply troubling. A common pattern exists in the manner in which we typically respond to unsettling stories in our region. A tragedy occurs, an inquiry reveals some unpleasant truth, social media erupts with outrage, high-profile individuals offer their condolences and opinions, and citizens call for accountability. Depending on the degree of disturbance created by the story, national discussion can dominate public discourse anywhere from a couple of days to several weeks. Once another story begins to gather attention, public focus will shift, and the individuals at the center of the original scandal will be left to deal with the consequences of the scandal, usually without the same amount of public outcry that originally surrounded them. This is a pattern that should worry us. The recent allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) have once again brought questions of child protection, institutional accountability and the safety of girls into Ghana's national conversation. Following an investigation by Joy News, the case prompted public outrage, government intervention and renewed scrutiny of the Ghana Education Service and its handling of complaints. The headmaster has been interdicted pending investigations, while the education ministry has announced support for 19 students identified in connection with the allegations, including psychological counselling, medical care and academic assistance. Each of these actions is an essential measure. However, I am currently focused on a larger question.What happens when the public stops paying attention? Because the uncomfortable reality is that the consequences of abuse do not disappear when a story stops trending. The fear, trauma, disruption to education, and struggle to rebuild a sense of safety do not operate on the same timeline as public outrage. One of the most troubling aspects of our response to humanitarian and social issues is how easily we become invested in the story but lose sight of the people experiencing it. We remember the headline and the outrage and debate who should be held responsible. Yet how often do we return to ask whether the people affected are actually receiving the support they were promised? In cases involving sexual abuse, particularly where children are concerned, the need for sustained attention is even greater. The immediate public reaction may create pressure for intervention, but recovery and protection require much more than a moment of national sympathy. For the students at Obuasi, the questions above should not conclude with an announcement stating that counseling and medical support will be provided. Will these services be provided? Will their academic development be supported? Will they be free from intimidation, victim-blaming, and unwanted public attention, and will their identities remain protected? Each of these points represents a critical component of what a meaningful response should look like. We must be careful not to assume that an announcement means an intervention has been fully implemented. Equally, we should not assume that nothing is being done simply because the public has not received every detail. What we need is appropriate transparency, sustained monitoring and evidence that the commitments made are translating into actual support. This problem extends beyond Obuasi and beyond sexual abuse cases. Disturbing cases of violence against women, child exploitation, among others occasionally generate sufficient national interest to warrant national attention. We show outrage over such cases and declare our solidarity with victims. Yet we frequently lack the ability to sustain our outrage beyond the initial controversy. Consider the reported sexual abuse of a 14-year-old autistic student at Bolgatanga Girls' Senior High School, which also reignited conversations about safeguarding and the vulnerability of children within educational institutions in September 2026. Different cases have different circumstances, and should be investigated on their own evidence. However, recurring concerns about the protection of students should prompt us to examine whether our responses are producing lasting improvements or simply reacting to each new incident. We cannot keep treating every disturbing revelation as an isolated controversy when similar questions about reporting, institutional responsibility and student safety continue to arise. The problem with reactive advocacy is that it places enormous attention on the moment of exposure but often insufficient attention on what follows. We become passionate about demanding action when a story is fresh, but less consistent in monitoring whether that action has happened. And when public attention disappears, the pressure on institutions to demonstrate progress can disappear with it. Accountability should never depend upon public pressure. One of the most significant lessons learned from the Obuasi case is that children should never suffer as a result of whether or not an investigative journalist exposes a problem or whether enough public outrage exists to compel action from authorities. Schools and educational authorities have responsibilities that exist regardless of whether or not the public is watching. As a young woman involved in humanitarian work and women's rights advocacy, I believe one of the largest challenges facing social advocacy is not always getting people to care. Sometimes it is getting them to continue caring long after the initial emotional response has passed. There is a difference between feeling sorry for someone and committing to support them, a difference between demanding justice and ensuring that justice was pursued, and there is a difference between sharing a story and being responsible for ensuring that the issues raised by that story were not forgotten. This is why journalists, civil society organisations, child protection advocates, women's rights groups and concerned citizens must continue asking questions long after the initial headlines disappear. We must follow up on investigations, monitor institutional commitments, demand appropriate updates and keep the needs of affected people in public conversation without compromising their privacy or dignity. Our advocacy must also extend beyond individual controversies to the policies, safeguards and social attitudes that allow harm to occur in the first place. The students of Obuasi and every victim of sexual abuse deserve more than just a moment of national sympathy. They deserve protection, support, a credible process for establishing the facts and an educational environment in which their safety is taken seriously. The headmaster is equally entitled to due process, and allegations must be established through the appropriate legal processes. Neither principle should be sacrificed. Ultimately, the measure of our concern cannot be how loudly we react when a disturbing story breaks. It must also be how consistently we demand answers when the excitement has passed. The people behind our headlines do not get to move on simply because the rest of us have. If our outrage disappears beforetheir painful experience had been addressed and prior to any accountability having been secured, then perhaps we must begin to question whether or not our outrage was worth anything.

Title: Power expires. Friendships shouldn’t
Content: There is something profoundly disturbing about people who occupy fixed-term public offices or privileged corporate positions and suddenly develop amnesia about the relationships that existed before their appointments. The phone numbers remain, but the friendships disappear. People who once shared ideas, dreams and ambitions are suddenly considered too ordinary to associate with. Friends in entrepreneurship are ignored. Calls go unanswered. Requests for modest assistance are treated as personal inconveniences. Some even become unnecessarily arrogant, as though their appointments have permanently elevated them into another species. Have we not learnt that appointments end? Governments change. Retirement comes. Contracts expire. Political fortunes reverse. The same corridors of power that once welcomed you will eventually become unfamiliar territory. The security detail disappears, the official vehicle is withdrawn, the privileges evaporate and suddenly, the world becomes remarkably quiet. Then comes the desperate scrolling through old contacts. You begin searching for people whose calls you once ignored. You remember friends whose businesses you could have helped nurture. You suddenly rediscover relationships you abandoned when you thought your position made you important. My intention is not to curse anyone. It is a caution. Never confuse the office you occupy with the person you are. An appointment is a temporary privilege, not a personal inheritance. The position is yours only for a season.
