The people you meet along the way are part of your permanent journey. If you have friends building businesses, creating jobs and developing ideas, help them where you legitimately can. Open doors. Share opportunities. Make introductions. Support enterprise. Do so ethically, transparently and without abusing your office. You do not have to compromise your integrity to be a good friend. One day, you will leave that office. When you do, may you leave with your dignity intact, your conscience clear and enough genuine friendships to remind you that you mattered beyond your title. Power is borrowed. Humanity is permanent.

Title: The $50,000 Passport Monster: How NPP built a syndicate, left it in Foreign Affairs, and now wants Ablakwa to carry it
Content: By Evans Mawunyo Tsikata It is rather interesting how, every now and then, the NPP seems determined to find fault with Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, almost at all costs. Today, I particularly appreciated the submission by Lawyer Brako-Powers. I listened to his contribution with keen interest, particularly his response to one of the allegations levelled against the Honourable Minister, and I found his arguments quite compelling. “But it appears to me that the NPP is stretching this issue to a ridiculous level. And we must call them out. They are stretching this issue to a ridiculous level.” “Let me point out that the multitude of allegations doesn't amount to guilt. In the entire conversation, the way the NPP is going about it is as though they've caught someone. And it's as though they've concluded that a crime has been committed. But when you address or you drive this conversation from this mindset or point of view, you lose the entire conversation and you lose the entire Ghanian. Because the Ghanaian is looking for real accountability.” The man at the centre of this whole storm is Alhasan Sumani. Let's be clear about who he is. In 2023, he was not an employee of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, yet his name reportedly surfaced in a similar scandal. He was what we commonly refer to in Ghana as a“goro boy”,an individual who operates around the Passport Office, allegedly maintaining connections with officials to facilitate certain activities. He was also known to be a TESCON activist at AUCC, with reported links to the NPP. It surprising how the NPP had never mentioned his name all through their allegations. It is important to emphasise that, as at 2023, Mr Yahaya Amantana Mahama was not the Director of the Passport Office. At the later part of 2024, when the NPP knew they were exiting power, what did they do? They quickly employed him. They regularized their own boy. They planted their seed. Because as one insider put it, "All of them will have to go home so that new people will be employed. The Chief of Staff and the President, being very kind men, decided let's leave everybody. They are all Ghanaians." So this is one of such employees. He knew his masters were leaving, so he secured himself a job before the door closed. Fast forward to May 2026. A Pastor and his wife report that Alhasan has taken money from them promising them Service Passports. This is not Diplomatic Passport. This is Service Passport. From a reliable source, the Minister, Hon. Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, asks the Director to produce a report. And here is where the NPP propaganda collapses: The Director, Yahaya Amantana Mahama, was not even in Ghana in May when the incident happened. His travel records will show it. How can a man authorize a passport when he is not in the jurisdiction? Let’s compare Ambassador Kadija's real signature with the forged one being paraded around. The difference is clear. It is fake. Forged on ministry letterhead that Alhasan had access to because NPP gave him access. The Minister has no hand in it. From a reliable source the Director informed the Minister that there was a similar case in August he was already investigating. This Director once upon a time has been a victim of NPP vindictiveness.  In 2023, just like many other persons, Amantana went for NDC primaries. Because NPP was in power, they wanted to punish him. They wanted to remove him. It took CLOSAG going to court on his behalf to protect him. CLOSAG to court in 2023 - that's documented. A man the NPP tried to victimize for being NDC cannot suddenly be their accomplice in selling passports for $50,000. Enter Waleed - Travel and Tour. Waleed, the travel and tours operator, has testified against Alhasan. The pastor, the wife, Waleed - all point to one man: Alhasan Sumani. So what did Minister Ablakwa do when it came to his notice? Did he sleep on it? No. He constituted a committee to investigate the matter. He has said he will come to Parliament himself to present the facts. That is what a responsible Minister does. But what does NPP do? They shout "$50,000 Diplomatic Passports for sale!" They want to publish all diplomatic passports since 2025. They want to create noise. Why? Because they are desperate to find dirt on Ablakwa at all costs. Why Ablakwa? Because Ablakwa single-handedly took them on for 8 years. He exposed National Cathedral, he exposed SML, he exposed the former government's thievery. They have never forgiven him. Now they think they have found a stick to beat him with - using their own boy they planted in the Ministry. This is diversion 101. You create a monster, you leave the monster in the system, and when the monster bites, you shout"Look, the new government is corrupt!" And let us be honest and blame the NDC itself. We have not learnt any lesson. The President's "father-for-all" game is killing the grassroots. You keep NPP appointees and NPP TESCON boys in sensitive offices like Passports, like Foreign Affairs, and you expect them to be loyal and committed to a positive course? The same people who were doing "protocol" and selling passports under NPP are still there, now sabotaging you from inside. NDC grassroots are still unemployed on the streets while NPP boys are still at post, forging letters with old letterheads. If you do father-for-all, this is what you gain. Alhasan Sumani must be investigated, and prosecuted when guilty to the fullest. He is not a mistake; he is a product of a deliberate syndicate that thrived under NPP. He was a goro boy who became a staff through the backdoor. His actions must not be minimized. And Hon. Okudzeto Ablakwa inherited a syndicate. He did not create it. When it came to his attention, he acted. He did not cover it. The Minority calling for a bipartisan committee is duplication. It is the same witnesses - Waleed, the Pastor, Alhasan etc. Wait for the Minister's committee report. Let Parliament interrogate it. But don't throw mud at an innocent Minister because you are embarrassed that your own boy is the centre of the scandal. At the end of the day, nothing will come out of this smear except embarrassment for the NPP. Because you cannot hang your own monster on another man's neck and expect Ghanaians to believe you.

Title: The New economy budget: Will Ghana finally build growth that lasts?
Content: Ghana’s reliance on the International Monetary Fund has become a defining feature of its economic history, with 17 programmes since 1966 shaping the country’s trajectory and leaving a legacy of short‑term stabilisation without long-term transformation. The ‘New Economy’ budget to be presented by Finance Minister Ato Forson on Thursday, 12th November 2026 is positioned as the decisive moment to break that cycle, and it carries the weight of expectation that this time the reforms must endure beyond the political calendar and deliver prosperity that is both tangible and sustainable. President Mahama first mentioned the New Economy program in May 2026. It is a $10- billion investment over five (5) years which would be spread across nine (9) pillars and designed to operate without new borrowing. Dr. Forson describes it as a shift from stabilisation to production, with priorities such as gas‑to‑power and gas‑to‑fertiliser projects, the Western Railway Line, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and industrial parks like Afienya. This is a vision every successive government in the 4th Republic has set. That Ghana must become a country that produces what it consumes, and the discipline required to achieve this lies in maintaining fiscal responsibility while unlocking space for investment. The need for this transformation is underscored by the lived experience of recent years. Inflation reached 54.1% in 2022, the cedi lost more than half its value, and bondholders absorbed a 37% haircut on US$13 billion while ordinary citizens bore the brunt/consequences through diminished purchasing power. Since then, growth has rebounded to 6% in 2025 and debt distress risk has eased; stabilisation alone has not translated into jobs. Youth unemployment remains alarmingly high, with 21.9% among those aged 15 to 35 and 32.5% among those aged 15 to 24. At independence, Ghana’s income per person was slightly ahead of Malaysia’s, but by 2022 Malaysia’s was more than 5 times higher. This is a stark and powerful reminder of how far the country has fallen behind. Ghana's economic history teaches us invaluable lessons. The 1983 Recovery Programme reduced inflation dramatically but failed to sustain growth. Debt relief in the early 2000s created fiscal space that was spent rather than invested, and industrialisation drives from the 1960s to 'One District One Factory' collapsed under weak foundations. Fiscal rules have been breached in election years and ambitious plans have too often evaporated with changes in government. The New Economy must be different from all the previously failed economic initiatives. Of course, the rhetoric is not new, but the institutions, laws, and bipartisan commitments that anchor it must ensure continuity beyond 2028. A bipartisan approach to the New Economy initiative is essential. The NPP, which governed from 2017 until 2024, may inherit the programme midway, and its criticisms, from unaccounted GH¢650 billion to the unimplemented 24‑Hour Economy, deserve serious scrutiny. Yet scrutiny must serve the national interest, not partisan gain. Buy‑in means agreeing on a scoreboard, verifying progress through independent institutions, and ensuring that factories, railways, and power plants are not hostage to political cycles. The credibility of the programme depends on both government and opposition recognising that economic transformation cannot be reduced to applause or obstruction. A programme beginning in 2027 runs until 2031, with 3 of its 5 years falling under the next government deserves continuity. Gas plants and railways require more than one electoral cycle to deliver returns, and a wise man once said, “half‑built assets are the most expensive kind.” Prez. Mahama has pledged to build gains that no successor can reverse, but only law, institutions, and bipartisan agreement can guarantee that promise. On 12th November 2026, clarity will be the measure of credibility. The country must see a single set of numbers, whether US$2 billion annually or US$1.6 billion, alongside detailed budgets, timelines, and job targets for each pillar. A binding fiscal rule with a debt anchor at 45% of GDP by 2034, quarterly reports verified by the Auditor‑General and Statistical Service, and multi‑year commitments anchored in law will determine whether the New Economy is more than a slogan. Scepticism about inflation risks, the mixed record of state‑backed industry, and the viability of projects like fertiliser plants is valid but such concerns should drive thorough scrutiny. Ghana does not need an NDC economy or an NPP economy at her age. What the country needs is a prosperity-centred economy. It needs an economy that survives its owners, one that is built on discipline, continuity, and shared responsibility. Thursday’s budget must be the beginning of that resolve not to return to the IMF.

Title: Is Sudan’s Army refusing, for a second time, to hand over an “International Criminal” accused of genocide?
Content: After the head of Sudan’s dissolved National Congress Party fled prison following the outbreak of the civil war in mid-April 2023, he resurfaced under the protection of Port Sudan authorities’ forces in territories under army control, raising questions about the possibility of his handover, given that he is a criminal wanted by international justice. The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an international arrest warrant for Ahmed Haroun in 2007. He is accused of 20 counts of crimes against humanity and 22 counts of war crimes, including murder, rape, torture, persecution and forcible displacement, as well as launching attacks on civilians through militias that he financed and recruited. The ICC in The Hague continues to demand Haroun’s surrender, confirming on its official website that the case remains active. Meanwhile, the United States has offered a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest, surrender or conviction, describing him as responsible for recruiting, financing and arming the militias that committed atrocities against civilians in Darfur. Accused of Genocide Under the Protection of the Sudanese Army Reuters revealed that officials from the party of Omar al-Bashir, Sudan’s former president who was ousted by a popular revolution in April 2019, confirmed that army authorities in Port Sudan had arrested Haroun, who is formally accused of committing genocide in Darfur in the early 2000s. Haroun appeared in a podcast interview in which he sought to justify the army’s cooperation with Islamists. However, he also disclosed details of their relationship, which Port Sudan authorities have consistently denied, in an apparent attempt to conceal an alliance that has drawn criticism from the country’s civil, popular and political forces. According to Reuters, the International Criminal Court has yet to issue any response, particularly given that Sudan’s military authorities had previously arrested Haroun but refused to hand him over to the ICC, before he escaped during a prison assault at the outbreak of the current civil war more than three years ago. Haroun belongs to the National Congress Party, which is deeply rooted in Sudan’s Islamist movement and the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood organisation. The movement dominated power in Sudan from the beginning of former President Omar al-Bashir’s rule in the 1990s until 2019. Although the party was dissolved, it continues to seek a renewed presence in territories and positions under the control of the Sudanese army. Sudanese politician and Secretary-General of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement, Yasser Arman, maintained that the Sudanese army was fully aware of every detail surrounding the podcast in which Haroun appeared, and that the recording took place at a location entirely under its protection. In an article published by several Sudanese newspapers, Arman confirmed that Haroun conducted his televised interview under army protection at the Al Salam Rotana Hotel, where he may still be staying to keep him out of public view. The Sudanese politician ridiculed the “set design, filming quality and programme, which are entirely at odds with the famine, economic collapse, water and electricity cuts in Sudan, and which mock the people.” Arman pointed out that the army had kept Ahmed Haroun and the programme crew who recorded the podcast at a hotel in central Khartoum, away from the war and its dangers in other locations, where people are being deprived of their right to life. He added: “Haroun sat addressing people from the ICC’s balcony, lecturing the hungry, determining Sudan’s future and distributing what he does not own to those who do not deserve it, with the ICC’s predicament and the December Revolution behind him.” He stressed that “the Al Salam Hotel that hosted Haroun has become a headquarters for warlords. Anyone who does not believe this should go there early in the morning, at breakfast time, to see militia commanders in the hotel lobby and dining hall.” He also sarcastically questioned the army’s seriousness about arresting him, asserting that Port Sudan authorities would most likely place him at the Al Salam Rotana Hotel “because the services and communications there are better.” Mark Kersten, an expert in international law and international criminal justice, wrote that Port Sudan authorities had “arrested Haroun for the second time, and on both occasions refused or failed to hand him over,” ultimately asking: “Who is protecting Haroun? And what are they hiding there?” The Sudanese human rights group Emergency Lawyers also called for Haroun to be handed over to justice, given that he is a criminal accused of dozens of crimes and atrocities committed against civilians in Darfur and other locations during the years preceding the December Revolution, which ousted Bashir in 2019. The group rejected the continued political manoeuvring and compromises by the leadership of the military authorities in Port Sudan, as well as the protection of a criminal who has evaded justice.

Title: Accra after Sunset: El Niño, a heating city and the sky above us
Content: By Petras Anaab Ali (MPhil) The sun has gone down, but the room still feels hot. The fan is running, yet sleep does not come easily. Outside, people seek relief on verandas, in compound yards and along the roadside. For anyone who has spent such an evening in Accra, the question is simple: why does sunset bring so little comfort? That question has become more urgent. On 30 October 2026, the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) warned that a very strong and still intensifying El Niño is developing, and that Ghana should prepare for a hotter, drier and dustier dry season. Heat stress is expected to peak between February and April 2027, especially in the north. The ocean data behind that warning are striking. In mid-October, the weekly Niño 3.4 index, the standard measure of El Niño, reached+3.3°C. Scientists classify anything above +2.0°C as "very strong." For Accra, the warning raises a practical question: how prepared is a densely built city for additional heat? Answering it means looking at three things together: the global climate, the city we have built, and, less obviously, the whole column of atmosphere above us. My MPhil research in Physics at the University of Ghana followed the last strong El Niño upwards through that column. What it found is thatEl Niño does not only change the weather at ground level. It disturbs the entire sky. El Niño begins with unusually warm surface water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Normally, trade winds push warm water westward towards Asia. During El Niño those winds weaken, and the warm pool spreads east. Warm water heats the air above it, the air rises, and storm clouds form where they normally would not. That shift in where the atmosphere draws its heat rearranges winds and rainfall across the globe. Scientists call these long-distance links teleconnections. The present event is far beyond the top of that scale. In September, the US Climate Prediction Center put the chance at 75% that it would exceed every El Niño recorded since 1950. The great events of 1982/83, 1997/98 and 2015/16 are remembered in Ghana for drought and bushfires, and the first two were followed by power rationing. Two cautions belong here, because they keep the argument honest. First, El Niño changes the odds; it does not dictate the weather of every community. Ghana's seasons also depend on the tropical Atlantic, and GMet notes that a cool Gulf of Guinea could shape how the 2027 rains behave. Second, the heat people feel today cannot automatically be blamed on a forecast for the coming months. Establishing how unusual Accra's present heat is requires local observations compared with the same season in earlier years. According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), September 2026 was thesecond-warmest September on record, with the global surface temperature1.33°C above average. NOAA's map for that month shows a bright red tongue of warm water stretching along the equator from South America across the Pacific: El Niño itself. Northern Canada and Siberia are deep red. Cooler-than-normal blue is now confined mostly to Antarctica and a few small patches. Ghana and the Gulf of Guinea appear in light pink, roughly half a degree to one degree above normal. That should not reassure us. Global temperatures usually peak a few months after El Niño itself peaks, because the heat released by the Pacific takes time to spread through the atmosphere. That is what happened after the 2023/24 El Niño, when 2024 went on to break global temperature records. On the evidence so far, West Africa's turn is still coming. El Niño will not arrive in a cool city. Local evidence over the past year gives the discussion a firm foundation. One clarification matters. Land surface temperature is the temperature of roofs, roads and soil as seen by satellites. A 4°C rise in surface temperature does not mean the air everywhere in Accra has warmed by 4°C. But hot surfaces are exactly what keep a city warm after dark, which brings us back to that sleepless evening. The physics begins with the energy received during the day. Sunlight heats roofs, roads and walls. Dark surfaces absorb more of it, and dense materials such as concrete and block store it. After sunset, that stored energy keeps flowing into the surrounding air and into rooms, partly as infrared radiation we cannot see but can certainly feel. A room can stay uncomfortable long after the sun has gone because it is still releasing the day's heat. How fast that heat escapes depend on ventilation, shade, roof design and how closely buildings are packed. Iron roofing sheets heat quickly under the sun; poorly ventilated rooms hold heat in. Trees and wetlands work the other way: they shade surfaces and cool the air through evaporation. As Accra has replaced vegetation with concrete, it has removed some of its own natural cooling. Humidity adds another layer. Our bodies cool mainly by evaporating sweat. In Accra's humid coastal air, sweat evaporates slowly, so a night at 27°C can feel far more oppressive than the number suggests. A thermometer reading alone cannot describe the experience of heat. Heat is shared, but the ability to escape it is not. One household can run an air conditioner all night. Another depends on a single fan in a poorly ventilated room. A trader may have to stay at a roadside stall through the hottest hours because leaving means losing income. That helps explain why indoor workers in crowded, unventilated spaces can be more exposed than people working outside. Accra's authorities have begun to document this. AMA's citywide Extreme Heat Perceptions Survey asks residents how heat affects their health, livelihoods, productivity, sleep, transport and daily routines. It complements a heat-mapping exercise in which temperature sensors were installed across the city to identify hotspots. Publishing those results in an accessible form would let residents understand their own exposure and let the public judge whether interventions reach the places of greatest need. Electricity sits at the centre of this. Every fan and air conditioner draws power, and a hotter dry season will push demand up. The supply side carries its own El Niño risk. GMet says Lake Volta is in good shape for now, but warns that the real risk falls on the 2027 rainy season, which determines how much water will be available for hydropower in 2028. When power fails on a hot night, the fan stops, and the people with the fewest alternatives suffer most. The heat we feel is only the bottom of the story. For my MPhil thesis,Investigation of the Potential Changes in Ionospheric Patterns Due to Climate Variability(University of Ghana, 2024), I compared the strong La Niña of 2020/21 with the strong El Niño of 2023/24. I used temperature profiles from the COSMIC-2 satellites, covering the atmosphere from the ground to 60 km, and navigation-satellite signals recorded in Bogotá (Colombia), Antananarivo (Madagascar) and Baie-Comeau (Canada). Those signals reveal the Total Electron Content (TEC) of the ionosphere, the electrically charged layer roughly 100 to 1,000 km up that every GPS signal must cross. To be clear, that work did not measure temperatures in Accra's streets or homes. But it showed that El Niño leaves a fingerprint at every level of the atmosphere. In plain terms: during El Niño, the stable morning layer of air that acts as a lid on the lower atmosphere was weaker and broke up earlier, so convection started sooner and reached higher. That churning launches atmospheric gravity waves, ripples in the air that grow as they climb into thinner air, much as a whip's crack builds towards its tip. A warmer stratosphere let more of those waves through, and when they reached the ionosphere, they stirred up its charged gas. The Sun is the ionosphere's main driver, so the two had to be separated. My La Niña year fell near solar minimum and my El Niño year near solar maximum. After statistically removing solar activity,El Niño still explained an additional 17–27% of the variation in the ionosphere's electron content. The study was among the first systematic analyses of El Niño's effect on the African equatorial ionosphere, and the African station responded as strongly as stations elsewhere in the tropics. The Sun has been active this season too. The provisional Dst index, which tracks geomagnetic storms, recorded six disturbances between September and October 2026. The strongest, on11 October, reached about −93 nanotesla, a moderate storm just short of the intense threshold. My thesis concluded that El Niño-linked ionospheric variabilitycan rival a moderate geomagnetic stormof that kind. The difference is duration: a solar storm passes in a day or two, while El Niño's influence persists for months. Why should anyone in Accra care? Because a disturbed ionosphere bends and delays satellite signals. My analysis suggests El Niño-linked changes can produceposition errors of a meter or more, and vertical errors of 2 to 3 meters for single-frequency receivers, the kind found in most everyday devices. That will not stop anyone finding a trotro station, but it matters for satellite-guided aircraft approaches, land surveying, precision farming, drones and radio communications. West Africa sits beneath the equatorial ionization anomaly, one of the most turbulent parts of the ionosphere, where irregularities after sunset are already common. My data showed night-time electron content rising 30 to 40% during El Niño, precisely when those irregularities are worst. I must add one honest note. None of my stations was in Ghana, because long, continuous, publicly available records of the kind this study needed were not available here. A Ghanaian physicist studying the African sky had to use data from Madagascar. Good decisions need better local data. Four things would sharpen the picture considerably: The purpose is to give residents a clear account of what is changing, where exposure is greatest, and which responses the evidence justifies. There is a foundation to build on. In April 2026, the Mayor of Accra announced plans to amend AMA's bye-laws to formally recognize heat as a public health risk, after a review found major gaps in how the city handles extreme heat. The new provisions are to focus on markets, transport terminals and temporary structures. AMA's public health leadership has also called for reforms covering ventilation standards, roofing requirements, shade and green infrastructure. The task now is delivery. I would urge the following: Africa needs to study Africa. The atmosphere does not stop at the top of the clouds, and neither should our science. The warm room after sunset and the disturbed ionosphere 300 km overhead are not separate stories. They are the same atmosphere responding to the same warm ocean. The data are clear: a Pacific running more than 3°C above normal, a planet in its second-warmest September on record, a city whose surfaces have heated by about 4°C in three decades, and a measurable El Niño fingerprint from the lowest kilometers of air to the top of the ionosphere. We cannot stop El Niño, but we can measure it, forecast it and prepare for it. GMet's warning gives Ghana a few months before the peak heat arrives. The sun will keep setting over Accra. Whether its residents find relief afterwards depends partly on decisions we make before the next hot day begins. Petras Anaab Ali (MPhil), also known as Sumaila Ali or Coach Ali (The Supreme Tactician), holds a BSc and MPhil in Physics from the University of Ghana and is reading a certificate program in Biblical Studies at Heritage Bible Institute. His MPhil research investigated how El Niño and other forms of climate variability affect the ionosphere. His academic interests lie at the intersection of cosmology, quantum theory, philosophy of science and Christian theology. He works with Ghana's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) as a Programme Officer, contributing to environmental regulation and sustainability efforts. He is also a Sports Analyst, Researcher, Writer and Commentator with Radio Univers and Legon Today. LinkedIn:www.linkedin.com/in/petras-anaab-ali-mphil-5703553a6 Email:petrasanaabali@gmail.com

Title: Appoint Clowns. Get a Circus
Content: One of the biggest obstacles to Ghana’s economic and social development is not a shortage of ideas, policies or even resources. It is the chronic appointment of incompetent people to positions that demand competence, leadership and results. Take our Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives. For decades, many have presided over communities that remain filthy, poorly planned, environmentally deplorable and barely liveable. Roads are neglected, drains remain choked, sanitation is appalling, public spaces are abandoned and basic urban management appears to be an alien concept. Yet, somehow, we keep changing governments without changing the conditions in which people live. What exactly do some of these appointees do? Beyond occupying offices, attending meetings, making political appearances and distributing photographs of themselves, what measurable difference have they made to the communities entrusted to them? We must confront an uncomfortable truth: political loyalty is not a qualification for administrative competence. Being a party activist, campaign financier or familiar face in the corridors of political power does not automatically make anyone capable of managing a district, municipality or metropolis. A government can have the most brilliant manifesto, the most ambitious development agenda and the most eloquent presidential speeches. But if the people entrusted with implementation lack imagination, discipline, initiative and basic managerial competence, the outcome is predictable: grand promises, mediocre execution and another four years of excuses. Development is not delivered by manifestos. It is delivered by people who know what they are doing. We must stop treating public appointments as political compensation packages. Critical positions must be occupied by people who can think, organise, innovate, mobilise resources and deliver measurable outcomes. Ghana does not need more ceremonial officeholders. It needs problem-solvers. If we keep appointing people who cannot transform their immediate surroundings, we should stop pretending they will transform a nation.

Title: Ghana’s Gold has finally come home, and your pocket knows it
Content: For years Ghana lived with a strange contradiction in which it was Africa's largest gold producer yet struggled to find the dollars needed to pay for fuel, medicine and machinery. The cedi weakened and prices climbed while businesses planned around the next bout of exchange rate panic. The gold kept leaving the country but too much of its value never came back. A report by the Swiss development organisation Swissaid found that about 229 tonnes of Ghanaian gold worth US$11.4 billion went unrecorded in official exports over the five years to 2023. That is not merely a mining statistic, because it represents dollars that never reached our banks, royalties and taxes that never reached the state and stability that never reached ordinary households. The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), established in 2025 under Act 1140, was created to confront that contradiction. The public argument about it has been loud and some of the questions are legitimate, but the noise has often hidden a simpler question about what the country has actually gained. The answer is substantial and it reaches well beyond the mining pits. The first gain lies in bringing a scattered trade into the formal economy, and it also gives the state records on which serious oversight can rest. GoldBod exported 104 tonnes of gold from artisanal and small scale miners in 2025 worth more than US$10 billion, and a further 85.4 tonnes worth US$11.6 billion between 1 January and 20 October 2026. These figures are export values rather than profit, and their importance is that the trade now passes through official channels where it is recorded and where its foreign exchange can serve the wider economy. The national accounts show the scale of the change since GoldBod began operating. Gross international reserves rose from about US$8.98 billion in December 2024 to US$13.8 billion a year later, and the current account surplus jumped from US$1.47 billion in 2024 to US$9.08 billion in 2025. By August 2026 total exports had reached US$22.4 billion and the trade surplus stood at US$8.86 billion, with gold earning about two thirds of all export receipts. World gold prices were exceptionally favourable during this period and cocoa and oil also played their part, so the credit must be shared. Yet high prices only help a country to the extent that it captures the proceeds. Reserves serve as the national shock absorber because they reassure investors, support the currency and give the country room to respond when the world turns difficult. The benefit Ghanaians watch most closely is the value of the cedi, which comes under pressure whenever dollars are scarce. Every legally exported consignment of gold helps to ease that scarcity, since foreign currency from gold supports the banks that trade dollars and builds the reserves the Bank of Ghana can draw on to calm the market. The cedi gained about 41 percent against the dollar in 2025, its first sustained annual gain in three decades, and the Finance Ministry has credited GoldBod's exports as a major driver of that recovery. The steadiness that followed matters even more than the size of the gain. The cedi has given back some ground in 2026, yet the Bank of Ghana reports lower volatility in the first 140 trading days of this year than in the same period of previous years, and the rate in September was still stronger than a year earlier. People can plan around a currency that moves less sharply. Nowhere are these gains felt more directly than in international trade, because Ghana is an import dependent economy with an almost constant demand for United States dollars. The country spent US$5.87 billion on imports in the first four months of 2026 alone, and about US$2 billion of that went on oil, with diesel the single largest item on the national import bill. Rice, wheat, sugar, vehicles, spare parts, medicines and industrial inputs all have to be paid for in foreign currency, and that demand peaks in the fourth quarter when importers stock up for Christmas and manufacturers settle their overseas suppliers. Reserves built partly from gold give this trade a firmer footing, and at the end of 2025 Ghana's reserves covered 5.7 months of imports, a buffer that reassures foreign suppliers, shipping lines and lenders that Ghanaian buyers will be able to pay. Banks with better access to dollars can open letters of credit more readily, and importers spend less time chasing foreign exchange and more time moving goods. A stable cedi matters just as much at the point of payment, since an importer commits to a dollar price months before the cargo arrives and then pays duties and charges at whatever rate prevails on the day of clearance. The Importers and Exporters Association of Ghana reported that clearance costs during the 2025 Christmas peak were significantly lower than in previous years because a stronger cedi reduced the foreign exchange component of duties, freight bills and port charges. A consignment valued at US$10,000 cost about GH¢124,200 to settle in September 2025 and about GH¢115,500 in September 2026, and that difference of GH¢8,700 is working capital a trader can put into the next order. Tema Port handled 2.29 million twenty foot equivalent units in 2025 according to Lloyd's List, an increase of 34.6 percent on the previous year. New terminal capacity and the diversion of vessels around the Cape of Good Hope drove much of that growth, but a better supplied foreign exchange market made it easier for importers to use the capacity that had been built. Shipping lines, freight forwarders and haulage firms whose costs are largely priced in dollars benefit as well, and predictable costs strengthen Ghana's hand against Abidjan and Lomé in the contest for transit cargo bound for Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. Most Ghanaians will never read a reserve report, but they feel the effect of a steadier currency in their daily lives. Inflation fell to 3.4 percent by April 2026, and while the Bank of Ghana's tight policy and fiscal discipline under the IMF supported programme deserve their share of the credit, a calmer exchange rate removed one of the main sources of imported inflation. In a country that buys so much of what it consumes from abroad, that shows up in the price of fuel, medicines, school supplies and spare parts. For business owners a calmer economy has proved as valuable as a cheaper dollar, and the cost of credit tells much of the story. Average lending rates fell from 27.40 percent to 16.33 percent in the year to April 2026, easing one of the heaviest burdens on Ghanaian enterprise, while the Ghana Stock Exchange Composite Index was up 72.5 percent for the year by that same month. A manufacturer can now quote a customer with more certainty, and a trader at Makola or Kumasi Central Market can restock without guessing what the dollar will do by Friday. The benefits may also prove more durable than a single good year because several reforms now point toward lasting change. The ban on exporting unrefined doré from 1 September 2026 encourages more refining, testing and skilled work at home, so that Ghana keeps more of the value of its own resource. Reclamation of mined forest land has also begun, although on a modest scale. Government states that its Big Push infrastructure programme, covering roads, energy, water and housing, is being funded from domestic resources including revenue tied to gold and mining royalties rather than new borrowing on international capital markets. After the debt restructuring Ghana has just endured, that direction deserves serious attention provided it is pursued with care. Honest praise must also acknowledge the limits of what has been achieved so far. The cedi depreciated by 9.5 percent in the first nine months of 2026, and reserves fell to US$11.07 billion in August, partly because of a pause in GoldBod exports, before recovering to US$12.05 billion by 22 September. Gold export volumes fell slightly in the first half of the year even as values rose 49 percent, a reminder that much of the gain has come from price and that a correction would be felt widely. None of these concerns argues for reversing course, but they do argue for finishing the job. Ghana should publish an analysis of what a fall in gold prices would mean for reserves and public investment, and GoldBod should keep exports flowing steadily rather than allowing pauses that drain reserves just before the busy fourth quarter. Consumers and importers should receive the benefit whenever the currency strengthens, and above all the breathing space must be used to build what gold cannot provide on its own in the form of more factories, more exports and more jobs. GoldBod did not create Ghana's gold, but it has given the nation a far better chance of keeping what that gold earns. For the family at the market, the entrepreneur at the bank and the young Ghanaian looking for work, that is the reform's real promise. Gold has always been in our ground, and the task now is to make sure that its value stays in our economy. By:Albert Derrick Fiatui Albert Derrick Fiatui is the Executive Director of the Centre for International Maritime Affairs, Ghana (CIMAG). Albert Derrick Fiatui, is the Executive Director at the Centre for International Maritime Affairs, Ghana (CIMAG), an Advocacy, Research and Operational Policy Think- Tank, with focus on the Maritime Industry (Blue Economy) and general Ocean Governance.He is a Maritime Policy, Ocean Governance and Coastal Development Expert. Email:info@cimaghana.org/albert@cimaghana.org

Title: The Politics of Reconciliation: A case for Lawyer Kwasi Kwarteng
Content: As the NPP embarks on the difficult but necessary task of rebuilding party unity, it has an opportunity to demonstrate that unity is not merely a political slogan, but a commitment reflected in deliberate choices, difficult compromises and tangible acts of goodwill. Kwasi Kwarteng, who served as spokesperson for Hon. Kennedy Agyapong during one of the party’s fiercest flagbearership contests, distinguished himself by placing the interests of the NPP above personal allegiance. He promptly embraced Dr. Bawumia’s leadership and has since consistently worked across factional lines to promote reconciliation, even at a time when the party faced the real threat of fragmentation. His subsequent decision not to extend the internal rivalry into the National Communications Director contest, together with his sustained efforts in working for the party, demonstrates a willingness to subordinate personal ambition to the larger interests of the party. It would therefore send a powerful and reassuring message if Dr. Bawumia, the National Executive and the party leadership were to recognise and protect this investment in reconciliation by supporting a consensus arrangement that allows Kwasi Kwarteng to go unopposed in the Asante Akyem North parliamentary primaries. Such a gesture would go beyond the political interests of one individual or constituency. It would reassure disgruntled party members that reconciliation is genuine, demonstrate that loyalty and sacrifices are recognised, and give everyone a renewed sense of belonging in the NPP. It would also be a tangible demonstration to party faithfuls and the Ghanaian public that the NPP has genuinely turned the page, values those who build bridges and are prepared to make practical sacrifices in pursuit of a united political front.

Title: Why Dr. Farouk Aliu Mahama remains NPP’s best bet to reclaim Yendi seat in 2028
Content: In politics, numbers do not lie. And the numbers from Yendi in the 2020 and 2024 elections tell a very clear story. From the numbers, it's clear Dr. Farouk Aliu Mahama did not lose Yendi in 2024 because the people rejected him; he lost because the NPP was divided, and because a national wave of apathy hit the party everywhere. If the NPP wants to win back Yendi in 2028 and maximise votes for Dr. Mahamudu Bawumia, there is only one politically wise decision: rally behind Farouk Aliu Mahama. Here are seven reasons: 1. 2024 was not a rejection;it was a split Let us look at the facts. In the 2020 Yendi parliamentary election, Farouk Aliu Mahama, contesting for the first time, polled 40,624 to win by a whopping 62.14 per cent. His main opponent, the NDC's Alhassan Abdul Fatawu, polled 24,755, representing 37.86 per cent. From the data, Farouk won by a massive 15,869 votes - one of the biggest winning margins in the entire Northern Region by the NPP. Then in the 2024 Yendi Parliamentary election, Alhassan Abdul Fatawu polled 30,770 to win the seat against Farouk Aliu Mahama, who polled 30,441 and NPP-affiliated Independent Candidate, Hussein Abdul-Karim, who polled 4,324. From the data above, Farouk lost narrowly by just 329 votes. That is the whole story. Farouk did not collapse. He was split. The independent candidate, who came from within the NPP family after the bitter and disputed primaries, took 4,324 votes - votes that in 2020 would have gone to the NPP. If the NPP had gone into 2024 united, Farouk would have, despite the widespread national apathy against the NPP, won with over 34,000 votes against the NDC's 30,770. Even in division, even in crisis, even when his own party members campaigned against him, Farouk still almost won. That is not weakness, but a proof that he is firm on the ground. In many NPP strongholds across the country, many MPs lost by 5,000, 10,000, 15,000 votes in 2024. But Farouk, battling serious internal division, lost by 329. In a year of disaster for the NPP, he held the line. 2. Apathy affected everyone, not just Farouk The second factor was widespread national apathy that hit the NPP in 2024 also hit Yendi too. The NPP's parliamentary votes in Yendi dropped from 40,624 in 2020 to 30,441 in 2024, just as in all constituencies across the country including the party's stronghold. The NPP's presidential votes also dropped sharply, despite Dr. Bawumia winning the constituency. There are two lessons from this: First, the drop was not personal to Farouk, nor was it to Dr. Bawumia. It was a party-wide problem across the country due to reluctance by party members to go out and vote, as the NPP's own Mike Oquaye report found. When apathy hits, every candidate suffers and Farouk was not an exception. Second, and most important, is that even in that difficult year, the NDC candidate who won Yendi did not win a significant share of the votes that dropped from Farouk's 2020 numbers; neither did President John Mahama. The NDC moved from 24,755 in 2020 to 30,770 in 2024 - an increase of about 6,000 votes. Farouk lost about 10,000 votes from his 2020 total. Where did the rest go? They did not go to the NDC. They went to apathy and to the independent candidate. That means the people of Yendi did not switch to the NDC. They stayed home, or they voted for the independent out of internal NPP anger. Those voters are recoverable. They are NPP voters, and the man who can bring them back is undoubtedly Farouk. 3. Maximising Presidential votes Note this carefully: In 2024, while Farouk narrowly lost the parliamentary race, Dr. Bawumia still won the presidential race in Yendi with 32,239 against Mahama's 31,664. How did Bawumia win Yendi when the NPP parliamentary candidate lost? Because Farouk's structures, his campaign, and his groundwork kept the NPP competitive in Yendi even in a divided house. He was able to complement Bawumia's campaign through the NPP's great record of development in the area. If Farouk is on the ballot as a united NPP candidate in 2028, he will not only win back the seat; he will maximise votes for Dr. Bawumia. A united Yendi means a bigger presidential margin. A divided Yendi means the party will fight itself instead of fighting the NDC. 4. A record the people cannot forget Beyond the numbers, there is Farouk's remarkable record from the only time he has been MP. And in Yendi, the record is visible and verifiable. In his first term as MP, Farouk Aliu Mahama delivered an impressive record of development and community support: Roads were built and reshaped. Schools were renovated and new ones built. Farmers were supported with farm inputs and equipment. The youth received skills training and business support. Communities received water, health support, and educational assistance. The beautification of Yendi township is a clear, visible example that everyone can see. It is not a promise on a poster; it is on the ground. The people of Yendi are attesting to it themselves. They saw development, they felt it and they lived it. 5. He did not abandon the people after losing Many politicians disappear after losing an election, only to resurface four years later to ask for votes again. But Farouk did the opposite. After losing in 2024, he did not abandon Yendi. He continued to show commitment to the progress of Yendi and its people. He continued to support community projects and individuals, especially in job-seeking and education. He stayed with the people in defeat as he did in victory. That is character! That is leadership! And the people have noticed. 6. The comparison is already being made Today, the people of Yendi are comparing Farouk's high standard with the incumbent, who is struggling to replicate it. The incumbent has not matched the expectations. The projects have slowed, the energy has dropped and the presence has reduced. When the people themselves are calling for the one who once made things possible for them, a strategic party listens. The electorate cannot forget a man who changed their community, supported their children, and stood with them. When they exchanged Farouk for someone else, they expected more but they got less. That is why the call for his return is growing louder every day. 7. The NPP must not deepen old cracks This is the political lesson for the NPP in Yendi: Do not reinvent the wheel to deepen old cracks and open new ones. The 2024 defeat was caused by division and the solution cannot be more division. The solution cannot be to bring a new, untested candidate who will reopen old wounds, create new factions, and start from zero. The solution is unity! The NPP must demonstrate unity and rally behind the young and dynamic Farouk Aliu Mahama, who has proven that he is firm on the ground even when faced with crisis. He has the structures. He has the youth. He has the women. He has the chiefs and opinion leaders. He has the track record. He has the love of the people. Why throw that away? Conclusion: Act politically right Politics is about winning. And winning requires choosing the candidate who can win. Farouk Aliu Mahama lost in 2024 by 329 votes while fighting his own party and the bigger "enemy". Imagine what he will do in 2028 with a united party behind him. The NPP in Yendi does not need an experiment; it needs a proven winner. It needs a man who has delivered, who has stayed, and who the people themselves are asking for. The party must repose massive confidence in the young man and unite behind him. And Yendi will return to the NPP, with Dr. Bawumia getting the votes he deserves from Yendi. The people have spoken through their calls. Now the party must act.

Title: The politics of reconciliation: A case for Lawyer Kwasi Kwarteng
Content: As the NPP embarks on the difficult but necessary task of rebuilding party unity, it has an opportunity to demonstrate that unity is not merely a political slogan, but a commitment reflected in deliberate choices, difficult compromises and tangible acts of goodwill. Kwasi Kwarteng, who served as spokesperson for Hon. Kennedy Agyapong during one of the party’s fiercest flagbearership contests, distinguished himself by placing the interests of the NPP above personal allegiance. He promptly embraced Dr. Bawumia’s leadership and has since consistently worked across factional lines to promote reconciliation, even at a time when the party faced the real threat of fragmentation. His subsequent decision not to extend the internal rivalry into the National Communications Director contest, together with his sustained efforts in working for the party, demonstrates a willingness to subordinate personal ambition to the larger interests of the party. It would therefore send a powerful and reassuring message if Dr. Bawumia, the National Executive and the party leadership were to recognise and protect this investment in reconciliation by supporting a consensus arrangement that allows Kwasi Kwarteng to go unopposed in the Asante Akyem North parliamentary primaries. Such a gesture would go beyond the political interests of one individual or constituency. It would reassure disgruntled party members that reconciliation is genuine, demonstrate that loyalty and sacrifices are recognised, and give everyone a renewed sense of belonging in the NPP. It would also be a tangible demonstration to party faithfuls and the Ghanaian public that the NPP has genuinely turned the page, values those who build bridges and are prepared to make practical sacrifices in pursuit of a united political front.

Title: Atonomics at KNUST: The Minister asked us to test his plan. Here is where to start
Content: It is not every day that a Finance Minister stands before a university audience and asks to be checked. Yet that was the most striking line of Dr Cassiel Ato Forson's pre-budget engagement at KNUST on Monday. "Test the assumptions behind the policies we will be announcing," he told staff and students, "and show us where correction is needed." The Minister deserves credit, first, for showing up. He told the audience he had returned to KNUST "with responsibility," and he stayed to answer five rounds of questions from staff and students. Our students heard the country's chief fiscal officer explain his choices in person, and many put their own questions to him directly. Pre-budget engagements like this should become the norm. Three days before he presents the 2027 Budget on 12 November, the Minister laid out what some have begun to call "Atonomics": spend only what you have, finish what you start, bring down the cost of credit, buy Ghanaian, and write the rules into law. As an economist at his alma mater, I want to take him at his word. The Minister's diagnosis is hard to dispute. Ghana's boom-and-bust cycles have been driven largely by fiscal indiscipline, and his call for discipline to become "a culture of our entire nation" is the right one. Rules that depend on one minister's temperament do not survive elections. His case on credit is equally strong. When he took office in January 2025, the 91-day Treasury bill paid about 29% and businesses borrowed at 35–36%. He reports the bill rate is now about 4.5%, with some firms borrowing at 9–12%. He was candid that government itself crowded out private borrowers: bank credit to the private sector was only about 11% of GDP, against 25–26% in Côte d'Ivoire. His goal of lifting it above 20% is the right target. And his insistence on phasing is overdue. Starting 111 hospitals when the money could finish 10 is how Ghana fills its landscape with abandoned projects. Spreading the US$10 billion New Economy programme over four years, about US$2.5 billion a year, is sensible macroeconomics, not timidity. The Minister invited scrutiny, so here are three places where his own 2027 Fiscal Strategy Document tells a more complicated story. First, the debt path after 2028.The Minister spoke of reducing debt by 0.5% of GDP a year. The FSD projects debt falling to about 42% of GDP in 2028 and then rising back to about 44.8% by 2034, just under the 45% legal ceiling. The New Economy uses up most of the headroom. A shock to growth, the cedi or interest rates would push Ghana to the line. Second, crowding out has not gone away.The FSD plans no Eurobonds and negative net foreign financing, so government will still borrow around 5% of GDP a year at home, mostly from banks. That sits uneasily with the goal of doubling private credit. Third, buy-Ghanaian has costs.Requiring Free SHS feeding to use local rice, and tying rice import permits to local purchases as Nigeria once did, will help farmers. But it may raise food prices, encourage smuggling, and test Ghana's commitments under the African Continental Free Trade Area. The Minister did not say how he will square these. The most valuable evidence on Monday came not from the podium but from the floor. A young graduate who answered the call to farm described registering his two-hectare farm and being asked for an upfront tax of GH¢5,000. That bill has since more than doubled to GH¢12,000. When his plantain reached the market, he was offered GH¢20 a bunch. A colleague who works with market women explained why: market queens control access and set prices, leaving farmers little bargaining power. A lecturer asked how his students could get an affordable loan of GH¢50,000 to GH¢150,000 for a truck to aggregate maize. A student asked what institution will give young people a real voice in economic policy, not just a place in government programmes. These are not complaints about the vision. They are the points where the vision meets the market. The New Economy will succeed or fail at the farm gate, the tax office and the loan desk, not in the Budget Statement. The Minister promised policies on agriculture, textiles, local procurement, AI and affordable credit. Citizens should judge the Budget against five simple tests: The Minister closed by telling students they are "the very reason" for this effort. KNUST, and every university in Ghana, should now do what he asked: measure the results honestly, publish what we find, and hold the policy, not the personality, to account. Prof. Eric F. Oteng-Abayie is an economist in the Department of Economics, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kumasi. The views expressed are his own.

Title: Eric Amofa positions himself as unifying candidate in Asante Akim South NPP
Content: The political landscape in the Asante Akim South Constituency is increasingly drawing attention ahead of the next New Patriotic Party (NPP) parliamentary primaries, with growing discussions about the need for a candidate capable of uniting the party following divisions that have characterised its recent political history. The constituency has experienced internal disagreements, particularly following the previous parliamentary primaries, which exposed competing interests and strained relationships among sections of the party’s grassroots supporters. The divisions have raised concerns about the party’s internal cohesion and its ability to consolidate electoral support ahead of the 2028 general elections. Against this background, Eric Amofa, a former parliamentary aspirant and community development advocate, is positioning himself as a potential unifying alternative. The challenge of factional politics The political disagreements involving supporters of the incumbent Member of Parliament and those aligned with other parliamentary aspirants have remained an important subject of discussion within the constituency. There have also been allegations that some supporters of unsuccessful aspirants engaged in skirt-and-blouse campaigning during the 2024 general elections. These claims, which require independent verification, have contributed to discussions about party discipline and the consequences of unresolved internal disagreements. The emerging concern is that the next parliamentary candidate must be someone capable of rebuilding relationships across political divides rather than deepening existing divisions. Why Eric Amofa is attracting attention Eric Amofa’s potential appeal lies in his positioning as a candidate seeking to build relationships across the different political camps. His supporters point to his community engagement, educational interventions and professional background as important qualities that distinguish his political approach. Through the EKAJ Educational Fund, Amofa has supported educational initiatives, including scholarships, the distribution of educational materials, restoration of 25 broken boreholes in rural communities and assistance to underserved communities. His professional experience in social work, international banking and finance, as well as community development and social safeguards, also provides a foundation for his development-oriented political vision. His message of Unity, Development and Dedicated Service appears particularly relevant to a constituency seeking to overcome internal political disagreements. For Amofa, the challenge and opportunity are to translate his community engagement into broader political acceptance and demonstrate that he can work with party members irrespective of their previous factional affiliations. Questions surrounding Bice Obour’s candidacy Bice Obour remains an important political figure in the constituency, having established a considerable delegate following during the previous parliamentary primaries. However, the forthcoming contest presents an important leadership test for all aspirants: their ability to demonstrate that they can unite the party and command confidence beyond their established political support bases. Obour’s supporters can point to his previous delegate performance and his public expression of support for party unity following the 2024 primaries. Nevertheless, the wider political discussion is increasingly centred on which aspirant can most effectively overcome the legacy of factional competition and establish a new basis for cooperation. The question is therefore not simply who has the stronger political following, but who can provide the most inclusive leadership. Concerns about internal party administration Another issue attracting attention is the perceived neutrality of the constituency’s internal party structures. Some supporters of Eric Amofa have expressed concerns about alleged partisan conduct by sections of the constituency executive, arguing that internal party structures should provide equal opportunities to all aspirants. The credibility of the forthcoming primaries will depend partly on the ability of party structures to maintain fairness, transparency and confidence among competing candidates and their supporters. A united party requires leadership and institutional structures that are trusted by all sides. The 2028 electoral consideration Beyond the parliamentary primaries, the NPP faces the broader responsibility of rebuilding its electoral fortunes in Asante Akim South. The next parliamentary candidate will need to appeal not only to party delegates but also to floating voters, traditional party supporters, young people, farmers, artisans and other community stakeholders. This makes reconciliation, accessibility, development-oriented leadership and electoral appeal essential considerations. Eric Amofa’s development activities and stated commitment to inclusive leadership provide a platform on which he could build such an appeal. However, his ability to translate these credentials into measurable delegate support will be a critical factor. Conclusion: A contest about the future of the constituency The emerging debate in Asante Akim South presents a fundamental question for the NPP: should the next parliamentary candidate be selected primarily on established factional loyalty, or should greater emphasis be placed on the capacity to unite the party and rebuild its relationship with the electorate? Eric Amofa is making a case for the latter approach. His potential strength lies in his development-oriented profile, community engagement, and opportunity to appeal across existing political divisions. Ultimately, the decision rests with the party delegates. Their choice will not only determine who leads the NPP into the 2028 general elections but will also shape the future direction of party unity and political organisation in Asante Akim South. The constituency needs more than another parliamentary candidate. It needs a leader capable of bringing the party together.

Title: Dr Amin Adam writes an open letter to Finance Minister ahead of 2027 budget presentation
Content: Ghana does not suffer from a shortage of economic slogans. What we lack are sufficient productive jobs, thriving businesses, rising real incomes and the economic freedom that allows ordinary citizens to improve their lives through enterprise and hard work. Tomorrow, you will present what your government has christened the “New Economy Budget.” But before asking Ghanaians to embrace another grand economic slogan, perhaps you should first account for the promises of the old one. Not long ago, the NDC government promised a transformative 24-Hour Economy, backed by ambitious investment and employment targets. Ghanaians were promised jobs, expanded production and new opportunities. Yet the government has not provided a sufficiently convincing and independently verifiable account of jobs created, investments mobilised or businesses transformed under that programme. Now comes the “New Economy.” What exactly is new, beyond the branding? The economic reality confronting ordinary Ghanaians is considerably less glamorous than the government’s slogans suggest. The KPMG pre-budget survey released today provides a sobering reality check. Some 71 percent of respondents identified jobs and youth employment as a national priority, while 54 percent cited the cost of living. These are not abstract economic indicators. They reflect the everyday anxieties of households struggling to make ends meet and young people searching for opportunities.Inflation may have fallen substantially, but lower inflation does not mean prices have returned to affordable levels. October’s headline inflation of 5.5 percent still masks sharper pressures in essential services. For households facing accumulated price increases and constrained purchasing power, macroeconomic stability must mean more than favourable statistics. The findings from KPMG’s survey highlight continuing pressure on household budgets despite the fall in headline inflation from its earlier peaks. Indeed, the pocket economy is hurting whilst the paper economy is being celebrated. Those concerns should be central to the 2027 Budget, rather than overshadowed by celebrations of macroeconomic gains.Honourable Minister, we acknowledge the importance of policy continuity. Your government has maintained important elements of the economic stabilisation and reform efforts initiated under the previous NPP administration, including the Gold Purchase Programme and the debt restructuring process. Indeed, inflation had already declined from its peak of 54.1 per cent in December 2022 to 23.8 percent by December 2024, before your administration took office. The fall in inflation was 31 percentage points. Under your government, it fell further to 3.2 per cent in March 2026, a decline of 19.8 percentage points. Therefore, the subsequent disinflation represents further progress, but it did not begin in January 2025.Yet recent developments also demand caution as we have observed a worrying trend of reversals in economic gains. Inflation, having fallen to around 3.2 percent earlier in 2026, increased to 5.5 percent by October. The cedi, following its substantial appreciation in 2025, had depreciated by approximately 9.5 percent against the US dollar by September 2026. These developments do not erase the stabilisation gains entirely, but they demonstrate how fragile those gains can be. Growth figures also warrant closer scrutiny. According to the Bank of Ghana, real GDP growth moderated from 6.6 percent in the second quarter of 2025 to 6.0 percent in the corresponding quarter of 2026. More importantly, non-oil GDP growth slowed from 8.5 percent to 5.4 percent, while agricultural growth declined from 7.1 percent to 3.9 percent. Interestingly, ICT continues to contribute significantly to economic growth. The same digital economy that the NDC, the President, you and your foot soldiers once sought to dismiss as a distraction from economic management is today an important source of growth under its own administration. This should provide some perspective on the digitalisation agenda championed by Dr Mahamudu Bawumia. Economic progress is cumulative, and governments should acknowledge the foundations upon which they build. Now comes your proposed US$10 billion New Economy investment programme, equivalent to approximately US$2.5 billion annually over four years. Where will the money come from, and how much of it is genuinely new? The reported financing framework proposes reducing the primary surplus target from 1.5 percent to 0.5 percent of GDP, alongside additional revenue mobilisation. But relaxing a fiscal target does not create new wealth. It permits additional spending, potentially at the expense of faster debt reduction. Why should the country weaken an important fiscal anchor so soon after a painful debt restructuring? If the government intends to amend the fiscal framework, it must demonstrate that the resulting fiscal space will finance genuinely productive investments, rather than recurrent expenditure, politically attractive projects or spending pressures ahead of the next elections. And if the government has yet to convincingly demonstrate the financing and implementation of its earlier US$4 billion 24-Hour Economy ambition, why should Ghanaians embrace another US$10 billion promise without demanding a credible financing plan, clear implementation milestones and measurable employment outcomes? The central issue is not the size of the announcement but the credibility of the financing, the quality of the investment and the economic returns it will generate. Ghana certainly needs economic transformation. But transformation is not achieved by renaming programmes, multiplying policy acronyms or announcing increasingly ambitious investment figures. It requires fiscal discipline, competitive businesses, affordable credit, reliable infrastructure, productive investment and institutions capable of delivering results. Economic growth is not a slogan. Jobs are not created by press conferences. Prosperity cannot be legislated into existence, and economic freedom cannot be delivered through political branding. As you present the 2027 Budget, the real test will not be how compellingly you describe the New Economy, but whether you can demonstrate how it will be financed, how it differs from previous promises and how it will improve the lives of ordinary Ghanaians. Before unveiling a New Economy, account for the 24-Hour Economy. Ghana needs a functioning economy, not another freshly packaged promise. See less

Title: Demystifying Derivatives: Yield enhancement through equity and credit-linked solutions (Part 1)
Content: Institutional investors traditionally gain exposure to equities and bonds by purchasing the underlying securities directly. While this approach remains central to portfolio construction, direct investment can sometimes present practical constraints, particularly when investors seek exposure to assets listed or issued outside their domestic markets. Derivatives can provide an alternative route. When combined with traditional deposits, they can create structured solutions whose returns are linked to the performance of equities, market indices, corporate debt or sovereign credit. These structures allow investors to gain exposure to selected markets without necessarily purchasing or holding the underlying securities directly. Equity-Linked Deposits and Credit-Linked Deposits illustrate how this can be achieved. Both can expand the investment opportunities available to institutional investors and provide additional sources of return. However, their use introduces risks that must be carefully assessed, including the performance of the referenced asset and the creditworthiness of the institution providing the investment solution. Equity-Linked Deposits Let us examine Equity-Linked Deposits. These are investment vehicles that track assets beyond traditional fixed income, such as equities. They are becoming increasingly common in the region, particularly in East and Southern Africa, where institutional clients seek returns associated with the performance of equity markets and equity derivatives. Generally, these products combine a deposit with an equity call option. The return enhancement is derived from the performance of the call option acquired by the investor. The option may reference the shares of a single company, an equity index or a basket of equities, such as the MSCI World Index or the S&P 500 Index. The investor places funds in the deposit and receives the principal at maturity, subject to the terms of the structure and the creditworthiness of the issuing institution. The call option provides the potential for an additional return if the referenced equity or index performs favourably over the investment period. This structure allows investors to participate in equity market performance without purchasing the underlying shares directly. It may therefore appeal to investors seeking exposure to international equities while retaining a deposit-based investment structure. The solution can also be customised to reflect the investor's preferred market exposure, investment horizon and return objectives. An investor may select a single equity where there is a specific market view or choose a broad index or basket to diversify exposure across several companies, sectors or markets. Furthermore, by using a cross-currency swap as an overlay, the structure can be converted into payouts in the local currency. This can allow the investor to receive returns in a currency aligned with its liabilities or investment requirements. Depending on market conditions and the design of the structure, the currency component may also contribute to the overall yield enhancement. As with the other derivative-based investment strategies discussed in this series, counterparty credit risk remains an important consideration. The investor relies on the institution offering the solution, often a bank, to fulfil its payment obligations. The creditworthiness of the issuer must therefore be considered alongside the potential performance of the referenced equity or index. Credit-Linked Deposits Another yield-enhancement strategy is the Credit-Linked Deposit. This product may be particularly relevant to investors in our region because of their familiarity with government and corporate bonds. A Credit-Linked Deposit allows an investor to gain exposure to a sovereign or major corporation without holding the underlying security directly. It can provide customised coupon payments similar to those that the investor might receive from owning the referenced bond. The structure can be created by combining a deposit with a Credit Default Swap, thereby creating a funded credit exposure. The investor selects a reference entity based on its risk appetite and receives a corresponding return. A reference entity with a lower perceived probability of default would generally offer a smaller coupon, while exposure to a higher-risk name may provide a larger coupon to compensate for the additional credit risk. The payment profile can also be customised. Instead of receiving the semi-annual coupon payments commonly associated with bonds, for example, an investor may structure the Credit-Linked Deposit to make quarterly payments. This flexibility can assist institutional investors in managing cash flows and matching investment income against expected liabilities. A distinctive feature of the Credit-Linked Deposit is that it removes the need for the investor to purchase the referenced bond or open a securities depository account in the issuer's country. This may reduce administrative requirements and eliminate some of the custody or depositary fees associated with direct ownership. For illustration, an investor in Ghana seeking exposure to the Kenyan sovereign could obtain that exposure without establishing accounts or a securities depository arrangement in Kenya. Instead, the investor could engage a suitable counterparty, preferably a bank, place an amount corresponding to the desired sovereign exposure and enter into a credit derivative referencing that sovereign. Under this arrangement, the investor obtains synthetic exposure to the referenced sovereign. The deposit and the credit component together generate the return sought by the investor. The structure does not eliminate credit risk. If a credit event occurs in relation to the referenced entity, the investor may lose part or all of the amount invested, depending on the terms of the product and the recovery value of the referenced obligation. Since the Credit-Linked Deposit is an over-the-counter structure, the investor is also exposed to the creditworthiness of the counterparty with which the transaction is executed. If that counterparty becomes insolvent or is otherwise unable to meet its obligations, the investor may suffer a loss independently of the performance of the referenced sovereign or corporation. Investors must therefore assess both the reference entity and the institution providing the structure. Regulatory Considerations and Market Opportunity Implementing these yield-enhancement strategies requires careful consideration of the applicable local regulations. Certain structures may fall within the alternative investment provisions under the Guidelines for Asset Managers and the Guidelines on Investment of Tier 2 and Tier 3 Pension Scheme Funds. Where a structure provides exposure to an asset or reference entity outside Ghana, it may also be treated as an external investment. Investors must therefore consider the applicable asset-allocation limits, approval requirements and foreign-currency rules before entering into a transaction. The foreign-currency component of these investments may require compliance with guidance issued by the Bank of Ghana. Pension funds, asset managers and other institutional investors must also ensure that any proposed investment is permitted under their governing mandates and internal investment policies. These requirements do not remove the potential value of the structures. They establish the conditions within which the investments must be assessed and implemented. Regulatory limits can restrict the proportion of a portfolio allocated to external or alternative investments, thereby containing the overall exposure of a fund to these instruments. For asset managers, pension funds and corporates, the potential opportunity lies in using permitted allocations more effectively to achieve diversification and pursue enhanced returns. Equity-Linked Deposits can provide access to international equity performance, while Credit-Linked Deposits can provide exposure to sovereign or corporate credit without requiring direct ownership of the referenced securities. Cash flows generated by these investments, including coupons or investment proceeds, may eventually be repatriated and converted into local currency. Investors must therefore consider not only the prospective return but also currency movements, repatriation requirements and the effect of the investment on their regulatory asset-allocation limits. A depreciation of the local currency, for instance, may increase the local-currency value of a foreign-currency investment and affect the proportion of the portfolio allocated to external assets. The investor may consequently need to rebalance the portfolio to remain within the applicable limits. The suitability of these solutions will depend on each investor's mandate, risk appetite, liquidity requirements and capacity to evaluate structured investments. Their adoption must therefore be supported by appropriate governance, transparent documentation and a clear understanding of the underlying market and credit exposures. Derivatives are widely used to manage market risk, but their application extends beyond hedging. Equity-Linked Deposits and Credit-Linked Deposits demonstrate how derivative-based structures can help institutional investors access new markets, diversify their portfolios and pursue additional returns without necessarily purchasing the underlying securities directly. These benefits must be considered alongside the relevant risks.
