His appearance at a sitting in Port Harcourt,Nigeria, reportedly prompted the ECOWAS Parliament to refuse to swear in Ghana's newly constituted delegation, deepening the impasse. Speaker of Parliament Alban Bagbin previouslyreferred Afenyo-Markinto the Privileges Committee following a petition by Majority Leader Mahama Ayariga, who accused him of defying a parliamentary resolution that had removed him from the delegation. A key development that helped break the deadlock came when Deputy Minority Leader Patricia Appiagyei pulled out of the proposed replacement list. She cited a lack of consultation and what she described as irregularities in the nomination process as reasons for her withdrawal. Under the arrangement approved by Parliament, George Kweku Ricketts-Hagan will lead the Ghanaian delegation, with Afenyo-Markin included as a member rather than in a leadership role within the group. The remaining members of the delegation are Emmanuel Kwasi Bedzrah, Laadi Ayii Ayamba, Eric Afful, Dominic Napare, Kwame Anyimadu-Antwi and Bryan Acheampong. Popular Ghanaian business mogul and lawyer declares intention to contest NPP parliamentary primaries Millicent Yeboah Amankwah will participate as an observer. The reconstituted delegation is expected to allow Ghana to fully re-engage with the ECOWAS Parliament and put an end, at least at the domestic legislative level, to the standoff that had disrupted the country's representation in the bloc. TheECOWAS Parliamentis the legislative body of the Economic Community of WestAfrican States (ECOWAS), representing the people of West Africa. It serves as a platform for dialogue and consultation on regional integration issues, such as human rights, infrastructure, and social affairs. Comprising representatives from all 15 ECOWAS member states, the Parliament works to foster integration through dialogue and consensus-building. The ECOWAS Parliament consists of 115 representatives from these 15 states and includes a Bureau (Speaker and Deputy Speakers) along with several Standing Committees focused on sectors like agriculture,energy, health, and more. It offers advisory opinions on matters like human rights, infrastructure, and social and cultural issues. Although Ghana were eliminated at the group stage in Qatar, the drum's place in the FIFA Museum ensures that tradition is not forgotten. Taken together, the three artefacts span different chapters of Ghana's engagement with football's biggest stage. One speaks to a painful near-miss that still resonates across the continent; another captures the cultural spirit a squad chose to carry onto the world's most watched platform; and the third marks a young player's moment of impact at the most recent edition of the tournament. Title: Customs Commissioner directs ports to detain right-hand-drive vehicles without import permits
Content: The Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) has directed all ports and stations nationwide to process or release right-hand-drive vehicles unless importers produce valid permits authorising their importation. The directive, contained in a memorandum dated November 16, 2026, and signed by the Commissioner of Customs, Aaron Kanor, follows concerns that some right-hand-drive vehicles are being presented for clearance without the requisite approval. The GRA has consequently instructed all sector commanders to ensure strict compliance with the directive. This follows a JoyNews report on the use of Toyota Voxy vehicles and their involvement in an accident titled "VOXY!! Blame Game Among State Institutions As Blood Flows On Ghana's Roads." Watch the full report below. The memorandum draws attention to Section 58 of the Customs Act, 2015 (Act 891), which prohibits the importation of right-hand steering motor vehicles into Ghana without approval from the Minister. It further states that prohibited motor vehicles are liable to seizure and forfeiture to the State. According to the directive, any right-hand steering vehicle presented for clearance without a valid permit from the Ministry of Transport must be detained and dealt with in accordance with the provisions of the law. The Commissioner has tasked sector commanders with communicating the directive to officers at all frontier stations, ports and collections under their supervision to ensure its strict enforcement. The directive is addressed to all ports and stations.

Title: Dangote challenges Ghana to tap into West African market of 450 million people, boost local production
Content: Nigerian business magnate Aliko Dangote has urged Ghana to look beyond its domestic market and position itself to exploit the vast commercial opportunities across West Africa, saying the country has access to a regional market of about 450 million people. He said Ghana could strengthen its economic position by attracting investment into productive industries, expanding local manufacturing and leveraging regional trade agreements to reach consumers beyond its borders. Addressing participants at the maiden Invest in Ghana Summit on Monday, November 16, Mr Dangote urged Ghanaian entrepreneurs and investors to adopt a broader business outlook by considering the entire West African subregion as a potential market. He argued that Ghana's economic potential should not be measured solely by its population, given the opportunities presented by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). “When you are talking about Ghana’s market, it’s not only the population of Ghana. Ghana’s market, I was telling you, is 450 million people’s market,” he said. Mr Dangote said regional economic integration offered businesses operating in Ghana an opportunity to scale up production and distribute their goods across neighbouring countries through trade arrangements designed to facilitate commerce among ECOWAS members. He therefore called for deliberate efforts to position Ghana as a regional manufacturing and distribution hub. Dangote proposes 1,000km road linking three West African countries Mr Dangote identified inadequate regional connectivity as a major constraint to cross-border trade and called for investment in transport infrastructure to help West African countries maximise their commercial potential. He proposed the construction of a 1,000-kilometre road linking Nigeria, Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, saying the project could improve the movement of goods and strengthen trade relations among the three economies. He said he intended to engage the President of Ghana and other regional leaders to ensure the proposed project received priority attention. “I think we are really going to engage with the President and the other Presidents to make sure that this road is given a priority,” he stated. The proposed route is expected to improve regional connectivity, facilitate the transportation of goods and make it easier for businesses to access markets across the three countries. Warns against excessive dependence on imports Beyond expanding regional trade, Mr Dangote urged African countries to reduce their dependence on imported goods, arguing that sustainable economic prosperity would require a stronger commitment to domestic production. He said countries that rely heavily on importing finished products without developing their own industries risk losing significant employment and investment opportunities to manufacturing economies. “If you are a consumer, you are not a producer; you will never, ever create jobs. You will never, ever create prosperity,” he said. He explained that when goods are imported, the employment opportunities associated with their production are largely created in the countries where they are manufactured. By contrast, investment in local industries creates jobs, supports businesses and enables countries to retain a greater share of economic value within their economies. Using Ghana's rice industry as an example, Mr Dangote encouraged consumers and policymakers to support locally produced rice, even when imported alternatives were relatively cheaper. “Even if today in Ghana you are producing rice at a little bit more expensive than the imported one, it’s okay,” he remarked. He argued that spending on locally produced goods would support Ghanaian farmers, processors and other businesses along the domestic supply chain rather than allowing those economic benefits to accrue to foreign producers. Dangote eyes major investments in Ghana's agriculture sector Mr Dangote also signalled his business group's interest in expanding investments in Ghana, particularly in sectors that could strengthen domestic production and reduce the country's dependence on imported commodities. He identified sugar production, cocoa processing and rice milling as potential areas for investment. On sugar production, he disclosed that discussions were ongoing with the government over a proposed investment that could create nearly 50,000 jobs. The project, if concluded, is expected to generate employment across agricultural production, processing and related activities. He also expressed readiness to consider establishing an additional 500,000 metric tonnes of rice-processing capacity in Ghana, subject to an agreement with the government. The proposed investment would provide opportunities to link local rice cultivation to industrial processing, while supporting efforts to increase the domestic supply of processed rice. Mr Dangote maintained that African countries must first build the capacity to meet a greater proportion of their domestic consumption needs through local production before placing greater emphasis on expanding exports.

Title: EXIM Bank-funded cashew factory targets 33,000-tonne annual processing capacity
Content: The newly commissioned NADKANSCO Cashew Processing Limited in Techiman has the capacity to process up to 33,000 metric tonnes of raw cashew nuts annually, in a major boost to Ghana's efforts to expand local processing and reduce exports of the commodity in its raw state. Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Export-Import Bank (Ghana EXIM Bank), Sylvester Adinam Mensah, disclosed this during the commissioning of the facility by President John Dramani Mahama on Monday, November 16, 2026. He said the factory's annual processing capacity was almost twice the total volume of cashew nuts processed locally across the country in the previous year. “Last year, Ghana produced more than 262,000 metric tonnes of raw cashew nuts. Yet only 17,000 metric tonnes were processed here at home,” he said. Mr Mensah explained that the facility had an installed capacity of 100 metric tonnes of raw cashew nuts per day under a two-shift operation. He said the factory was already operating close to its installed capacity and had employed nearly 1,000 people directly, while supporting another 3,000 livelihoods indirectly. The additional jobs, he said, covered activities across the cashew value chain, including farming, aggregation, transportation, packing and loading. “That is 4,000 livelihoods sustained in one decision to process here at home instead of shipping raw nuts abroad,” he said. Mr Mensah said the Ghana EXIM Bank had committed approximately $12 million to support the project, including financing for modern automated processing equipment, working capital and workforce training. He explained that more than $3 million of the funding was used to acquire the factory's automated processing equipment. The investment, he said, was intended to strengthen Ghana's capacity to process its cashew produce locally, create employment and retain more economic value within the country. The factory is expected to produce cashew kernels, cashew nut shell liquid and briquettes for export, while supplying cashew cakes, briquettes and roasted kernels to the domestic market. Mr Mensah urged the company's management to scale up operations and operate at full capacity, assuring them of the bank's continued support through affordable, long-term financing. He said the facility was consistent with the government's 24-hour economy agenda, which seeks to maximise productive capacity through extended operations, industrial expansion and job creation. NADKANSCO Cashew Processing Limited, a private initiative, is an EXIM Bank-funded factory.

Title: PwC Post Budget Forum: Government spending to hit 16-year high in 2027 – Fitch Solutions
Content: Fitch Solutions says Ghana faces limited fiscal risks in 2027 despite an anticipated increase in government expenditure under the administration’s New Economy Agenda. The research firm expects the fiscal deficit to widen to about 2.7% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) next year, representing the largest deficit since 2023, largely driven by increased government investment. Speaking at the PwC Post-2027 Budget Forum, Director at Fitch Solutions, Mike Kruiniger, said capital expenditure is projected to rise significantly as government steps up investment in support of its economic transformation agenda. “We expect capital expenditure to rise to around 5% of GDP next year, which would be the highest level Ghana has seen since around 2010. So quite a substantial uptake,” he said. Despite the anticipated increase in spending, Mr Kruiniger expects Ghana to maintain a primary budget surplus in 2027, supported by improving debt conditions, relatively low domestic treasury yields and sustained economic growth. “Importantly, though, in line with the Ministry of Finance projections, we still expect the primary balance to remain in surplus,” he stated. He added that with the public debt-to-GDP ratio falling below 50%, the country's fiscal position provides some room to accommodate higher investment without creating significant immediate risks. “With the debt ratio having fallen below 50%, pretty low yields on domestic treasuries, pretty robust amount of GDP growth, we think that fiscal risks stemming from the increase remain very much limited as we go into 2027,” he said. On economic performance, Mr Kruiniger noted that Ghana's economy recorded strong growth, with activity expanding by 6.2% year-on-year in August, driven largely by the services sector, particularly information and communications technology (ICT). He attributed the sector's performance to continued growth in data usage and mobile money transactions, alongside low inflation, which has helped sustain consumer purchasing power. Mr Kruiniger also said Ghana's position as a relatively small net importer of energy has helped cushion the economy against the global energy shock arising from the US-Iran conflict. Although the country's energy trade deficit has widened, he said the impact remains relatively modest compared with other economies. “The energy trade deficit has widened as a result of the U.S.-Iran conflict this year. But when we put that into perspective, that deficit only accounts for around 0.3% of GDP. So that is very small by global standards,” he explained. He noted that Ghana's crude oil exports provide an important buffer against its dependence on imported refined petroleum products, helping the country remain relatively insulated from fluctuations in global energy prices. Mr Kruiniger further linked Ghana's fiscal resilience to stronger domestic revenue mobilisation, particularly from income and property taxes, which has helped keep the primary balance comfortably in surplus in 2026. The Fitch Solutions assessment suggests that while the government's increased investment ambitions could widen the fiscal deficit in 2027, the country's improving debt position and continued economic growth could help contain the associated risks.

Title: ‘Twenty-three cripples walked to me and left their sticks’ – Agyinasare4 hours
Content: Archbishop Charles Agyinasare has recounted what he describes as a remarkable healing experience at a church gathering in Orlando, Florida, in 2011, where 23 people with physical disabilities allegedly walked towards him using sticks and later left the walking aids behind. The Founder of Perez Chapel International said the incident happened during a meeting organised by renowned American evangelist Dr Morris Cerullo. According to Archbishop Agyinasare, he had told the congregation that he believed three people would approach him carrying walking sticks. He then invited those who felt led to respond to come forward. He said the response exceeded what he had anticipated, with 23 people making their way towards him. “Twenty-three cripples walked to me and left their sticks. We have it on video,” he said. He was speaking on Channel One TV’sThe Point of View, hosted by Bernard Avle, on Monday, November 16, 2026, where he reflected on his experiences in healing ministry and the approach he adopts during church meetings. Archbishop Agyinasare said he often addressed people suffering from various ailments directly during his ministry, rather than depending only on conventional prayer sessions. “So for most of my meetings, I just speak to the sick, and the things happen,” he added. The account forms part of the archbishop’s wider ministry of evangelism, which has taken him to several countries. He founded Word Miracle Church International in Tamale in 1987, before the ministry expanded and was renamed Perez Chapel International in 2013. Through his evangelistic work, he has conducted campaigns and ministry activities across Africa, Europe, Asia and the Americas, according to his church’s published profile. Archbishop Agyinasare said the Orlando incident remained one of the experiences that shaped his confidence in speaking directly to people seeking healing during his ministry.

Title: Africa must reject unfunded climate obligations at COP31 — Zanetor4 hours
Content: African countries should not accept new climate obligations without adequate financial, technological and capacity-building support, Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, Minister of Environment, Science and Technology, has said. She also called for a united African position at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) to secure concrete commitments on climate finance and adaptation. Dr Agyeman-Rawlings made the call at the African Ministerial Conference on the Environment (AMCEN) High-Level Ministerial Consultative Meeting, held on the margins of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. She said African ministers should defend three key positions during the conference’s high-level segment: maintaining the commitment to triple adaptation finance, rejecting additional obligations without the means to implement them, and preventing double-counting of climate finance or excessive reliance on loans. The Minister said African countries had demonstrated commitment to climate action by submitting Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), developing carbon markets, and preparing implementation plans. However, she noted that the resources pledged to support those actions had not been delivered at the required scale. Dr Agyeman-Rawlings said African countries should not be expected to take on additional commitments without corresponding financial, technological, and capacity-building support. She stressed that climate finance must be accessible and credible, warning against funding arrangements that counted the same resources more than once or increased developing countries' debt burden through loans. The Minister called on African negotiators to maintain a common position throughout the negotiations, describing unity as the continent’s greatest strength at the conference. She pledged Ghana’s support to the Chair of the African Group of Negotiators, Nana Dr Antwi Boasiako Amoah, and other African delegations throughout the conference. Dr Agyeman-Rawlings said Ghana would continue to advance Africa’s climate priorities as the country prepares to assume the expected chairmanship of the African Union in 2027. She urged African ministers to seek concrete financing commitments and clear implementation plans rather than declarations unsupported by resources. The AMCEN meeting reviewed key issues under negotiation at COP31, including climate finance, adaptation, just transition and the relationship between climate policy and international trade. Ministers were also briefed on preparations for COP32, scheduled to be hosted by Ethiopia in Addis Ababa in November 2027, and discussed support required from African countries to ensure its success. The meeting further considered preparations for a joint session of African Ministers of Environment and Ministers responsible for Finance, Planning and Economic Development, expected to be held in Addis Ababa from March 17 to 23, 2027.

Title: Richmond Adu-Poku: Record labels are dead in Ghana
Content: Ghana has become exceptionally good at producing music stars. We churn out hit songs, manufacture viral sensations and export artistes who command attention beyond our borders. But when it comes to building the powerful businesses that turn these stars into sustainable commercial empires, our performance has been rather less impressive. We have the talent, the sound, the audience and the occasional international breakthrough. Yet, somewhere between the recording studio and the international bank account, the money seems to lose its way home. Perhaps it is time to bring back an old friend we have neglected for too long: the Record Label. This is not an invitation to resurrect an era when artistes needed permission from a label executive to sneeze, let alone release a song. It is about rebuilding the business infrastructure that makes music commercially sustainable. From Gramophones to Global Highlife Ghana's recording industry did not begin with Spotify, TikTok or an artiste discovering the magic of a digital distribution account. Its history stretches back nearly a century. In the 1920s, recording companies such as Zonophone and His Master's Voice were already documenting Ghanaian music for commercial distribution. Among the pioneers was Kwame Asare, popularly known as Jacob Sam, whose 1928 recording ofYaaAmponsahbecame a landmark in recorded highlife. In 1948, Decca established a permanent recording studio in Accra, widely recognised as the first of its kind in West Africa. It became an important recording centre for influential musicians, including E.T. Mensah's Tempos, King Bruce's Black Beats and E.K. Nyame's Guitar Band. By the 1960s and 1970s, Ghana had developed a formidable recording and manufacturing ecosystem. Ambassador Records, Record Manufacturers Ghana and the Ghana Film Studio contributed to production, while local studios and vinyl-pressing facilities helped take Ghanaian music to commercial audiences. In other words, we were doing more than making music. We were manufacturing records, employing people, distributing products, developing businesses and exporting culture. Highlife was not just a sound. It was an industry, complete with machinery, investment and commercial ambition. When the Vinyl Stopped Spinning Economic difficulties, declining local pressing facilities and the popularity of cassette duplication weakened the old system from the late 1970s into the 1980s. The industry adapted. Cassettes became the new currency, while businesses such as Frimprince Music, Prince Dave Records, Megastar and Soul Records helped keep Ghanaian music commercially alive. Later, labels such as Slip Music became important players in highlife, gospel and popular music. The packaging changed, the technology evolved and distribution found new routes. But one principle remained constant: music needed investment, organisation and businesses willing to take risks. Somebody understood what we occasionally forget today: a microphone can create a star, but it takes a business to build an empire. The Modern Label Era: Building Stars and Brands The emergence of hiplife and contemporary Afropop introduced another generation of producer-led and artiste-led music companies. Lynx Entertainment, founded by Richie Mensah in 2006, became a notable example of structured talent development, contributing to the careers of artistes such as Asem, Eazzy, MzVee, KiDi and Kuami Eugene. Other notable players included Samini Music, Black Avenue Musik, BBnZ Live, Highly Spiritual Music, Legacy Life Entertainment, Sarkcess Music and Burniton Music. These companies understood that releasing songs was only the beginning. There was branding, artist development, production, promotion, management and commercial partnerships to consider. Some have evolved, others have scaled down, while most have disappeared from the industry's spotlight. The problem is not that every label has vanished. It is that Ghana has not built enough strong, sustainable music businesses to match the extraordinary talent it produces. We have plenty of people interested in discovering the next superstar, but far fewer adequately capitalised institutions willing to invest in what happens after the discovery. Distribution Is Not the Music Business Digital technology has made it easier than ever for Ghanaian artistes to take their music global. Today, an independent musician can release a song without waiting for a traditional executive's blessing. That is progress, and nobody should romanticise unnecessary gatekeeping. But let us not confuse access with capacity. Having a distribution account does not automatically make someone a music entrepreneur. Uploading songs and chasing streams are one thing; financing campaigns, building brands, negotiating licensing deals and turning music catalogues into wealth are entirely different ball games. That is where modern record labels become relevant. Artistes may not need old-fashioned record deals, but they certainly need transparent partnerships that provide investment, expertise and commercial muscle. Independence is beautiful, but being your own artiste, accountant, lawyer, marketer, distribution manager and CEO can quickly turn musical freedom into corporate slavery. Even stars need a team! Let'sCelebrate the Businesses Behind the Music The Telecel Ghana Music Awards should seriously consider restoring its Record Label of the Year category. Stars do not magically manufacture themselves, and the businesses investing behind the hits deserve their moment in the spotlight. The Ghana Association of Phonographic Industry must also reposition itself to champion modern labels, distributors, music rights and stronger industry partnerships. Beyond awards and applause, Ghana needs investment, better contracts, effective copyright protection and locally owned music catalogues. International partnerships are welcome, but Ghanaian businesses must develop enough commercial muscle to negotiate from positions of strength. We must stop exporting our talent while importing the business power to profit from it. Ghana does not lack musical talent. What we lack are sufficiently strong institutions capable of turning that talent into enduring commercial power. We need labels that think beyond the next release, executives who understand intellectual property and investors who recognise that music catalogues can be valuable assets long after the latest hit has disappeared from the charts. Our history proves that we have built such structures before. Our contemporary successes prove that the talent remains. What is missing is the ambition to connect the two. Because an industry that can produce stars but cannot build businesses around them will spend its lifetime celebrating other people's commercial victories. After nearly a century of making music, Ghana deserves more than applause. It deserves ownership, investment and power.

Title: Ato Forson has earned his chance to grow the economy: 2027 budget preview
Content: The 2027 budget, which the Finance Minister presents on Thursday, 12th November, is expected to come with the unveiling of the "New Economy", estimated to inject $10 billion over four years into critical sectors of the economy. In 2025, I wrote that Dr. Ato Forson faced a choice between pushing for growth and protecting the stability that was only just emerging. He chose stability, and I said it was the right call, but that the real test was what came next. In July, I made the same point about the Big Push, which he funded without front-loading. The New Economy is the logical next step to transition from stability to growth. Before we get into it, let us look at the record that earned him the room to attempt this. In 2024, the government was running a primary deficit, spending more than it earned even before paying a cedi of interest. By 2025, he had turned that around into a primary surplus of 2.6% of GDP. Based on IMF numbers, it is the largest primary surplus we have seen in at least 25 years. And he did this while clearing old debts. The government paid off GH¢23.7 billion in arrears in 2025 without building up new ones. He also scrapped the E-Levy, the betting tax, the emissions levy and the COVID levy, while cutting effective VAT from 21.9% to 20%. In addition, he backed that discipline with a law that sets a floor of 1.5% of GDP for the primary surplus. The results are there for all to see. We exited the IMF programme in July, rating agencies upgraded our credit, and inflation dropped from 23.8% at the end of 2024 to a low of 3.2% in March 2026, and stood at 5.5% in October. Under his watch, GDP also crossed $100 billion in nominal terms for the first time in our history. To be fair, high gold prices and a strong cedi helped a lot. But the hard parts belong to him. Paying bills you could easily delay and writing a law against your own spending are things finance ministers usually avoid. Dr. Forson is proving to be the disciplinarian the economy needs. Looking at IMF figures since 2000, we have managed a primary surplus in only four years: 2003, 2015, 2017 and 2025. And in every election year since 2004, the primary balance has been worse than the year before. No finance minister in the Fourth Republic has held the line straight through an election. So here comes the challenge. The New Economy is set to cost 1.5% of GDP every year from 2027 to 2030, targeting agriculture, energy, mineral processing, textiles and pharmaceuticals. Two-thirds of its funding will come from lowering the fiscal rule's surplus floor from 1.5% to 0.5% of GDP. The argument for spending is solid, though. Capital spending at 1.4% of GDP is far too low for a developing country, especially when a third of our young people aged 15 to 24 who want to work cannot find jobs. However, the real risk is the timing. Lowering the floor just 19 months after passing the law could send mixed signals to financial markets. But so far, we haven’t seen much to worry about.  Going into Thursday, here is what I will be watching for. First, we need a self-correcting trigger on the fiscal rule. The relaxed floor should come with an automatic rollback to 1.5%, for example, if capital spending misses targets or new arrears begin to cross a set threshold. Second, we need to measure the jobs the New Economy creates and be able to show they came from the program. Finally, state support to industries under the New Economy should follow actual output, with government paying private firms only after they deliver results. If Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson creates verifiable jobs through the New Economy and holds this new fiscal rule firmly through the 2028 election, he will be the first finance minister in our modern history to fix a fiscal mess and expand the economy right through a full electoral cycle. Salim Nuhu is an economist at a global e-commerce and technology company and a former World Bank economist. He holds a PhD in Economics from Michigan State University and a BA in Economics (First Class) from KNUST. He writes in his personal capacity. Contact:salim.nuhu@outlook.com

Title: Father says Peki SHS son was brought in dead before school called to say he was sick
Content: The father of a 19-year-old Peki SHS student who died after an alleged dormitory row says the school called to say his son was sick almost two hours after the boy had been brought to hospital dead. Gabriel Tsetsekple gave the account in an interview published on Monday, telling GhanaWeb how he learned of his son Joseph's death. Joseph Tsetsekple, 19, was in his final year at Peki Senior High School. Wereported his death and the arrest of a fellow studenton 10 November. He said the school called him on a Monday to ask for money, and he sent it. Between 3pm and 4pm the next day, he said, the school phoned to confirm it had arrived. "On Monday they told me that they needed money, so I sent them the money, and then I didn't hear from them," he said. At about 19:00 that Tuesday, he said, a staff member asked whether he was Joseph's father, told him the boy was ill and had been taken to hospital, then asked whether his health insurance was active. "He said he has been admitted to the hospital, and then I can't get to him. So, I began to worry, because I know Joseph is not having any specific illness," he said. He asked his wife to make enquiries. What students told her, he said, was that Joseph was pushed by a friend: "he fell backwards, and he used his head to hit the metal box, and so he fell unconscious." That account has not been independently confirmed. Our 10 November report said investigators were also examining claims that he did not get medical care quickly enough. School authorities declined to speak publicly at the time. The Volta Regional Director of Education, Marian Jemima Akua, confirmed the death at the time and urged boarding schools to tighten supervision and emergency response. Her call came the same week a Funsi SHS student's video exposed athree-year blackout in a boys' dormitory. In February 2024, the parents of a 16-year-old student who died atAburi Girls' Senior High Schoolalso alleged delay and negligence, and police opened an investigation. The family went to the school for answers, he said, and were left dissatisfied. "We realised that the school were trying to cover things up when we went to the school to speak to the authorities," he said. He then went to the emergency unit at Peki Government Hospital. Staff there told him his son had arrived dead at about 17:20, well before the school's call. "I quickly went to the hospital's emergency ward and they told me he was brought in dead around 5:20 pm so meaning he died in the school and nobody bothered to attend to me from the school," he said. As of 17 November, the school, theGhana Education Serviceand the Volta Regional Police had made no public response to the father's account.

Title: Reported fraud in Ghana jumped 48% to 24,778 cases, and most of it is digital
Content: Reported fraud across Ghana's banks, deposit-takers and payment firms rose 48 per cent to 24,778 cases last year, as a global fraud awareness week runs to Saturday. The figures are from theBank of Ghana's 2025 Fraud Report, set out by Second Deputy Governor Matilda Asante-Asiedu in Akosombo on September 10. The count takes in payment service providers as well as banks and specialised deposit-takers. In 2024 it was 16,733. The trend matches what theCyber Security Authorityhas seen, withonline fraud dominating its incident counts. The value at risk grew from GH¢99 million to GH¢101 million. Fraud inside banks and deposit-takers fell significantly, so almost the entire increase came from payment service providers. Mrs Asante-Asiedu said fraud is migrating from banking into electronic money and digital payment channels. Fraud incidents within payment firms rose 98 per cent between 2022 and 2025, following the growth ofmobile money. The Cyber Security Authority counted 3,876 cyber incidents from January to July 2026, and online fraud made up about 47 per cent of them. Director-General Divine Selase Agbeti gave the figures at the launch of the 2026 National Cyber Security Awareness Month. He added that electronic fraud in the payment provider segment rose by 54 per cent. The awareness week, organised by the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, runs fromNovember 15 to 21. Fake investment schemes cost victims the most. The CSA logged 352 cases in the first half of 2026, with losses of GH¢3,429,447, from promises of high returns advertised on social media and paid by mobile money. The scammers pose as subsidiaries of foreign firms and rebrand often; names the CSA has flagged lately are Darazz, Daily trade, Ghstore, KUKA and Edollar. Its advice: returns that look too good are the cue to walk away and check through official channels. In business impersonation scams, fraudsters createfake listings of real firmson search engines and maps. The CSA received 54 such cases between January 1 and April 26, 2026, with losses of GH¢266,195. Victims are asked to fill forms with their phone number, network, transaction amount and mobile money PIN, which the criminals use to steal from accounts. The CSA says never disclose PINs, one-time passwords or banking credentials to anyone. Romance scammers use model-like photos and always find an excuse to avoid meeting. The CSA advises an image search on the photo, cutting off contact at the first suspicion and never sending cash to someone known only online. Phishing messages use familiar company names, demand passwords or bank details and press for immediate action. Arecent CSA and NITA alertcovered scams that followed the Microsoft outage. Never share your PIN, even with agents and telecom workers. Avoid birth years and patterns like 1111 or 1234, and never hand your phone to an agent. Wait for the confirmation text at a merchant's shop, and check it truly came from your network. Treat texts and calls from strange numbers with suspicion, and never follow their instructions. Report fraud to the CSA at any hour on 292 by call or text, on WhatsApp on 0501603111 or by email to report@csa.gov.gh. Itswebsite formand the CSA Ghana app take reports too. "It is a duty owed to every customer whose money and data you hold," Mr Agbeti said, urging firms to do more than comply.

Title: All 261 MMDCEs face independent review, with Mahama expecting the report by December 20
Content: President John Dramani Mahamawants the country's Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), all 261 of them, put through an independent assessment, with the final report on his desk by December 20. Local Government MinisterMahama Ayarigaset out the directive in a signed statement dated November 17 in Accra. The review starts at once and runs until December 15. It builds on the President's October order that MMDCEs report to residents through a twice-yearlyAccountability Series. Ayariga has also warned them againstmisusing assembly vehicles. MMDCEs are the government appointees who run the country's local assemblies. The review looks at what each has delivered since taking office and how residents rate that delivery. Six indicators decide the score. The heaviest, at 35 per cent, is general development: roads and drains, sanitation and waste, new schools, CHPS compounds, markets and lorry parks, local jobs, social programmes, poverty reduction and how the Common Fund is spent. Revenue and financial management count for 20 per cent, covering internally generated funds and whether Common Fund accounts are filed on time. Another 15 per cent rests on peace, security and relations with chiefs, including how land and chieftaincy disputes are handled. Ayariga has proposed a National Eminent Chiefs Committee todefuse the triggers of conflict in northern Ghana. Governance and accountability are worth 15 per cent too. That covers whether the General Assembly, its sub-committees and Area Councils actually meet, and whether the assembly sticks to the rules on procurement and public spending. Citizen engagement and inclusion make up 10 per cent, from town hall meetings and live broadcasts of assembly sittings to answering petitions and reaching women, young people and persons with disabilities. A final 5 per cent rests on presidential directives and national programmes such as housing, sanitation and the 24-Hour Economy. Sanitation is already under pressure in some regions. This month the Western Regional Minister warned chief executives oversanitation and wetland encroachment. Each MMDCE has until November 30 to upload a self-assessment, backed by evidence, to a dedicated portal. From December 1 to 15, field teams will check those claims district by district. They will inspect roads, markets and the books, and speak with assembly members, traditional leaders and residents. Residents get their own platform to rate their chief executive. Presiding Members, District Coordinating Directors and intelligence agencies can also be called on for confidential peer reviews. Officials from the ministry and the Regional Coordinating Councils lead the exercise, alongside the Common Fund Office, the National Development Planning Commission and the Office of the Head of the Local Government Service. The ministry says the results will give the President hard evidence for decisions on local governance, and the report goes to him for "consideration and further action". The statement does not say what happens to chief executives who score poorly.

Title: Weija-Gbawe MP gives government until November 23 to restart abandoned STEM school
Content: Weija-Gbawe MP Jerry Ahmed Shaib has given the government until November 23 to resume work on the abandoned Upper Weija STEM school or face a march to the Finance Ministry. He issued the ultimatum after touring the stalled site with some constituents on Friday. It is not his first appeal over an unfinished project in the constituency: in March, he urged the government toopen the near-complete Weija paediatric hospital. The school is about 70 per cent complete, he says, and work has stood still for more than a year. "If by November 23 we do not see any effort by the government to complete this abandoned project, we will organise a serious demonstration," he said. Shaib, the NPP MP who is also Second Deputy Minority Whip, said he would lead chiefs, the Wulomo and residents to the Finance Ministry to press for the money to finish the school. It would not be the constituency's first march over a stalled project: in May, residentstook to the streets over the idle 120-bed children's hospitalin Weija-Gbawe. "The government must complete this facility for it to start running, so that students in Weija will not have to travel to other regions to continue their education," he said. The project began under the Akufo-Addo/Bawumia government, he said. He has asked the Finance Ministry to free up money for the Education Ministry, so that the contractor can return to site. Education MinisterHaruna Iddrisu, who has argued fora STEM revolution in the education sector, has assured him the government will complete the school, he said. But promises by word of mouth are no longer enough, he said. He wants work restarted so the school can open its doors by the next academic year. Built on the site are dormitories for boys and girls, bungalows for the principal and the headmaster, a dining hall, libraries, science labs and blocks of classrooms, among other buildings. He said the site was well suited to a modern secondary school and, once finished, would be among the best STEM schools in Ghana. He also hinted that politics may be behind the delay. "I don't want to believe that the government is abandoning this project because it was started by the NPP," he said. "But if that is the intention, then it is wrong. Government should not use politics to punish my people." "When this school is completed, it will admit children of both NPP and NDC parents, so we should not politicise everything," he added. In September, he urged the government to prioritise the school, and the Weija Queenmother said finishing it should come before buildinga 24-hour marketin the municipality. Neither the Education Ministry nor the Finance Ministry had publicly responded to the ultimatum by Monday night.

Title: Agyinasare wants to see the National Cathedral accounts before churches put in more money
Content: Archbishop Charles Agyinasare says the National Cathedral's accounts should be made public before anyone decides whether churches should pay to finish it. The founder of Perez Chapel International said churches, his own among them, gave money to the project but have never seen how it was spent. "Let's see what the account says first. And then when we see what the account says then we can know, because I know churches and us contributed some monies but we don't know what the account is," he said. He made the call in an interview with Bernard Avle on Channel One TV's The Point of View on Monday. The Archbishop said the reported spending on the project worried him. If that sum was all the country had to show for it, he said, it was a problem, and he wanted to see the accounts. President John Mahamaput the public money spent atalmost 90 million dollarsin September. He said a forensic audit of that spending was ready and with the Attorney-General, and promised the Christian Council a copy. Mahama has also said Christians couldfund the cathedral at GH¢1,000 eachinstead of using taxpayers' money. Days later hedissolved the project's Board of Trusteesand ordered the site handed back to the Local Government ministry by the end of October. Agyinasare said the politics around the project had become the real obstacle. "I think that the politics of it is a problem and we should move past the politics of it and then pick it up from there," he said. He still wants a cathedral on the site where building began. He suggested the state could take it on as a national venue rather than one man's pledge. "It wouldn't do too much harm if one day the government decides that, look, we are moving past somebody making a personal pledge," he said. A national cathedral could host the state's indoor ceremonies, he added, down to the swearing-in of a president. TheChristian Council set up a committeein September to work out a way forward. The Minority Leader, Alexander Afenyo-Markin, hasaccused the government of inconsistencyover the project. On illegal mining, Agyinasare said a nationwide state of emergency was not needed, butthe worst-hit areas needed one. "For some areas where the forest is desecrated and where the rivers are bad, there should be some form of state of emergency, because some areas are getting worse gradually," he said. "The government needs to be decisive in some of those places and say that in this particular area, because of what has happened to this forest and because of what has happened to this river, we declare a state of emergency." He has visited Dunkwa and nearby mining sites, and said some of the damage there was being repaired. "From the pictures I have seen and the videos I have seen, some places are being reclaimed. But I think more needs to be done," he said. His call comes two days after theCatholic Bishops' Conference demanded a state of emergency in galamsey hotspots. Mahama has said he willdeclare one only if the National Security Council advises it. Agyinasare also said Mahama wasdoing better in his second term than in his first. "I think he's done better than the first term," he said. "I see the cedi has done well. I see we've been able to pay some of our bills." He pointed to projects being built without loans. "Some of the projects we are doing, we are not borrowing money for them. That, for me, I think, is progress." Flying home from India in September, he said, he was told Emirates now flew to Ghana twice a day. He took that as a sign that more people were travelling out to buy goods again.

Title: BTS wins six awards at 2026 Melon Music Awards, including Artist of the Year
Content: South Korean music group BTS has emerged as the biggest winner at the 2026 Melon Music Awards, taking home six trophies at the two-day ceremony in Seoul on 14 and 15 November, including Artist of the Year and Album of the Year, following its return as a full group with its fifth studio album, ARIRANG. BTS received three awards on the first day of the ceremony: Album of the Year for ARIRANG, Stage of the Year, and Global Top 10. The group added three more on the second day, winning Artist of the Year, Top 10, and Best Group – Male. Artist of the Year and Album of the Year were among the most significant honours of the ceremony. They recognised the group’s overall performance during the year and the reception of its fifth full-length album. BTS did not attend the ceremony at Gocheok Sky Dome but sent video messages to acknowledge the awards and thank its fans, known as ARMY. In one of the messages, Suga described 2026 as a year the group and its fans would not forget. Jimin also reflected on the group’s return, saying the members were happy to release ARIRANG, reconnect with fans, and perform for them again. Released in March 2026, ARIRANG marked BTS’ return as a complete group after its extended break. The album and its lead single, “SWIM”, recorded strong performances on international charts. BTS topped the Billboard 200 with the album, while “SWIM” reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The song also made an immediate impression on Melon’s domestic chart, reaching the platform’s Top 100 within an hour of its release. All 14 tracks on the album entered the chart. These performances provided important context for the group’s success at the Melon Music Awards, where chart performance, audience engagement, and industry recognition contribute to the awards process. While BTS led the awards tally with six trophies, other K-pop acts also secured major honours. Girl group IVE won five awards, including Song of the Year for “BANG BANG”. The group also received Top 10, Global Top 10, Best Group – Female, and Music Video of the Year. Rookie group CORTIS took home Record of the Year for “REDRED”, alongside Top 10 and Global Top 10, bringing its total to three awards. Meanwhile, aespa became the first recipient of the newly introduced Global-K Artist of the Year award. The Rookie of the Year honours went to ALPHA DRIVE ONE and LNGSHOT. The 18th edition of the Melon Music Awards was held over two days for the first time, bringing together 26 performing acts at Seoul’s Gocheok Sky Dome. The ceremony attracted more than 36,000 attendees and introduced new award categories designed to recognise the growing international reach of K-pop. BTS’ six-award achievement placed the group at the centre of this year’s ceremony, with its wins spanning major album and artist honours, group recognition, and stage performance. Coming after its return as a complete group, the recognition at MMA 2026 adds another milestone to BTS’ career and underscores the continued reception of its music among audiences in South Korea and internationally.

Title: Issakaba is back after 25 years, but you can't watch it in Accra yet
Content: If you grew up on the Issakaba VCDs, the sequel is finally in cinemas. Just not in Ghana, for now. Issakaba Returns opened on Friday, November 13, at Silverbird cinemas in Lagos, Abuja and Kaduna, according tothe cinema's film page. The Accra Mall and West Hills screens are not on that list, and their programmes for 13 to 19 November don't include it. So check before you head out. Lancelot Imasuen, who directed the 2001 original, directs again. Silverbird bills Sam Dede, Chidi Mokeme, Iyabo Ojo, Regina Daniels and Nosa Rex. Dede returns as Ebube, the man who led the Issakaba Boys,3News reported in 2024when the return was first announced. The new story is set in a place called Amangwa, where a governor turns to the old Issakaba group, and Ebube wants to stop that return. It runs for 2 hours 26 minutes, in English and Pidgin, and Silverbird rates it 18. That's a long sit, so plan your snacks. The title flips the letters of Bakassi, a nod to the Bakassi Boys, the vigilantes who emerged in south-eastern Nigeria in the late 1990s. Nosa Rex, one of the cast, is the producer whoapologised to Ghanaiansin August 2025 after an outburst over piracy. The Nollywood Reportersays Blue Pictures Distribution is handling the release. Whether it reaches Accra cinemas later is down to them and the cinemas.

Title: Mahama puts public debt at 45% of GDP while Amin Adam says it is 47.5%
Content: President John Mahamasays Ghana's public debt stands at 45 per cent of GDP, while former Finance Minister Mohammed Amin Adam puts it at 47.5 per cent. Mahama gave his figure on Monday at the Ghana Investment Summit in Accra, telling investors the debt had held broadly steady at 45 per cent of GDP as of July. The summit also heardDangote Group's plans for sugar and cocoa factories in Ghana. Amin Adam said in a television interview later on Monday that the ratio had risen from 44 per cent at the end of 2025 to 47.5 per cent in October 2026. On Sunday, the former minister hadaccused the government of announcing policies without plans to fund them. In dollar terms, he said the debt stock moved from US$49 billion at the end of 2024, when the NPP left office, to US$65 billion in October 2026. He put the rise at almost US$16 billion. "Our debt stock has moved from $49 billion at the end of 2024, when we were leaving government," he said. He said the stock grew 18 per cent in the ten months to October, adding GH¢118 billion since the end of 2025. Only about GH¢30 billion of that came from the cedi's slide, he said, asking: "If the minister is not borrowing, how can your debt stock increase by 18%?" The two figures describe different months, July for Mahama and October for Amin Adam. Borrowing, repayments and currency moves sit between them. They also come from different sides of the argument. Amin Adam conceded that restructuring and the cedi's earlier appreciation cut the stock in 2025, but said currency moves cannot explain the 2026 rise. Mahama's pitch at the summit rested on wider numbers. He cited inflation easing to 5.5 per cent in October 2026, from 23.5 per cent in January 2025, and a primary surplus of 1.6 per cent of GDP. Amin Adam rejected the claim by Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson that the NPP deliberately pushed repayments into 2027 and 2028 to set up the NDC government for default.Ato Forson has recounted the pain the restructuring imposed on households. He said 98 per cent of the restructuring was finished before the election. "And so, how on earth could we know that the NDC was going to be in government at the time the repayment will be done in 2027 and 2028?" The exercise secured US$11 billion in relief, he said, made up of US$5 billion in outright cancellation and US$6 billion in debt-service savings. "And so you are happy to take credit for the benefits, and when it is time for repayment, you are complaining." He linked borrowing to a projected GH¢61 billion interest bill in 2027. That, he said, is more than the GH¢34 billion set aside, combined, for the ministries of agriculture, energy, tourism, and trade and industry. What would settle the argument is the Finance Ministry's debt bulletin, alongside theBank of Ghana's Summary of Economic and Financial Data. No bulletin with an October figure was on the ministry's website on Tuesday. We could not find a debt-to-GDP ratio in the Bank of Ghana's latest summary, for September. Until an official October figure lands, neither man's number can be checked against the record.

Title: How to spot a genuine new cedi note: hold it up, tilt it and feel it
Content: Anyone handed a new Heritage Series cedi note can test it on the spot by holding it to the light, tilting it and feeling the print, theBank of Ghana's brochure on the series says. The notes enter circulation from 1 December, and the banknotes already in use remain legal tender alongside them, as ourexplainer on when the notes arrive and what happens to the old onessets out. The brochure covers all eight denominations, GH¢1 to GH¢200. Ourguide to the faces, landmarks and symbols on every noteexplains who and what each one honours. This one sticks to the security features. Counterfeiting is on the Bank's mind too. It says it isworking on a new Currency Act to replace the 1964 law and tackle counterfeiting, with clearer procedures for detecting and surrendering counterfeit notes. Beyond the five shared checks, each denomination has its own thread or stripe, according to the brochure. Every note from GH¢2 to GH¢200 also carries a gold stripe: tilting the note reveals a shiny band of gold bars. The Bank hasclarified that the GH¢50 portrait is Theodosia Okoh, developed from her own photographs, after days of public debateover who the image shows.

Title: Ahenfie is crowned Miss Malaika Ghana 2026 after the Aura Night finale
Content: Miss MalaikaGhanahas named Ahenfie its 2026 winner, posting the result just after midnight on Monday. Thepageant's accountwrote: "Congratulations to @_Ahenfie_ our winner for Miss Malaika Ghana 2026 Aura Season." Ahenfie is the contestant name. Her Instagram profile is titled A.A. Dorothy. The finale was billed as the Aura Night, for 7pm on Sunday, 15 November 2026, at "The palms convention center".Miss Malaika Ghanaposted that venue the day before. On Instagram, the pageant wrote: "A massive congratulations to @_ahenfie_ the winner Miss Malaika Ghana 2026!" It added: "Welcome to your reign." The reelcarries that caption. A later post said she "didn't just compete for a crown" and "competed for a platform to impact generations through education."That notewent up on Monday morning. Senam is first runner-up. The pageant said she "graced the stage with elegance" and "spoke with power" through the Aura Season. Boatemaa is second runner-up.Miss Malaika Ghanapraised her "poise" and "radiant energy", and told her "this is just the beginning of your beautiful journey." Photographs of the crowning are credited to @chocolateshotit. On Instagram the pageant wrote "SHE IS THE AURA!" and "Congratulations to AHENFIE, Miss Malaika Ghana 2026!"That postcredits @chocolate_shot_it. The pageant calls itself an Accra-based reality show first broadcast in Ghana in 2003 and produced by Charterhouse. The same day,US visa rules kept African contestants out of Miss Universe 2026.

Title: Bernice Offei's son recalls the 5:51am call and the morning she died at UGMC
Content: Gospel singer Bernice Offei's son Daniel has recounted rushing to the University of Ghana Medical Centre (UGMC) after a 5:51am call to find doctors trying to revive her. Speaking on Saturday, November 14, Daniel said the family had learned that his mother,banker and gospel songwriterBernice Ofeibea Offei, was in the intensive care unit under doctors' monitoring. At 5:51am, a caller asked him to come to the hospital with his family because her situation had changed. Pressed for details, the caller said they had only been asked to call them in. "With no time to waste, I rushed to UGMC and there you lay with the doctors making every attempt to resuscitate you," Daniel said. His father joined them later, before a doctor said: "Let's call it in." Her body went to the UGMC mortuary and then to Transitions, afuneralhome. At both places, attendants asked the family to identify her barely five minutes after they arrived. After the first identification, Daniel said, he broke down in tears. "At the second identification, it felt like the Lord was telling me, 'Take a second look.' Standing over what remained of you, I noticed that a slight smile was on your face," he said. Her husband, Professor Samuel Kwame Offei, dated her death to the early hours of Saturday, September 12 in the UGMC intensive care unit, calling it "the darkest moment of my life". "It is the hardest thing I have ever had to bear," he said. She wasbriefly reported missing in Accra on September 1, before her family and the authorities confirmed within 24 hours that she was safe. Professor Offei said church members and friends joined the search, and the family was overwhelmed with relief when she was found. "We thought the worst was over," he said. In the biography read at the church, the family said she died "after a brief period of hospitalization following her unceremonious departure from home on the 1st of September 2026", having been taken suddenly to hospital that day. At Saturday's service, one of her sisters spoke of the years before her health declined, and of several nights spent with her at the hospital. The sister said she left her reluctantly on the Thursday to attend a camp meeting, hoping to come back and find her recovered. The news of her death reached the camp early on Saturday morning. Inhis family tribute, Daniel also referred to her illness: "Unfortunately, due to your health, you never got to catch a glimpse of what you prayed for." At Wednesday'sremembrance night at the church, Most Rev Prof J. Kwabena Asamoah-Gyadu, Presiding Bishop of the Methodist Church Ghana and Legon pastor from 1991 to 1996, said the family "has gone through a lot in the last couple of years" during her illness. "The health struggles of our dear sister Bernice were not unknown to us," Asamoah-Gyadu said. The family has not publicly named a cause of death. Kwasi Ernest, a former manager who is not family, said in a television interview in September: "For four to five years, she had been battling dementia that affected her brain." He said the illness was triggered when she left home and could not find her way back to the house. The family has not confirmed his account. At the close of theburial service at Legon, the head of family, speaking for the Djoleto family on her father's side and her mother's family, announced that "there's going to be a private burial", a church reception afterwards, and a thanksgiving service on Sunday at 10:30am. The family released doves before the casket was taken away. A small family team went to the cemetery, which was kept private and not named, while other mourners moved to the funeral grounds.

Title: Archbishop Agyinasare says Mahama’s second term outperforms first4 hours
Content: Founder of Perez Chapel International, Archbishop Dr Charles Agyinasare, has rated President John Dramani Mahama’s second administration ahead of his first, citing improvements in the performance of the cedi, government payments and the financing of public projects. He said the developments since Mr Mahama returned to office showed signs of progress, particularly efforts to meet outstanding financial obligations and undertake some projects without resorting to additional borrowing. Archbishop Agyinasare also cited increased flight activity between Ghana and other countries as an indication of growing commercial activity and movement of goods. He recounted that during a trip from India in September, he was informed that Emirates was operating two daily flights to Ghana, a development he considered encouraging. “They told me Emirates was coming to Ghana twice a day. So I came with the midnight flight, and there was a seven o’clock flight. Now, that should show you that people have started going out to buy things. That alone, for me, was an encouragement,” he said. The renowned preacher further pointed to the performance of the local currency and the government's efforts to clear some outstanding bills as indicators of improvement. “I see the cedi has done well. I see we’ve been able to pay some of our bills,” he stated. He also referenced the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy presented to Parliament by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson on November 12, particularly the government's account of payments made and projects being undertaken without new borrowing. “Some of the projects we are doing, we are not borrowing money for them. That, for me, I think, is progress,” Archbishop Agyinasare added. “I think he’s done better than the first term,” he said. He made the assessment during an interview on Channel One TV on Monday, November 16, where he gave his views on the performance of the Mahama administration since its return to power. “I think he’s done better than the first term,” he said.
